She didn’t feel the need to break the silence though, enjoying the feeling of not being quite so alone, but eventually, the loneliness crept back in and she wanted to know that someone else was there.

     

                “If you’re an alien, what do you look like?”

     

                “Me? Oh, I’m- I’m just … your standard alien, you know? What’s it called here? A stereotype? What do stereotypical aliens look like?”

     

                “Green skin. Big heads. Sometimes they have antennas.”

     

                “Oh, well … that would be more like J’onn, across from me.”

     

                Lena hadn’t bothered to look into the other cells yet and catch a glimpse of her new neighbours - save for the two meta-humans she’d showered with that morning - but she softly laughed.

     

                “So you’re not green?”

     

                “Blue. Blue skin, twelve fingers and three eyes.”

     

                “Really?”

     

                “Well I’m not going to tell you the truth. It’s hard to find fun here so don’t spoil mine for me.”

     

                Smiling thinly at her words, Lena swallowed thickly. “How long have you been in here?”

     

                “I’m the longest in this cell block. J’onn was about a year later.”

     

                “How long ago was that?”

     

                “Oh … about eighteen years.”

     

                Lena’s stomach jolted and the air was expelled from her lungs, her chest aching as a cold feeling spread through her. Tears blurred her vision and her voice was hoarse and cracking when she replied.

     

                “No. No, you can’t have just- you can’t have stayed here for that long. They couldn’t just- why haven’t you broken out?”

     

                “There’s no way out.”

     

                Choking on a loud sob as she reached up to cover her mouth with her hand, Lena broke down, tears leaking from the corners of her eyes, stinging as they hit the cuts on her cheek. Eighteen years. How could someone last that long in this place? How could they keep someone there for that long? What had Kara done that had made her deserving of being imprisoned? Lena was too afraid to ask and so wrapped up in her own fear to go down that line of thought.

     

                “It’s not so bad,” Kara whispered. “I have friends here now. And you have me. It’ll be okay, Lena.”

    Chapter 3

                The morning dragged into lunch and Lena tried to nap through the pain of her beating, a headache blossoming behind her eyes as she lay on the hard metal mesh of her bare cot. Kara had made a few more attempts at conversing with her since she’d fallen apart with the devastating horror of imagining decades spent in the prison, but Lena had been silent as she wallowed in her misery.

     

                She hadn’t touched her lunch and didn’t so much as move when the forcefield was brought down and then put back up, the tray slid in and then removed hours later. Sleeping a little and feeling stiff and aching as she used the toilet and splashed cold water onto her bruised face, dabbing it dry with the hem of her sweatshirt, Lena retreated to her bed and drew her knees up to her chest as she hugged her arms around them. It was cold, the storm making the prison frigid as vents pumped out warm air, which wasn’t quite warm enough.

     

                Lena wished for her blankets, the thin pillow and mattress, anything to make herself more comfortable. Most of all, she wished for her own bed, for the thousand thread count Egyptian cotton, the king size mattress and the blackout windows controlled at the touch of a button. She wished for silence and linen pyjamas, Darjeeling tea and her research. If she didn’t manage to get herself killed with her stubbornness, Lena imagined the boredom would drive her to insanity and finish her off instead.

     

                Listening to the shifting of her fellow inmates, the sound of quiet conversations, someone’s snores and the rapid breaths of someone doing push-ups, Lena bided her time. In her mind, she tried to map the layout of the prison, of each turning she’d passed, the airlocks and which scanners required two people to open it - just the cells so far - and the guard rotations and crews. For such a remote black site, so covert and off-the-grid that they’d managed to hide aliens right under the sea, Fort Rozz was far from the high-tech prison she would have designed.

     

                Perhaps it was for the best that they’d had to rely on old technology to contain the earlier prisoners, upgrading over the decades as progress was made. The old locks became electronic, and then retinal scans. The iron bars of cells became forcefield and the shock collars were introduced. Some places, like the pitiful bathrooms, retained the old plumbing systems with freezing seawater filtered through, non-essential upgrades overlooked in pursuit of funding the medical centres with the most up-to-date equipment.

     

                Yet, the guards were lax. She’d been left alone with Alex, left alone with Doctor Danvers. They’d been confident enough to beat the shit out of her with few repercussions, leaving Lena to believe that the government wasn't very involved in the running of the place. They could do as they pleased, pass the long hours of their shifts and rosters as they saw fit, perhaps working out on the black site as a punishment for some misbehaviour at their DEO main office.

     

                The guards came and took the prisoners in small groups or individually, leaving Lena alone as she wondered what they were doing with them. It was leniency for her broken ribs that left her behind, ignoring the sound of people coming and going, the prisoner’s names called out by guards as manacles were clapped onto wrists and the doors hissed open and closed at the end of the block.

     

                Her musings as she tried to take stock of things carried her all the way through to dinner. She was hungry, she could admit that, but Lena made no move when her dinner was slid towards her. Closing her eyes to the fluorescent lights overhead, Lena breathed slowly, trying to banish the heavy pressure behind her eyes, the pulsing feeling of her injuries - especially her ribs, which ached with each breath. She could hear Kara speaking in the cell next door.

     

                “Agent Danvers.”

     

                “Prisoner KZ64.”

     

                Lena strained her ears to pick up on the conversation, a painful frown creasing her face at the barely perceptible softening of Alex’s exasperated tone.

     

                “I was wondering if you could bring some painkillers.”

     

                “Are you feeling okay?”

     

                “Not for me.”

     

                There was a pause and she heard Alex’s sigh. “Kara … don’t make trouble for yourself.”

     

                “Me? Trouble?” Kara softly exclaimed with a short laugh, teasing and almost fond of the guard who kept watch over her. “I’m a model inmate.”

     

                Alex clicked her tongue, although she sounded amused when she replied. “Don’t go ruining that for yourself, or you’ll be demoted from my favourite prisoner.”

     

                “You’re a gem.”

     

                Snorting, Alex disappeared and Lena frowned as she kept her eyes closed, turning over the conversation in her mind. Perhaps being a long-term prisoner had afforded Kara some leniency with the guards. They’d seemed almost friendly, in a reserved sort of way, and the thought left Lena uneasy. 

     

                She didn’t have time to broach the topic with Kara before footsteps made their way towards her cell, scuffing on the concrete floor. Staying still, Lena drew in a shallow breath and waited for them to leave her alone but was disturbed a moment later anyway.

     

                “Prisoner LL93.”

     

                Lena didn’t respond to Alex calling out her new ID, just feigned being asleep until someone else spoke.

     

                “Open the cell.”

     

                Cracking open an eye at the sound of the doctor speaking, Lena pushed herself up onto her elbows slightly. Watching as the bluish forcefield shut down, Lena eased herself up into a sitting position as she watched Doctor Danvers cross over to her cot, standing before her.

     

                “Look at my finger,” she murmured, taking a light out of her white coat pocket and shining it in Lena’s eyes. “No concussion. Good. I brought you some painkillers.”

     

                Turning to look toward the wall, Lena let out a quiet scoff of laughter, realising that Kara had been asking for her benefit.

     

                “I don’t need any painkillers.”

     

                “You really should take them.”

     

                “No, thank you.”

     

                “You need to eat as well.”

     

                “I’m not hungry.”

     

                Sighing, the doctor put her light away and sank to a crouch before Lena, giving her a pained look, something like genuine worry shadowing her blue eyes.

     

                “Sweetie, it’s no good torturing yourself.”

     

                “Why would I bother when the lovely agents here can do it for me?” Lena quipped as she gestured to Alex.

     

                She let out a short laugh and ran a hand over her swollen face, feeling worn out. Grimacing, Doctor Danvers rose to her feet and walked over to the metal tray with Lena’s dinner on it, picking it up and walking over to the bed. She set it down between them and Lena braced her elbows on her knees as she leaned forward.

     

                “Did she ask you to come and make sure I eat?” Lena asked, jerking her chin toward Alex.

     

                “Yes.”

     

                Lena scoffed and shook her head. “She’s not very smart if she thinks you have any influence over me.”

     

                “She’s smart about many things. Come on; eat.”

     

                It was childish but Lena turned her head aside, jaw clenched tightly together as she inhaled shallowly through her nose, trying to stifle the tremors that wracked her. Fingers grasping the material of her pants, she spoke to the floor as she cast her eyes down.

     

                “What’s the point? If they’re just going to keep me here … I may as well get it over and done with quickly.”

     

                “A fair point,” the doctor agreed, “but you’re forgetting the vital information that they won’t let you starve yourself.”

     

                Her voice was low and strained as she reached for the tray, picking up the plastic fork and nudging it into Lena’s unwilling hand. Glancing sideways at her, Lena hesitated. Taking the fork in her hand, she stared down at it, too flimsy to be a weapon and too many guns and batons and bodies to take her down even if she tried. Not to mention that it would be nigh on impossible to get out of the prison.

     

                “And how are they going to make me?”

     

                “They’ll get someone to put a tube down your throat - not me, they know I won’t cooperate with things like that - and they’ll put you in a straight jacket to make sure you can’t bring it back up. I’ve seen it more times than I care to admit. Trust me when I say I’m trying to make it easier for you.”

     

                “Why would I trust you?” Lena snorted.

     

                “Because I’m one of the few people here who is sorry that this is happening to you.”

     

                Snorting, Lena smiled faintly, her scabbed over cuts twinging as they pulled. “Sorry won’t change anything.”

     

                “No, but neither will forcing yourself to suffer. Here. The painkillers.”

     

                Eyeing the white little pills in the small paper cup, Lena shook them into her palm and picked one of them up. She read the markings on it and realised it wasn’t anything nefarious, pausing before she put them on her tongue, the powdered coating making them stick, and swallowed them dry.

     

                Turning her fork over in her hand, she turned to the tray and eyed the sad green beans, the congealed fat of the casserole and the greyish mash. None of it was particularly appetising, and Lena didn’t think she’d ever eaten anything as bad as that, but what else did she expect in prison? She apprehensively scooped up a forkful of limp green beans - the safest option, she deemed - and put it into her mouth, chewing with great reluctance.

     

                Forcing herself to swallow, Lena met the doctor’s blue eyes. “Satisfied?”

     

                The doctor gave her knee a quick pat and climbed to her feet. “Finish it all, and then we’ll see. Let someone know if your ribs are bothering you; I’ll sort out more painkillers for you. Maybe something stronger to help.”

     

                Nodding in acknowledgement of her words, Lena moved the food around on her tray. The best thing on there was a slice of vanilla cake, entirely unnutritional but a surprising treat, and Lena forced herself to choke down some of the lukewarm casserole with the grim reward of cake once she was finished. The forcefield went back up and the guards left and Lena picked at her food with all the enthusiasm of someone on death row.

     

                “You shouldn’t have done that,” she called out, just loud enough for Kara to hear her.

     

                “You’re in pain.”

     

                “I can handle it.”

     

                “You shouldn’t have to. Besides, Eliza’s nice.”

     

                Lena’s face crumpled as she ate a mouthful of mash. “Eliza? Who’s that?”

     

                “The doctor. When you've been here as long as I have … well, making friends is the only thing that keeps you sane. Not all of them are bad. The agents are pretty nice if you get to know them.”

     

                “No offence, Kara, but I’m not going to sit in a cell and make friends with the people keeping me here.”

     

                There was a long pause and Lena closed her eyes, sighing heavily before shaking her head. Alienating the one person who’d made an effort to comfort her wasn’t the way to go either. Kara quietly replied before Lena could say anything else though.

     

                “That’s fair. But they don’t want to be here either. Eliza’s husband was killed for hiding J’onn - he’s the one in the cell across from me-”

     

                Lena climbed to her feet and walked across to the other side of her cell so she could see J’onn in his one and her stomach jolted, the breath stolen from her lungs as she quickly moved over to the forcefield and slammed a fist against it. She felt dread and shock sweep through her, her face pale and slack as she stared at the familiar face.

     

                “Hey! Asshole. You want to interrogate me and put me away and then pretend like you’re stuck in here with the rest of us? Huh? What the fuck is this?”

     

                “Ah, I see you’re acquainted with Hank Henshaw,” J’onn chuckled as he waved a hand at his face. “An unfortunate face to be stuck with, no?”

     

                Kara’s soft laugh drifted from beneath the bed. “I told you, J’onn’s green . He’s a Martian; he can change his form to mimic other people’s appearances. Didn’t stop the real Henshaw from throwing him in here though.”

     

                Lena frowned as she looked at J’onn, the similarities identical and unsettling as she licked her lips. “How do I know this isn’t some trick to lull me into a false sense of security and get me to confess to things?”

     

                “You’re already in here; what’s longer than a life sentence?” Kara murmured.

     

                Feeling like she’d been winded by the gentle truth, Lena ran a hand through her hair and returned to her cot. Sitting down onto the cold metal, she rubbed at her forehead, everything so muddled and unsettling.

     

                “Henshaw was the partner of Eliza’s husband,” Kara continued. “When they killed Jeremiah for hiding him, they sent Eliza and Alex here. It’s been seventeen years; Alex was only sixteen when she got here.”

     

                “How do you know all of this?”

     

                Kara’s huff of laughter was rueful and resigned. “She was the only other kid, only two years older than me. We became … friends.”

     

                “That doesn’t make it okay,” Lena whispered, her voice so soft that she didn’t intend for Kara to hear her.

     

                “Maybe not,” Kara replied, “but … in a place like this, you have to take what little kindness is offered. If it’s between the doctor who fought to let me be schooled with her daughter, and the agent who helped me with my English and sometimes sneaks me extra food, and the agents who spit on my kind … you bet I’ll take the nice ones.”

     

                Grinding her teeth together as her throat tightened, Lena stretched out on the cot and blinked back the burning feeling building behind her eyes. She found herself swallowing the painful lump, and then again, unable to banish the feeling. Rubbing her temple as she breathed slowly, she couldn’t make her tense body unwind.

     

                “That makes you angry,” Kara said after a few minutes. “I get it. Everyone else has been there too. Most of us have been here long enough that … you just give in. And it doesn’t make you weak , it just- it’s tiring. Resisting them, being punished … you get tired of it after a while.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena let out a sharp exhale, pinching the bridge of her nose. “I’m not a quitter. I’ll get out of here, or I’ll kill myself trying. I’m not okay with sitting in a cell singing Kumbaya with these people - if you can call them that. I’m sorry. I’m sorry that they’ve held you here for that long but … I’ll never be okay with it.”

     

                “It’s okay,” Kara murmured. “Who knows, maybe you’ll be the one to free us all.”

     

                With a snort of laughter, Lena grimaced faintly. “I don’t think I’d ever manage a prison-wide jailbreak.”

     

                “Ah. Well, when you make it out … let them know we’re here.”

     

                “Of course.”

     

                They lapsed into silence and, after a while, Lena heard the quiet scuff of Kara moving on the other side of the wall. There was a lull that blanketed the cell block and she was left with too much time on her hands, the space between dinner and lights out stretching out until she felt like time itself had stopped.

     

                Her eyelids were getting heavy and she was about to cave to sleep, an unfortunately uncomfortable one at that on the hard mesh of the cot, when there was a rap against the forcefield.

     

                “Prisoner LL93, up against the back wall.”

     

                She cracked open an eye to look at Alex, and then slowly eased herself up, ribs protesting, as she took in the sight of the agent with her arms full. Moving over to the back wall, leaning against it as she waited for Alex to remove the barrier with a sullen look on her face, Lena watched as a thin mattress was unrolled and tossed onto her cot, a pillow and a scratchy blanket following suit.

     

                Backing away and putting the forcefield back up, Alex fixed her with a firm stare and Lena gave her a piercing one in response. Lena thought she was waiting for a thank you, which was the last thing Lena intended to give her, and after a moment Alex’s lips twitched slightly before she raised her eyebrows.

     

                “Lights out in one minute; I’d make your bed quickly if I was you.”

     

                Dipping her head in a slight nod, Lena pushed off the wall and walked over to her cot, straightening the mattress and shaking the blanket out over it. Kicking off her shoes, she climbed into bed a moment before the lights went out and spent half of the night staring into the darkness as sleep eluded her.

    Chapter 4

                “Don’t they ever let us out?” Lena pouted.

     

                It was just after breakfast, Lena’s hair still slightly damp and her temperament a little prickly that morning. She was growing restless being cooped up in the cell all day with nothing to do except wait for their regular meals and then to sleep. Lena was sick of sleeping; she hadn’t been particularly good at that before prison, but now she just felt lethargic all the time.

     

                “We get a monthly social. Just for our block. Best part of the month, to be honest.”

     

                Lena snorted, rubbing her forehead. “Not that it’s hard, right?”

     

                Kara let out a quiet chuckle and Lena rolled onto her side, pressing her hand against the wall as if she could feel her on the other side. A wan smile crossed her face and she closed her eyes.

     

                “We get daily walks too.”

     

                “So, I’ll finally be able to see what you look like,” Lena murmured, a thrill of anticipation running through her as her smile grew a fraction. 

     

                Her curiosity was too great and she couldn’t explain why she needed to know, only that she did. There were few things to look forward to from the inside of a prison cell, but meeting the inmate beside her was about the only thing that kept Lena interested. If she wasn’t housed in the cell next to Kara, Lena imagined she would already be on her way to insanity, too unstimulated by a lack of anything to occupy her time that she surely would have given up already without the conversation.

     

                “No,” Kara whispered, “they don’t let me go at the same time as the other girls. It’s the same with showering. Too dangerous.”

     

                “Ah,” Lena muttered, disappointment knifing through her.

     

                “I already told you though,” Kara lightly replied with forced levity. “Blue skin and all that. But you will see me at the social though.”

     

                “When’s the next one?”

     

                Kara hummed for a moment, tallying the days. “Two weeks.”

     

                Making herself comfortable as she faced the wall, fully under the bed with her knees curled up to her chest in an effort to stay warm on the concrete, Lena made a low sound of interest at the back of her throat. 

     

                “And what do these socials entail?”

     

                “Well … you can read a book from the well-stocked library of Fort Rozz.”

     

                “Actually?”

     

                “They have two Jane Austen books, half of a dictionary and a few on marine life and trees.”

     

                Lips twitching with amusement, Lena’s voice was laced with laughter as she replied. “Which half of the dictionary is it?”

     

                “A through to M. Did wonders for my English vocabulary when I first ended up here, but N to Z could use a bit of work,” Kara quipped.

     

                Quietly snorting, Lena shook her head, her cheek pressed into the gritty floor as her eyelids shuttered. “Was it hard?”

     

                “Learning English? No, it was my … eighth language. Ninth? We travelled a lot when I was younger.”

     

                “To different planets?”

     

                “Mhm.”

     

                They lapsed into silence as Lena processed that. It was easy to forget at times that she was talking to an alien , one from a different universe, a different solar system, who could have torn the underwater prison to shreds if she’d been allowed the use of her powers. Lena didn’t know what those powers were, but clearly something to be feared if they’d imprisoned her for so many years.

     

                “So … what else can we do at the social?”

     

                “Well … they have a few decks of cards - Psi is really good at tricks so don’t trust her in a game - and they have an old TV that sometimes gets enough reception to play old episodes of Jeopardy. J’onn likes it so we usually let him enjoy it, but sometimes Mon-El forces him to put The Green Mile on. Have you ever seen it?”

     

                “No.”

     

                “It’s pretty good. You’ll get sick of it after the twelfth time though.”

     

                Lena let out a quiet huff of laughter. “Do they have chess?”

     

                “Ah, chess. Noun. A board game of strategic skill for two players, played on a chequered board on which each playing piece is moved according to precise rules. The object is to put the opponent's king under a direct attack from which escape is impossible - checkmate.”

     

                Kara rattled off the dictionary definition and Lena’s answering laugh was louder this time, almost sharp with delight and wry amusement. “You have an eidetic memory,” she said with approval.

     

                “Eidetic. Adjective. Relating to or denoting mental images having unusual vividness and detail, as if actually visible,” Kara replied with laughter in her voice. “I do. We were … a little more advanced on my planet. No one ever locked me up for being inhumanly intelligent though.”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                As her mood soured slightly and her thoughts turned brooding, Kara continued in an effort to lighten the moment, distract her from the black hole that would have consumed her if Lena had let it. She could wallow there indefinitely but Kara wouldn’t let her entertain the thought of it.

     

                “They don’t have a set though. I’ve never actually played chess before; do you like it?”

     

                “I do. I used to be a chess champion when I was younger.”

     

                “Really? I wouldn’t want to play against you then.”

     

                Rolling onto her back, Lena stared up at the metal mesh of the cot, crossing her legs at the ankle and smiling faintly to herself. “I’d go easy on you.”

     

                “You’ll have to teach me then. There’s a checkerboard there - half the pieces are missing but we can make our own chess ones out of paper.”

     

                “Alright then,” Lena softly replied, an ache in her chest as she swallowed thickly. “I’ll teach you at the next social.”

     

                “Well, now it’s definitely going to be the best day of the month.”

     

                Lena was still laughing when the thudding sound of a baton being struck against the concrete walls separating the cells tore her from her conversation. She craned her head to peer through the end of the cot, taking in a pair of polished black boots.

     

                “Prisoner LL93, out from under the bed,” Alex flatly ordered her.

     

                Sighing, Lena grimaced as she turned back to the gap. “Fun’s over,” she muttered.

     

                Kara let out a snort of laughter and Lena’s lips twitched in response as she shuffled out from under the bed, ducking her head under the lip and then pushing herself to her feet. Smoothing her hands over her uniform, she arched an eyebrow at Alex, who gave her a disgruntled look.

     

                “Doctor Danvers has cleared you for your daily walk.”

     

                “Lucky me,” Lena sarcastically replied.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Alex made a shooing motion with her hand. “Back against the wall,” she muttered, pressing a hand to the panel.

     

                The forcefield came down as Lena propped herself up against the wall, arms folded over her chest as she watched Alex walk towards her, the other guard, Vasquez, lingering outside. She straightened as Alex approached, making them eye level, and gave her a faint sneer as she put her hands out for the cuffs to be clapped around her wrists.

     

                Alex gently held her arm as she led her out of the cell and Lena tried to crane her neck to catch a glimpse of Kara but was quickly pulled towards the door on the other side of the cell block. Andrea and Gayle were already there, similarly shackled, and the three of them were led through the door and into the hallway, through a few more corridors and airlocks, until they reached a metal door with peeling paint and were guided inside.

     

                Lena found herself in a large room, bare with concrete walls and floors, patches marked from the damp that seeped through the prison, a few overhead lights illuminating the windowless space. Alex took up position in front of the locked door and Vasquez walked to the other side of the room, mirroring the same stance, hands on stun guns, feet a shoulder-length apart. Cameras winked with red lights from each corner.

     

                When Andrea and Gayle started walking, Lena followed suit, lagging at the back of the line they made as they slowly shuffled along. It was boring and Lena would’ve preferred to return to her cell and talk to Kara, rather than walk around the depressingly empty room in endless laps. 

     

                “Is this all we do?” Lena asked, her voice too loud in the echoing space.

     

                “You’re permitted an hour of exercise each day,” Alex said.

     

                “Can I choose not to?”

     

                “No.”

     

                Snorting, Lena shook her head, “of course not.”

     

                “Keep walking.”

     

                A bitter smile twisted her lips and her stare was piercing and brimming with animosity as she caught the eye of both women each time she passed them by. It felt like slowly going insane, walking in pointless circles, the damp smell of the room laced with salt and brine making her want to gag, the air so cold that Lena was surprised she didn’t see her breath before her. She shivered and hunched her shoulders as she walked her laps, no ventilation to offer fresh air, no windows for sunlight, no sunlight even if there had been windows. It was like her own personal hell to be trapped beneath the weight of the ocean and her chest felt tight at the thought of the structure buckling beneath the pressure and drowning her to death.

     

                The hour felt endless and Lena was relieved when it ended, no warmer and perhaps even stiffer as her body shuddered from the intensity of the cold, leading her to believe that the old room was on the outskirts of the prison, closer to the water, badly insulated and without the warmth generated by the power required to keep the forcefields, pressurised doors and airlocks running. She was glad for the sweatshirt they’d given her that morning after she’d showered and Lena wished they were allowed to keep them, but even that luxury wasn’t afforded to them unless the weather above sea level was bad. 

     

                She was taken back to her cell then for lunch, a tray of wilting salad, a bread roll and a tub of vanilla yoghurt slid across the floor of her cell. Lena ate the roll and the yoghurt and picked at the salad before drinking her cup of water and setting the tray against the far wall, a petty habit that she’d started doing to annoy the guards, although they offered no signs of irritation whenever they came to collect her empty tray.

     

                As soon as the trays had been collected, Alex stopped outside her cell again and jerked her chin. “Back against the wall.”

     

                “If it’s another walk, I’ll pass,” Lena drawled as she obeyed with antagonising slowness.

     

                Alex ignored her snide comments as she put her cuffs back on her and gave her a gentle prod between her shoulder blades, urging her onwards. They left through the door on the right end of the cell again, and Lena didn’t even bother trying to catch a glimpse of Kara this time - the guards seemed insistent on the prisoners keeping their heads down and one foot in front of the other. 

     

                They walked through the hallways and only made a few turns before they stopped a couple of minutes later. Alex pressed a hand against the panel and the lock clicked before she jerked the door open. Lena was surprised to find a comfortable office inside, the concrete walls painted a faded pale blue, the bare floors covered with a large rug that took up most of the small room. A small desk was wedged up against the wall with a desk and a computer, a shelf with a few books and then two chairs arranged opposite each other.

     

                A woman at the desk turned to look at them, wearing a sweater and glancing curiously at Lena with dark brown eyes. Her eyes strayed to Alex and softened minutely, noticed by Lena, who wondered where she was and what torture she was going to be subjected to this time.

     

                “Prisoner LL93,” Alex said. “I’ll be back in an hour.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Alex backed out and pulled the door shut, the sound of the lock clicking back into place making Lena feel cagey, trapped inside the small office with too much furniture crammed inside for her to walk around freely. She lingered just inside the door, her cuffs still securely limiting her range of motion.

     

                “Prisoner LL93,” the woman hummed, picking up a manila folder on her desk and then opening it. “Lena.”

     

                Her tone warmed as she said her name and she offered her a kind smile, gesturing to a chair as she climbed to her feet. “Please, take a seat.”

     

                The woman sank down onto one of the two, leaving the other one free for Lena, who stood there, stony-faced and silent. Making herself comfortable, the woman shifted and cleared her throat.

     

                “It’ll be a long hour if you stand the whole time.”

     

                “Why am I here?”

     

                “Inmates are required to attend one session with a registered psychologist on a monthly basis.”

     

                With a breathless scoff, Lena ran her tongue over her teeth, a sharp glint in her eyes. “A shrink? Really?”

     

                “Doctor Kelly Olsen.”

     

                Crossing over to the chair and settling down onto it with a contemptuous air of amusement, Lena leaned back, shackled hands in her lap and eyed the woman. Her lips were twisted in a wry smile and she didn’t respond, just waited.

     

                “So, how have you been adjusting?”

     

                Letting out a disbelieving laugh, Lena shook her head, “oh, just great. This is very on par with my lifestyle before I wound up here.”

     

                “I understand that you might be angry-”

     

                “You don’t understand shit,” Lena snapped.

     

                “I’ve read your file,” Kelly replied, tapping the manila folder in her lap. “The circumstances that brought you here are … unfortunate. What do you think?”

     

                Seething silently, Lena curled her fingers into fists and then flexed them again, biting the inside of her cheek. “Seems like a mistake to let prisoners in here unguarded.”

     

                “Not really.”

     

                “I could hurt you.”

     

                “You really shou-.”

     

                Kelly’s placid tone was enraging. Lena would’ve preferred the cold indifference of the guards or even the mockery and brutality of some of them - at least they were clearly defined enemies - but the psychologist’s earnest warmth unsettled her. Lena’s stomach twisted itself into knots and there was a sourness to her expression as she lunged from her chair.

     

                Before her outstretched hands could so much as lay a finger on Kelly, who didn’t even flinch or move a muscle, Lena stiffened as her shock collar jolted her with a course of electricity. Dropping hard to her knees in the space between the chairs, Lena drew in a strangled breath as her face stiffened at the pain. Visibly paler, she glanced up at the hand reaching out to her. 

     

                “I told you you shouldn’t; all of our sessions are strictly confidential, but they’re visually monitored for safety.”

     

                Glancing up, teeth grit against the ache in her body, Lena spied the blinking red camera watching them from the corner. She ignored Kelly’s hand and dragged herself back to her feet, sinking heavily onto her chair as she tossed her dark hair out of her face.

     

                “What’s the point of this?”

     

                “The mental health and stability of the inmates. Some … aren’t quite sane, others have been here for too long to have regressed in cognitive functioning. My job is to check in on everyone and make sure they’re doing okay and see if there’s anything I can do to help.”

     

                “The only thing that can help any of us is letting us go.”

     

                “That’s not within my power, but I’m interested in getting to know more about you. As I understand it, you’re quite intelligent. I have your IQ test results here - well above average, well above the ordinary high level too - what do you think about the DEO’s claim that it’s inhuman intelligence?”

     

                Mouth thinning as she looked aside, a muscle twitching in her jaw, Lena ran her fingertips over the thighs of her prison pants. The feeling of the coarse weave was enough to distract her from her anger, focusing on the feeling of it as a way to rein in her frustration, which wasn’t directed towards the woman before her. She was just an easy target, a present one to spend her anger on.

     

                “They’re even bigger idiots than I thought the government could be,” Lena bitingly replied.

     

                “It upsets you.”

     

                “I’ve been locked up . Of course it fucking upsets me!’

     

                “No,” Kelly mused, “that’s true, of course, but there’s underlying anger there too. It offends you, doesn’t it? To have all of your hard work discredited, made out to be the product of something you’re not guilty of. It strips you of any achievement and leaves you incapable of defending yourself with any concrete proof.”

     

                Bristling, Lena’s look was positively haughty as her lips twitched with annoyance. “You make it sound like it’s about my ego and not the fact that I’ve got a life sentence for scientific research.”

     

                “Harmful research.”

     

                “According to the government.”

     

                Kelly nodded, “yes, according to them. Though, I admit, from the information they’ve provided about your research … it does seem intentionally harmful when its only use is to harm people.”

     

                “It was something I discovered , never used. The only person who got hurt in the process of creating Anti-Kryptonite was me . How is that any different to research into nuclear warfare, into deadly viruses?”

     

                “You’re right. I believe it is the intent that matters most, not the purpose. However, the government feels otherwise, especially with your brother’s past.”

     

                “Yes, I’m well aware of my brother’s actions. He casts a long shadow, which I’ve never been able to escape.”

     

                “Tell me about your relationship with him.”

     

                Making a low sound of objection at the back of her throat, Lena scowled while smiling faintly. “No. All I’ll say is I’m glad he’s dead.”

     

                “Is that feeling from before he caused you to wind up here or as a result of it?”

     

                “Before.”

     

                “But you blame him for your incarceration.”

     

                Lena tersely nodded and Kelly hummed softly in understanding. There was a brief lapse before she continued speaking, diverting the conversation to a new topic as she crossed her legs and cocked her head to the side.

     

                “You’ve been reported as disruptive,” Kelly said, idly tapping the folder on her lap.

     

                “And?”

     

                “You’re a scientist - you don’t strike me as impulsive. Is there a reason for your behaviour?”

     

                A ripple of amusement crossed Lena’s face and she shifted in her seat, tilting her chin up a fraction. “I won’t go quietly. I won’t give in or accept that this is my life now.”

     

                “The rest of us have been here a lot longer than you have; do you think we all came so quietly at the beginning?”

     

                Lena stilled at the mention of Kelly being kept in the prison too, on the other side of it like Alex and Eliza. “What did you do to wind up here?” Lena asked, not expecting honesty.

     

                “I was in the military for a while. I found out some information about a DEO’s operation that I shouldn’t have. Lost my fiancée in the process. I was given the option to make myself useful here or be killed - they never outright said that was the alternative, but it was strongly implied.”

     

                “So, you know I’m innocent then.”

     

                “I know the DEO twists the truth and takes harsh precautions. They’re a secret organisation dealing with the protection of the whole planet from the kinds of beings locked up alongside us here. I … understand that the strict measures are a fear response to what they don’t know.”

     

                “Ignorance isn’t an excuse.”

     

                “No, it’s not. But there’s nothing we can do from in here except adjust to our new reality.”

     

                Lena’s eyes prickled with tears and her anger flared white-hot at the easy submission to the violation of their human rights. How could the people who weren’t locked behind bars just go about following orders from people who would never let them leave?

     

                “There has to be more than that,” Lena hoarsely replied, her voice trembling as desperation bled through. “I don’t believe that we can just be locked up here and that’s it. I never got a trial, I never got a lawyer. I have a business to run; I’m a billionaire. People will notice I’m gone.”

     

                “No, they won’t. There’ll be some story about how you’ve been locked up over some crime, that you fled the country to escape arrest or something along those lines.”

     

                “My mother-“

     

                “Will cooperate with whatever they tell her to or risk being locked up here too. I know all about the kind of person Lillian Luthor is, and she doesn’t strike me as a sentimental kind. Her Cadmus organisation pioneered the work the DEO does - I can guarantee she already knows you’re in here.”

     

                Feeling like the air had been knocked from her lungs as she struggled to breathe, Lena rocked forward, forehead nearly touching her knees, and clenched her teeth in an agonised grimace. 

     

                “Look, I won’t insult your intelligence by lying to you; as long as you’re relatively sane and healthy, they don’t care about anything else. They just want me to talk to you once a month and recommend prescriptions to Doctor Danvers if necessary. But … for what it’s worth, you seem like you’ve got enough tenacity to survive in here without losing your mind.”

     

                Silent for a long minute, Lena didn’t look up from her lap as she whispered, “I’d like to go back to my cell now.”

     

                “Agent Danvers will be here in five minutes to collect you.”

     

                The rest of their time together passed in tense silence and Lena was grateful that Kelly afforded her those few minutes of silence to collect herself. Sorting folders at her desk, Kelly left her sitting on the chair until there was a knock on the door and Alex admitted herself.

     

                She led Lena back to her cell, neither of them speaking then either, and her cuffs were removed as she was locked back in her cell. Crossing over to her cot, Lena sank down heavily onto the edge of it and dug the heels of her palms into her eyes, exhaling sharply.

     

                “You’re back.”

     

                Glancing over her shoulder at the blank wall, Lena swallowed, misery and frustration threatening to overwhelm her as a prickle of pity for her neighbour joined it.

     

                “Yeah.”

     

                “Where’d you go?”

     

                “To see the shrink.”

     

                “Shrink?”

     

                Lena closed her eyes and felt a stab of fondness for the gentle curiosity of the alien next door. “The psychologist.”

     

                “Oh. How’d that go?”

     

                “I don’t like shrinks.”

     

                Kara made a vague hum in response and Lena hesitated before climbing off the bed and working her way beneath the cot. She shifted closer to the wall, feeling the cold seep into her as she exhaled slowly, a weary sigh of resignation.

     

                “Ask me something.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “You sound like you need a distraction so ask me a question.”

     

                The tense set to Lena’s face softened minutely and she considered it for a second before speaking.

     

                “What’s space like?” Lena whispered.

     

                Kara’s voice lowered as she spoke through the gap. “Terrifying. It’s claustrophobic, just … endless darkness.”

     

                “Why’d you come to Earth, if you don’t mind me asking.”

     

                The silence stretched on for so long that Lena thought the conversation had ended, Kara effectively shutting her out. She didn’t hear her move on the other side of the wall though, that gritty shift of the canvas shoes against concrete, the quiet footsteps from the rubber soles padding away to distance herself from Lena’s questions. Eventually, she answered, but it was a long time coming.

     

                “My parents sent me here. Our planet … it was dead. They had the means to send me here to look after my cousin.”

     

                “What happened to them?” Lena whispered.

     

                “I don’t know. They died, I assume. I got … stuck. Our planet blew up and the shockwave blasted my pod. I ended up in a place called the Phantom Zone and … I got here late. I was frozen in that place for twenty-four years, trapped inside a pod, in and out of consciousness. I was only thirteen. By the time I got to Earth … I was too late.”

     

                Lena’s mouth was dry and she struggled to swallow. Her voice was hoarse when she spoke, barely above a whisper, her heart beating rapidly in her chest. Dread pooled in her stomach and she had the distinct feeling that she knew what the answer to her question would be before she asked it.

     

                “What happened to your cousin?”

     

                She heard Kara’s shuddering inhale, as if she was fighting back a sob. “He’s dead.”

    Chapter 5

    Chapter Notes

                “Ready for the big social?” Kara whispered in the dark.

     

                Although they had no concept of time, the cells had been plunged into darkness and they’d been ordered into bed. Waiting until it was silent in their block, the cell neighbours had eased themselves up off their steel grille cots and underneath, shifting close to the wall. 

     

                Curled up on her side, Lena was cold and huddled for warmth, but she was reluctant to get back into bed. Those long hours of talking with Kara were all that kept her sane, although she’d started to integrate herself more with the rest of the cell block over the past week, with some reluctance on her part and great enthusiasm on Kara’s. There was Nia directly across from her, a human-alien who had oneiric and astral projection abilities; Mon-El, an exiled prince who seemed to hate Lena for her friendship with Kara; Brainy, who spent most of his time pacing; J’onn, who offered wisdom and tried to lead them all in meditation to small success; Imra, a Titanian from the 31st century, who’d arrived with Brainy and had psychic abilities; Andrea and Gayle, the two meta-humans - the former with umbrakenesis powers and the latter with telekinesis and telepathy. Kara eluded any talk of her own powers, and in comparison, Lena felt comically normal .  

     

                To pass the time, they each took turns picking a category and naming something through the entire alphabet until someone drew a blank and was eliminated. There were shouts back and forth about repetitive categories and cheating answers, riling up a few of the prisoners to the point where a shock collar was employed more than once, and when it became evident just how smart Lena was, they objected to her playing. Everyone except for Kara and Brainy said she was making her own words up, and the former was only on her side out of principle, her knowledge of the English language fluent to the point of conversation but not educated on obscure scientific terms Lena pulled out. Instead, they questioned her about the outside world and news on what they’d missed out on.

     

                Lena’s life had settled into a routine over the following two weeks; frigid showers, sad meals, stolen conversations with the meta-humans she spent most of the time out of her cell with, and daily walks that she loathed. Laying on the concrete floor talking nonsense with Kara was just about the only thing that she didn’t abhor, and only then because the alien was the only friend she had.

     

                “Mhm. Are you excited for me to thrash you at chess?”

     

                “Oh, definitely. It’s all I’ve been looking forward to for days,” Kara murmured with a laugh in her voice.

     

                “That’s a bit sad.”

     

                “Just you wait until you’ve been in here long enough to go mad, then you’ll be excited for a monthly social.”

     

                Kara said it lightly but it made Lena’s chest ache with grief at the thought of being locked away for that long, wondering how the alien had managed to stay sane, to seem so well-adjusted with no one but prisoners and guards to talk to, nothing but a handful of minutes a day to walk properly and years hidden away from the sun. Lena loathed the sun, conscious of harmful UV rays and skin cancer, and yes, the vanity of ageing, but she would’ve given her entire fortune to be able to bask in the warmth of the sun, to feel the bracing sea air and not feel damp to her core in the dingy prison that was always cold with wet stains seeping through the concrete.

     

                It wasn’t even winter yet, and she imagined storms would make things worse, might make the prison lurch underwater with the tumultuous current, and might leave them all with pneumonia as the temperature plummeted. The whole thing was an affront to human rights and she felt her faint humour evaporate as she seethed in the dark.

     

                “I’m only joking,” Kara whispered a moment later, quick to reassure Lena. “You’ll get out of here before then, right? With your plan and all.”

     

                “I don’t have much of a plan,” Lena rasped, face spasming with pain as she came up without an answer for one of the few times in her life. 

     

                But she was too stubborn to not turn over every rock, biding her time before finding her way out, even if escape came in the form of her mother relenting and asking for her release. Lena would take it, she’d allow her to lord it over her for years to come if it meant getting the hell out of that cell. It was a stretch to rely on her mother though, knowing that trust was thin and rare between them, and Lena knew she’d have to come up with her own plan as a primary way of escaping; she’d never been good at relying on anyone else but herself. 

     

                “Yet,” she quietly added, her voice a weary sigh.

     

                “Well, if you need help, just let me know,” Kara tiredly replied, “I think I’d like to see this planet I’ve landed on. I’d like another sunset.”

     

                “Where were you living when you got here?”

     

                Kara hesitated, confused for a moment, “I- my pod crashed in America - I’m not sure where - just as the sun was going down. It was summer, I’m not sure what day. The sky was pink; I’d never seen anything like it. That’s all I got. About an hour at sunset before they came and took me.”

     

                Cold pierced Lena like a knife as she went rigid and pushed herself up slightly, staring at the dark wall as if she could see through to the other side. Her stomach knotted itself and her mouth was dry, unable to bring itself to work as she tried to form a sentence. Kara just sighed softly, resigned, the sound of someone who’d gotten used to their lot and wouldn’t fight it.

     

                “I never got to see where my parents sent me. I was there in that desert with a pink sky and these things flying around - I’d never seen a bird before - and then I was in a room being questioned, and I’ve been in here ever since then. This is all I know about Earth.”

     

                “I- you never- you never got to live here? You didn’t-”

     

                “No.”

     

                Anger flashed through Lena, hot and quick, and she kicked the wall, her canvas shoes scuffing along the concrete. “You were just a kid. Just a fucking kid.”

     

                “I’ve heard there are loads of kids just like me. I’m just one more that no one even remembered to forget.”

     

                “I’d remember you. If you were gone, I wouldn’t forget.”

     

                Kara’s soft huff of laughter made Lena’s chest ache, her breaths shallow and pained as she closed her eyes. The world had been cruel to her, yes, but she was starting to realise that there were worse things to be subjected to, and she didn’t think she would’ve had the strength to hold out for so long. If her mind hadn’t given in, if her body hadn’t failed her, her heart might’ve given up. Eighteen years was an immeasurably long time to imagine cooped up in a cage; she would’ve dashed her head against the wall after even one if this was how it was like.

     

                “I wouldn’t forget you either.”

     

                Swallowing thickly, Lena’s lips twitched with a faint smile. “Of course you wouldn’t; you have a perfect memory.”

     

                “So do you.”

     

                “And how do you know that?”

     

                “Because someone couldn’t be so threateningly smart if they didn’t have the ability to remember what to be smart about.”

     

                “Ah. Touché.”

     

                Kara made a faint sound of confusion, humming through the stillness of the night. “What does that mean?”

     

                “Touché? It’s French for touched. It’s used in fencing.”

     

                “Fencing?”

     

                “A sport with foils. It’s like sword fighting … did you have swords where you’re from?”

     

                “Yeah, we had swords. But that still doesn’t make any sense.”

     

                Smiling thinly as she rolled onto her back, the hard floor making her body ache as the cold seeped it. Her elbow was hurting from where the bone had been pressed against the concrete and she rubbed it idly, trying to stifle the shivers as her shoulder blades were numbed by the chill radiating from the ground.

     

                “It’s used in conversations to say … someone made a good point or a clever point at someone’s expense.”

     

                “Oh. I see. Do you speak many languages?”

     

                “Only Irish, Latin and Ancient Greek.”

     

                Kara let out a short laugh and Lena’s brow creased with bewilderment. “What?”

     

                “What’s Latin?”

     

                “Oh, it’s a dead language from Italy. A couple thousand years old. No one speaks it anymore in everyday conversation; that’s why it’s a dead language.”

     

                “Why do you speak it then?”

     

                “It’s useful in science. A lot of the scientific names for things are in Latin. And it’s been used in literature for centuries. It’s just … useful. I was raised taking Latin lessons, and Ancient Greek - I don’t even know modern Greek, but I know all the old stories in their original form. That’s just what my family was like.”

     

                Silent for a moment, Kara’s reply was hesitant. “Will you tell me one of those stories?”

     

                Lena hesitated too, blinking in surprise and faltering before she inhaled quickly and swallowed. “Sure. How about Pandora’s box? It’s fitting; the moral is that unchecked curiosity and disobedience can cause trouble. I guess that only applies to me.”

     

                Bitterness bled into her words and Kara let out a quiet, humourless laugh, the sound of her shifting closer to the wall, making herself comfortable, softening Lena’s hardness for a brief moment, as she searched her memory for the beginning of the story. As she opened her mouth to speak, there was the heavy thump of something hitting the forcefield.

     

                “Prisoner LL93, in bed.”

     

                Jolting with surprise at the disturbance, Alex’s voice sounding too loud in the stillness of the night, Lena tried to sit up and whacked her head on the underside of the bed. “Ow, shit,” Lena hissed, rubbing at her forehead.

     

                Scowling as she scooted out from under the bed, Lena shot Alex an irritable look, sneering slightly as she stiffly pushed herself to her feet. Sinking down onto her cot, she angrily pulled the blanket up over herself, the scratchy fabric rubbing her chin as she huddled for warmth. She heard Alex’s footsteps move to the next cell and a murmured conversation with Kara that was too quiet for her to overhear before the cell block fell silent again.

     

                They didn’t speak for the rest of the night and Lena slept fitfully, the thin mattress doing nothing to soften the metal grille of the cot, the scratchy blanket barely managing to keep the cold at bay, and only then because she was curled in on herself so tightly that it hurt to stretch herself out in the morning when she was woken up. The shower made her teeth ache from the cold and she couldn’t stop herself from shivering violently as she briskly washed the suds from her skin, the harshness of the water leaving her skin a mottled pink. 

     

                Sniffing and damp haired, Lena dressed and welcomed the sweatshirt she was given that day, along with the long-sleeved undershirt and the usual prison scrubs, the colour washing her out completely. There were bruises beneath her eyes from her exhaustion and her skin was positively grey, the lack of sunlight making her ghostly in comparison to her usual luminescent paleness. She didn’t engage in the other women’s conversation as they dressed and groomed themselves as best as they could, feeling only emptiness where they felt a prickle of excitement for the social in the afternoon. 

     

                Walked back to her cell, her wet hair leaving damp patches on her clothes, she sat on the edge of her cot and shivered, drawing the blanket around herself and huddling as breakfasts were brought around on a groaning trolley. Lena didn’t so much as acknowledge hers as it was slid inside to her feet, kicked with more force than anyone else’s by Jensen, the one who’d beaten her black and blue, watching her with cold, hateful eyes before the barrier blipped back between them. Even then, she didn’t eat, cold and resentful as she looked at the cold, lumpy porridge and the wilting apple she’d been presented with. She’d quickly learnt that the food was hit or miss, and even the better meals were worse than anything she’d ever had the misfortune of eating out before landing in prison. It wasn’t that Lena was expecting Michelin star meals, but decent food would have gone a long way with the prisoners. She might even have listened more often if the incentive to eat well had been on the table.

     

                As it was, she was in no mood to eat her scraps and grimly ignored the tray until they were collected, a guard warily moving into each cell to pick it up and add it to the trolley. When they stopped outside Lena’s, she didn’t move, didn’t obey the order to move back against the far wall, or the instruction to finish her breakfast when the tray was found untouched. Turning her attention to Jensen as he watched closely, shark-like in his clinically cold aggression, waiting to rip into her, she watched as he waited for a long minute before slapping his hand against the panel and stalking over to her.

     

                Leaning down to pluck the apple from the tray, Lena kicked the rest of it over to him, bringing him up short before she rolled the withering apple in her grasp, her fingernails a faint lavender from the chill, and then threw it with as much force as she could put behind it. Lena had never been one for throwing sports, never had the hand-eye coordination for it, preferring more intellectual pursuits like chess and puzzles, or fencing, where the foil remained firmly in her hand, in her control, but her hatred for the man made her aim true as she lashed out, the crack of the apple hitting him squarely in the nose filling her with savage pleasure.

     

                A smirk twisted her lips as she watched him double over, blood seeping through his fingers as he swore, but her satisfaction and amusement was short lived as a jolt of electricity shuddered through her, making her stiffen as her body locked with the seizing effects of her shock collar. Slumping, she slid off the bed, the hard edge of it biting into her back before she sagged on the floor, and she looked up to greet a boot to the face, the triumph dimming from her eyes as pain made her vision dim.

     

                Lena let out a small laugh, defiant and pleased with herself as her lips curled with a smile, his blood splattering on her cheek as he leaned over her. She could hear Kara’s voice shouting out from next door, demanding to know what was going on as Lena fought back against him, hauling herself to her feet and straightening up in time for him to punch her right in her smiling mouth. She felt the lip split, cut inside too where her tooth dug into it, and she spat right in his face as his fingers curled around her neck.

     

                “Do your worst,” she encouraged him, her voice oddly serene.

     

                “Lena.”

     

                Kara’s voice was sharp with panic next door and she wanted to call out and tell her that she was fine, but she didn’t want any undue attention poured upon her friend. Instead, she clenched her teeth and swallowed, a muscle twitching in her jaw. The next punch made her jump before it landed as the sound of something heavy striking the forcefield sounded from next door. Even Jensen hesitated, his grip loosening around Lena’s neck as his fist dipped, a spasm of panic crossing his murderous face. He looked pale and worried and, not for the first time

     

                Lena heard the thudding sound again and her eyes strayed towards her open cell. A moment later Kara started screaming, the harsh fluorescents of the cell dimming to an apocalyptic red, making everything seem bloody and brutal. The sound of her shouts made Lena’s hair stand on end and she ducked around the distracted guard calling for backup and lunged out of the cell. She didn’t make it more than two steps out before she was tackled to the ground, the small one - Maggie - grinding her knee into Lena’s back as she scrambled on top of her, dragging her arms behind her back and cuffing her.

     

                She couldn’t see, the gritty floor pressing into her cheek as she faced the opposite way to Kara’s cell, finding herself staring at Nia, the young woman across from Lena’s cell, shaking her head as she looked at her with wide eyes. It was clear, hand pressed against the forcefield and her attention distracted, that Nia wasn’t deterring Lena for her own well-being, but for Kara’s. Perhaps she would have fought more and struggled harder, but she went limp all at once at the thought of her cell neighbour being hurt.

     

                Breathing heavily, feeling clammy and faint from fighting back, Lena squeezed her eyes shut for a moment, the commotion around her seeming distant, her ears ringing and muffled like cotton wool had been stuffed inside them. She could hear shouting and thuds and she tried to turn her head to catch a glimpse of Kara, her curiosity over her appearance slipping to the back of her mind; Lena just wanted to see if she was okay.

     

                Instead, her head was roughly pushed back down and a minute later she was dragged up, struggling to catch her feet beneath her, before being hauled out of the cellblock. Her breaths were shallow wheezes and she could taste blood but felt no worse for wear. Her face would be sporting a nice bruise tomorrow, along with the rest of her, but it wasn’t as bad as last time, she could already feel that much. She imagined that it would be a much shorter trip to the doctor’s this time and she wondered if she’d be able to slip cookies through the small vent in the cell walls if she brought them back from Eliza. 

     

                It was a shock to her then that she wasn’t taken to see the doctor this time, her injuries left untreated as she halted before a door with a rusting industrial wheel locking mechanism on it. The thick hinges screeched as the cell door was pulled open, revealing a cramped space with room for a cot, toilet and sink. It was a fraction of the size of her cell, barely space to walk between the bed and the toilet, no room to pace, no room afforded for the luxury of stretching out. It was a punishment, plain as day.

     

                Uncuffed and shoved onto the cot, catching herself against the wall as her knee banged on the edge of the bed frame, Lena let out a soft hiss through her teeth and turned at the sound of the hinges screeching and the door clanging shut. She watched as the internal mechanism of the clunky lock turned, metal groaning as she was sealed inside. 

     

                Her anger hadn’t evaporated yet, only been concealed with worry for Kara, and now it came back white-hot as she slammed her palm against the metal, her hand stinging and no satisfaction taking the edge off her fury. Curling her hands into fists, she grit her teeth and then sat on the cot, drawing her knees up to her chest as she leaned back against the wall. 

     

                It was warmer in the cell, the air holding a muggy quality to it, as if the generators powering the prison were just on the other side of the wall, somewhere in the middle of the warren of hallways. But Lena was grateful for it as the chill that had crept into her bones and joints thawed out a little. She was grateful for it until the minutes crept into an hour, the solitude giving her worry time to grow, until she was stretching out, sweating in her layers as she thought about Kara. What had made her scream like that? Like she was being tortured, like she had lost her mind, throwing herself against the forcefield and causing such a fuss that the guards had seemed terrified at the prospect of her getting out. It was enough to make Lena's heart pound, her mind turning over every possibility of what they were doing to her; surely a mere shock collar that even Lena could withstand a few jolts from wasn't enough to have caused her so much pain.

     

                No one came, no one disturbed her, and the hours bled together as she waited. It grew hot in there, even as she shed her pilled sweatshirt, and then the grey scrub top and white long-sleeved cotton shirt. The air was thick and Lena’s hair stuck to her forehead as sweat beaded on her brow and her pale cheeks flushed pink. There were no vents, but pipes that were scalding to the touch ran down one wall. In the end, she had to strip down to her underwear, stretched out on the mattress as she stared at the blinking camera in the ceiling corner, wondering how long they’d keep her there.

     

                She imagined she’d be back in her freezing cell that evening, or perhaps tomorrow morning, but she underestimated how much she’d stretched their patience. Falling asleep at some point, on top of the cot and the scratchy blankets, she slept fitfully and rose with flushed cheeks and a sheen of sweat coating her skin. They’d dropped off breakfast for her, a punishment in itself if it hadn’t been a slice of relatively fresh bread, better than half of her usual meals, and a plastic cup of water was pushed through the hatch in the bottom of the door as well.  The floors were crunchy with grit as she stood, and the sink was scummed with dried soap stains as Lena refilled her cup after draining it. The water was so cold it made her teeth hurt, and there was the copper tang of the pipes in it, but she was more concerned with dehydration and drank freely. Collapsing back onto the bed, she settled in for a nothing day, the edges blurring together as hours passed by.

     

                Lena was sure they’d let her out later that afternoon, after giving her a day to cool off in the sweltering heat of the cramped cell, but nobody came and the single light stayed permanently on. Days passed by until she couldn’t be sure if it had been weeks or merely hours. There was no hurry. A slice of bread appeared periodically - she couldn’t tell whether they marked three regular meals or if it was whenever someone remembered she was there. All she knew was that she was hungry.

     

                Growing irritable, even more so than in her cell, which now seemed like a luxury with the conversation, space and the merciful cold she never thought she’d appreciate, Lena was restless and crabby as she tried her best to sleep through the duration of her punishment. She’d always been so good at being by herself but never had she felt so lonely. Even the voice inside her mind has lost its breath, until a numbing emptiness consumed her. 

     

                When the door groaned open, it could have been midday or midnight for all Lena knew, and she pushed herself up off the mattress, blinking owlishly at the guard slipping inside. Alex. Rubbing at her face, feeling dirty and greasy and too hot, her ribs a shade more prominent and her bruises faded to yellow. There were never any mirrors around for Lena to inspect her reflection, which she was grateful for, unsure how she’d handle seeing the beaten version of herself in prison clothes.

     

                Alex gave her a hard look, easing the door shut behind her. There was a spark of anger in her brown eyes and Lena knelt on the bed as she stared at her, far too close in the confines of the isolation cell.

     

                “Is she alright?” Lena blurted out before she could help herself, betraying her air of indifference she’d been aiming for.

     

                Mouth a flat line, Alex stared at her for a long moment. “Fine.”

     

                Deflating as she exhaled, Lena rubbed at her forehead, first and sweat mingling beneath her touch. She felt faint and weak, from relief, borderline heatstroke and starvation. Sinking back down onto the bed, she nodded, not looking at Alex.

     

                “She’s fine for now, but you ,” Alex ground out, “are going to get her hurt if you carry on. You could get her killed.”

     

                Looking up, Lena gave her a scornful look. “If you care about her so much, why haven’t you helped her escape.”

     

                “I can’t even help myself escape,” Alex bitingly replied. “Or my mom. I’d be shot for helping her.”

     

                “Ah. Self-preservation, is it?”

     

                Anger sparked on the guard’s face and Lena couldn’t help the smile that curled her lips, mocking and satisfied. She wouldn’t have been surprised if Alex locked her back inside and left her there for another undefined length of time, but she just loomed over Lena instead, only mildly intimidating, and only then because of the gun and the baton at her sides.

     

                “Cause any more trouble and you’ll find yourself in here for a month - and I won’t be able to get you out next time.”

     

                Blinking, Lena straightened up as Alex grabbed the ball of wadded up clothes shoved in the corner of the cot and dropped them on Lena’s lap. 

     

                “Get dressed.”

     

                Trying not to think about Alex’s contrarian moods - indifferent one moment and then doing her small favours the next - Lena pulled her clothes on quickly and shoved her feet into the canvas daps before she allowed herself to be cuffed. 

     

                Walking out of the hot cell and into the sudden chill of the hallway was like sinking into the freezing waters of the Arctic, and Lena was grateful as much as she was reluctant to enter back into that world of freezing to death. It was even worse when she was taken to the bathroom, empty and as grimy as ever, having to take even longer to scrub herself clean properly with the paltry sliver of soap and the harsh water making her want to shut the shower off.

     

                Still, once she was dry and in clean clothes, she did feel marginally better, as far as that went while being in prison. Hair clean and skin pink and pimpling from the cold, the smell of cheap soap and detergent enveloping her in the sweetest cloud, Lena was more obedient as she was led back to her cell. And for one awful , shocking moment, it felt like coming home, her heart buoyed with the thought of hearing Kara’s voice again, of laying beneath the cot and stretching out in the cold, and Lena wanted to laugh and cry at the thought.

     

                It was both chilling and numbing and she was silent as she sank down onto the edge of her cot, staring blankly at the opposite wall, not saying a word as she let her reality sink in. It was only Kara’s quiet, prompting voice a long minute later that broke her out of the black pit of her despairing thoughts.

     

                “How long was I in there for?”

     

                “Ten days.”

     

                “Oh. I’m sorry for missing the social,” Lena murmured, a pang of guilt stabbing through her.

     

                Kara laughed quietly, “it’s alright. Turns out, I wasn’t feeling up to it anyway.”

     

                "What did they do to you?"

     

                "Oh ... well, I guess I really did it to myself."

     

                "No, you didn't. It was my fault."

     

                "No, it wasn't."

     

                A lump constricted Lena’s throat and she swallowed thickly. “Are you alright?”

     

                “I’m alright. Are you? I’ve been in isolation before; I know it’s enough to make you lose your mind.”

     

                She turned and let her forehead rest against the wall between them with a thunk, closing her eyes. “Don’t worry, I have no intention of going mad. At least not today.”

    Chapter 6

                “You know, I never thought I’d be grateful to be cold while I was isolated,” Lena said the following day as she shivered, teeth chattering. “But now I think I might cause some trouble to wind back up in solitary. At least it was warm there.”

     

                “Don’t do that again,” Kara murmured, a faint plea in her voice.

     

                Lena’s trembling lips thinned with a smile as she closed her eyes, arms wrapped tightly around herself. It would have been warmer if she got off the floor, but that would’ve meant having to talk louder to converse with Kara, and she was a private person by nature and didn’t want to broadcast their friendship.

     

                “What did they do to you? Agent Danvers said I could’ve gotten you killed.”

     

                “Oh,” Kara softly murmured. “I mean … she’s not wrong. They wouldn’t have, though. It’s just … well, I’m a lot stronger than anyone else here.”

     

                “On this block?”

     

                There was a delayed pause before Kara slowly responded, wariness threading through her words. “In the prison.”

     

                Left speechless, Lena opened and closed her mouth, her eyes open as she stared at the concrete wall. “Oh.”

     

                “They’re … a bit more, ah, cautious with me.”

     

                “In what way?”

     

                “The red light the other day was to make sure I couldn’t use my powers. Then the collar … well, mine’s got something a little bit extra in it.”

     

                “What?”

     

                Lena’s mouth was dry and she felt guilt claw at her as she waited for Kara’s reply. It wasn’t forthcoming though and her concern made her brusque, worried that her rash behaviour would hurt her friend if she wasn’t mindful of the truth. 

     

                “Kara.”

     

                “It’s- well, it’s a sort of poison, I guess. Only for my kind. But don’t worry; they rarely use it and it’s slow, so it wouldn’t actually kill me - unless they exposed me to it for too long. It’s like radiation, I guess. Too much too fast is lethal, but otherwise, it’s fine.”

     

                Choking on a bewildered laugh, Lena pinched the bridge of her nose. “That’s not how radiation works.”

     

                “Isn’t it? That’s what it’s like back home. We didn’t have a yellow sun though so our levels were a lot lower. And I didn’t really get much of a scientific education here so I’m not sure how that converts.”

     

                “Where are you from?”

     

                “Ah, you wouldn’t know it,” Kara said with a resigned sigh. “It’s gone now, anyway.”

     

                “Do you miss it?”

     

                Kara’s laugh was quiet and choked. “Of course. Don’t you miss your home?”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena hummed contemplatively, digging her fingertips into her arms as she envisioned her cold apartment, empty and unlived in, the office where she’d slept on the sofa some nights, the lab where she hadn’t slept at all but spent more time in than she did at home, the room at boarding school where she’d spent a good portion of her childhood, and the home of her childhood. None of them were particularly comforting or welcoming places, least of all the latter. They were just places to her.

     

                “Not particularly. I suppose I just miss being free. I miss … drinking my imported coffee, my nice clothes, my soft mattress and sheets. I miss being able to use my computer for my notes and my aged whisky, I miss being able to use my wealth to get whatever I wanted. I’ve never really had a home that felt like a home. If it wasn’t for the living conditions here … it would be much the same as anywhere else to me.”

     

                “That’s … sad.”

     

                “That’s life.”

     

                “Is that the life you want to return to if you get out of here?”

     

                “When.”

     

                “Right, when you get out of here.”

     

                Blowing the air out of her cheeks, Lena rubbed at her cold nose and frowned. “I don’t know. Maybe I’d like to shake up the world a bit now. Bring this place down in the most public fashion.”
