                With a soft huff of laughter, Kara shifted on the other side of the wall, and her voice faded a little, as if she was speaking to the underside of her cot. Lena shifted closer to the wall, turning her ear to the small ventilation shaft. 

     

                “So you’re going to get out and then develop a death wish that will have you assassinated by the government?”

     

                “Did you study politics here?” Lena dryly asked with a quiet laugh. “You know US history well.”

     

                “Governments are tragically the same in any galaxy.”

     

                “Of course they are. They’re all corrupt, which means they can all be bought. So I’ll buy my life and they’ll find a scapegoat and they’ll buy my research that landed me in here as part of the deal for my safety. I’ll be the poor little rich girl, wrongfully mistreated by some unlawful division of the government that went off-book. They’ll have to free everyone in here though; isn’t that a good enough win?”

     

                Kara hummed faintly. “For some people. Somehow, I don’t think that’ll satisfy you though.”

     

                “Probably not,” Lena agreed, “but it’s a start.”

     

                “And how are you planning on getting to that point? What’s your plan?”

     

                Smiling thinly to herself, wry amusement softening her face as she blew onto her cold fingers and then jammed them into her armpits, Lena let out a withering sigh. “Unfortunately, I’m still in the reconnaissance stage. Which involved getting brutalised a lot more than I initially anticipated, but it’s all worthwhile.”

     

                “How are cracked ribs and bruises worthwhile?”

     

                A light laugh escaped Lena, a shred of warmth in her chest as her cheek dimpled and her eyes closed. “It helps me uncover more knowledge.”

     

                “And …”

     

                “Knowledge is valuable, is powerful,” Lena murmured, keeping her voice down as she mentally walked through the map in her mind. “I’m not going to waste any opportunities to learn more about this place, no matter how rash or violent my methods are. I refuse to sit by idly.”

     

                “What benefit did you get out of isolation?”

     

                Smiling thinly to herself, Lena’s eyelids shuttered. “Ah, well, now I know that further into the centre of the prison, in the older sections, there’s a room with pipes full of boiling hot steam where they send people to punish them. What does that tell me? There’s probably a room with all the boilers for the gas and water, or a room for the generators and electricity powering every inch of this prison. What’s the quickest way out of a prison? Turning off anything that can power lights, doors, cameras and these collars. So, there’s the first target.”

     

                “Okay, I’ll bite,” Kara said with a quiet laugh. “Now, say you’re in isolation … how do you get into that room with the power source?”

     

                “Ah, well, I wouldn’t. Every plan has the brains and the brawn. I’d just need someone strong, and in a prison of aliens with all kinds of powers, it wouldn’t be too difficult to find one strong enough.”

     

                “Except for the fact that we’re all kept docile and weak.”

     

                “You don’t seem docile and weak to me,” Lena countered.

     

                Quietly snorting, Kara clicked her tongue, lowering her voice as amusement washed through it. “Don’t blow my cover, or they’ll up my dose.”

     

                “Your secret’s safe with me,” Lena whispered, smiling to herself. “Say, you wouldn’t be able to burst through a wall by any chance, would you?”

     

                “Like paper,” Kara softly replied with a terrifying edge of power. 

     

                “Ah, so you’re my brawns then, huh? If you’d like to blow this joint and get the fuck out of here, that is.”

     

                With a long, wistful sigh, Kara let out a short laugh. “I do have a mind to see another sunset before my days are over.”

     

                “So … partners?”

     

                There was a pause and she could hear the quiet hesitation before Kara sighed defeatedly. “Lena-”

     

                “We could do it,” she firmly whispered. “I’m being serious. If you helped, if everyone did, I could get us out.”

     

                “You’ll get yourself killed,” Kara whispered, her voice sad and pained.

     

                “I’ll take a quick death than the slow descent into madness they have planned for all of us here. I should be grateful; at least I’m not immortal, so my imprisonment has an expiration date.”

     

                Her weak laugh and attempt at humour fell flat as Kara remained silent. After a long minute, her voice came through, slow and quiet.

     

                “Then you’re luckier than me.”

     

                “You’re …”

     

                “I’m not technically immortal, but … centuries, at the very least.”

     

                Lena’s mouth went dry and she drew in a shallow breath, rattling in her chest. “Kara, you can’t survive here that long. That’s- you’ll go insane.”

     

                “I’ve done alright so far,” she hedged.

     

                “Out of pity and rare kindness from a guard and a doctor who will be dead in a few decades, if being stuck in this shithole doesn’t kill them faster than that. I’m going to get them out too; they can help me.”

     

                There was a pause and then a shifting sound before Kara thickly spoke. “I don’t … think I want to talk about this anymore.”

     

                She heard Kara shift away from the wall, working her way out from under the cot, shoes scuffing on the floor. Biting back a sigh, Lena similarly scooted out and climbed back onto her bed, wrapping herself in her blanket and huddling for warmth. 

     

                Kara didn’t speak to her much for the next few days and Lena brooded, removing herself from the word association game they all decided to play as she turned her back to the cell block and sat in the middle of her cell. The chill of the concrete seeped into her and the freezing showers only made her colder, so cold that they were given boiling cups of water to stop them from getting hypothermia as they weathered out the storm. 

     

                Andrea developed a cough that kept everyone up all night and then a few days later the lights in the cell went out, plunging them into darkness. It was a minor electrical issue, they were informed, guards coming around with torches to hand out meals they had to fumble with in the dark. Lena’s eyes couldn’t make out a thing in the darkness and it was suffocating to be left in so much darkness, her ears picking up on every little sound.

     

                “Winn’s out sick,” Alex whispered to Kara, “chest infection from the damp. We’re going to have to wait for him to get back on his feet before we take a look at the wiring.”

     

                “Is the rest of the prison out?”

     

                “No, just whatever wiring leads to the lighting fixtures for this block and the next one.”

     

                Lena’s stomach jolted with excitement, her head pounding in her chest, and she loudly cleared her throat. Listening to the scrape of boots and the heavy tread stopping beyond the invisible forcefield, Lena climbed to her feet and walked blindly towards it, hand outstretched to make sure she didn’t walk into it.

     

                “Prisoner LL93,” Alex wearily greeted her. “What?”

     

                “I hear you have an electrical issue.”

     

                “What’s it to you?”

     

                Smiling slightly, eager to get inside the prison, perhaps find something useful, even if it was just looking at the innards of the structure. The circuits they used could reveal valuable information, and perhaps present an opportunity for sabotage. She wasn’t likely to pass it by if it presented itself so willingly.

     

                “I’m a scientist and engineer. I know pretty much everything there is to know about electrical circuits. I’ve built my own machines since pre-school. You couldn’t hire a better electrician.”

     

                “Are you asking me to let you fix the lights?”

     

                “Are you going to let me?”

     

                The only response she got was the scuff of retreating footsteps, followed by the hiss of the doors parting to let the guard out. Shrugging nonchalantly, although disappointment curled in her stomach, Lena moved over to her cot and sat back down, wrapped in her scratchy blanket as she stared into the blackness and waited to feel tired enough to sleep.

     

                An hour later, the door hissed open and a bright beam of torchlight cut through the darkness of her cell as she squinted and held a hand up to protect her eyes. Alex’s face looked ghostly and disembodied, floating in the dark as her black uniform melted into the shadows of the cell block, but her dark eyes drilled into Lena and she beckoned her.

     

                “Prisoner LL93, up against the wall.”

     

                Stiffly uncurling, Lena obeyed and was cuffed before dragged from the cell and escorted out. The hallway beyond was dark as well, the lights in the whole sector out, but Lena counted the turns - right, right, left, straight, left - and once they reached the lit portion of the prison, started noting the doors and cameras. 

     

                When they stopped outside a door, Alex admitted them and Lena found herself in a partitioned room, a metal grille door with an old fashioned keypad lock separating her from the multitude of tools beyond. Alex pulled a pair of cuffs from her belt and latched one onto Lena’s wrist and the other onto the bars of the grille.

     

                “What do you need?”

     

                “Electrical tape. Pliers. Screwdriver; Phillips, probably, but bring one of each and a few sizes. Wire cutters. Wire strippers. Potentially a soldering iron with 60/40 tin-lead based-”

     

                “Okay, well, I’m not giving you that.”

     

                Shrugging, Lena smiled faintly. “I’ll make do with what you have.”

     

                Alex fetched the tools that she requested, occasionally moving back over to the grille to show Lena something through the mesh, ensuring she had the right materials for her. Afterwards, she stopped by a guard room, dingy and austere with patches of mold blooming around the edges of a tiled splashback, a hot water urn reheating itself as someone made a cup of coffee, a luxury Lena would have killed for, and a boxy TV playing a staticky hockey game from a few years back.

     

                “Hey, Vasquez, with me,” Alex called out.

     

                The woman with cropped hair groaned and hauled herself to her feet, her chipped mug abandoned on the sticky surface of a folding table, and she tucked her thumbs into her tactical belt as she followed them out into the hallway. Sandwiched between them, Alex holding a red metal toolbox with all the necessary materials, Lena walked along at a leisurely place, filing information away for later.

     

                “So, is there a generator room? Are there localised points for different wings? What’s the deal?”

     

                “The deal is you’re going to get up in the ceiling and figure it out,” Alex grimly informed her.

     

                “Alright, so … no leads?”

     

                “Nope.”

     

                “Super,” Lena dryly replied, rolling her eyes.

     

                She wasn’t that put out by the thought of crawling through years of dust and potential rat shit - would they have rats on an underwater raft? That didn’t seem likely and she hadn’t seen any so far - but it was cold and she wasn’t used to doing dirty work like that herself. Still, it would give her enough time to go poking around, and that was her main goal here. Lena didn’t care if the lights were off for another week; one could get used to anything after long enough. Except prison. She refused to get used to prison.

     

                Walked to a room overflowing with bundles of wires, Lena was given a brief moment to double-check what they’d already inspected, and confirm that it wasn’t any loose plug sockets, although she couldn’t confirm whether there were any flaws with the wiring, which she very much imagined there would be considering how half of the prison was an ancient, rusting and moldering mess. 

     

                Shrugging as she straightened up from the junction box with the labeled switches for different circuits, she faced Alex. “Well, it hasn’t tripped. Must be the wiring.”

     

                Sending Vasquez off to search for a ladder, Alex leaned against the metal door while Lena glanced around, drinking in the sight of everything. There were a multitude of junction boxes, a couple of generators and stacked towers with so many wires and extension cords that it was a walking fire hazard. Lena wondered if this was the room near the isolation cell, or if perhaps that one was a boiler room; either way, it was palpably warmer in the room and she plucked at the front of her sweatshirt.

     

                “So, do you like your job?” Lena conversationally asked, trying to probe.

     

                Without even looking at her, Alex let out an exasperated sigh. “No talking.”

     

                “Just trying to get to know you better,” Lena said, clicking her tongue. “Kara seems to think highly of you, at any rate. Not sure why.”

     

                “Prisoner KZ64 and I have known each other a lot longer than a measly few weeks. You might take a leaf out of her book and improve your behaviour, or I don’t imagine you’ll last long in here.”

     

                Humming, Lena’s eyes roamed around the room. “What makes you think I want to?”

     

                “I said no talking.”

     

                “Right. Got it. Mouth shut,” Lena slowly replied, enjoying watching Alex restlessly shift with annoyance as she continued to talk. 

     

                It was petty, but Lena would take pleasure in being a nuisance if that was all she could do. She’d learnt at a young age that sometimes the only way to get attention was to get a rise out of someone, and she’d gotten good at manipulating emotions to get what she wanted. This was no different; if she kept pushing the right buttons, eventually she’d find the one that let slip a nugget of information out of anger or frustration. And information was all she had to rely on at this point.

     

                But Alex didn’t bite, and when Lena continued to talk, Alex escorted her out into the hallway and locked her in a storage cupboard with nothing but an empty bucket and a box of unopened bleach. When Vasquez returned with the ladder, Alex let her back out again, looking more composed as she gestured Lena back into the room. 

     

                Setting up the ladder and reaching up to shift one of the square ceiling tiles aside, Alex climbed back down and dusted off her hands. “Alright, good to go.”

                

                “You’ll have to uncuff me,” Lena pointedly said, holding out her hands.

     

                There was a tightness to Alex’s expression before she slowly moved, unlocking the cuffs and hanging them at her belt. 

     

                “Don’t do anything stupid.”

     

                “Yes, ma’am.”

     

                Alex gave her a flat look in response to her sarcasm, and Lena met her eyes with a hard stare, a faint smirk curling the corners of her mouth. Perhaps it would work against her to provoke the one guard she was trying to get on her side to help break out of there, but for whatever reason, Alex seemed perpetually annoyed by her and little else. Lena wouldn’t have said she liked her, but she didn’t treat Lena with the same contempt as some of the guards did, and she gave her a little more leniency.

     

                “I’ll go first-”

     

                “What, you’re coming up there?” Lena snorted.

     

                “As if we’re going to trust you to go up there alone,” Alex said with an eye-roll. “You’d probably booby trap the wiring and hide up there until we could drag you out, and I’d personally rather not deal with that. God knows, you’re enough of a headache without the extra drama.”

     

                “You know me so well,” Lena crooned.

     

                Prodding her forward, Alex’s mouth turned down at the corners as she tried to mask her irritation. Glancing over at Vasquez, Alex jerked her chin at her. “Give her your flashlight.”

     

                Unhooking it from her belt, Vasquez held it out and Lena took it, testing it with the click of a button, on and off. Alex climbed up the ladder and paused near the top as Vasquez lifted the toolbox up to her, leaving her weapons ready for the taking. Lena made a note of that but hung back, arms folded across her chest as she observed. It was better to be patient and lull them into a false sense of security than make her move prematurely without a well thought out plan.

     

                She watched as Alex disappeared up into the dark, and the crawl space lightening a fraction from the shaft of light radiating from the flashlight. Hauling herself up the ladder, Lena clamped her own flashlight between her teeth and pulled herself over the lip of the ceiling and into the cramped space. 

     

                On hands and knees, she pulled the flashlight from her mouth and coughed as she stirred up a thick layer of dust. Clicking it on, she swept the beam of light around and shuddered at the sight of cobwebs and evidence of rats or mice. Apparently, vermin survived just fine in an underwater prison.

     

                Crawling through the space, just wide enough that she could manage on her hands and knees, albeit a little crouched, Lena made her way to the snaking wires congregating from the gaps within the walls of the room downstairs. The bundles were thicker than her torso and labelled, but it still took her fifteen minutes of coughing and spluttering her way over the numerous bundles before she found one for the lighting.

     

                “It’s these ones,” she hoarsely informed Alex, patting the mass of black wires, indistinguishable from the other bundles of black.

     

                “And now?”

     

                “We’ll need to follow it to the section without power. Check the entire length.”

     

                “Right.”

     

                Lena crawled onwards, trying to visualise the space beneath her - they would’ve taken a right here, then a left and another left, which meant they should follow the bundles snaking right ahead - and made slow progress as she tried to narrow the thick bundle down to a smaller one for that sector. The minutes passed by quickly and they were up there for an hour, crawling around vent shafts obstructing their path, beneath wide pipes - some frigid and some radiating heat from a few feet away - and the entire time Lena was left with the cold feeling of dread at the tonnes of ocean above her. All that separated her from the outside was a few feet of solid metal sheeting and insulation. Each drop of water in the damp and dusty space made her shiver at the thought of rivets and sheet metal tearing apart to admit a flood of saltwater.

     

                Another hour slipped by as she started inspecting the individual wires branching off the bundle as thick as her bicep, which itself was a run-off of the main bundle. She ended up following the wires to their end, asking for a screwdriver and spending twenty minutes making sure some were tightened while others were loosened, pulling a wire loose and then backtracking to a point where a dead rat lay near a bundle of chewed through wires, declaring it the cause of the outage. 

     

                Alex acted as her assistant but was oblivious to what Lena was doing, only doing a cursory check at the beginning to see that the wires were, in fact, frayed where they’d been chewed through. That left Lena to tamper a little as she fixed the wires, cutting the plastic casing off and trimming the wires, splicing the ends together and wrapping them in electrical tape. It was a shoddy repair, all that she could do with the tools afforded her, but it would fix the lights and the doors at the very least. 

     

                Still, she didn’t stop there, fiddling with the other nearby wires as well, cutting certain ones that she prayed would last for a week or so before being noticed, fraying some to short on their own, and crossing a few wires, splicing them together to malfunction. Anything to get the opportunity to get back up in the crawl space once she was better prepared. 

     

                “All done,” she rasped almost three hours later, her throat parched and her brow beading with sweat even as she shivered from the freezing temperatures.

     

                Alex counted every tool put back into the box and then fixed Lena with a piercing stare before reaching for her radio and pushing a button. “Vasquez, we’re all done up here. Can you give us a light to guide us back?”

     

                In the meantime, they started crawling back the way they’d come, and five minutes later there was a pinprick of light sweeping through the darkness, pinpointing their exit. It was quicker on the way back, following the light as they crawled beneath pipes and around ventilation shafts, Lena trying her hardest not to kick dust into Alex’s face as she shuffled forward, her back aching and the dust wracking her with coughs.

     

                Once they reached the hole in the ceiling, she shuffled out and down the ladder, looking grey and ghostly with the sheer amount of dust caking her. She looked like she’d gone prematurely grey, her dark hair almost white, and she tried to shake it off her clothes as she sneezed. Clicking off her flashlight, she handed it back to Vasquez and flicked the switches in the junction box as Alex shimmied through and descended the creaking ladder.

     

                “I’ll take her from here,” Alex informed the other guard, the two of them exchanging curt nods, before she was escorted out of the room.

     

                As they wound their way through the hallways, they came to a previously dark section and Lena felt a flicker of smug pride to find the lights on, despite her subtle sabotages, and Alex was silent as she guided her onwards. When Lena bore left, making for the path back to the cell block, potentially betraying her increasing familiarity with the prison, Alex made a small sound of objection.

     

                “Keep walking.”

     

                Lena slowed mid-step for a moment before she continued onwards, her stomach jolting before she tried to keep her composure, wondering what was going on now. Alex walked beside her, allowing her the freedom to walk without being roughly handled along the way, and they walked down a hallway that was identical to many of the others, but Lena was distinctly sure she had never been down before.

     

                Unlocking the door with her handprint, Alex opened it to reveal a bathroom similar to the one that the prisoners were brought to each day. It was empty and the mirrors were still faintly fogged, a fact that seemed off to Lena. Gesturing her inside, Alex stepped in and locked the door, fixing Lena with a wry look on her face.

     

                “Cooperation can lead to benefits.”

     

                “Wha-”

     

                “This bathroom is for DEO agents and other employees. It has hot water.”

     

                Blinking at her, it took Lena a second to realise she was doing her a favour in return for fixing the lights. Under ordinary circumstances, Lena might have thanked her, but considering it was from inside a prison, she wasn’t very forthcoming with her gratitude, even though she felt weak with it.

     

                “I’ll fetch you a clean uniform. I’d make the most of your time, if I were you.”

     

                Lena didn’t have to be told twice as Alex uncuffed her. She was already pulling off her dusty clothes before the other woman had left, weeks of freezing communal showers leaving her with very little self-consciousness as she strode over to a shower head.

     

                The hot water was scalding after she gave it a minute to heat and Lena couldn’t help herself as she stood beneath the hard spray, a small cry escaping her. As dust sluiced off her skin with rivulets of steaming water, she let out a forceful breath and her eyes filled with tears, and then she was actually crying, shaking as she let the heat drill into her. Never had anything felt so good and she wept for how something as small as a hot shower could break her apart.

     

                She was still crying when Alex returned, her hitching sobs audible over the hissing sound of water, but Lena didn’t have the energy to feel embarrassed. Alex set her clothes down on the counter near the sinks and leaned against them, eyes downcast as she let Lena shower for another five minutes, this time hurrying to wash her hair with real shampoo , and wash herself with soap that wasn’t some twisted lump in various stages of disintegrating.

     

                Eventually, Alex cleared her throat. “Time’s up.”

     

                Reluctantly shutting off the water, Lena shivered violently in the sudden chill of the bathroom, but was still somewhat warmed to her core as she wrapped herself in one of the worn towels. Drying herself off, feeling refreshed and soft, she dressed in the clean uniform and freshened up - deodorant, toothpaste, running her fingers through her wet, tangled hair. 

     

                She caught a glimpse of herself in the fogged up mirror for the first time since that first day, usually intent on avoiding looking at her reflection in the spotted mirrors, and her stomach knotted at the sight of her. Her face was thinner and her skin was positively ghostly, although the heat of the shower had instilled a slight flush of pink to her cheeks. Lena looked sallow, sick, and she was far from the billionaire businesswoman that had been thrown in there a month ago.

     

                Once she was done, Alex wordlessly clapped her manacles back on her and escorted her out into the hallway and Lena was struck by the bizarre urge to thank her. It was the most subdued she’d felt since arriving in the prison, the most defeated, and most of all it was the most human she’d felt. Despite her earlier interest in ferreting out information, she didn’t say a word as they walked back the way they’d come.

     

                Fighting back the urge to cry the entire walk back to her cell block, Lena was distracted, not even taking stock of the turnings and doors, the locations of the cameras and wide ventilation shafts that possibly might allow someone to crawl through it, if necessary. She would need to size Kara up first, see how brawny her muscle was before planning a more covert way out, if bursting through the walls and tearing the prison apart failed. 

     

                As they turned into the hallway leading to the cell block, they found the doors already sliding closed as another prisoner was brought out. Alex guided Lena over to one side of the hallway as a trio walked towards them. Alex nodded at them as they drew level before ushering Lena onwards, but her attention caught on the sight of the prisoner being escorted along. 

     

                The woman was young, perhaps of an age with Lena, although her blue eyes were wide and mournful, as if she was perpetually sad, and she had dirty blonde hair falling down to her waist in a tangled mess. She was quite tall and her thinness made her look gangly, although there was something childish about the softness of her face. Perhaps worst of all was the grey prison uniform that differed from Lena’s; the woman was trapped in a straitjacket, unable to use her arms as black straps restricted her movements even further.

     

                Still, as Lena passed her by in the hallway, the young woman gave her a wide smile, blue eyes crinkling at the corners and her nose wrinkling slightly. A faint glow of happiness filled the pallid grey of her cheeks, making her look healthier than she was for a brief moment. Staring at her with a faint crease of bewilderment between her eyebrows, Lena’s expression was grave and troubled. And then the woman spoke.

     

                “Hello, Lena.”

     

                Slow shock dawned on Lena’s face as her lips parted and her eyes widened. Her stomach jolted, swooping with breathless surprise, elation running through her as the arms on her hair stood on end. Trying to turn as the doors to the cell block parted, Lena caught only a brief glimpse of blonde and faded grey before Alex turned her back around, her question hanging in the air as her heart pounded in her chest.

     

                “Kara?”

    Chapter 7

                Lena was restless as she paced in her cell, back and forth, back and forth, waiting. The warmth of her shower faded, leaving her shivering as she hunched her shoulders and ignored the guessing game the other inmates were playing. Her mind was fixated on Kara, on the straitjacket she’d been bound in, her lanky frame and her face. Lena had assumed she must have been lying about her appearance, finding some small entertainment in keeping Lena guessing about what type of alien she was, but Lena hadn’t expected her to look so human. So ordinarily human in such a fragile way, her cheeks a little hollow, her warm smile a little brittle, an eagerness to her as if years spent in prison had transformed her into something a little eccentric, if not mad.

     

                It felt like an hour before the cell door was opening and Kara was being led back inside, the retinue of guards more than any of the others had ever warranted. Pressing up against the forcefield, Lena’s eyes tracked her across the cell with rapt attention, taking in the delicate bones of her hands, the meek slope of her shoulders, and her hair, far too long and wet from her freezing shower, although Kara didn’t so much as shiver. Turning to look at her, Kara gave her a quick wink and Lena stumbled back a step, her lips parting. She couldn’t bring herself to indulge Kara in her amusement, couldn’t form her numb lips into a smile as she watched her with wide eyes.

     

                The moment Kara passed out of her sight, no amount of pressing up against the force field offering a better angle to see her with, Lena hurried over to her bed. Dropping to hands and knees, cold concrete freezing her palms as she crawled beneath the bed, scooting as close to the vent in the wall as she could. Her heart was pounding in her chest and Lena’s teeth chattered ever so slightly as she huddled, waiting.

     

                A moment later, a warm voice laced with laughter drifted through to her, the sound of it like a shock to Lena’s system as the hairs on her body stood on end, skin rippling with goosebumps that weren’t because of the cold.

     

                “Have you been waiting for me?” Kara lightly asked.

     

                “You-” Lena started before faltering. She pressed her lips together and swallowed before letting out a sharp exhale, eyes shuttering. “You’re not blue.”

     

                It wasn’t what she’d planned on saying, but it fell from her lips when she couldn’t force anything else out. Kara’s answering laugh made her shiver. Lena could tell that she was enjoying herself, and it struck a pang of sadness inside her to think of how little there was for Kara to enjoy after almost two decades inside a cell.

     

                “No,” Kara murmured, quiet glee in her voice. “No, I’m not blue.”

     

                “You lied to me.”

     

                “You have to let me have my fun.”

     

                Lena made a rough humming sound of agreement at the back of her throat as she struggled to process her thoughts. “Kara,” she whispered.

     

                “Lena.”

     

                Swallowing a rising sob, Lena let out a shaky breath and wiped at her eyes with her frozen fingers. Her nails were a pale shade of lavender and Lena jammed her fingers into her armpits as she pressed a cheek to the floor, tense as she curled in on herself.

     

                “The straitjacket-”

     

                “Oh, they’re just cautious,” Kara dismissively replied, making light of something horrific. “I guess it helps me not fidget, though. Which is good, because I’m a fidgeter.”

     

                “Kara.”

     

                “You were holding out on me though,” Kara forged on, keeping her tone light even as her voice wavered. “I might’ve told you I was blue but you didn’t tell me you looked like that .”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena’s chin dimpled as she suppressed the overwhelming emotions rising in her chest. It felt awful , it felt wrong and heartbreaking that they could just lock them all up there, keep them caged and subdued like dangerous animals at a zoo.

     

                “And what’s that supposed to mean?” Lena asked, her voice rasping.

     

                “I think you already know. You’ve seen your reflection.”

     

                “Only twice in the last month, and it wasn’t pretty.”

     

                “I don’t think you could ever be anything other than that.”

     

                Kara’s voice was a whisper, intimate and deep as it faintly travelled through the vent. She didn’t respond, let the words wind through her mind, knotting her stomach with a deep ache. Lena wasn’t prone to lying, didn’t think it admirable to dismiss a compliment one knew was true, and she wouldn’t have before, knowing what she looked like. But the last glimpse of herself in the mirror, only an hour ago, showed a hollowed-out version of herself, carved from white marble, hard and thin. It was a shadow of herself.

     

                When no response was forthcoming, Kara let out a soft sigh, and now Lena could envision her, her tall frame curled up in a mirror image of her own pose, her chapped lips parting, dishwater blonde hair drying in a tangled mass on the gritty concrete floor of her cell. How strange it felt to know how someone would be, how seeing Kara had opened up a corner of Lena’s mind to imagine all the ways her face would look as she spoke, sighed, laughed. It cut a little deeper to fit the straitjacket into that mental image, to imagine her wriggling under the bed without the use of her arms, laying on her side with her arms strapped across her chest, useless.

     

                “What did you find?” Kara eventually asked.

     

                Letting out a small laugh, the sound hollow and defeated, as her earlier triumph and smug intelligence receded in light of how truly awful these people here were. It wasn’t something she could reason her way out of, Lena was starting to understand. Her freedom was something that would have to be taken by brute force - perhaps not entirely, but it would be inevitable.

     

                “Well … I know my way to the tool room and the junction boxes. And there’s enough crawl space to get through the ceiling. The wiring’s a mess … it would be a shame if a few of them got snipped and crossed and needed repairing again. Another blackout would be awful .”

     

                Her sarcasm towards the end grew and Kara was silent for a long moment, her breaths shallow and quick before she spoke. “Do you have a plan?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “What is it?”

     

                Squeezing her eyes shut, Lena’s mouth thinned for a moment before she replied. “I’m going to get you and me out and sink this place to the bottom of the ocean.”

     

                Kara hesitated, the silence weighted with expectation before she slowly responded. “Is that it?”

     

                Lips twitching in a wry smile, Lena made a sound of objection. “No, not quite. I’m still in the early stages, unfortunately. I find it’s better to plan thoroughly than rush in.”

     

                “Haven’t you been rushing in this whole time?”

     

                “No, it’s planning. Brutal, and careless, but lessons have been learnt and intelligence collected. I’m not stupid enough to get beaten to a pulp for the sake of nothing. Well, not after the first time - just to establish boundaries, you know? Knowing how far someone will go is perhaps the most valuable piece of information of all, and I know that they won’t kill us. Not unless we’re a direct threat to them, and even then I think they’ll find themselves in hot water with the chain of command.”

     

                “Do you think maybe you’re overestimating our worth?” Kara asked, a strained note of humour in her question.

     

                Humming as she considered it, Lena shifted onto her back, idly tapping a finger on the underside of the metal grille. “No,” she curtly replied. “No, I don’t think so at all. By your claim, you’re the strongest being in this prison, no? The American Government is a war machine, the biggest one in the world, profiting off of its weapons. You’re the biggest weapon on the planet, if you’re not exaggerating.”

     

                She said the last part with a short laugh, tapping her finger against the metal again as she considered it. What would make the skinny woman in the cell next to her so powerful that they took extra precautions when she was already imprisoned miles beneath the sea? Kara couldn’t have been exaggerating, and that’s what led Lena to believe her importance.

     

                “They won’t want to give up their greatest weapons. There could come a time when they’ll need you, so they’ll keep you here just in case. That’s why they don’t kill us all.”

     

                There was no response but she didn’t hear Kara shift away, and so Lena stayed beneath the bed, waiting for her to speak as she processed Lena’s words. It was a few minutes of silence before she let out a weary sigh of resignation.

     

                “I want in.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing in surprise, Lena blinked rapidly. “I- you what?”

     

                “I’m going to help you. But … you need to get Eliza and Alex on board. If Alex is on board, Kelly will be too. You’ll need a way to get them all out. They won’t leave without each other.”

     

                Speechless, Lena let out a breathless laugh, elation flooding through her. “I can arrange that.”

     

                “Once you get them on board … then you come up with a plan.”

     

                “Yes,” Lena murmured.

     

                And then Kara let out a fleeting laugh, warm and light and just mad enough to make Lena’s stomach flutter. Nothing had killed Kara, and she’d never given up, not after years inside. She might not have escaped , and might have only merely existed, but she was still alive and sane and it struck Lena like a heavy-handed blow to hear her laugh, where she only felt like she was unravelling. The solitude hadn’t killed her friend, nor the guards or the cold, or her own mind. More than half of her life had been spent in a cell, but Kara still laughed and it broke Lena’s heart a little.

     

                “I’m going to get you out,” Lena whispered to her. “I promise you. I’ll get you another sunset.”

     

                “I believe you.”

     

                “Do you?”

     

                “I do. I have no choice but to,” Kara sadly replied. “I’ve gotten used to it. Being stuck inside here. But I remember. I remember and I- Lena, I’m frightened. The only thing keeping me sane is my friends … but when they’re all gone, when I’m the only one left …”

     

                “That won’t happen,” Lena firmly told her. “I promise you.”

     

                “Humans only live eighty years and they spent so much of it just … waiting for things to be over. But this is the in-between. This is the waiting that happens in the space between when you’re born and when you die. I … I’m getting tired of waiting here in a cell; I don’t want to stay here anymore. I just- I want to go outside.”

     

                “What would you do if you were out?” Lena asked, trying to lighten the mood a little.

     

                Silent for a moment as she considered her answer, Kara let out a small laugh. “I’d watch the sunset. On the beach. With seagulls. And I’d like to try ice cream for the first time; Alex said I’d like it.”

     

                It was the answer of a child and Lena felt her throat close up and her eyes sting. She felt that white hot anger within her flare to life, the coals stoked. It wasn’t right that they’d taken a child, a little girl with no home and no family, from a different world and left her to rot in such a miserable place. She should’ve been insane, should’ve been ready to tear the place down. Instead, she was gentle and content with her lot - although perhaps willing to fight her way out with Lena’s help - and that made it even more unbearable for Lena. To know that someone so good had clung to innate kindness, hadn’t let her conscience break over all the atrocities she must have seen over the years, was a feat in itself, and Lena would not rest until she got Kara the freedom she’d been denied for eighteen years. She wouldn’t rest until she saw another sunset.

     

                “I wish more people were as uncomplicatedly good as you,” Lena hummed.

     

                “You are.”

     

                That response was enough for a shaky laugh to escape Lena, her face creasing with surprising amusement. “Not like you. I’m a good person, but … I’m a bad person too. I guess that’s just like most people. We’ve all got a little bit of good and bad in us, the trick is just learning how to be good all of the time and bad none of the time. I think … most of us aren’t very good at that.”

     

                “Well, I think you’re a good person. I don’t think you’d ever be capable of hurting anyone,” Kara replied. “I mean, I don’t think you could ever kill someone.”

     

                Swallowing the flicker of fear in her heart, knowing that there was something inside her, like all people, that would be capable of anything, under the right circumstances. It was such a naive statement for Kara to think of things in such simple terms, that someone kind must be inherently good and incapable of doing awful things. Lena could do a lot worse than awful if she was pushed to it; Lena could tear the world apart with her own mind - and at the moment, she had half a mind to.

     

                “Don’t ever underestimate what a person is capable of,” she whispered, her voice soft but holding the threat of violence, of what she was truly capable of.

     

                “Is that what you’ll do to get us out of here?” Kara asked, her voice a tremulous whisper as if she feared Lena’s answer.

     

                Hating the truth of her honesty, Lena grit her teeth for a moment before answering her. “Yes. If I have to. I’ll do anything to get us out if I have to.”

     

                “Can you promise me something?”

     

                “Sure.”

                

                “Don’t make me kill them. I know that I’ll be- I’ll be the muscle, but if we don’t have to, I don’t- I just- not all of them are bad. They’re stuck too, and I know we can’t get them all out, so …”

     

                Eyelids shuttering as she softly exhaled, Lena knew that she would falter even for the ones that did deserve it. Every single guard that had shown unnecessary force, any who had left a bruise or left them bloody, she would hesitate at every one, wondering if she had to kill them for her freedom, if it came down to it. She couldn’t fault Kara for not wanting to do the same thing that made her falter, especially when she would be the one to do it if it came down to it. Lena just hoped that the gentle alien would have it in her.

     

                And she knew Kara wasn’t as vengeful as her, had long since relinquished any anger towards the guards, any hope for getting out. Eighteen years was a long time to stay angry at people, to not grow to love the people on the other side of the force field. How could Lena blame her for her signs of Stockholm Syndrome, for wanting to save the ones that left her trapped in a straitjacket and debilitated with a shock collar? 

     

                “Of course,” Lena thickly replied, her throat bobbing at the difficulty of speaking. “We do what we have to. Nothing more. Nothing less.”

     

                They didn’t speak of it any further after that, Lena preoccupied with how she’d convince the doctor and her daughter to help her. Out of the two of them, Doctor Danvers was more likely to help her, but even that seemed like a slim chance. Alex didn’t trust her as far as she could throw her, although she might feel more inclined to help for Kara’s sake. All in all, Lena figured that the easiest way to a straightforward answer was to merely ask.

     

                Her opportunity came a few days later with her delayed monthly checkup with Doctor Danvers. Lena ought to have gone a week ago, but on accounts of her being in solitary, she’d missed the one-month anniversary of her imprisonment date. Perhaps that had been for the best; Lena didn’t know how she would’ve coped with that knowledge if she’d been forced to confront it. All she wanted to do was get out.

     

                It was an effort to rein in her willingness to go to her checkup, knowing her eagerness would be suspicious, and she kept a slow, measured pace at Agent Sawyer’s side as she was escorted through the hallways. As usual, Lena kept up her vigilant reconnaissance, mapping cameras and turnings, considering getting to the medical bay one of the more important routes to memorise. She would need to know how to get there to get Eliza out. She was still wondering how to broach the topic when they came to a stop outside.

     

                “Lena,” Eliza greeted her with wry exasperation, gesturing her towards the padded table. “Come in. Take a seat.”

     

                Allowing the cuffs to be unlocked, Lena rubbed at her wrists as she followed Eliza’s instructions, climbing onto the table and folding her hands in her lap as she listened to the sound of latex gloves snapping onto the doctor’s hands. Eliza picked up her clipboard and plucked a pen from her coat pocket before scrawling down a few details while Sawyer retreated outside to allow for confidentiality.

     

                Nearing the bed, she hooked the wheeled trolley with her foot and dragged it closer before fixing Lena with a stern stare. “How’re you feeling?”

     

                “Oh, I’m great,” Lena snorted, rolling her eyes as her mouth twisted contemptuously and she shed her grey sweatshirt. 

     

                “Causing more trouble, I hear.”

     

                “I’ve always been a bit theatrical.”

     

                “Might I offer a suggestion? You should consider being less theatrical, for your own safety.”

     

                Giving her a thin smile, Lena cocked her head to the side and watched Eliza write down the date. “And then how would I gather my intel for a prison break?”

     

                Lowering her clipboard and dropping her shoulders as she gave her a resigned look, Eliza set everything down on the tray and unwound her stethoscope from around her neck, poking the ends into her ears.

     

                “Talking like that is going to get you in trouble,” Eliza warned her as she pressed the metal disc to Lena’s chest. “Breathe in. And out.”

     

                Lena obeyed, breathing deeply and evenly as Eliza listened to her heart and lungs, before looping the wire around her neck again. She used her pen light next to check Lena’s eyes, the darting beam making her pupils contract and dilate, before checking her mouth and throat. 

     

                “What if I promised to get you out?” Lena asked, her voice a low murmur. “You and your daughter. Would you help me?”

     

                Softly sighing, Eliza shook her head and made a few notes before checking Lena’s ears. She was silent for a moment, her mouth a hard line, standing before Lena as she felt the lymph nodes under her jaw and then met her eyes for a fleeting moment.

     

                “Even if I wanted to, it would be pointless.”

     

                “So that means you don’t want to.”

     

                “We’re beneath the sea, in case no one has informed you of that yet. How are you planning on escaping? You’d get us all killed. And I’m not sure how much use I would be.”

     

                Swallowing thickly, Lena gave her an uneven smile with more arrogance than she felt. “I’ve pulled off more impossible feats before.”

     

                “If you talk like this around the wrong people-”

     

                “That’s why I’m talking to you about it.”

     

                A small smile tugged at the corners of Eliza’s mouth. “Do you think I’m going to do you a favour just because I don’t want to see my prisoners brutalised?”

     

                “Maybe.”

     

                “Lena-”

     

                “I’ve got money,” she blurted out. “They’ve frozen all my assets, my accounts, everything, but once I break out and expose them-”

     

                Eliza gripped her arms and shook her, just once, roughly, but it silenced Lena. She blinked in surprise, her sentence trailing off, and disappointment sank in her stomach as she realised she wouldn’t find an ally in the doctor. It was a long shot anyway, but it would complicate Kara’s willingness to help her if she couldn’t convince the doctor and her daughter to cooperate.

     

                “Enough,” Eliza gently said.

     

                Stiffening at the rejection, Lena resolved to make life difficult for the doctor after that. She kept her arms clamped to her sides as Eliza tried to work the cuff around her bicep to measure her blood pressure, refused to lay down for the doctor to delicately press on her abdomen, and didn’t answer any of the multitudes of questions posed.

     

                When Eliza filled a needle from a vial, Lena hopped off the table on the opposite side and found herself in a stand-off with the doctor. Clicking her tongue softly, Eliza gave her an exasperated look.

     

                “Please don’t.”

     

                “Or what?”

     

                “You know what will happen. We’ve been through this before; I’d rather administer your treatments properly, but if you don’t let me they’ll use unnecessary force. And it won’t be gentle.”

     

                Lena bared her teeth, looking cagey, her voice cracking as she replied, anger making her voice rough as her eyes darted over to the trolley. “I won’t sit quietly while I wait to die. I’ll find a way out with or without your help, but if you don’t help me, I’ll leave you here to rot with the rest of them. I’d be doing you a favour.”

     

                A sad smile graced Eliza’s mouth as her sloped shoulders dropped a fraction. “Sweetie, just humour me for a second. Just how are you getting out of here? Because I’ve been here a lot longer than a month and trust me-”

     

                “Not likely.”

     

                “There’s no way off here that doesn’t involve a monthly supply aircraft flying in from the mainland.”

     

                Lena filed that information away for future use, making a mental note to try and find the date that the shipments came in each month. If that was the only way off, that’s how she’d get off. She just needed the muscle to break them out, she’d have the mental map, and Kara … well, she’d be coming too, regardless of what she provided to the cause.

     

                “I’m not going to tell you my plan,” Lena snorted. “I’m not that much of an idiot. But I know you won’t tell anyone anyway.”

     

                “That’s very trusting. I could hand you over to the guards, make them put you in solitary.”

     

                “But you won’t.”

     

                “What makes you so confident?”

     

                “I don’t trust you, but you’re one of the few people who’ve been nice to me since I got here, so … that warranted some offer of freedom. I wouldn’t want to be indebted to you in any way,” Lena replied, a lump forming in her throat.

     

                Eliza gave her a pleading look but Lena was uncooperative, rounding the bench as Eliza circled it from the other side, both of them looking at each other, one hard and stubborn, the other reluctant and patient. Perhaps it was childish to be avoiding the inevitable like it was a game of tag, putting whatever she could find between her and the doctor before whoever was monitoring the cameras must have tipped off Sawyer.

     

                The short guard let herself in and gripped her baton with annoyance in her brown eyes, “Prisoner LL93, on the floor.”

     

                “I’ll pass.”

     

                “She’s fine,” Eliza assured Maggie, holding her free hand up in a placating manner. “Just give me a second.”

     

                Turning to look at Lena, she gingerly smiled and reached out with the needle, beckoning her. “Lena, be reasonable. It’s just a little needle. You’re almost done; don’t make it worse for yourself.”

     

                Grinning, Lena’s eyes creased at the corners as she came to a strategic stop. “Maybe that’s exactly what I want to do, Doctor Danvers.”

     

                Her posturing bought Sawyer enough time to shift to the right, parallel to Lena with a clear path between them. Lena was still grinning as her eyes slid sideways at the motion of the small woman barrelling towards her, and she could do little else but turn to meet the collision, eyebrows rising in mild surprise. 

     

                Lena was tackled to the tiled floor and let out a resigned sigh as she went slack, resisting the stubborn urge to fight. She couldn’t see the benefit of getting hauled off to solitary again just yet - not until she knew what she was looking for - so she played nicely, pinned to the floor as Maggie reached up and snatched the needle from Eliza’s hand and rammed it right into Lena’s arm. It was unnecessarily deep and painful, slamming down into muscle tissue before the sting of the contents seeped through Lena’s arm. Doctor Danvers was aghast.


                “Sawyer.”

     

                “Ow, fuck,” Lena exclaimed, a thunderous look on her face as she craned her neck, trying to look down at her arm. “You vicious bitch.”

     

                “Cooperate or you’ll be made to cooperate,” Sawyer muttered as she drove her knee into Lena’s spine, eliciting a squawk of pain from the prisoner.

     

                Lena would have seen red if it hadn’t been a carefully coordinated plan, situating herself right next to the tray on the wheeled trolley. It had been knocked over, rather deliberately on her part, when Sawyer tackled her, little silver medical instruments clattering to the ground as Lena had fumbled for whatever was in reach and felt the sharp bite of metal against her palm. She’d tucked it against the side of her body while Maggie was preoccupied.

     

                Now, arm throbbing dully from the pain of the rough injection, Lena was cuffed as Sawyer discarded the empty needle and Doctor Danvers cleaned up the mess. As she lined everything up on her tray, she cast a sharp glance at Lena, whose face was turned to the side, cheek pressed against the floor. 

     

                “Can you uncuff her, please,” Eliza said a minute later as she climbed to her feet. “I just- I need to measure her weight and the cuffs will add to the result. She needs to put her sweatshirt back on as well when we’re done; she’ll catch pneumonia in this cold.”

     

                Fixing the doctor with a disgruntled stare, Sawyer undid Lena’s cuffs and moved back to the door, her eyes trained on Lena. Sliding the instrument beneath her as she pushed herself up, not having to affect the slow, stiff pace, Lena plucked it from the ground as she paused on her knees and then pushed herself up. Eliza was turning towards the scales and Lena pretended to be adjusting her scrubs as she slipped the instrument into the waistband of her pants, tugging the shirts down and clearing her throat.

     

                Standing on the scales, she sweated as her pulse fluttered rapidly in her throat, waiting to be frisked any moment and get caught out. She knew it wouldn’t be a pretty punishment if she was found with stolen contraband on her, but Lena was willing to risk it. Her face was bone white with a sheen of sweat on her brow, and she curled her fingers around the warm blood in her palm, her throat dry as she swallowed.

     

                When Eliza told her to get off and handed over her grey sweatshirt, Lena looked into her blue eyes and read the intensity there, the sharp knowing look of someone who knew exactly what she was up to. Opening her mouth as she inhaled shakily, prepared to quietly beg, Lena was cut off as Eliza spoke first.

     

                “You’ve lost weight. I’ll make a note for the kitchen staff to increase your calories,” the doctor quickly said as Lena warily slipped her arms into the sleeves of her sweatshirt, a piercing look in her eyes as she studied Eliza’s face, both of them keenly aware that the other one knew they knew.

     

                Hand balled into a fist to keep the blood hidden, Lena pushed her head through the hole and dragged the warm fabric down with her left hand. Eliza’s eyes remained glued to her face and Lena avoided looking at her directly, tensed as she waited to see if the doctor gave her away.

     

                “That’s all,” Eliza announced a moment later, writing down the results and clearing her throat. Her head stayed ducked down as she busied herself with her work. “I’d recommend not doing anything stupid and you’ll stay in good health. Doctor’s orders.”

     

                “I’ll take that into consideration,” Lena wryly replied, catching Eliza’s warning look.

     

                Still, the doctor didn’t say a word as Lena’s wrists were clapped back into her cuffs and she was led back out of the medical bay. For whatever reason, Eliza wouldn’t help her, but she apparently wouldn’t stand in her way either. Lena thought she might just be able to bring her around if she had enough time.

     

                Her mind was preoccupied as she was taken back to her cell, slipping beneath the bed and removing the medical instrument. It was a small scalpel, the edge stained with blood where it had gouged her, and Lena felt a smug prickle of glee as she hid it in a slightly warped part of the bed frame, where the edge of the frame pulled away from the grille.

     

                “How’d it go?“ Kara asked.

     

                “Better than expected,” Lena replied, although she rubbed her hand as she grumbled.

     

                “Did she say-“

     

                There was a bang on the force field and Lena instinctively sat up, smashing her head against the metal grille of the cot. Cursing, she poked her head out from under the bed, scowling. Alex raised her eyebrows, gesturing impatiently.

     

                “Up against the wall.”

     

                “I just got back from seeing your mom.”

     

                “And? Time for your walk,” Alex said with a weary sigh, gesturing for Lena to get up.

     

                Scowling as she rubbed her forehead, Lena crossed over to the wall and allowed herself to be cuffed. Then she was escorted out with Andrea and Gayle, at the back of the trio with Alex sandwiching her in from behind. 

     

                Deciding to take advantage of their time together, Lena licked her lips and glanced to the side, turning her head slightly.

     

                “I spoke to your mom earlier. She wasn’t too keen, but I think you might be more easily swayed.”

     

                “Eyes forward,” Alex loudly replied.

     

                Slowing her steps, Lena allowed a few feet to separate her from Gayle, in front of her, and she kept her voice low as she dragged her feet. “Do you want to get out of here?”

     

                “Stupid question, Luthor,” Alex muttered.

     

                “I could help you. I could get you, your mom and your girlfriend off. All you have to do is help me out.”

     

                “Not likely.”

     

                “But-”

     

                Alex grabbed the back of her sweatshirt and pulled her to a stop, her voice low and urgent in her ear. “You need to stop this. I don’t want to hurt you, but I won’t let you cause trouble and get the people I care about killed. You think we all haven’t plotted a dozen ways out of this hell? It won’t work.”

     

                “And how many of you were imprisoned for superhuman intelligence?” Lena softly replied.

     

                Silence answered her question and she smiled faintly. Keeping her eyes trained forward, she watched as the other guard at the front of their procession turned, baton out to halt the other two prisoners.

     

                “You good, Danvers?”

     

                Lena heard Alex audibly swallow, “all good. Her shoe slipped off.”

     

                Her fingers loosened in the sweatshirt and she gave Lena a gentle prod to propel her forward. Lurching back into motion, Lena’s mouth thinned and they didn’t speak a word as they caught up with the other prisoners and followed the path to the exercise room. Lena had it memorised by that point, her eyes taking in every hallway, every door, trying to map her way out of the mentally constructed prison. 

     

                Inside the spacious room, she dutifully walked her laps, keeping her pace slow and measured as she caught Alex’s eye half a dozen times within the hour. Her expression was unreadable but there was a flicker in her eyes, her gaze intense and thoughtful, and Lena wondered if perhaps she’d fucked up immeasurably by confiding in the agent. But she cared about Kara, and that was enough to convince Lena she wouldn’t rat her out - for what little she knew about her fellow inmate, Lena knew she would trust her instincts if it meant a potential ally.

     

                At the end of the hour, as the other guard unlocked the door and Alex escorted them out individually, she approached Lena and grabbed her arm, her eyes fixed forward and mouth barely moving as she spoke so softly it was barely audible.

     

                “Mention this again and I’ll tell the Deputy.”

     

                Disappointment sank in her stomach like a stone and Lena ground her teeth together as frustration made her rankle. Still, she couldn’t help but feel a prickle of curiosity for this Deputy, wondering who it was following the order to keep her locked up alongside everyone else.

     

                Out of luck, Lena was returned to her cell and she sat on the edge of her cot, rubbing her wrists as she brooded. A while later, a knock came from the other side of the wall and Lena scooted beneath the bed.

     

                “Hey.”

     

                “Did you ask?” Kara anxiously asked.

     

                Wincing slightly, Lena chewed on her lip for a moment. “Yeah.”

     

                “And?”

     

                She considered her answer for a moment before deciding that a lie was the simplest one. There was time to bring the two people Kara seemed to care for, for some bizarre reason, across to their side, to convince them to help her from within. What there wasn’t time for was any further delays in her plotting. So Lena lied, and a part of her hated herself for it, knowing Kara wouldn’t doubt her for a second.

     

                “They’re in.”

    Chapter 8

                Time passed by differently inside the prison and soon enough it was time for the next social. Kara had held back any excitement over them spending time together at the function this time around, perhaps holding on to some lingering apprehension that Lena would fuck it all up again and get herself thrown into isolation days before the allotted day. She didn’t though, she might even have been considered to be on her best behaviour, eating her food, taking her daily mandated walk and keeping her bluish lips pressed closed at the frigid shower each morning.

     

                Her motivations weren’t purely driven by the chance to sit with Kara face-to-face, but she’d be lying if she said it wasn’t an enticing prospect. Lena had a lot of questions to ask her in relation to her escape plan, which admittedly wasn’t progressing as quickly as she’d hoped, although Kara still hadn’t worked out that Alex and Eliza weren’t on-board with it yet, and she needed to get a better idea of the prison layout to get her bearings. Her world had been reduced to a few rooms and hallways in the sprawling underwater prison, and she knew she’d need to know more information to map out her blind spots and account for any trouble, and Kara had been there longer than anyone else.

     

                But, yes, Lena was eager to sit and drink in the sight of her, and she wasn’t above admitting it. Her perfect memory kept replaying their brief interaction, the thin and wild look of the tall woman, so human , despite being restrained like the dangerous alien that she was. Lena was fascinated, and she’d be lying if she said her heart didn’t lurch slightly whenever she thought of seeing her again. 

     

                The next social arrived with a palpable shift in moods, a hum of eagerness filling the cell block. J’onn and Mon-El played rounds of games, keeping a tally of who won the most so they could fairly decide who monopolised the TV for Jeopardy or The Green Mile . Kara was the most excited, having Lena explain the rules of chess to her over and over again over the course of the week leading up to the social. Lena indulged her and silently vowed to go easy on her the first couple of games. She didn’t want to kill Kara’s excitement for something new.

     

                On the day of the social, they were all taken through the usual routine, eating their foul breakfasts and enduring cold showers and a change of clothes. After their walks and waiting in their cells for everyone else to finish their turn walking around the big room, they were taken to the communal space with old metal tables and chairs, a shelf with a few mismatched books and board games and a TV bracketed to the corner near the ceiling.

     

                Lena sat down at a table with her cuffed hands on the scratched surface. The bench and table were both bolted to the floor and Lena shifted restlessly as she kept her gaze on the door, the other prisoners from her cell block led in in order of danger. She’d been brought in with Andrea and Psi in their usual group, deemed relatively harmless and able to claim their own spots while they waited for the others. They were brought in in small groups, the same way they were showered or walked and Lena looked at the door every time, anticipating Kara’s arrival.

     

                She watched as J’onn, with his uncanny appearance of Hank Henshaw, took a seat near the boxy TV attached out of reach up on the wall and turned it on. As Kara had said, an old episode of Jeopardy was playing and he seemed content to sit and watch, a serene look on his face. Psi was shuffling cards and Imra was conversing quietly with Mon-El, their body language speaking for themselves. Lena pitied them; falling in love in prison must be the worst kind of fate.

     

                Naturally, Kara was last, escorted by four guards, two of them remaining outside the locked door while the other two stayed inside with the other four. One of them was Alex, who tracked the alien’s movements as she slowly loped across the room with a bright smile on her face, her shoulders curved inwards and her movements slightly exaggerated, as if making herself as innocuous as possible.

     

                Green eyes unreadable as her heart stuttered in her chest, stomach clenching with nerves, Lena swallowed as she drank in the sight of Kara. Blue eyes like the sky, shining with delight, her skin a washed-out alabaster from so many years locked away without sunlight, and her hair a dirty blonde, limply waving past her waist. The grey of her prison uniform only leached the colour out of her further - except for those eyes. Lena’s mouth went dry and she half-rose from the bench as Kara stopped across from her.

     

                They’d let her out of the straitjacket and placed cuffs around her wrists as well, and Kara seemed pleased by the freedom of it, sinking down onto a bench as her smile turned crooked with sudden shyness. Lena sank back down onto her seat and cocked her head to the side as she continued to stare at her; she couldn’t stop.

     

                “Hi.”

     

                “Hi.”

     

                There was a pause and Kara let out a quick laugh, her eyes creasing at the corners. Lena felt her breath catch in her throat; how could she seem so human? It was bizarre but she thought blue skin and three eyes and whatever features Kara had joked about having would have been easier to process. 

     

                “This shouldn’t feel so awkward,” Kara said with another smile.

     

                Lena wondered if she always smiled so much, and how she could stand it after so long cooped up in a cell. Swallowing, she glanced down at the table, forcing herself to break her stare.

     

                “It’s weird seeing you,” Lena confessed.

     

                “I was hoping you’d think I was better to look at than a concrete wall, but to each their own.”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena looked back up as her face crumpled, mystified. She watched as Kara awkwardly managed to cross her legs on the bench - her feet were cuffed as well, the rattling chains filling the silence.

     

                “So … what do you normally do here?”

     

                “I usually draw. I like drawing.”

     

                “What do you draw?”

     

                Shrugging, Kara gave her a thin smile, “birds. There’s a book on bird species; I think they’re interesting.”

     

                “Because you didn’t have birds at home?”

     

                “You remembered,” Kara warmly replied, a pleased note of surprise in her voice.

     

                Lena shrugged slightly, her eyelids shuttering as a small smile quirked the corners of her mouth. “I’ve been known to pay attention at times. What’s your favourite kind of bird?”

     

                It felt like a strange question to ask but they were strange circumstances and Kara seemed all too eager to answer. “I like hummingbirds.”

     

                Making a polite, inquisitive sound at the back of her throat, Lena smiled faintly. “We’ll have to go and find some for you when we get out of here.”

     

                “I’d love that,” Kara earnestly replied as she nodded, a wide-eyed, almost childish look of innocent delight on her face. “What’s your favourite bird?”

     

                Considering it for a moment, propping her chin in her hand, Lena hummed. “I don’t know. Maybe a storm petrel.”

     

                “Storm petrel,” Kara murmured to herself, closing her eyes and then nodding before opening them again. “The smallest form of seabird in the world. Migratory species and prey to falcons, gulls and owls. Interesting choice. Why?”

     

                Shrugging, Lena pursed her lips slightly. “They’re bad omens. I have a soft spot for anything that gets a bad reputation for things out of their control. Just because they’re best seen during storms, it doesn’t mean they caused the storms.”

     

                “Ah. Your empathy is deeper than I thought.”

     

                “Did I come off as indifferent to the suffering of others?”

     

                “No, no,” Kara quickly replied, “only that I think you can get a better sense for people based on how they treat animals.”

     

                “Not humans?” Lena countered, arching an eyebrow.

     

                Kara smiled crookedly and her eyes creased at the corners. “A little, but … you can’t manipulate animals. The way you treat them is your true nature because you have nothing to gain from it.”

     

                “Not entirely true. A farmer would treat a lamb well, right up until it’s led to the slaughter.”

     

                “But the act of slaughtering it speaks for itself.”

     

                “Maybe the farmer is poor and hungry and has no other choice.”

     

                “Maybe, but that also speaks for itself, right? The way someone kills, the way they show their desperation. You humans are funny things; it’s a lot more complex on Earth.”

     

                “And what about where you’re from?”

     

                Grinning, Kara shifted, uncrossing her legs. “Easier.”

     

                She climbed to her feet and slowly crossed the room, squatting before the shelf and rummaging around. Returning a few minutes later, she set a stack of paper down, a checkerboard and a few crayons in varying colours. Apparently, pencils were too much of a threat, capable weapons in the hands of this supposedly violent bunch, and Lena picked up a worn-down orange crayon, snorting as she turned it over in her fingers. 

     

                “What do the pieces look like?” Kara asked.

     

                “The knight like this,” Lena said, picking up a blue crayon and using it for the black pieces as she drew a side-on horse head.

     

                “That’s the L formation?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                Kara mirrored it with a yellow crayon on another sheet of paper. Lena drew all of the pieces as Kara copied them and checked her knowledge on them all. They tore the pieces apart once they were done, placing them down on the checkerboard. Lena let Kara keep the white pieces and go first, explaining the rules again as they started their game. She had her favourite openings but Kara didn’t know enough to play to them, so Lena kept it simple and they kept up a steady stream of conversation as they played.

     

                She beat Kara, of course, and with relative ease as well, but it didn’t deter Kara from demanding another game. Lena thought she’d be a good player once she knew the game a bit better, but it didn’t stop her from beating her another two times before they’d lulled the guards into a relaxed sense of security and let the conversation slip to their escape plan as they drew on the empty pieces of paper Kara had brought over to the table.

     

                Kara’s hands moved with precision, the crayon scraping across the paper as she swiftly mapped out the lines of corridors, circling spots where cameras were situated and drawing thicker lines where doors were. The colours melded together to create a labyrinth that the paper couldn’t contain, but Kara had a lot of blind spots too. She spoke quietly over the page as well, her lips barely moving as she explained things to Lena, who was drawing molecules and writing down chemical equations to keep up the pretence of innocent drawings.

     

                “There’s a long hallway here with no doors on the left. I’ve been out there … twice? Coldest place in the whole prison, steel beams wider than me and no vents, which means …”

     

                “That’s the outer wall.”

     

                “Mhm. As far as I’ve assumed. They were moving me between cell blocks so I don’t have much information to go on.”

     

                “If we’re underwater … we have to assume they’re surfacing to let new prisoners embark and supply runs make their deliveries. Doctor Danvers said it’s aircraft flying in so there has to be a helipad on top of this place.”

     

                “I’d guess it’d be accessed by a central elevator but I can’t be sure. We’re all out cold on the way in and the only way out is in a box, so we’ll need to check with Alex-”

     

                “We can hold off on that for now,” Lena quickly dissuaded her, “we should focus on the inside first. Getting off the prison isn’t the hardest part-”

     

                “How is that not the hardest part?” Kara quietly exclaimed, her face furrowing with disbelief.

     

                Giving her a thin smile, Lena raised her eyebrows slightly. “Because we’ll just time it around the supply drop-off. Easy. We’ll keep track of it over the next couple of months so we can narrow down the date to pull it off, and then we’ll get your friends to confirm it for us. I’m assuming it’s a regular schedule.”

     

                “We get more fresh foods after a delivery.”

     

                “Well, there we go.”

     

                “Hey!”

     

                The two women jumped, straightening up as they jerked away from each other. Lena’s eyes darted over to Alex, who was storming over to them, all eyes training on the duo as the other prisoners watched warily. Kara grabbed the piece of paper, crumpling it up and shoving it in her mouth as Lena gave her an alarmed look. 

     

                “Spit it out,” Alex demanded as she stopped beside Kara with a grim look of exasperation on her face.

     

                Swallowing thickly, wincing as the sharp corners of the balled-up paper scraped her throat, Kara hoarsely replied. “Sorry. Couldn’t help myself. Not enough calories in my rations and crayons do smell good.” 

     

                A muscle jumped in Alex’s jaw as she stood over them, shooting Lena a venomous look before she snatched up a page. Staring at the letters and numbers and circles, Alex let out a quiet snort of laughter and set it back down, jutting her chin towards it.

     

                “You’ve written down the formula for ethyl acetate wrong.”

     

                “It’s for butyric acid,” Lena murmured. “Different atom arrangement.”

     

                Giving her a flat look, Alex arched an eyebrow slightly, “you don’t help your case, you know. You’re lucky I’m not going to tell the Deputy that you’re writing chemical formulas down.” 

     

                “Butyrate esters are used to produce paint, perfumes, food additives,” Lena off-handedly listed, her voice a slow drawl of annoyance. “What interest would the Deputy have in that? Afraid I might start a black market scheme to make the slop you serve here taste better? That would probably improve the mood a bit, that’s for sure.”

     

                Staring at her for a moment, her mouth a flat line, Alex waved a dismissive hand towards the crayon-covered paper before Kara. “Stick to drawing ducks.” Then she turned her attention to Kara. “And you … don’t be dumb, Kara. And don’t let her drag you into her mess.”

     

                “But …”
