Pausing in the mudroom, Lena shoved her feet into the boots and laced them tightly before pulling up the hood and opening the front door. Cold air assaulted her and she didn’t feel nearly warm enough after hours of cold, even with her new, thick layers limiting the effects of the piercing wind. 

     

                There were two large fuel tanks situated to the left of the building and Lena trudged over to them, finding a small shed beside one of them with all manner of equipment, including a hose. It was difficult work by herself, the hose heavy and unwieldy, but she was nothing if not stubbornly persistent and spent twenty minutes connecting the hose to the fuel tank and to the helicopter after locating the hatch. There were also two fuel drums in the body of the massive helicopter and Lena filled those up, knowing she’d need some for the return flight, locating a side compartment with filters, a hose, a standpipe and pump and a pair of gloves that she pulled on as well for warmth. 

     

                Once the chopper was refuelled, she made her way back inside and went through the left doorway, finding four desks and eight monitors taking up the bulk of the room. Pulling out a chair, she sat before the first desk and moved the mouse, the computer monitors flaring to life. It was password protected and it took Lena all of five seconds to turn over the keyboard and find the sticky note on the bottom, snorting as she snagged it free and entered the string of letters, accessing the computer and staring at an inventory spreadsheet.

     

                Clicking around through files and documents, clicking her tongue at how poorly protected it all was, even for a place as remote as the northernmost point of Alaska, she still came up empty-handed. There were logs to the prison, of course, stocktake of the supplies, received deliveries and dispatches and timesheets for the four employees who had been squirrelled away in the building, now dead. She was still looking, hunched over the keyboard, when Kelly stepped inside, similarly suited up.

     

                “Are you ready?”

     

                “Obviously not,” Lena impatiently replied.

     

                “What’s the holdup?”

     

                “That’s not your concern.”

     

                “Lena-”

     

                “Leave me alone.”

     

                Kelly sighed heavily, crossing her arms over her chest, the snowsuit rustling. “I’m just trying to help.”

     

                “If I wanted your help, I would ask for it.”

     

                “I’m offering it.”

     

                “Well I don’t need it, okay? How about you focus on your girlfriend making it through the night instead of bothering me?                 “We’re not going anywhere. We want to rescue Kara as much as you do. I haven’t known her as long as Alex and Eliza but we all care about her, so we’re not done . Not by a long shot. And I’m all you have right now because Alex can’t come and Eliza needs to stay with her, so let’s go.”

     

                Eyes glued to the screen, Lena’s mouth thinned as she tried to search Fort Rozz by keyword, the system was loading too slowly as she bounced her knee, all of her aches and pains nagging her now. “Well, it would be helpful to know where I’m going, so ...”

     

                With a quiet huff of laughter, Kelly crossed the room, pausing at Lena’s side and leaning across to tap her finger against a map pinned to the wall. There was a little pin set off-shore, in the middle of the Arctic Ocean, and as Lena’s head jerked up, she blinked in surprise. Chair wheeling backwards, she was on her feet, hand splayed against the map as she drank in the information, memorising it and safely tucking it away.

     

                “Sometimes it’s good to let other people help.”

     

                It was still a few minutes of research on the computer before Lena could calculate an approximate range of latitude and longitude the prison could be located in, still a large swathe of water they’d have to search.                 Satisfied that she had enough information to go by, although Lena knew very little about aerial navigation, she brushed past Kelly and stalked outside without pause for anything else. Jerking open the heavy door of the chopper, she struggled to climb inside but eventually managed to get into the pilot’s seat, fiddling around with it, donning the headset this time in case the communications system was back up once she neared the prison - that was purely wishful thinking but it helped - before Lena started the engine, flipping switches as she made her best guesses based on what she’d done to turn it off after landing. 

     

                The propellers picked up speed and Lena was readying for takeoff when Kelly jerked open the door Lena had shut behind herself and climbed in. Their eyes met, expressions wary and reserved beneath the bruising and blood from their escape, neither of them having time for even a hot shower or a bite to eat, and Kelly gave her a firm nod.

     

                It was a shaky takeoff and Lena gingerly winced as the wind buffeted them around as they climbed higher, before she managed to hold them steady, still climbing as grey clouds greeted them. She didn’t like the look of the weather but she angled them northwards and set off, picking up speed as her heart hammered in her chest, the power of controlling such a monstrously big machine getting the adrenaline pumping as she understood the gravity of their situation, how their lives were dangling by a thread. It was one thing to risk it all on the gamble of an escape but they’d pulled that off and now she was potentially dooming them to a watery death in the freezing waters of the Arctic if she lost control of the chopper now. 

     

                But she’d done it before and Lena was good at replicating results, at picking things up easily, her intellect prevalent from the time she could walk, a knack for machines and puzzles that had been stoked by the thorough education Lillian had given her.                 Within half an hour, only a sliver of land was visible behind them, water and ice ahead, grey clouds crowding in as Lena kept her eyes focused on the horizon, her fingers stiff around the control stick.                 “How are you feeling?” Kelly asked, finally breaking the silence, her voice crackling in the headset as she looked at Lena.

     

                Mouth flattening to a hard line, Lena’s eyes cut across to the other woman, angry and indignant as her eyes grew dangerously bright.

                “Don’t.”

     

                “I’ve killed someone before. When I was in the military. I was a psychologist but I still got shipped out, still found myself in terrible situations. I remember the first time - after the first time. It was a lot to come to terms with.”

                “Lena …” Kelly started before trailing off and letting out a weary sigh. “You need to think rationally about-”

     

                “Don’t tell me what to do,” Lena snarled, jerking the controller as she sharply turned towards Kelly, reeling them off course before she righted them, her anger simmering. “If it wasn’t for me , you’d still be in there.                 “That’s not what I’m doing. I just think you need to be prepared-”

Surely the sunlight would catch the edge of metal still sticking out of the water, or the dark shadow of it would be visible beneath the waves, but it proved fruitless. The day was too overcast, afternoon on the verge of giving way to evening, too early in the year for the season of a midnight sun, and Lena knew that their time was running short. Not only because of daylight hours but because of the limited fuel they had.

     

                The air grew colder as the sun started to sink, and they’d been circling the area within the confines of the coordinates for nearly an hour, the conversation between them limited as they went lower and lower, spotting nothing with their eyes or the equipment on the control panel.                 “Lena-”

     

                “Wait,” Lena said, holding a hand up, leaning forward, eyes squinting against the sparkling tips of the rippling water where the sun turned it to silver and gold. 

     

                “Lena,” Kelly tried again, her voice thin and rasping with exhaustion, “we can’t stay out here much longer.”

     

                Clenching her teeth as her chin wobbled, Lena blinked back the stinging in her eyes as she scowled. It was petulant and stubborn and Kelly was looking at her with aching pity, her hopes dashed by the empty sea around them. She didn’t want to be the one to voice the likelihood that they’d find Kara and the prison but she also couldn’t bring herself to speak a hopeful lie that maybe she’d gotten out and flown her friends somewhere safe, had perhaps landed wherever she’d found hard soil and was now looking for directions to where they were. That would have been cruel and Lena would have known it for the lie it was.

     

                They searched for another twenty minutes and Lena could feel Kelly’s restless unease as the light waned a little more and the risk of their return journey increased. Eventually, Lena let out a quiet snarl and banged her hand on the edge of the control panel before angling down to a large sheet of ice that looked thick enough to land on. By the time Kelly realised what she was doing, Lena was already too low for her to do much about it, the helicopter wobbling as she tried to make the landing. Stomach knotted tightly with apprehension, Lena let out a relieved breath as the skids touched down, bouncing slightly as they skittered across the ice, the propellers still whirring, before she cut the engines.

     

                Kelly tore off her headset and gave her a heated look of disbelieving anger. “What are you doing? We need to-”

     

                “Refuel,” Lena cut her off. “We need to refuel first.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “It’s seven hundred miles back. The tank isn’t big enough for that.”

     

                “But we made it back-”

     

                “They refuelled at the prison.”

     

                “Oh. But how-”

     

                “I took care of it,” Lena impatiently replied, unbuckling herself and climbing to her feet. 

     

                Struggling with the fuel drum secured in the expansive back of the helicopter, Lena lined it up near the side door and dragged it open, fighting with the wind until Kelly gave her a hand. Climbing out, she lost her balance on the ice and crashed down in a heap, hissing with pain as old bruises were pressed on and new ones were sure to form. 

     

                Climbing to her feet, Lena moved over to the side hatch and started removing equipment, opening the fuel cap, setting up the standpipe and the pump, connecting the pieces like a vaguely familiar puzzle. Kelly crouched at the edge of the open door, rubbing her hands together as her breath hung white before her, watching Lena work.

     

                “Have you done this before?”

     

                “No, but it’s not difficult,” Lena curtly replied.

     

                Kelly choked on a laugh. “It is to a normal person.”

     

                “When have I given you the impression that I was that?”

     

                “You haven’t, but it is fascinating to see someone seemingly be good at everything. It’s little wonder to me that the government saw you as a big enough threat to imprison you. They fear anything dangerous they can’t control.”

     

                “They should have been more afraid of the threat I’d be once I got out.”

     

                “Plans of overthrowing the government, hm? Ambitious. I would have thought you’d disappear, vanish somewhere with a new identity and keep a low profile.”

     

                Lena flashed a quick smile, dangerously thin and wry. “I’m not frightened of them. And they should have thought twice before wrongfully imprisoning someone like me. I have money, information, fame and a brain; that makes for a dangerous combination when you’d like to keep a covert government organisation a secret.”

     

                “So, that’s it, huh? The goal is revenge?”

     

                “The goal is a beach somewhere, at sunset - with ice cream.”

     

                Kelly fell silent for a moment, her face crumpling with confusion. “Right.”

     

                “It’s done.”

     

                Dismantling the equipment, Lena quickly packed it all away, the frigid air like a knife to her lungs as her gloved hands trembled and the sea ice swayed with the rising and falling of the water. The thought of being surrounded by so much water was stomach-turning and Lena didn’t want to linger there any longer than necessary, especially not with night encroaching, but it was amazing what one could endure when something was more important than their fears. She had always hated the water but it was a trivial thing compared to the tunnel vision determination of finding Kara. Lena would have suited up in diving gear and scouted the ocean herself if that was what it took, blotting out memories of her mother’s death with the sole purpose of finding Kara and breaking her out of prison a second time. 

     

                Loading the supplies back into the chopper, Lena hauled herself back in, accepting Kelly’s offered hand, and strapped herself back into the pilot seat. With her growing confidence, undercut by the bitterness of their failure to locate the prison, Lena had them in the air again with only a little panic as the ice beneath them started to crack from the shifting weight of the chopper, and it wasn’t long before the sunlight truly started to fail.

     

                It was disconcerting to be flying blindly as blackness blanketed the sea and sky, the veiled moon offering no light to navigate by, and Lena was on edge as she referred to the panels in front of her to keep them on course. Still, it was hours of flying through the darkness and the air grew colder, both of them flagging from the exhaustion of the day, Lena’s eyes prickling as she stared out at the nothingness and willed the time to pass by quickly.

     

                They eventually made it back, after coming in too far southwest and having to circle back slightly, making a jolting landing off the pitted tarmac as Lena missed her mark. Killing the engines, her failure sat heavily in her stomach, a yawning pit in her chest, and it took her five minutes to unbuckle herself and stiffly rise to her feet. Kelly had waited with her, the silence between them deafening, and Lena was grateful that the psychologist didn’t try to speak to her; she didn’t know what she would have done in response.

     

                Kelly made her way inside first, immediately going to Alex’s side, and Lena lingered in the mudroom for a moment as the warmth of the place rolled over her before she continued on to the bathroom. Pulling the light string, she shut the door behind herself and stared at the austere bathroom, dismal and cold, and turned the hot water of the shower on before she methodically shed her layers. The water took an age to heat up but Lena had long since grown used to cold showers, stepping beneath the spray with the glazed, absent look of someone in shock. 

     

                Slowly but surely the tears came then, the breath catching in her throat, tight and shallow, as she slowly came apart at the seams. And then the ragged gasps became muffled sobs as she buried her face in her hands, her skin stinging as the water finally grew hot, pounding over the notches of her spine, making limp ropes out of her dark hair as she bowed her head, despair slowly driving her to her knees. She was grateful for the noise of the water as her sobs turned rough and hitching, unable to be swallowed as they scraped the sides of her throat, but the truth was that Lena wouldn’t have cared even if the other occupants of the building could hear her - and they could.

     

                She stayed on the shower floor for half an hour, crying until she exhausted herself, so defeated and drained that she didn’t have the energy to move until her knees and back started to ache. The shower wasn’t the indulgence she’d dreamed of, the shampoo and soap cheap, the water a hard beating against her battered and bruised skin, but it warmed her through at least and Lena was clean and soft when she finally shut the water off. There were clean towels in a stack, one damp and hung up, which she assumed had been Eliza, and she wrapped herself up and dried off quickly before dressing in the stolen DEO uniform, sans snowsuit. 

     

                Swilling her mouth out with the mouthwash on the edge of the sink, Lena was left looking at her splotchy face in the speckled mirror, her eyes hollow and dull, and she could barely meet her own gaze as the knowledge of her failure weighed heavily on her. The fact that Kara was out there, still trapped in the prison, without its full functioning capacity, filled Lena with so much dread and anger that she was convinced she would find her just to berate her for her stupidity. 

     

                If there was one thing Lena was good at, it was seeing something through to the end, and she wouldn’t be able to rest until she found her again. How quickly was another matter entirely and despite her exhaustion, despite the scored lines from the bullets that had scraped her skin, the bruises from punches and the ice, from sleepless nights leading up to the escape, she didn’t rest.

     

                Emerging from the bathroom, she pulled up short at the sight of Eliza sitting on the bottom bunk of the other bedroom. At the sight of Lena, she climbed to her feet and picked up a cup of strong tea, stepping into the doorway so they were almost face to face. Holding the mug out, Eliza uncurled her other fingers to reveal a few pills. 

     

                “Tylenol, for the pain,” the doctor explained.

     

                Lena hesitated, unsure whether she trusted her, but ultimately concluded that there had been plenty of opportunities for Eliza to cause her harm. Plus she’d just helped save her daughter’s life, so Lena thought that constituted some level of a debt to be repaid on Eliza’s end. Swallowing the pills dry, she chased it down with a mouthful of tea, deliciously strong but starting to cool. Draining the rest of it, Lena nodded in thanks.

     

                “Kelly will be sleeping in the other room with Alex so you’ll have to share with me, I’m afraid,” Eliza continued, filling the silence. “I hope you don’t mind if I take the bottom bunk. My joints aren’t what they used to be with the cold.”

     

                Offering no reply, Lena set off down the hallway as if the doctor hadn’t spoken, bearing right into the office and claiming the computer she’d logged into earlier. She didn’t bother turning on the lights, the computer screen lighting up the space enough for her to work by, and she blocked out everything else as she got to work, combing through the thousands of files on the server as she compiled research, creating a new folder for anything useful and copying it across.

     

                Eliza had followed her, watching from the doorway for a while before she left and returned with a bowl of reheated box mac and cheese. She left it at Lena’s elbow with another cup of tea, talking to her as she tried to convince her to get some rest but Lena didn’t even acknowledge her presence as she continued to work. She did drink the tea while it was hot though, but despite her ravenous hunger, she left the mac and cheese untouched, working tirelessly throughout the night. 

     

                It had already been late when they’d returned, verging on midnight, but Lena was used to the long hours of research. How many consecutive days had she spent at her office, private workshop or research lab working away at problems without pause? She found herself slipping back into that old familiarity of being utterly consumed by something, although she wasn’t up to it like she used to be, her eyes burning fiercely as she forced herself to keep them open, a tension headache forming from too many hours away, an aching tautness to her neck and shoulders from her awful posture over the keyboard.

     

                Still, by the time a pale dawn broke over northern Alaska, she had a legal notepad filled with rough calculations and estimations based on the prison schematics and blueprints she’d found. Staring at the dimensions in the files she’d found, Lena had spent hours determining the mass from the materials, the combined weight of the contents and prisoners, her rough calculations letting her know what she was looking for before she could figure out how she would locate and lift it. Her knowledge of physics and engineering was broad and she applied what she knew, filling pages and pages with methods of weight distribution, tension and weak spots. By morning she’d run the numbers enough to conclude that nothing short of hundreds of millions of dollars of military equipment would get the job done. And she’d pay it too.

     

                It was mid-morning by the time she heard someone stirring, still working away at her plan as she raked a hand through her frizzy hair, consumed by her research on deep-sea recovery from what little she could find on Google. It wasn’t much and wasn’t very helpful, the only comparative sort of recovery being shipwrecks that were cut into pieces, weakening the structural integrity in the process. To cut the prison into pieces would mean to completely flood the entire thing, drowning the prisoners in the process, if the pressure of the ocean didn’t get to them first. The one saving grace was that, from Lena’s knowledge, the prison wasn’t already completely filled with water, which meant it wasn’t as heavy as it could have been.

     

                Still, the only method she could see that had any validity was the use of sea cranes mounted on giant ships, and that was after she’d managed to locate the prison, which would take SONAR and satellite systems, and a dynamic positioning system to help position the vessels in the ocean, altering their course with the wind and the waves as they tried to retrieve the prison. Once it had been located, she’d need remotely operated vessels as well to study the prison with cameras before the best way to enter could be determined. Tallying the cost and trying to determine how much money she had hidden in various off-shore accounts and hidden in bundles of cash around her safe houses, her other bank accounts and assets no doubt frozen, Lena didn’t hear Eliza enter the room

     

                “Lena,” Eliza said gently, setting down a cup of coffee and reaching out to touch her shoulder, startling Lena, who scowled as she shrugged out of her grasp. “How long has it been since you slept?”

     

                Lena couldn’t have known, proper rest evading her since Alex had gone up into the ceiling at least, and then a total lack of sleep for more than twenty-four hours now. Running the pads of her thumbs over her eyes, she exhaled sharply and blinked owlishly as she looked down at the bowl of porridge set beside the cup of coffee. She hadn’t touched her mac and cheese last night and Eliza held the bowl with its congealed contents in hand, looking concerned for the young woman.

     

                Glancing at her, Lena cleared her throat. “Thank you.”

     

                “You should get some rest.”

     

                Nodding in acknowledgement of her words, not so much in agreement, Lena took a sip of the coffee, bitter and strong, and returned to her work. She didn’t eat her breakfast either, months sustained on porridge leaving her with the contemptuous decision to never eat it again - or at least not for several years. Draining the coffee quickly as caffeine hummed through her, filling her with the artificial buzz of energy, she found it insufficient to cut through the fog of the drugs lingering in her system. Frustration bubbled up at her limitations, at how hard it was to concentrate, how long it was taking her to calculate things that she would have been able to do in her sleep before, and how difficult it was to keep things straight in her mind. 

     

                By lunchtime, Alex and Kelly roused themselves too, the former remaining in bed while the latter drifted around the building, poking her head in to see Lena hard at work and leaving her be. Lena kept at it all afternoon, flagging as her shoulder sloped and she started making errors, her rabbit holes of research going nowhere, stuck with nothing more than estimations and a list of companies that could potentially be hired, if only she had the funding and the ability to reach out without rousing suspicion. By the time dusk was settling in, the temperature plummeting again, Lena’s patience was wearing thin and she tossed her pen down onto the desk, jerking the chair back and snagging her coffee cup.

     

                Her legs ached as she moved for the first time in hours, briskly crossing into the kitchen, where the other three women gathered around the small table. Making herself a cup of coffee, her taut back to them, oblivious to the shared glances, Lena gritted her teeth and closed her eyes.

     

                “There’s soup in the pot,” Eliza ventured after a moment. “It’s from a tin but … it’s filling.”

     

                “I’m not hungry.”

     

                “You haven’t eaten a thing in days.”

     

                Turning, Lena cupped her coffee in her hands, letting out an amused huff as her mouth twisted. “Look, you’re not my mother. I don’t need you to look after me.”

                

                “You need to keep your strength up. We’re in this together and-”

     

                Cup halfway to her lips, Lena paused, letting out a sharp laugh and setting it down on the counter untouched. Crossing her arms over her chest, she haughtily arched an eyebrow, a thin smile on her lips as she rounded the island and leaned against it, a few feet away from the table of three.

     

                “Oh, really? And what have you done all day, hm? Don’t pretend that the three of you give a shit about anyone else. You got your family out, you got your freedom. You don’t give a shit that she’s stuck in there.”

     

                “Of course we-”

     

                “No, you don’t. Don’t you sit there eating and chatting away and tell me you care-”

     

                Eliza climbed to her feet, annoyance in the lines of her face as her mouth turned down at the corners disapprovingly. She moved into the kitchen, pulling out a chipped bowl and scraping the rest of the pot of soup into it, the cutlery drawer rattling open and closed before she let the spoon clatter against the rim. Setting the bowl down heavily on the island, she gave Lena a cutting look as she paused at her side.

     

                “She was a girl when I met her,” Eliza stiffly replied, her voice wavering, her eyes softening to aching dismay. “Only a girl. It broke my heart to see her in there, as much as it broke my heart to have my daughter in there, and I have watched her grow up and looked after her as much as I could, held her as she cried for her mother, nursed her through the things that they did to her, loved her as much as I could so she would at least know what that felt like, so don’t tell me that I don’t care. Call me a coward, call me complicit, call me every name under the sun, but I love that girl like she’s my own daughter and I will regret that I couldn’t do more for her every day for the rest of my life.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena smiled thinly, exasperated by them all as she rounded on Eliza, arching an eyebrow. The chair scraped the concrete floor behind her as she stared at the doctor, angry, frustrated, tired. “If you care about her so much, why did you leave her behind?”

     

                “You left her too, you know,” Alex retorted.

     

                Whirling around, eyes blazing with anger as the truth struck home, Lena punched her square across the face, sending Alex staggering backwards, weak and pale with surprise as her mother lurched forward and caught her before she struck the fridge. Kelly had reached for her girlfriend too but changed her trajectory, on Lena in an instant, grabbing fistfuls of her fleece as she drove her backwards, dark eyes hard and appalled.

     

                “What the fuck is wrong with you? She was shot yesterday, are you out of your mind?”

     

                “Get your hands off me,” Lena tightly replied, her fingers encircling Kelly’s wrists as she tried to pry her hands off. 

     

                “Calm down,” Kelly said through her teeth, glancing back over her shoulder at her girlfriend, concern flickering across her face.

     

                Using the preoccupation to shrug off Kelly’s touch, Lena brushed past her, teeth clenched, shoulders taut, and slipped out of the room. She was tempted to barge outside, into the sub-zero temperatures, and potentially take the chopper north again in search of the prison, but she knew that it would be pointless, even if the distance allowed her anger to simmer. And, truthfully, Lena was tired, so tired; she wouldn’t have made it there and back in one piece. Instead, she relegated those plans to tomorrow and, after a brief hesitation, she turned right at the hallway and walked into the bedroom allocated to her and Eliza. 

     

                Kicking off her boots, she hauled herself up the rickety ladder as she stewed in her frustration, eyes smarting with tears, a headache pounding behind her eyes, her body aching everywhere and stiff from the cold. The quilt on the bed was thick, with an extra thermal blanket too, and she burrowed beneath them, the mattress thicker than anything she’d slept on inside the prison, piling the blankets on top and laying on her back as she splayed her fingertips along her brow bone and inhaled sharply through her nose. Hunger gnawed at her stomach and Lena regretted her hasty decision to snub the soup, feeling somewhat faint and hollow.

     

                Still, she couldn’t sleep. Body limp like a puppet with cut strings, she sank into the soft mattress and didn’t move but her mind was another thing altogether. Trying to parse through the information she’d crammed into her brain over the last sixteen hours of searching for something , she closed her eyes to the damp-stained ceiling two feet above her face and felt her frustration knot in her chest, a tangible thing that made her ache as she listened to the quiet of the building. It was a stark difference to the noise of the cell block and Lena found it difficult to sleep without the sounds of the prison and the prisoners. She was still awake when the door cracked open a while later and Eliza slipped inside, the bottom bunk creaking as the other woman climbed into bed and then let out a weary sigh.

     

                “We need to trust each other, if only for her sake.”

     

                Lena didn’t respond, just rolled over and tugged the blankets up higher. Eyes closed, she listened until Eliza’s breathing evened out and then the residual tension bled out of her, the sound of someone else nearby familiar enough for her to finally fall asleep. Her body needed the rest and desperately kept her asleep for as long as possible, until the sun was fully up and she felt groggy as she woke to the grey room, sunlight leaking through the blinds. Sitting up, she dug the heels of her hands into her eyes, rubbing furiously and letting out a rasping sigh.

     

                Having slept more than anticipated, Lena climbed out of bed, the ladder shuddering beneath her feet, and laced her boots back on before she made her way out of the bedroom. Making directly for the control room, Lena blinked as she pulled up short at the sight of three of the desks already occupied, three faces turning towards her as her expression turned wary.

     

                “Coffee and breakfast are in the kitchen,” Alex told her, still looking grey and weak, a shadow of a bruise on her cheek, but with a determined set to her jaw as she tapped her pen against the legal pad on her lap. “Help yourself and then we can get started.”

    Chapter 18

                After pulling the hatch closed, water still poured in around the edges as the gap where it should have sealed, pressurised against the weight of water surrounding them, remained open, Kara let go of the ladder and dropped. It was a long way and she fell quickly, knees bent as she braced for impact, the floor shuddering beneath her feet as she splashed into the ankle-deep water swirling around. The drainage system was struggling against so much water and Kara looked around in the dark, her keen eyesight making the colours drab but as visible as broad daylight as she took stock of things.

     

                Her goal was to get through the prison and let everyone out, get her friends to the central chamber and give the strangers in their own cells a chance at their own freedom, but as she stood in the icy waters, Kara faltered. The prison was eerily silent, the normal overwhelming hum of the electricity, the engines, the rumbling pipes of gas, water and steam absent, the drum of so many heartbeats greatly diminished. It was the latter that gave her the greatest pause, bodies drifting about, riddled with bullets and broken bones.

     

                Standing in the gloomy chamber with the water level slowly increasing as the sea flooded it and slipping through the open doors of an adjoining section of the prison, Kara felt her chest tighten with panic. Running her bloody hands through her hair, she drew in shallow, ragged breaths as she squeezed her eyes shut, hunching over as she tried to think of what to do, or how to get everyone out of this mess. The prison was slowly sinking, that much was clear, and the water would just keep rising in this section, the few still alive inevitably drowning unless she helped them. And Kara hadn’t meant to kill anyone, had just been trying to get out, get Lena and her friends out, the people who’d been a sort of family to her on the other side of the cell walls, but there was a whole other group of friends who’d gotten her through the darkness of the years, and Kara had felt split in half by the whole thing, knowing she couldn’t leave them behind without a guilty conscience. Now, she couldn’t leave them in the sinking prison without giving them a fighting chance.

     

                Disoriented by the dim lighting, the sound of running water and the sparking electrics, coupled with the sound of Lena above her, tearfully begging her, sobbing and arguing with Kelly as it cut Kara deeply, regret at what could have been minging with resolve to do what she had to do, Kara took a minute to get her bearings. She could already feel her power diminished by the blotted out sun, the radiation soaked air feeling so dull after the intensity of the dawn breaking over the Arctic Circle, and she knew she had to act quick, regardless of what she would do with the time afforded to her. 

     

                Turning in a slow circle, she listened to the heartbeats of the unconscious guards and one prisoner and grimaced as she blurred into action, dragging limp bodies into the hallway of the section they’d broken through. Making a row of guards, feeling the terrified gaze of administration staff cowering in the dark on top of desks as water rushed through, lapping at their chairs, she went back and reluctantly grabbed the heavy Daxamite by the neck of his sodden sweatshirt, wading through the water and tossing him unceremoniously through. Cuffing them all, she straightened and grimaced.

     

                Then she went back for the pallets with the realisation that they would need supplies, the ones she left behind, the guards and staff that she didn’t feel obligated to rescue, who could rely on the covert organisation that put them there to rescue them. Her guilt only went so far, and her pity was reserved solely for the prisoners, not the ones who had kept them there, behaving cruelly towards her, feeding her kryptonite, shocking her and starving her. And she knew there were other prisoners who’d suffered worse than she had, who didn’t have the natural invulnerability beneath a yellow sun to withstand the beatings, who couldn’t heal broken bones and fresh bruises in a few hours. 

     

                Still, she couldn’t let them die, hadn’t wanted to hurt anyone until her senses had been overloaded, so acute, so sharp and sensitive that it had overwhelmed her, like every feeling had been magnified a thousandfold. It had been blinding, deafening, the touch of her clothes against her skin coarse, the smell of salt, steel, blood enough to make her gag, the mere taste or the air fetid as it coated her throat, worked into her lungs. It almost felt like a kindness, what they’d done to her, putting her beneath a red sun lamp where she’d been weakened, the world dulled without the full force of the radiation overpowering her. Kara hated to think it, hated to perceive herself as weak, but it was somewhat a relief to feel it slipping away, like a fading echo of a loud shout.

     

                The pallets were too big to get through the airlock doors without dismantling it, and Kara made quick work of tearing through the plastic-wrapped mass of boxes and cartons of food and supplies. Streaking back and forth, she left them littered throughout the sector on any surface that was out of reach of the water, stacking bottles of bleach on top of tins of coffee, a pallet of tinned peaches on top of boxes of oats and crates of bagged and powdered milk on top of medical supplies and drugs and vitamins. There were perishables as well, fresh apples and loaves of bread, cheap cuts of meat, rolls of bandages and surgical towels, standard-issue DEO uniforms and boxes of toothpaste and bars of soap. Once she’d unloaded all of the pallets, Kara was almost knee-deep in the central chamber, her hair plastered to her face and a part of herself that deliberated over the idea of leaving.

     

                Instead, she turned and waded through the water, passing through the first set of doors in the airlock and dragging each one shut before repeating it with the second set. It wasn’t a perfect seal but it was the best she could do and stopped all but a trickle of water from pouring through. The chamber beyond would continue to fill, which was concerning, given that was the only way out, and Kara worked quickly, ducking into the first office, climbing onto the filing cabinet and pushing open the ceiling panel. Climbing through, she crawled through the ceiling space blindly until she was sure she was far enough to be in the next section.

     

                Dropping down from the ceiling, Kara’s shoes squeaked on the dry floor and she looked around expectedly, seeing no one in the dark. This wasn’t her section, the familiar hallways she’d walked for eighteen years, but it was still somewhat familiar to Kara, who had been through the adjoining sections of her zone numerous times over the years. Moving swiftly through the hallways, she took stock of the bodies that they’d left in their wake, shifting the dead into a row with a wince, staining her hands and her clothes further, and stretched out the unconscious guards in one of the offices, cuffing them all with their own gear so they couldn’t cause any trouble for her. 

     

                Making her way to the next airlock, she ducked into a janitor’s closet just off the hallway and scaled the metal shelves to remove a ceiling panel and circumvent the powerless doors. Kara didn’t want to destroy what could very well end up being the last thing holding back the water if the prison flooded entirely, and truthfully, she was a little uncertain of her strength at the moment, feeling it wane away from direct sunlight, her muscles aching as if she’d had a good workout, the sensation unfamiliar to her after years of relative disuse for anything beyond the daily functions of existing. Crawling through to the other side, she landed in a crouch just beyond the sealed doors.

     

                Padding through the hallways, wary of any guards who hadn’t been caught in the fray as she listened to their heartbeats and nearby footsteps, Kara made her way to her cell block. There were four in each section and she knew the layout of the prison by memory well enough to make her way directly to the one she’d been housed inside, repeating the process of finding an adjoining room - this time an office - and stealing through the ceiling until she judged herself to be right over the block, by the sounds of things.

     

                Removing the panel, she dangled her legs through and fell right into the middle of the shouting match between the two groups her fellow inmates had lumped themselves into. They all fell silent at the sudden appearance of her standing in their midst, those with sensitive eyes taking her in while the metahumans blindly stared into the dark, unable to make out more than the shadow of her.

     

                “Kara?” J’onn started, his voice low with wary confusion. “What-”

     

                “We need to go,” Kara breathlessly interrupted him. “Now. The prison, I- it’s sinking, it’s- it’s flooding. I- we broke it so we need to go now or we’re going to be trapped here.”

     

                “Trapped?” Andrea indignantly replied. “I am not dying here.”

     

                Arm around her shoulder, J’onn guided her away from the group, their heads ducked together as he spoke quietly to her. He must have read the ripple of panic on Kara’s face, the taut nervousness of her body as she shifted restlessly, a stone sitting heavily in her stomach. 

     

                “What happened?”

     

                “They got out,” Kara whispered, her voice trembling. “They got out but … the damage. I-”

     

                She faltered, closing her eyes, pressing her fingers to her eyebrows as she breathed slowly through the building pressure in her chest. “I didn’t mean to. It was all so much, I- the guards. I killed some of them, I- Alex got shot and I-”

     

                “It’s okay,” he murmured as her frantic whispering turned rough as she fought to swallow a sob. “Tell me what’s happening to the prison?”

     

                “Mon-El was there,” Kara rasped. “We fought. Um … he’s still alive out there with some of the guards. We damaged a lot of stuff. The control panel got crushed. The doors stopped working and um … the engines are dead, and we burst a lot of pipes. It started sinking a bit and water started coming in, and I guess the pipes were helping, but the whole centre of the prison is flooding. And without electricity, I couldn’t seal the hatch properly and now there’s water coming in and it’s the only way out and if we don’t go now ...”

     

                She couldn’t bring herself to say it, fear tightening her throat as she looked at her friend, her blue eyes wide and mournful, his own dark and softly resigned as he gently squeezed her shoulder. Kara’s eyes filled with tears and her bottom lip trembled as she let out a choked breath.

     

                “We’re all going to die in here.”

     

                Letting out a defeated sigh, J’onn gave her a grim look of respect. “You shouldn’t have come back for us.”

     

                “I couldn’t-” Kara said as her voice frayed, agony wrenching her. “I couldn’t-”

     

                “It’s okay, it’s alright. You acted selflessly and that’s a very brave thing - more than most people would do. Thank you, Kara, for coming back for your friends.”

     

                She shook her head, covered in the blood of so many others as she stared hollowly at J’onn, feeling sick as her hands shook. “It was so easy ,” she gravelly confessed, the breath hitching in her chest as she stared down at her red palms, blood dried in streaks over the backs, worn into the grooves and nail beds. “I was so … strong. I shouldn’t be that strong, J’onn. I hurt them - badly. I- I put my hand through him and- oh, God, there was so much blood. They didn’t stand a chance.”

     

                Letting out a pitiful whimper, Kara clamped her mouth shut as she screwed her eyes closed, hands balling into fists. “They were right about me; I can’t go out there. I should- I should stay. Stay here. Shouldn’t I? You agree, don’t you? I’m- I’m a- a monster, a killer. It wasn’t supposed to … happen like this but Lena-”

     

                Just speaking her name made Kara’s shoulders go slack, a cutting moment of clarity, of peace and focus through the haze of panicked horror, and then shame washed over her in a tidal wave of nauseating revulsion. Drawing in a shaky breath, her face ghostly beneath the blood, Kara’s mouth moved soundlessly, her face wrenched pleadingly as she looked up at J’onn.

     

                “They would’ve killed her and I promised her I’d get her out. All of them. And I did. I did get them out but … I didn’t think it would be like that. I- I don’t know what to do now. We need to- we need to go, right? You can fly and I can fly and-”

     

                “Kara, Kara,” J’onn gently interrupted her, cupping her face in his hands, softly shushing her. “Slow down, okay? We need to think about this; I’m not as strong as you, the metahumans definitely aren’t. They wouldn’t survive out there, they won’t be able to swim up and the cold … without a chopper, there’s no way we can get everyone out safely.”

     

                Lips parting, Kara’s expression went slack with worry. “But … we have to. There’s no other choice.”

     

                “Let’s take a look at things first, okay? Is there-” J’onn faltered, wincing slightly before he cleared his throat. “Did you … kill everyone?”

     

                Blanching, the breath catching in her throat, Kara shook her head. “I tied the guards up. The admin staff and janitors are still loose. The lights are off though, um … I think they’re scared.”

     

                Nodding, J’onn sighed and ran a hand over his buzzed hair. “Yes, I’d say there’s a good chance they are. But is anyone in charge still alive?”

     

                “The Warden was there. She was bleeding pretty badly when I pulled her out. But, um, the Deputy is cuffed in the next section - at least she should still be there.”

     

                Nodding again, somewhat distracted, J’onn gave her shoulder a reassuring pat. “Okay, we’ll find her and we’ll see what we can do.”

     

                He turned away from her then, calling out to Querl and Imra, conversing quietly with them before bickering broke out with the other prisoners and he eventually reconvened with Kara. J’onn boosted Kara up first, back through the hole she’d used to enter, and then she braced herself against the edge of the hole to reach for him and haul him up after her. Crouching in the ceiling, they told the remaining five prisoners they would be back soon and moved quickly through the crawl space without the need to be quiet or cautious.

     

                Emerging on the other side of the sealed cell block doors, Kara led J’onn through the hallways until they came to the next airlock, both of them standing on the edge of a sink to climb through to the ceiling again and go over the airlock. There was the sound of movement on that side, voices that Kara tuned into as guards hissed back and forth about what was happening, and she led them through to the supply closet she’d left the unconscious form of the Deputy inside while corralling Eliza and Kelly, easily finding the one without a handle and breaking it down. Lucy was cuffed and angry as she looked around blindly in the dark at the intrusion, struggling to her feet until Kara reached down to grasp her cuffs and hauled her up with ease.

     

                “Who’s there?” Lucy roughly asked. “Schott, is that you?”

     

                “It’s Kara,” the Kryptonian murmured, surly and still a little unbalanced by the trajectory her morning was taking.

     

                “Kar- you-”

     

                “No time for that, the prison is damaged and … well, we’re all dead if we don’t figure out how to at least fix it so I need you to tell me everything you can about this place.”

     

                “What do you mean it’s damaged?” Lucy demanded. “What did you do?”

     

                A strangled laugh escaped Kara as she dragged the Deputy out into the hallway. “I broke us out. Lena, Alex, Eliza and Kelly - they’re gone. Half of the guards are dead, maybe more than that. The power’s out, we have a very big leak and if we don’t get out of here …”

     

                Mouth opening and closing as she floundered, Lucy stared in Kara’s general direction with stunned disbelief. “But …”

     

                “Tell us what you know,” Kara softly pleaded before she hardened. “Or I’ll have to go and find someone who won’t hold back getting it out of you.”

     

                “How have you been in here so long and you still can’t bring yourself to fight back like everyone else?” Lucy wondered, her voice barely a whisper. “I can’t tell if you’re a coward or if it’s self-preservation.”

     

                “Neither. Tell us, quickly. I can keep you safe if you help us.”

     

                Hesitating, Lucy clearly saw the wisdom in cooperating. “What do you want to know?”

     

                J’onn stepped forward, his calm demeanour turning brusque as he wasted no time, startling Lucy, who had thought it was just Kara. “Are there any evacuation submersibles for emergency escapes?”

     

                Flinching with surprise, Lucy shied away as she tried to make out the shadowed figure of the other alien. Kara held her fast and the Deputy’s eyes strayed back in her direction.

     

                “How many of you are out?”

     

                “All of us,” Kara bluffed, knowing that the other cell blocks had no power either, the sounds of curious conversation, arguments and banging on the sealed doors audible throughout the prison. “I suggest you tell us quickly or I’ll leave you for the other prisoners to deal with. I don’t think they’ll be too fond of you. Now, J’onn asked you a question, Deputy.”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lucy shook her head, eyes swimming with tears. “No. No, of course there aren’t.”

     

                “What’s the protocol for an emergency then?”

     

                “There isn’t one. The higher ups at the DEO would rather we all go down with the prison than risk anyone being free. Even the staff. I mean … we’re all sentenced here for a reason.”

     

                Eyes flitting to J’onn, Kara’s mouth thinned. “We’re trapped.”

     

                “How manoeuvrable is the prison?” J’onn asked, a determined set to his face.

     

                “Not very,” Lucy whispered. “It goes up and down. That’s about it. It’s- it’s too big to move like a submarine. We’re anchored-”

     

                “Anchored? How?”

     

                “Big winches beneath the prison with anchors to make sure we don’t drift too far. They put some slack into the chains when deliveries come in so we can surface.”

     

                Kara gritted her teeth, closing her eyes as she let out a shaky breath. “So we’re stuck.”

     

                “We were always stuck.”

     

                “Kara,” J’onn warily murmured. “How bad is the leak?”

     

                Raking a hand through her hair, she faltered, mouth opening and closing as she shrugged. “I don’t know. Bad. I tried to shut the doors from the central chamber to the admin section but … it’s still coming in.”

                

                “And the supplies are out there?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Deputy, how well-stocked is the prison?”

     

                “We can last three months without a new delivery if we have to. On rations.”

     

                “How many are dead, Kara?”

     

                Chewing on the inside of her mouth, she swallowed thickly, the taste of bile caught at the back of her throat. “I don’t know. A third? Half?”

     

                “Let’s say we can stretch it to four or five months on rations-”

     

                “We won’t need rations. It’s fine, we can get out. I got them out, so-”

     

                “You can get out. You should have gone,” J’onn grimly sighed. “The others won’t make it. Not even with just the cold but the water pressure; if you open those doors to get us out, all that water is going to come rushing in. You might not even be able to withstand it until the section is fully flooded and the pressure stabilises.”

     

                “So what do we do?”

     

                His shoulders went slack and he ran a hand over his face, eyes going to Lucy. “We conserve supplies and hold out for as long as we can.”

     

                Kara met his gaze, her own apprehensive and frightened as she thought of Lena. It would be Lena who could get them out, Lena who had the brains and money to find a way to start a manhunt for the sinking prison, it would be Lena who knew they were there and what the government had done in secret. J’onn’s stare was piercing, weighted, as if waiting for confirmation from Kara that she thought her friend would come for them, if they could buy her enough time. She never even entertained the idea that Lena wouldn’t. She knew, in her bones, in her heart, in the corners of her mind, that Lena would come; she had seen it on her face when she’d left her standing on the sinking deck that she was not someone who ever gave up. All that mattered was how long they could give her to succeed.

     

                “That’s not enough,” Kara hoarsely said after a tense pause, frustration filling her chest as she tried to stop her hands from shaking. “There’s no power, no gas, no water. No oxygen. Oh, God, the oxygen lines. J’onn, we’re all going to-”

     

                Laying a hand on her shoulder, he squeezed gently, silencing her before he looked at Lucy. “Was there a backup generator?”

                

                “The Warden has one. A small one in her office, for emergencies. Enough to power her computer and message for aid.”

     

                “Show us.”

     

                Kara towed Lucy by her cuffs, the trio making for the airlock as the Deputy stumbled in the dark. Slipping through the ceiling first, Kara reached through to grab Lucy as J’onn passed her up, before he climbed up himself. Lucy’s breaths were shallow and loud in the close confines of the ceiling and Kara felt a flicker of pity for her before she turned and started crawling forward.

     

                “I can’t see.”

     

                “Just follow me.”

     

                They only went a short distance and Kara cocked her head, listening to the sounds of the guards below waking up, their voices trembling as water splashed and trickled, arguments breaking out and the click of cuffs coming loose. Most of them would still be out cold, or injured enough to have no energy to move as they lay submerged in the rising levels of water below and she was glad that there would be few interruptions of their task as she slipped through and dragged Lucy down with her.

     

                Climbing off the desk she stood on, Kara splashed into the water and she pulled the Deputy down with her, the breath catching in Lucy’s throat at the freezing temperature of it, shin-deep and rising.

     

                “Is that- is that water?” she gasped. “There’s so much, I-”

     

                J’onn dropped onto the desk and then into the water beside them and Kara tugged impatiently on Lucy’s cuffs. “Which way?”

     

                “I have a flashlight. I have a flashlight on my belt. If you- if you turn it on I can show you. I just- I can’t see.”

     

                Mouth tightening at the corners, Kara yanked the flashlight free and flicked the switch, the sudden brightness hurting her eyes as she narrowed them to slits, the beam making her look ghastly as Lucy let out a hoarse shout, clapping a hand over her mouth as she turned her head aside.

     

                “Oh God, oh God. What the fuck?” the Deputy breathlessly babbled, her voice breaking. “Please don’t hurt me. Please don’t hurt me.”

     

                Kara could feel the blood that had dried on her, soaking into her grey prison clothes, her blonde hair dark and stiff, skin barely visible beneath the flaking patches on her face. Some of it had washed away in the water as she’d dragged the guards out but Kara knew she looked gruesome, had anticipated a hot shower - preferably away from the prison - to wash it off and change into something clean and dry. Instead, she was wading through the dark of a flooding prison as her hope guttered like a feeble candle.

     

                “Take us to the Warden’s office and we won’t.”

     

                She didn’t want to tell Lucy that she felt sick at the thought of having to hurt anyone else, that the blood coating her was enough to make her hands tremble, that she was fighting to stifle down her emotions because if she let herself feel them she’d collapse into a sobbing heap and be no good to anyone. Let the Deputy think that she was a bloodthirsty murderer, as long as it got the results that they wanted. Kara would deal with the stain of what she’d done with no inhibitors to dim her power once they’d resolved their immediate problems.

     

                Keeping a tight grip on Lucy’s upper arm, Kara waded to the door and opened it before casting the flashlight around for the agent to illuminate the hallway beyond. The only thing near them was a bobbing tactical helmet and a broken riot helmet but further into the section there were the clear sounds of voices and she heard Lucy inhale as if about to shout for help.

     

                “Go ahead, shout. It won’t make a difference to me. My collar’s off and they don’t have any kryptonite bullets, so they wouldn’t stand a chance.”

     

                Clamping her mouth shut, Lucy paused and then angled her body. “It’s left.”

     

                They moved through the hallways as water lapped around them, their movements slower, sluggish as they carved ripples through the slowly rising levels, until they came to an office. It was similar to the others, boxy and drab, made from concrete and a standard issue desk and chair, clunky computer, a row of filing cabinets and a wall of doors and panels. Lucy made her way over to one of them, opening the door and beckoning Kara closer, the flashlight landing on a generator stored on the shelves, the rising water levels very close to overtaking it.

     

                “There.”

     

                “How strong is this thing?”

     

                “It could probably keep a computer running for a day or two. I’m not sure; it was only for emergencies.”

     

                “And the power?”

     

                Mouth twisting, Lucy shrugged. “I don’t know. I don’t know anything about electrical circuits, I’m not good with machines or anything like that.”

     

                “Winn,” Kara murmured, her eyes darting to Lucy and then J’onn. “Here, take this.”

     

                She handed him the flashlight and then dragged the generator from the shelf, holding it safely above water, the thing almost half the size of the Warden’s desk. Wading out of the office, Kara paused as a beam of light cut across her, her mouth flattening with annoyance as she walked forward.

     

                “Halt!”

     

                “I don’t want to hurt you,” Kara called out, “I’m just trying to help. We need to cooperate-”

     

                The sound of a gun firing deafened her momentarily, so loud to her ears, and she faltered as she worked her jaw, the bullet pinging off the top of the generator and hitting her shoulder. Picking up the shell, Kara rolled it between her fingers and tossed it into the water, exhaling forcefully.

     

                “Stop!” Kara ground out. “We’re sinking, so unless you want to die-”

     

                Another bullet struck her, this time flattening against her forehead, the smell of hot metal filling her nose, and Kara made a low sound of frustration at the back of her throat. Elbowing the closest door down to the shrieks of the three desk clerks inside, Kara swiped a computer aside and set the generator down with a heavy thud before stalking back out. 

     

                Walking over to the guard with an exasperated set to her shoulders, she reached him as he finished emptying his pistol on her, his hand violently shaking, blood covering his face from getting caught up in the fighting beforehand, and Kara reached out to pluck the gun off him like it was a toy. Pulverising metal in her hand, she tossed it aside, chipping concrete from the bullet-riddled walls with the impact, and jerked him close by the front of his Kevlar vest.

     

                “I said stop.”

     

                He pulled his baton free and stabbed the electrified end of it into Kara, who looked down and bit back a groan. She had to admire his determination to fight, regardless of how stupid it was, and plucked the baton from his grasp before bouncing his head off the wall hard enough to knock him unconscious. It was difficult, trying to manage her strength, which was nowhere near its peak but was more than she’d had to deal with since she’d first arrived on Earth, for those handful of hours she’d been free beneath a yellow sun. Reserved, not wanting to hurt anyone badly, not wanting to hear the way their bones broke, their heart stop, their breaths cease, she set the guard down in the water with his back leaning against the wall, trying to prop him up so he wouldn’t topple and drown.

     

                Looking over her shoulder, she caught sight of J’onn and Lucy and shooed them. “Go, go. I’ll be right behind you.”

     

                More guards were coming and she caught a few bullets but heard a cry of pain from Lucy as one struck, J’onn cursing and picking her up, letting the flashlight fall into the water. It cast a ghastly light over the hallway, the moving water casting white ripples on the austere walls and ceiling. Most of the guards were injured in some capacity, their heartbeats faltering with panic as they advanced on Kara with little desire to do so, mere annoyances to her than anything else without the use of kryptonite. 

     

                Holding her hands up, giving them a pleading look, Kara’s shoulders slumped. “You need to start getting each other out. I can’t help you right now but if you use the ceiling panels-”

     

                “Surround her!”

     

                “You’re all going to drown if you don’t listen to me. Can’t you feel how cold it is? How high the water is? I’m trying to help you.”

     

                They were having none of it though, and after she'd picked up the first to advance and thrown her into the guards crowded behind her, Kara ducked into the office for her generator and moved quickly, bullets riddling her sweatshirt and pinging off her as she ran down the hallway and made a turn, retracing their earlier path. It was a struggle to get the generator up through the ceiling and she ended up breaking a hole to make it fit before coming out on the other side, covered in dust and plaster and holding their prize. 

     

                She landed heavily with the generator and staggered for a moment before forging onwards, leaving the other two to catch up. They weren’t aware that she’d locked Winn inside the control room after Alex had held him at gunpoint to disable the comms, but she led them to the room, listening to his frantic heartbeat as he struggled to get the door open, having removed his cuff once he’d regained consciousness.

     

                “Step back!” Kara called out, waiting until Winn obeyed before she kicked the door in, her hands otherwise full.

     

                Winn looked terrified in the glow of his flashlight, eyes wide as he shrank back against the control panel, desk chair skittering aside. “Please don’t hurt me,” he blurted out. 

     

                Sighing at the presumption, Kara walked inside and set the generator down on the floor, gesturing to it. “Can you please connect the generator to the battery or the electrical mains or something so everyone can see what they’re doing?”

     

                “I- wha-” he stammered as J’onn ushered Lucy inside, making Winn straighten. “Deputy?”

     

                Lucy had a hand pressed to her bleeding arm, a hole all the way through where the bullet had passed, and she swallowed thickly, giving Winn a solemn nod. “Do as she asks, Winn.”

     

                “I- I would,” he said, nervously wringing his hands. “It’s just, um … well, it’s not a big generator, and I need something to plug into it. There’s not really a plug for the lights so …”

     

                “Well, what can you plug into it?” J’onn asked.

     

                “I don’t know. A lamp, I guess. A computer, but … well, the servers will be down, so I wouldn’t be able to connect to the drive. No internet. We- we have generators for electricity but … I don’t know what’s happened. They should be working, they’re powered by the turbines.”

     

                “There was a lot of damage done.”

     

                Going white, Winn looked from Kara, to Lucy, to J’onn. His mouth opened and closed, no sound coming out as he looked like he was about to pass out. “Where?” he hoarsely asked.

     

                Kara floundered for a moment, confused. “In the middle chamber. Where the elevator is. The control panel got broken, some pipes, I-”

     

                “Just there? You’re sure?”

     

                “I- yes. But it’s been cut off, it’s flooding.”

     

                Sagging, pressing his hand to his chest as he let out a frayed sound of relief, face clammy with fear, Winn scrabbled for the desk chair and sank down onto it. “Oh, thank God.”

     

                “What?” Kara demanded.

     

                “The prison,” he weakly explained. “It’s powered by a nuclear reactor.”

     

                There was a stunned moment of silence, Kara’s lips parting as her eyes darted to J’onn and then Lucy before returning to the agent. Licking her lips, she swallowed past the lump in her throat. “What do you mean?”

     

                “I mean it’s powered by a nuclear reactor. The heat from the atoms splitting releases the heat, which is used for the high-pressure steam. The steam turns the propulsion turbines which- which powers the engine for us to surface, and the- the turbines for electricity. When the water cools … it restarts the process. It’s how we get our oxygen as well. Desalination, electrolysis, everything. It- it’s enough to run the place for twenty years. ”

     

                Stiffening at the thought that she’d potentially put the entire prison population at risk, Kara was brimming with nervous energy. “Where is it?”

     

                “Near the isolation cells. It’s protected but if it breaks …”

     

                Biting back a curse, frustration making her throat close up, Kara rubbed her eyes as she tried to think. “Okay, okay, that’s okay; we weren’t near there. It’s far enough away from the escape hatch to be safe.”

     

                “When they installed it a few years ago, they, um, they said … it would be better to expose the aliens to the radiation than the staff,” Winn admitted. “Just in case. So … that’s why it’s that far out.”

     

                “How do you know all this?” Lucy asked.

                

                “The Warden used to make me do maintenance sometimes on the other equipment it powers. I’m an engineer - used to be - not- not a reactor engineer though. I guess I’m just good at … fixing things. Um, but it’s not safe to go in though. It’s in a separate compartment and no one can go in when it’s operational because of the radiation.”

     

                “But you could fix the rest of it? The oxygen? The power?”

     

                “Well … I’d have to see what I’m working with first but in theory, yes. There are valves in the pipes so I could divert-”

     

                “Come with me,” Kara cut him off, reaching out to haul him to his feet.

     

                Leaving the generator behind, she dragged Winn with her as she set off down the hallway, J’onn following with Lucy. Struggling to stay on his feet, Winn let out a small sound of objection, tripping forward and stopped from falling face-first by the tight grip of the Kryptonian.

     

                “Wait! Wait! I can’t- I can’t fix it if I can’t see what I’m doing.”

     

                Pausing, Kara glanced at him and considered it for a second. “We have a flashlight, isn’t that enough?”

     

                “No. ”

     

                “Oh. Well, unless you’d like to suffocate, you need to make it enough.”

     

                “Wait,” he breathlessly insisted as Kara started to lead him on. “There’s someone else. A prisoner. She has powers. Electrical powers.”

     

                Stopping again, Kara turned around and stared at Lucy. “Is that true?”

     

                The Deputy hesitated and then sighed, closing her eyes as she grimaced and nodded. “Yes. Prisoner LW90.”

     

                “Where is she?”

     

                “She’s in your section. Different cell block.”

     

                Nodding, Kara set off again, determined and purposeful. Climbing through the ceiling, listening to the muffled cursing of the Deputy as she was led back and forth, and Winn’s shallow breaths loud in the confined space, she paused to confer with the staff which cell block they were looking for and then deliberated between breaking down the doors or climbing through the ceiling. The latter won out and she removed a panel and stared down into the dark cell, hesitating.

     

                “Hi, sorry, excuse me,” Kara called through the ceiling. “Which one of you is LW90?”

     

                “Why?” a woman with white hair asked, sauntering forward, her arms folded over her chest as she stopped almost directly beneath Kara as she looked around in the dark.

     

                Kara took her to be the woman in question and dropped out of the ceiling, landing in a crouch and straightening, giving the woman a grave look. “My name’s Kara Zor-”

     

                “I don’t give a shit who you are. What do you want?”

     

                “Oh, um, the prison is, uh, well, it’s in bad shape.”

     

                “And?”

     

                “Um, well, I was hoping for some help. See, I’m a prisoner too-”

     

                “You’re a prisoner? Then how are you out of your cell?”

     

                “Well, I broke out. That’s- that’s how the prison got damaged. Um … but now it’s flooding and some panels got broken and the oxygen- it’s a long story. Anyway, we’re trying to fix it to buy some time for a rescue and-”

     

                “Kara?”

     

                “Siobhan!” Kara softly exclaimed with relief as she turned to look at the dark-haired woman she hadn’t seen in years .

     

                Mouth twisting with annoyance, Siobhan jerked her chin towards Kara. “She’s telling the truth, Willis. She was an inmate on my old block.”

     

                “What’s this got to do with me?”

     

                Wringing her hands, Kara tried not to sound too desperate, grateful for the darkness as she tried to bargain with the metahuman. “You have powers, right?”

     

                “Wouldn’t be in here if I didn’t.”

     

                Biting back a laugh at how there had been a powerless human in here until recently, Kara’s lips twitched with an uneven smile. “Right, so, do you think you’d be able to power the prison again? Get the lights going so we can see what we’re working with?”

     

                “Can’t,” Leslie said, reaching up to adjust her collar. “They blocked my powers.”

     

                “Oh, right. Hang on, let me,” Kara murmured, stepping in and reaching up to break the collar apart, marvelling at how easy that was after so many years of being saddled with her own collar. 

     

                Tossing it aside, Kara dusted off her hands, pausing at the feeling of the blood, and then looking back up as she watched Leslie flex her fingers, her breath hitching as she must have felt the power rush back in. Kara’s stomach jolted a moment later at the wide smile that stretched across the other woman’s face, a little too eager and slightly manic for comfort.

     

                But then Leslie turned her hands, lightning flitting across the backs of them, and she laughed before flicking her fingers, the lights stuttering back on a moment later. There was a momentary pause as the eyes of the prisoners on that block focused on her, surprise and shock rippling across faces at the sight of the blood-drenched Kryptonian before Siobhan arched an eyebrow.

     

                “Whose blood is that?”

     

                “Everyone’s,” Kara winced. “Um, thank you. I’ll, uh, I’ll come back once everything’s … you know, sorted. I’ll bring some food.”

     

                Snorting, Leslie gave her a dismissive look, “and who put you in charge? If you think I’m sitting in here for a minute longer than I have to, you’re crazy, lady.”

     

                With a wave of her hand, Leslie had the doors to the cell block sliding open as she powered it and overrode the security system. Kara’s eyes widened with panic, realising the error of her mistake too late. Still, she darted forward, quicker than anyone else as she stood in the open doorway, holding her hands up.

     

                “Wait! Wait, wait, hang on. Just hang on a second, there are guards out there. I need you to stay in here where it’s safe or they’ll-”

     

                “No, I don’t think I will,” Leslie drawled, her eyes darting sideways to Siobhan before she flicked her fingers and the other woman’s collar clattered to the ground.

     

                Eyelids shuttering, Siobhan smiled, rolling her neck as her banshee ability made itself known to her again. “I don’t think so either.”

     

                “Fuck,” Kara softly swore, moments before a bolt of electricity was directed right at her.

     

                Fortunately, she could withstand that, absorbing it with no effect, but it was when Siobhan joined in that she faltered, the prison seeming to pitch around her as her eyes widened and she staggered back out of the doorway, clapping her hands over her ears as the sound pierced her eardrums. It disrupted her balance, so overwhelmingly loud to her sensitive hearing, and Kara struggled to stay on her feet as she watched the two women step out of the cell block and the rest pause before they followed suit.

     

                Once Siobhan’s attention was off her, she let out a ragged breath as J’onn reached her side, gripping her elbow as she straightened, giving him a fearful look. “This is bad.”

     

                Nodding, he hesitated and Kara patted his arm. “You take Winn to patch things up; I’ll sort them out.”

     

                “Are you sure?”

     

                “We need to keep it running. Without oxygen-”

     

                “Right. Be careful, okay?”

     

                “And you.”

     

                “Shall I bring the Deputy with me too?”

     

                Eyes landing on the bristling form of a prisoner stalking out of the cell, Kara felt on edge. “She’ll be safer with you. I don’t trust this lot.”

     

                Taking off down the hallway without another word, Kara listened to the sound of more doors sliding open and bit back a curse as she honed in on the sound of Leslie’s heartbeat. Putting on a burst of speed, she tackled the woman to the ground too late, more prisoners venturing out of their cells with curiosity at the sudden freedom offered to them. The sound of collars clattering to the floor was audible to Kara’s ears down various hallways.

     

                “Stop,” Kara quietly snarled. “Stop it, you’re going to get them all killed.”

     

                Letting out a sharp laugh, Leslie grinned. “At least they’ll have their chance at revenge, huh? Just like you.”

     

                Mouth twisting derisively, Kara scoffed and dragged Leslie up, wrapping an arm around her throat as she choked her off, blue eyes flitting around nervously. It took a minute for the lack of air to get to the woman and then she went slack, and Kara felt reassured that she hadn’t killed her by the irregular heartbeat she could hear within her embrace. 

     

                Climbing to her feet, Kara dragged Leslie’s unconscious body over to a janitor’s closet and left her on the floor, snapping off the door handle so she couldn’t escape, leaving her there to cause no further trouble - she hoped. Setting off down the hallway, Kara found her own cell block and fellow inmates milling about outside the open doors and she saw the way their eyes widened at the sight of her but she didn’t have time for the embarrassment that slammed into her.

     

                “I need help,” she hoarsely called out as she approached.

     

                “What the hell happened to you?” Andrea sceptically asked.

     

                “Everyone in this section is loose. All of the prisoners. The doors to the next section are open and … I think they’re going to kill the guards. I- I need help. Please. I need help stopping them.”

     

                Querl shared a look with Nia and they nodded before stepping forward, Imra hesitating before she also nodded. Psi and Andrea lingered back, the latter folding her arms over her chest, the former cocking her head to the side, eyes narrowing.

     

                “Why should I care about the guards?”

     

                “You shouldn’t,” Kara thickly replied. “But the prison is sinking, it’s flooding, the oxygen and electricity and- and water is all messed up and J’onn’s got Agent Schott trying to fix it but … if everyone else tears the prison apart, we’re all dead.”

     

                “No offence, Kara,” Andrea snorted, “but what good are any of us? You’ll be fine but none of us have our powers. I’m human, she’s human.” She jerked her thumb at Psi. “May as well let them deal with the guards and protect ourselves as best as we can.”

     

                Crossing over to Andrea, Kara grabbed her collar, the other woman freezing in fear as she stared at Kara with wide, baby-blue eyes. Tearing the collar off, hoping she wouldn’t regret it this time, Kara tossed it aside and raised her eyebrows.

     

                “There.”

     

                Rubbing her neck, Andrea smiled thinly. “Thanks and all, but mine came from an amulet, so …”

     

                “Oh.”
