                “Mine doesn’t,” Psi coyly told her, arching an eyebrow.

     

                Making quick work of everyone else’s collars, the inhibitors inside them made useless as soon as the collars were off, Kara gave them all an expectant look. “Well?”

     

                “Let’s go,” Nia murmured, touching Kara’s arm. “They can decide for themselves.”

                

                “Querl, what do you know about nuclear reactors?”

     

                “Nuclear reactors,” he hummed. “Well, what don’t I know? I-”

     

                “Great, go and find J’onn and give Winn a hand,” Kara interrupted, clapping him on the shoulder.

                

                Then she set off as fast as she could, following the sounds of chaos that led out of their section and into the next, the doors wide open, cursing LW90 as she caught sight of the inmates fighting the guards who had been smart enough to follow her lead and crawl through the ceiling, ending up in the section that wasn’t flooding. Grabbing the back of Siobhan’s grey top, Kara clapped a hand over her mouth to silence the wailing banshee, her ears ringing as she gritted her teeth against the pain, and slammed her head into the wall to knock her out. 

     

                Lowering her to the floor, Kara turned her attention to the next inmate, a redhead she’d never seen before. She was spreading fire everywhere, a man screaming on the floor as his uniform burned away, the cheap polyester mingling with the skin that was bubbling and charring. Horror stole over Kara and she tackled the woman from behind, both of them going down, and the woman reached behind to grab a fistful of Kara’s sweatshirt, a smoking hole burning through it as if she expected it to work on Kara.

     

                “That won’t work on me,” Kara growled. 

                

                “Scorcher, don’t waste your time!” a man called out. “That’s the Kryptonian that Siobhan was telling us about.”

     

                Turning, Kara caught him holding two guards aloft and she straightened, stepping over the woman and landing her fist across his jaw. He was clearly an alien from his looks, so the punch didn’t rip his head off from the force, but he went flying, guards staggering before his grip on them fell slack and they fell over. Picking himself up, his face crumpled with anger and he charged at Kara, who was trying to reason, until it turned into an all-out brawl.

     

                Exchanging punches, only slightly feeling them, Kara grew weary of it quickly and was too preoccupied with the safety of her friends as she caught sight of Nia using her powers to lasso a man who’d been in the middle tossing a guard into a wall when she’d caught him. Imra was using her telekinesis to stop bullets in their tracks as the guards tried to retaliate, tearing guns from their hands as she held her own aloft, directing the objects. Kara was surprised by the Titanian’s power as Imra showcased it, using psionic blasts on guards and inmates alike as she tried to defuse the situation, and it gave Kara the time she needed to round everyone up quickly, knocking people out as swiftly as Imra, although hers was more physical and would leave everyone with a nasty headache from her pulled punches.

     

                Still, there were more guards and more inmates than they were quickly able to manage and the guards who had been busy climbing through the ceiling were backtracking back into the slowly flooding section. This, naturally, led to some of the smarter inmates finding their way up into the ceiling to pursue them, and so Kara followed suit. Tired of it all by now, the constant back and forth, the rapidly rising water and the chaos of the prison, she dropped into water that was almost to her knees, cold even though it didn’t affect her, which made the guards panicked enough without the newfound horror of being chased by loose prisoners.

     

                Unfortunately, enough time had passed for all of the guards who were still alive to have regained consciousness and helped each other out of their cuffs - if they were bound - and to get themselves in enough order to retaliate at the inmates that hunted them down. Most of the aliens weren’t invulnerable like she was, although they proved hard to kill and strong or powered enough to cause harm to the guards, and whether it was limbs torn free or bullets striking home, there were soon patches of water that were a troubling shade of red. Kara didn’t have to question why.

     

                The trouble really started when she came upon a knot of guards firing at the prisoners wading down the hallway towards the exit, the overhead lights flickering as Leslie’s electricity struggled to combat the water and exposed wires of the central section. Kara pushed her way through the prisoners at the rear, forcibly setting some aside or giving the hardier aliens a swift punch, before she reached the gap separating two groups. Holding her arms back, she held them back and scowled, looking gory and angry, further incensed by the guard who tried to shoot her.

     

                “Enough!” she shouted. “There’s no time for this.”

     

                “Hand them over,” one of the prisoners demanded.

     

                “No. We have bigger things to worry about.”

     

                And then Mon-El was there, bleeding profusely where she’d bested him, pushing past the aliens at the front and spitting into the water, his lip curling contemptuously. “You would defend them, wouldn’t you? After helping three of them escape.”

     

                “Escape?” one of the aliens exclaimed.

     

                “Fighting me to help them,” Mon-El scathingly continued. “And all four of them are out now, and where are you? Stuck here with the rest of us. And I’m not so sure you’ll get lucky again.”

     

                Scoffing, Kara jutted her chin forward. “You’re wasting time when we should be making sure we can all survive in here.”

     

                “In here? You’ll help them escape but expect us to happily sit in here instead of getting out too? God, you’re spineless.”

     

                “Spineless? I’m not the one who cut a deal to get a promotion to guard instead of prisoner. I’m not the rat.”

     

                “Call me a rat again,” Mon-El growled.

     

                Chaos ensued as Mon-El stepped forward, bristling as his face flushed, and when one of the prisoners behind him gave him a shove to egg him on, Kara’s fist connected with the side of his face to alter the trajectory of his motion as he came towards her. Then a guard shot a metahuman in the face, the man going down in a spray of blood, immediately limp, and one of the inmates picked him up and threw him at the guards, two collapsing beneath the impact and the rest scattering.

     

                As Kara beat back Mon-El, she found it hard to keep the prisoners and the guards separated, snagging a sweatshirt here to jerk someone back, slammed into the wall by the Daxamite with enough force to crack it, catching a pistol in her grasp and tearing it free, blocking a punch from Mon-El with her forearm as she squeezed the gun into a lump of metal. It was all so loud and bright after the darkness, the ringing of gunshots, the taste of metal and blood in the air as Kara felt overwhelmed, disoriented, trying to manage the riot of sensory information while trying her best to stop the fighting. 

     

                Mon-El distracted her too much though, a nuisance that wouldn’t go away, even as she beat him bloody and earned a few bruises too, unusual for her. Still, that was enough for a few prisoners and guards to have slaughtered each other, the water turning red, churned up by fighting bodies as bullets riddled the hallway until the guards started to run out. It was enough of a distraction for a couple of the prisoners to get the first set of doors open before they waded forward to the second set before Kara noticed, but when she did, it was too late.

     

                “No! Don’t-” she yelled, wading forward and then staggering at a blow to the back of her head. 

     

                Shaking it off, her vision swaying slightly, Kara reached the doors and tore the first woman away and then reached for another dressed in prison grey. They’d clearly heard Mon-El’s talk of Kara helping to free the others and planned on making their own escape, but they made the grave error of underestimating just how fucked the prison was. Already, a small wave of water had rippled down the hallway, the level inside the airlock slightly higher as it acted as a bottleneck for the water seeping in through the doors at a steady pace, but that was nothing compared to the water beyond, the spacious central chamber so large and filling with freezing seawater that when she dashed forward to stop the other prisoners with their fingers jammed in the faint seam between the doors, she felt a moment of horror. Right before the doors were forced apart and the brunt of the freed water barrelled right into Kara.

     

                Her mouth was still open, a shout halfway up her throat, when she was swept backwards by the force of the water, an unending torrent dangerously churned as it frothed through the doors and knocked guards and inmates over alike, dragging everyone under and tossing them about. Clamping her teeth shut, Kara’s eyes stung fiercely as she opened them, her vision still sharp but the tiny bubbles of the churning water limiting what she could see. Fortunately, her body density was greater than a human, which meant that she sank to the bottom with the force of the water but was also able to withstand it better, grounding herself against the floor and staggering upright as she braced herself against the wall.

     

                The water was up to her waist now and rapidly rising, swept down the hallway and lagging at the bottleneck of the open doors as the water ran in, the choked sounds of people drowning audible even with the roar of the water. Cursing, Kara found the nearest person, a birdlike alien that was floundering, even this far down the hallway, and grabbed the woman by the collar. The alien let out a choked sound at the pressure around her throat but Kara didn’t let up as she ducked into the closest office, out of the direct current of the water, and climbed onto the desk, alien in tow. Punching a panel upwards, Kara grabbed the alien and shoved her through.

     

                “Go,” she roughly ordered her.

     

                Jumping off the desk, she moved as quickly as she could, the water almost up to her ribcage, forcing her to practically swim as she fished out the nearest warm bodies, guard and prisoner alike, ducking into open doors to force them up through the ceiling. The taste of salt was strong in her mouth and she laid eyes on her friends, making a beeline for them, shepherding a few more live people into doors and ordering them to get into the ceiling. She got Nia first, tossing her over a shoulder and catching sight of the Warden floundering about, her mouth thinning even as she snagged the woman’s arm and dragged her through the water.

     

                A fair amount of the bodies were dead, had already been dead from the prison break, and Kara had to use her hearing to sift through the deceptive corpses as she tried to rescue as many people as possible. Still, there were a number that drowned before she could get them, their heartbeats faltering in her ears and then coming to a stop, making her stomach lurch each time they gave in, too tired to keep their head above water and find a way out. Then there were the ones who had been too injured to begin with, bleeding out from bullets and injuries, their irregular heartbeats pitiful as the water had closed over their heads immediately and they’d drowned with little objection. 

     

                She stayed in there, the whole section flooding as the water from the central chamber flooded in, levelling out until it was higher than she was tall, yet more water rained in from the leaking hatch in the middle and she knew that in a few short hours, the central chamber would be completely flooded again and the entire section would be underwater. Her biggest concern then was whether the ceiling panels would be able to cope with the rising water levels, all but the ones she’d broken through or removed stuck fast with decades of grime, but they were only plaster and PVC and she didn’t think they would hold in the long run. The water would soak through and the damp would spread and anyone who’d survived would be subjected to the frigid temperatures without the gas lines fixed, and would die of dehydration without the desalinator working for clean water. It was a complete and utter mess.

     

                Once everyone was out of the section, Kara got herself out. She had to swim underwater, past bodies moving with the current of her strokes, trying not to stare into the lifeless eyes, and surfaced beneath an open panel. Nia was waiting for her, teeth chattering from the cold that Kara never felt, and Kara heaved herself up through the hole as saltwater ran off her in rivulets. Her throat felt rough from the salt and she was tired, so tired, feeling what little strength her stint in the sun had given her waning now as she was shut off from the source. Of course, she had that little bit of radiation in the air to boost her just over that edge of inhumanly strong, quick and invulnerable, but it felt pale in comparison to what she’d tasted for a moment, no matter how overwhelming it had been to exist as herself for a short while.

     

                Following the damp trail over the others through the ceiling, she came out in the adjoining section to find guards and inmates, everyone doubled over or slumped on the floor, many bleeding in pools of water, coughing and spluttering and soaked through. She landed hard on the floor, staggering slightly, her pallid face furrowed with anger as she caught sight of Mon-El, pale and wide-eyed as she sat at the base of the wall. Stalking over to him, Kara hauled him up by the front of his torn sweatshirt.

     

                “You asshole,” she snapped, shoving him back against the wall as he blinked in surprise. “The supplies were in there, everything from the new shipment. We needed that to survive.”

     

                “I didn’t open the doors.”

     

                “But you couldn’t let go of your grudge for me to stop them, could you?” Kara fumed. “We’re in this mess because of you, and the lives of those that just drowned are on you.”

     

                Scoffing as he shrugged his sweatshirt into shape, he scowled. “We’re in this mess because of you. You tore this place apart, and there were plenty of dead out there before those doors opened.”

     

                Flinching as if he’d slapped her, which would’ve hurt far less, Kara stepped back, her hands falling limply to her sides. Mouth opening and closing, she closed her eyes and shook her head, trying to dislodge the thought. Psi stepped forward then, her eyes locked onto the Warden, who was nursing a bullet wound and slumped with defeat.

     

                “No, it was her fault. If anyone should be blamed, it’s the person in charge.”

     

                “We’re all prisoners too,” a janitor shot back, sullen and scared.

     

                One of the inmates gave the man a surly look, clenching hands into fists. “Are you? Let’s see how you like sitting in a cell all day, being tormented and beaten.”

     

                Rubbing her forehead as things started to spiral again, Kara wished that Alex was there to take control, her hard demeanour and firm hand for ordering people about giving her a natural edge for leading people. If she’d been there, gun in hand, she would have straightened it all out quickly with the threat of Kara’s strength behind her, but Kara had no head for ordering people about, trying to get two groups to cooperate. All she knew was that she was starting to get a headache and was tired, wet and uncomfortable by the sheer amount of blood covering her.

     

                “Everyone stop! From now on, we work together, okay? If we want to survive, no more fighting,” she blurted out a moment later. “We need to work together. We need to ration our food and water, we need to help clean this place up and get it running again. We have to figure out how to survive together.”

     

                “Over my dead body am I wasting supplies on pieces of shit like them,” one of the prisoners said, spitting on the floor. 

     

                Kara folded her arms over her chest. “That’s not up to you.”

     

                “And who put you in charge?”

     

                “You’re alive because of her,” Nia said, stepping forward, her stance protective and firm. “And you’ll survive long enough to get out of here if you listen to her too.”

     

                “Yeah? And how is she going to manage that?”

     

                Nia smiled slowly, “well, because she managed to free the one person smart, rich and crazy enough to free us.”

     

                “We just need to give her time,” Kara said, her voice small and wavering, full of desperation and conviction as she ached for Lena to come back. “She’ll come back if we give her enough time, I’m sure of it.”

    Chapter 19

                They spent the next two days working tirelessly, combing through prison files, uncovering concerning information about a nuclear reactor that had Lena connecting the dots and sitting white-faced at her desk as she tried to convince herself that they hadn’t caused that much damage to the prison. The other three women weren’t as obsessive about it as her, or rather they felt the need for breaks, to eat and sleep and stretch their legs, while Lena didn’t move an inch from the desk unless strictly necessary.

     

                There was a bitter argument between her and Alex about using the chopper for another trip to scout the area and see if they could find the prison, the guard of the opinion that they’d be wasting fuel they might need to escape, while Lena thought that Alex was selfish for thinking of herself. Still, she didn’t take the chopper out again, stewing in her anger as she saw the wisdom in conserving their fuel stores. If things went to plan, they’d need fuel to fly out for their rescue mission. If they went badly, they’d need fuel to fly as far towards Anchorage as they could get before abandoning the chopper. 

     

                Already sleep-deprived, Lena pushed herself to the limit, dry-eyed and slumped over the desk as she picked through the information and conferred with the others on their findings, bickering back and forth about ideas and plans. Alex had invaluable information on the inner workings of the prison and Lena was reluctant to cooperate with her but couldn’t deny that it was useful to have someone shut down her ideas before she could invest too much time into developing them. But the list of possibilities was growing slim and her patience was wearing thinner by the hour.

     

                They were arguing again, had been for the last fifteen minutes, Lena explaining physics with the conviction that she could only ever be right, while Kelly hummed indecisively, Eliza remained mostly silent as she refilled their cups of coffee and added some logic to both sides as required, while Alex took issue with practically everything. Mostly it was the risk, which they all knew there would be, but she was completely against anything that could go even slightly wrong, thinking they were going about it the wrong way. The problem was there didn’t seem to be a right way to do it either.

     

                “We can’t do it,” Alex slowly enunciated. “I know you think you can do everything but how do you suppose we lift a hundred-thousand-tonne prison out of the water to get her out? At best, diving to it to open the hatch would work, but the water pressure would fuck us and we risk flooding the rest of the prison to get her out.”

     

                “Well we have to do something,” Lena hotly replied. “If you don’t like my plans, you come up with something.”

     

                “Why don’t we all take a break?” Kelly suggested.

     

                Scoffing, Lena climbed to her feet and made her way to the front door, shouldering out into the cold, which slammed into her like a stinging wall. She didn’t have the stolen snowsuit on and she hugged her arms to her chest, shoulders hunched as she stalked off into the blue of dusk. Putting some distance between herself and the suffocating confines of the prison dark site seemed like a good idea.

     

                Cold air scouring her lungs, she walked a fair way before stopping, sure to be within easy reach of the squat house. Her long strides in her too-big boots allowed her to vent some of her frustration and she curled her hands into fists, jammed into the warmth of her armpits, and exhaled plumes of white in steady breaths as she tried to remain in control. She wanted to break something and with the irritating guard bickering with her at every opportunity, there was a good chance it would be Alex’s face if she didn’t stifle her dislike and learn to get along with her for Kara’s sake.

     

                She paced a while, back and forth across the frozen earth, hard-packed and dusted with frost, trying to wrestle with her emotions as her lips grew chapped and the wind bit her cheeks. Lena was used to being in control, had been CEO with a whole staff at her beck and call, but she hadn’t been in control for the better part of a year now and it was difficult to come to terms with that. Even now, on the outside. 

     

                The sun sank lower over the horizon and Lena felt the cotton wool thickness of her mind as she tried to focus. Running her hands over her face and through her hair, Lena could feel the knot of frustration in her chest, a physical thing that made her sternum ache.

     

                “Think, think, think,” she muttered to herself, digging the heels of her hands into her eyes as she came to a stop.

     

                Standing in the dimness of dusk, the vacant landscape making her feel even lonelier, with nothing but her thoughts to listen to, Lena exhaled sharply. It was almost similar to that helplessness she’d felt inside the prison, at a loss for what to do, but she’d actually managed to make it out and in hindsight, that felt a lot easier than breaking back in. Especially knowing that the prison wouldn’t be surfacing anytime soon, and didn’t have eight months to wait for her to hatch her next plan. Alex had informed them of their reserved resources, and Lena had run the numbers herself from invoices of stock sent out to the prison each month, and they could last a few months, sure, but time would pass by quickly and they had none left to waste.

     

                It very quickly became too cold for her without proper gear on, that chill that had settled in her bones never seeming to go away, no matter if she took a hot shower or dressed warmly in the snowsuit and thick layers. Lena felt like there would always be a part of her that was cold now, after so many months tucked away in the Arctic, as if it had burrowed into her and could never be burnt out. Her footsteps crunched across the ground as she plodded back to the black site, depressingly grey with the glow of a couple of lights seeping through the windows. 

     

                Letting herself back in, she stamped her feet on the bristled mat to dislodge any ice and blew on her frozen fingers, bitten pink, before glancing left. The other three women were still seated at their desks, facing each other as they continued to discuss their options. There was a palpable air of caution as they turned their attention onto Lena, who angled towards the doorway, hovering on the room’s threshold.

     

                Kelly met her gaze, eyes dark and grave with worry. She had her elbows on her knees as she swivelled the desk chair back and forth in a restless manner. “We need to go public with it,” she softly declared.

     

                “Absolutely not,” Lena flatly replied, making a cutting motion with her hand. “We’re all fugitives, in case you have forgotten.”

     

                “I’m well aware of the gravity of our situation. If it wasn’t for the fact that we’re all supposed to be ghosts, if it wasn’t for the fact that the DEO agents stationed here are on probation and just narrowly missed being carted off to prison as well, everyone would already know we’d escaped. But they don’t because the DEO thinks we’re going to die of old age out there, and they’ll continue doing what they’re doing because people don’t know.”

     

                “And once they do , we won’t be able to continue our search. It’ll be nigh on impossible to fly out there and comb the ocean until we find her once we’ve got a government organisation after us.”

     

                “I know you think that you can do it alone, and if it was purely about intelligence I’d believe you, but this is time-sensitive and I worked for the military. I know, okay? I know how it works. The government will cover up anything and everything possible and they’ll get away with it unless there’s enough attention and a media storm to put a massive spotlight on them. Only then will something have to be done. And yes, maybe you’re right and the something that’s done is they try to track us down, but at least the entire world will know that Kara, along with everyone else, is in an underwater prison, and there will have to be investigations.”

     

                Lena curled her hands into fists, her teeth clenched as she tried not to bite. “You don’t know that.”

     

                “I do. I do know it. I’m not saying go to the government, I’m saying go to the media. You have connections, right? Surely you can contact … someone.” Kelly’s confidence faltered at the end, hitching slightly with uncertainty as if she hoped she was right.

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena rubbed them and scrambled for a solution, for someone who could help, someone who she trusted. That list was practically non-existent; Lena didn’t trust anyone. Her lips moved soundlessly as she ran through a list of government officials, lawyers, human rights activists, and reporters who’d interviewed her at some time. Lena was well connected, and knew people in practically every field from charity galas and conferences she’d attended over the years, but there weren’t any that she knew the number off the top of her head to call and discuss the situation, and there were only a few that seemed appropriate to begin with.

     

                The more she thought about it, the more a person nagged at the back of her head, and Lena didn’t want to consider it but the idea grew and grew until it was practically unignorable. With a withering sigh, she grimaced and opened her eyes, warily nodding.

     

                “I know someone.”

     

                Eliza nodded and pushed herself to her feet, moving over to the brick-like phone that they’d very quickly checked was untraceable and unmonitored. There was something to be said for squatting in a government black site; the government agents hadn’t wanted to be found there either. Taking the phone from her with a murmured thanks, Lena hesitated, and it wasn’t because she couldn’t remember the number. She knew the number by heart and had dodged the calls from it as much as possible, and it was almost ironic now that it was the one number she needed to call for help. 

     

                Walking out of the room, she made her way down the hallway to her shared bedroom and sank onto Eliza’s bottom bunk. Dialling, she pressed the phone to her ear and felt her heart pound in her chest. It took a moment for the call to connect, the sound of it ringing making Lena’s adrenaline spike, her hands going clammy, her mouth dry. If the situation hadn’t been so dire, she might’ve hung up. Instead, the call connected and there was a momentary pause before she spoke first.

     

                “Mom.”

     

                “So, you’re alive after all,” Lillian’s voice came through on the other end, the line bad but her mother’s smooth amusement still audible.

     

                It made Lena’s throat close up, a pang in her chest as her eyes filled with tears. She may have had a difficult relationship with her mother but right then, Lena didn’t think she’d ever been happier to hear her voice. It was like a shock to her system, the contrasting reality of her circumstances and the life she’d had before.

     

                Letting out a frayed laugh, pitifully small, Lena closed her eyes, swiping a thumb over one lid. “I am.”

     

                There was a brief pause before Lillian spoke, her voice tight with what sounded unmistakably like worry. “What happened?”

     

                “I was arrested.”

     

                “Arrested? There was nothing in the news.”

     

                “I was sentenced without a trial. They came in the middle of the night and took me. Put me straight in prison.”

     

                Her mother’s voice sharpened, the razor edge of outrage colouring her words. “Where are you now?”

     

                Licking her lips, Lena hesitated. “I can’t say. I broke out.”

     

                “Of course you did.”

     

                “I-” Lena faltered, gritting her teeth and trying again. “I need your help.”

     

                “Oh. Now, that’s surprising. What do you need?”

     

                “It was the government, a covert sector of it, the DEO. It was all signed off by the President. There are a couple hundred more still in prison. I need your help getting the story out.”

     

                “Alright. Send me information to verify your story and I’ll go to the media.”

     

                “Thank you,” Lena whispered, her voice soft and exhausted.

     

                “Give me two days. Call back then.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                There was an awkward pause then, Lena divulging nothing further and her mother asking no questions, and neither of them knowing how to end the call. She opened her mouth to speak and nothing came out, anything she could have said dying in her throat as she clamped her lips shut again and swallowed thickly.

     

                Then Lillian spoke, her voice a little tender, gentler than Lena was used to. “It’s good to hear your voice.”

     

                The line went dead before Lena could reply and she curled her hand around the brick of a phone, letting her hand fall limply to her side as she bowed her head, so much tension knotted in her muscles as she tried to straighten out her feelings. Things with Lillian had never been easy, not by a mile, but there had always been a certain level of respect for their mutual intelligence and a touch of respect for Lena’s obstinate decision to oppose her family at every chance. Lillian may have pitted Lex against his sister in what she deemed healthy competition, but Lena had clearly come out the victor and that counted for something in her mother’s eyes. If Lillian said she would help, she would. The cost of that help was another matter entirely; Lillian would need to benefit from this somehow.

     

                Taking a moment to compose herself, the ripple of confused agony on her face smoothing out into aloofness, the slightly damp sheen to her eyes drying, Lena climbed to her feet, the bunk creaking at the motion. Swallowing thickly, she stepped out into the hallway and returned to the control room, the murmured conversation between the other three women cutting off at her return. It was glaringly obvious to Lena that she was the outsider amongst them, only there out of necessity’s sake, and she didn’t care that they’d so clearly been whispering about her, except for the fact that it was irritating.

     

                “It’s done. I need to send as much information to corroborate it as I can,” she announced, tapping the phone against her hand. “I have to call back in two days.”

     

                They all nodded, a palpable air of relief as some of the tension faded from their shoulders, expressions softened minutely, but some suspicion as well, sideways glances and flickers of curiosity. No one was brave enough to speak for a moment, to ask what they so desperately wanted to, and Lena set the phone down on Eliza’s desk, nodding before she turned and walked out of the room. 

     

                It was dark outside and she hadn’t eaten dinner yet, although there was a frozen lasagne cooling in the kitchen that Eliza had put in the oven for her. Making her way into the kitchen, she picked up the foil container and fished a fork out of the drawer before dragging out a chair and sitting heavily. With her cheek propped up in her hand, she attacked the congealed meal, a deep furrow between her eyebrows as she brooded. 

     

                Slow footsteps sounded behind her a minute later and she let out a heavy sigh. Sitting back, she waited until Kelly walked into her line of sight and set down her fork, climbing to her feet and walking into the kitchen. Pulling out a scratched plastic cup, Lena cleared her throat and filled it with water from the sink. Taking a sip, she kept her back to the psychologist, who had taken a seat at the table, across from her. The water was so cold it made Lena’s teeth ache and she lingered for a moment, shoulders taut.

     

                “Who’d you call?” Kelly asked a moment later, her curiosity getting the better of her.

     

                Lena paused, almost considered not responding too, before she turned and walked back over to her dinner. Setting her cup down, she sat and dragged the chair in, legs grating against the concrete, and picked up her fork. Toying with the lasagne, Lena cleared her throat again, scooping up a forkful.

     

                “My mom.”

     

                Taking a bite, she kept her eyes down as she chewed slowly, the weight of Kelly’s eyes making her want to shift restlessly. It almost felt like they were back in the prison, in one of their sessions together. The thought made Lena’s mouth tighten at the corners.

     

                “Oh. I didn’t know you had any family that was alive. I mean … you never spoke about them in our sessions.”

     

                “Wasn’t relevant,” Lena shrugged.

     

                “I- well, I mean … most people would have wanted to call their mom the minute they were out. Even if only to tell her what’s happened. Surely she’s been worried sick looking for you for the last eight months.”

     

                “I wouldn’t count on it. She probably assumed I was off-grid for research. We don’t talk.”

     

                “Oh. But she’s going to help?”

     

                Shrugging again, Lena ate another bite and was slow to reply. “She said she will.”

     

                “So she will, then.”

     

                “No, she said she would; doing something not in her own interests isn’t really her style.”

     

                “But … she’s your mom.”

     

                “Do you know anything about my brother?”

     

                Kelly shrugged noncommittally. “I was already inside before he did … all of that. I guess he always kind of appeared … mentally unstable.”

     

                “Right, so, imagine the middle ground between me and him. That’s our mom.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                Kelly seemed unconvinced, as if she didn’t know what to make of Lena’s explanation. Not that Lena had really given her a solid basis of mental stability for Kelly to understand the stark difference between Lena and her family, but that was entirely due to her imprisonment. And it wasn’t to say that they didn’t have any similarities - Lena had been raised a Luthor after all - but that tended to be more so in their nurtured intelligence and skills, their dedication to research and solving puzzles, their aptitude for business. That was where it ended though, Lena had made sure of that. Except, now people were dead and more could die and it left a pit in her stomach and a queasiness that wouldn’t go away.

     

                Losing her appetite, Lena set her fork down and picked up her water. Taking a sip, she grimaced, her mouth a flat line, and then climbed to her feet as she met Kelly’s curious stare. “I should get writing.”

     

     

                “That’s the last of it,” Kara said, water streaming off her, pooling on the concrete floor as she set down a soggy cardboard pallet of canned corn. 

     

                Wiping water off her face with her equally as wet hand, she could taste the salt at the back of her throat, breathing in grateful lungfuls after her blind searching through the dark, flooded section beyond their current one. She’d insisted on doing it, on recovering as many of the sealed bottles and tins as she could so they could add to their provisions. Some were useless, of course, sacks of flour dissolved to nothing, boxes of oats bloated as they’d soaked up the water and congealed on the floor, but many items were airtight and hadn’t been spoiled.

     

                Nia grimaced, a pucker between her eyebrows as she looked down at the meagre piled and then raised her brown eyes to Kara’s face. “That’s it?”

     

                “Well, all of the good stuff at least.”

     

                “That should stretch the rations out a week or two longer,” Querl estimated, eyeing the stacks of cans and bottles.

     

                Most of the prisoner’s food was preserved in some manner, which meant that they did recover quite a decent chunk of food to pad out their stores, but Kara worried that the estimated four months of supplies would run out faster than they assumed. It was already hard enough trying to enforce the rations rule, and to insist that the prison staff be allowed to eat. The dead bodies floating in the section beyond were a twisted blessing, lowering the number of mouths to feed, and that was the only way she could cling to the hope that they’d have enough time.

     

                “Let’s get this locked up,” she sighed. “Querl, you stay in case someone tries to poach.”

     

                Heaving a stack of cartons from the floor, she set off down the hallway and followed the turns to one of the isolation cells they’d commandeered for food stores. The heavy door with the vault lock made it secure and easy to guard, along with the other isolation cells on either side, where they’d had to lock up some of the staff for their protection. J’onn was patrolling the hallway to ensure none of the other prisoners tried to break in and snap anyone’s neck, and he appeared at the sound of Kara and Nia, giving them a helping hand as he twisted the wheel of the cell door and jerked it open on squeaking hinges.

     

                They made several trips until the small cell was bursting with tins of carrots, peas, Spam, coffee ordered for the guards and fruit cups. There were better things in there that had never made it to the prisoners before, things that almost felt like a treat in such a bleak place in a dire situation. Doling out packets of sealed chips to the prisoners as a snack often felt like that human Christmas celebration Kara had heard so much about. 

     

                “It’s getting colder in here,” J’onn said after he’d sealed the door on the second vault, his words hanging visibly in the air before him as his eyes strayed towards the other doors. 

     

                Some of the staff had been locked inside other rooms, for lack of space, and most of them were on Kara’s old cell block, kept under close watch by the prisoners. The force fields still weren’t up, Lena’s meddling leaving them glitching or disabled even after Winn had successfully restored the lights, water and oxygen systems. There was steam as well, running the electricity to keep everything going, but the prison used limited natural gas and what they had been using for heating and the gas stoves in the kitchen had been stored in tanks in the central chamber that Kara had helped destroy. The chefs she’d roped into making meals for all on board Fort Rozz had to make do without any gas and the microwaves from a few guard break rooms had been moved to the kitchens to at least help give out warm food, if nothing else.

     

                Things could’ve been worse, but still, they could have been a lot better. As she listened to the heartbeats of everyone in the nearby vicinity, hearing whispered conversations between prison staff, scared and helpless, she couldn’t help but wonder what she would be doing if she was on the outside now. She couldn’t help but wonder if Lena was okay, whether Alex had survived that bullet wound, if Eliza and Kelly were well and if the four of them were looking after each other. She knew that her powers would have helped them on the outside but she also knew that her duty was to the prison and the people she’d grown up with, the people who were in the same predicament as her, who she would’ve left to a watery grave if she’d gotten on that helicopter instead of staying to help fix what she could and wait through the agonising days, and potential weeks, of a rescue effort.

     

                It had already been three days. Three days and it felt like an eternity. She ran a hand over her face and thought for a second, confused as to how she’d ended up as the person to consult on matters, to keep people in line and dole out commands. Kara had been a child when she’d been arrested, and all she knew of leadership was her parents and their mismanagement of Krypton that had led her to Earth in the first place. They weren’t shining examples. Feeling out of her depth and wishing for Alex and Lena, two different minds that were good at leading in different ways, she grimaced.

     

                “Hand out extra clothes and blankets to anyone who feels the cold. We don’t want them dying of hypothermia; we’ll have no gas to burn the bodies.”

     

                “Somehow, I don’t think they’ll be dying of hypothermia,” J’onn wryly replied, his eyes sliding sideways to Kara.

     

                Mouth thinning, she nodded, knowing that he was right. There was a palpable hum of violence in the air amidst the prisoners, and she had fought her hardest to keep the other sections of the prison closed off for now, not wanting every sector to get loose. Worst case scenario, one of the prisoners would be stupid and strong enough to pry open one of the other entrances to the central chamber and flood another section of the prison. So far, they had relied on ignorance and guard uniforms to explain the power outages and inaccessibility of the cell blocks, passing food through the ceiling and reassuring everyone things would be okay.

     

                Still, the freed prisoners in her section were enough to contend with, and she’d had to forcible restrain a couple and lock them in isolation as well to stop them from crawling through the ceiling and freeing the others, or at the very least spreading word of the truth and inciting a riot. It was purely due to her strength, being stronger than anyone else in the prison, that had set her at the top of the pecking order, and being able to strongarm a man twice the size of her to his knees and choke him unconscious afforded her a little bit of respect amongst the others. She could imagine things would only get worse as hunger, claustrophobia and fear-mongering of being trapped until they died started to set in.

     

                So far, unlimited use of the boxy televisions strewn throughout areas of the prison, as well as clunky gaming consoles, radios and CD players, helped boost morale, and Kara could hear the overlapping staticky sound of music, movies and the beeping of Space Invaders as she walked through the prison. There were a few people she trusted and they’d all been trying their hardest to keep watch, to occupy everyone’s minds and check on the other prisoners, scavenging the other sections for medical supplies, stored food, spare clothes, blankets, pillows, pens and paper for drawing, board games from the guard rooms and tattered novels the staff had passed around. It was more entertainment than most of them had had in years and at least it was something.

     

                “Where’s Imra?” Nia asked, in step on Kara’s other side.

     

                “She went to the kitchens to watch over the chefs. Lunch should be ready soon.”

     

                Up ahead, Kara caught sight of Winn, mousy and pale-faced with fear as he stood at an intersection wringing his hands. Perking up at the sight of him, picking up speed, Kara quickly loped across the distance separating her from him.

     

                “Winn! How’d you go with the comms-”

     

                He started shaking his head before Kara could continue her line of questioning, the small bubble of hope in her chest bursting as her shoulders slumped. The guard looked similarly defeated and Kara let out a weary sigh.

     

                “System’s completely fried. Sorry. I tried, really, I did.”

     

                “I know, I believe you.”

     

                “Sorry.”

     

                “It’s fine,” Kara said with more bravado than she felt, setting off down the hallway. “People know we’re in here, know where we are, so even if we can’t contact them it doesn’t mean they’re not looking or coming for us. We just have to hold on until help gets here.”

     

                Andrea was perched on the counter in a break room, the door wide open as Kara walked past, talking, sipping a cup of coffee. As Kara’s words reached her, she let out a quick laugh and jumped off the counter. Pausing and stepping back to look at the other woman, Kara raised her eyebrows a fraction.

     

                “If you’re holding out hope for them to come back for us, you’re wasting your time,” Andrea snorted.

     

                “I’m not wasting my time,” Kara softly replied, insistent and slightly irate.

     

                “Yes, you are. Sorry to break it to you but we’re all going to die down here so … well, if you find any liquor on your searches, let me know. I’d hate to go out sober.”

     

                “We are not dying down here,” Kara growled. “They’re going to come for us, you’ll see. We just have to give them time.”

     

                Andrea rolled her eyes and smiled ruefully, pale blue eyes defeated. “Look, I know you want to believe your genius girlfriend is scouring the Arctic for us right this moment but the truth is she’s going to go back to her cushy life and forget any of us ever existed - you included. She’s a billionaire; you really think she gives a shit about us?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Well, she doesn’t. Believe me, I know, I grew up exactly like her, surrounded by other people like her. My family was wealthy until my father ran the business into the ground and if I got out of here and had her kind of money, the last thing I’d be doing would be coming back to break out a bunch of strangers I don’t owe anything.”

     

                “She and I are not strangers. We’re … friends.”

     

                “Right. Well, for everyone’s sake, I hope you’re right but otherwise … keep me posted about the alcohol.”

     

                Mood souring as Andrea spoke to the small voice at the back of Kara’s mind, giving attention to her doubts, Kara stalked off. Dressed in her damp clothes, she ducked into a store room and grabbed something clean and dry before heading towards the bathroom that had previously been reserved for prison staff and good behaviour rewards. Kara had showered there most of the time, the hot water pleasant against her skin but without the heating working now she had a cold shower, washing the salt from her skin as she brooded over Andrea’s words.

     

                Lena would come. Lena would come for her, not because she owed the prisoners anything, not because she harboured any loyalty towards any of them, but because she cared about Kara and had promised to get her out.

     

     

                Two days later, Lena called Lillian back, standing outside as the cold bit at her exposed face, each breath raw and scouring as she held the brick of a phone to her ear and squinted against the brightness of the sunset. She breathed slowly as she listened to the phone ring in her ear, her chest feeling tight, her whole body coiled with anticipation. It connected a moment later.

     

                “Lena?”

     

                “Mom.”

     

                “Are you okay?”

     

                “Fine. Did you do it?”

     

                “Of course I did. There’s an award-winning reporter at CatCo; I took the story to him and it was printed this morning. It’s just about to hit the evening news. Is there a TV where you are?”

     

                “Yes, but it barely gets any reception.”

     

                “Turn it on.”

     

                Her heart pounding in her chest, Lena turned and opened the front door, stepping into the gloom of the place and winding her way through the kitchen to the small living room. Switching the TV on, she adjusted the antenna until the static cleared and voices jumped into clear words.

     

                “-her mother, Lillian Luthor, CEO of the biomedical company Cadmus, has informed CatCo Media that her daughter has been uncontactable for the last eight months. This news comes on the heels of the article that was published by CatCo this morning, detailing the harrowing imprisonment Lena Luthor experienced. She claims that a secret sector of the government has imprisoned more than three hundred aliens and metahumans in an off-shore prison north of Alaska. It is believed that Miss Luthor has escaped the facility and is now a fugitive; police have asked that any sightings of the billionaire businesswoman be reported to your local authorities. The White House has been contacted for a statement on the matter, but so far they have declined to comment-”

     

                The other three women crowded behind Lena to watch the news, pale-faced and mildly surprised that it had worked. Lena felt her throat tighten, even as some of the stiffness in her shoulders loosened.

     

                “Thank you,” she murmured into the phone.

     

                “Everything you wrote … is that- is that … really what happened to you?” Lillian hesitantly asked.

     

                “Yes.”

     

                Her confirmation was met with silence and she could practically feel the cold anger radiating from her mother on the other end. After a moment, Lillian replied, her voice clipped and faintly worried. “They’ll be coming for you now. You need to get as far away as possible, disappear until it’s been sorted. Can you do that?”

     

                Sighing forcefully, Lena closed her eyes, tuning out the news and rubbing her forehead. “I can’t. I can’t do that; I need to find a way to-”

     

                “Leave it to me,” Lillian brusquely cut her off. “You stay safe - and hidden. I will handle the rest. I’ve already called the family lawyers.”

     

                “I don’t care about that,” Lena said with frustration. “There are people inside the prison that I need to get out-”

     

                “And the best way you can do that is by staying alive and letting me kick up a fuss for you. I will have this on every newspaper, magazine, news station, radio. The White House will be forced to respond, the President will be forced to step down, whichever government officials involved will be prosecuted and punished and-”

     

                “Okay, okay. Fine. Do what you can, but it needs to be quick-”

     

                “I understand that but you’re a fugitive so my priority is clearing your name-”

     

                “I don’t care,” Lena hotly replied. “I don’t care if I’m a fugitive for the rest of my life. Don’t prioritise that. If you care about me at all, you will help me do this one thing and save those innocent people.”

     

                “They’re just aliens,” Lillian murmured, her voice lowering. “They’re not worth more than your own life.”

     

                “They are worth the same, at least.”

     

                “What is it? The real reason for this … altruism. You’ve always been soft-hearted but this is an unusually foolish crusade you’ve set yourself, so why are you so determined to rescue them all? This is outside the realm of your usual charity.”

     

                “Is it so unbelievable that I would want to rescue them because it’s the right thing to do? That they have been wrongfully imprisoned too?”

     

                “No, it isn’t unbelievable but you have practically bitten my head off at the mere suggestion that we have some patience to find the best solution. What is it? Have you grown fond of one of them?”

     

                Pausing, gritting her teeth, Lena jerked her chin forward, as stubborn and proud as ever. “Yes.”

     

                Her mother let out an exasperated sigh. “Oh, you silly girl.”

     

                “Please,” Lena murmured, her voice wobbling slightly.

     

                “Okay. Okay, I will do it as quickly as possible, I can promise you that. I will do everything in my power, so whatever comes of it … know that I did try my hardest for you.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “Now, you need to go. Take the others with you, if you must, but leave as quickly as you can. Now that the story has hit the news, they will be looking for you.”

     

                Lena’s stomach jolted as her eyes strayed to the window, thinking about how long it had been since the first article had hit the web. It would be a long flight, depending on the aircraft, and this was the first place the DEO would look, knowing it was the waypoint between the prison and headquarters, and Lena reached forward to turn off the TV before she turned to look at the others.

     

                “Okay.”

     

                “Call me again once you’re somewhere safe.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                “I love you, Lena,” her mom said after a moment, uncertain and a little surprised by her candour.

     

                Pausing, Lena faltered for a moment before she jerked the phone away from her ear and hung up. Closing her fingers tightly around the brick, she was silent for a moment, the quiet curiosity of Kelly’s words washing over deaf ears as Lena sank into a stupor for a moment, before shaking herself out of it. 

     

                “We need to go,” Lena quickly ordered, leaping into action.

     

                The other three women were staring at her helplessly, confused by the sudden desire to leave when she’d been so insistent that they stayed until they freed Kara. More insistent than any of them. Voices overlapped as they started to question her and Lena tore through the house, shaking slightly in her haste, the panic of being caught before she could help free Kara rising in her chest. They would be shot on sight, she knew that much, and Lena would be useless then. 

     

                “Just- hold on,” Alex roughly shouted as she managed to snag Lena’s arm, looking greyish and exhausted, her left shoulder held lower than the right as her bullet wound still pained her. “What the hell is going on?”

     

                “My mom’s sorting it out but we’re all fugitives now. Publicly. So we need to get out of here as quickly as possible. They’re coming , okay? This is the first place they’ll look and they have a headstart that spans hours , so we need to go now. Pack a bag.”

     

                That was all the explanation she would give and all the explanation they needed, Alex nodding as she let go of Lena’s arm and started to help her. They ransacked the stores, filling bags with food and water, Eliza grabbing medical supplies, Kelly grabbing spare clothes and all of them dressing in the stolen snowsuits before they filed outside. Lena had the clunky phone in her bag and she patted her pocket absentmindedly as she sat in the pilot seat of the chopper, glad she’d had the foresight to refuel it in case of emergencies. 

     

                No one spoke as she started the engine and flipped switches, remembering the way she’d done it the last few times, although still not confident in her abilities. It was getting late as well and the clouds were grey, the wind biting and howling. Alex sat in the seat beside her and Lena shared a glance with her before the guard nodded and Lena set her jaw, feeling angry and frustrated as she took off, putting more distance between herself and Kara, wondering if she was making a grave mistake, wondering if she’d ever see her again.

    Chapter 20

                Lena put them down on the outskirts of the Brooks Range, miles away to the southeast of Barrow and far enough from their starting point to give them a fighting chance without getting flagged on the radar of any incoming aircraft. There was more fuel in the chopper but she didn’t want to risk it, figuring that they’d put enough distance between them and the black site to throw off the chase a little.

     

                She’d set them down to the south of Atigun Pass, near the Dalton Highway, with the intention of them stealing a car at some point. The logistics of that plan hadn’t been well thought out yet and she hadn’t dared voice them, knowing that it would put them at risk, leave people on their tail, and leave a trail for others to piece together to track them down. It was all they could do though, the only solution in sight to her, knowing that they were in remote, unpopulated areas that were usually only accessible by air. At least she’d put them down as close as possible to a chance . 

     

                It was late now, and dark too, and that was a consolation at least, meaning that no one would have seen them by sight. Lena just had to hope they hadn’t shown up on any radars, and with the sparsely populated regions they’d passed through, she knew that there was a good chance they’d remained unnoticed. A good thing, too, as she’d taken off the tops of a few trees while blindly descending, trying to make out the terrain and landscape by the faint moonlight seeping through the clouds. They’d touched down heavily and the propellers had damaged a few trunks, gouging out the bark, before she killed the engine.

     

                Her bumpy landing rattled them about but at least they were decently hidden by the surrounding trees and shrubbery, and that was all she could really hope for once day broke and any potential pilots flew overhead. Shutting off the engines, the propellers slowing to a final stop, Lena climbed to her feet and started fumbling around in the dark. She’d already disabled the GPS at one point, ensuring no one could track them, had gutted what she could and scoured the chopper for anything that would tip off the DEO to unusual activity after that first day, and now she came up with a fire extinguisher and smashed the control panel to bits, amid exclamations of surprise from the other women.

     

                Breathing heavily, warm in her thick layers, Lena tossed the canister aside and cast the shadowed figures a quick glance. “We sleep here tonight and set out at sunrise.”

     

                “And go where?” Alex asked. 

     

                She still had a rattle in her chest, the cold and damp getting to them all, and she was still weak and recovering from her bullet wound, and now slightly pissed off that Lena had ruined their only way forward that wasn’t on foot.

     

                “Fairbanks.”

     

                “Fairbanks? I may not have officially graduated from high school or had an Ivy League college education like you but I’m pretty sure Fairbanks is days away by foot and you just killed our chopper.”

     

                “We’ll figure something out,” Eliza sighed, stepping up behind her daughter and carefully gripping her arms. “Come and rest.”

     

                It was cold inside the chopper, with no blankets or pillows for them, and even though it was spacious enough for a month’s worth of supplies and a few agents to fit, the four of them huddled together, just behind the seats. Food was fished out and passed around, cold and miserable, packets of jerky and muesli bars shared with mouthfuls of water before they slept. 

     

                Lena didn’t though, keeping watch through the long night until her eyes were prickling and her body felt leaden. The sun started to rise and she could make out their bearings as she climbed to her feet and slipped between the chairs, looking out of the windshield to take in the south-facing view of greenery as the land sloped downwards, away from the mountains behind them. In the far distance, she could see the grey sliver of the highway that travelled north. It would take them hours of walking to reach it but it was their best bet.

     

                Rousing Eliza first and then the other two, Lena didn’t say much as they had a pitiful breakfast of tinned pears and trail mix. Taking measured sips of their water and divvying up further supplies so the weight was shared equally, they made their preparations to leave and Kelly squared her shoulders, looking around from their elevated position.

     

                “This way,” she nodded, setting off.

     

                Lena and Alex didn’t argue over taking the lead, with the memory of an off-handed comment from Kelly about her military service making Lena realise that she was probably the only one out of the four who had ever had to navigate through some sort of unfamiliar terrain. Perhaps Alex and Eliza had gone camping, Lena wasn’t sure, but she certainly hadn’t and so she put her faith in the ex-soldier as Kelly confidently manoeuvred down the sloping rock and shrubbery on nimble feet. 

     

                For her part, Lena was less than graceful, slipping a few times, falling hard on her ass, bruising her already bruised elbows, skinning her palms, getting herself worked up into a hot sweat in her bundled layers, even as the cold bit her cheeks and scraped her throat raw. Eliza followed at the rear, close behind her, hands steadying her, helping her up, quiet words of encouragement, and Lena felt her cheeks turn rosy as she resented the doctor’s gentleness, her willingness to help. After everything, Lena didn’t want her help - because of her Lena just wanted to sink down and sleep.

     

                They walked for hours, the landscape seeming unchanging even as they reached flatter ground, as the trees grew patchy and sparse and they trudged through grass and mud. Her too-big boots gave her horrendous blisters and she stopped being able to feel her feet after the first hour, unused to such exertion, feeling faint and weak. Still, she was faring better than Alex at least, who was grey and stumbling, and Lena did feel a small flicker of guilt at not setting the chopper down closer to the highway, their evident destination. It wasn’t like she could have had the foresight for it though and she kept her mouth shut, uncomplaining as she staggered onwards, the wind blowing them about, grey clouds gathering overhead with the threat of rain. 

     

                Her dark hair was plastered to her cheeks and forehead, the swishing of the snowsuit an irritating accompaniment to their walking, and Lena was almost wishing they’d stayed at the black site and tried to hole themselves up inside it instead of traipsing across the middle of Alaska on foot. They had to stop after a couple of hours, Alex sagging to the ground as her breaths came quick and short, cheeks flushed and face hard with pain. 

     

                Flopping down beside her, closing her eyes, Lena breathed raggedly, leaning against her bulging backpack as it weighed her down. Her limbs ached, her chest ached, her head ached and Lena regretted not sleeping all night, even though the fear of being caught unawares by anyone on their trail had been greater than her need for rest at the time. Now it was catching up to her and she blinked back black spots as she stared up at the grey expanse of sky.

     

                “Here,” Kelly murmured, giving Lena a few saltine crackers from a packet, and half a bottle of water handed over to her.

     

                Thanking her, Lena managed to push herself up enough to drink some water, her dry throat soothed by it. Wolfing down the crackers with the rest of it, she watched as Eliza gave her daughter painkillers for her shoulder injury, not strong enough to stifle the agony of the stitched wound that should have had her in a bed, resting, and as soon as the other two had a bite to eat and some water, they were off again. Cursing their predicament, Lena didn’t have the energy to complain as she put one foot in front of the other, walking onward until she felt like she might pass out. 

     

                Their pace was slow and they had to rest a few more times, the uneven terrain making it harder as the ground rose and fell, icy rock slippery underfoot, patches of mud sucking at their boots. It was getting dark when they finally made it to the highway, the grey stretch of road vanishing into the distance. They still had the purplish light of twilight though, and they had to make good use of it while it lasted, pulling back from the road slightly and finding a good patch of shrubs and small trees with a sloping, rock wall to their backs.

     

                “Here will be a good spot,” Kelly said with a confident nod, as if they had many other options.

     

                “We need a fire,” Eliza said, dropping her pack and sinking to the ground with her daughter, Alex’s forehead shiny with sweat as her eyelids closed and she leaned against the rock behind her. “Do either-”

     

                Lena’s mouth turned down at the corners as she spoke curtly. “No fire.”

     

                Rounding on her, Kelly looked aghast, eyebrows drawing together over dark eyes. “We have to have a fire. We’ll all freeze to death without it. Hell, we’ll be lucky if we don’t freeze to death with one.”

     

                “A fire increases our risk of being seen.”

     

                “The trees will shelter the worst of it.”

     

                “We’ll be seen.”

     

                “It’s either risk being seen or risk freezing to death. I know which one seems more likely.”

     

                Faltering, her own feet and hands numb, cold even in the bundled layers of her snowsuit, Lena’s mouth flattened. She knew that Kelly was right and that Alex needed a fire more than any of them, needed to stay warm and dry before pneumonia settled in, her body already weakened from her injury. She’d managed well so far and Lena knew that it would be three against one if she tried to argue, that deep down she knew they needed a fire and even if she objected, she wouldn’t be able to stop them, wouldn’t be able to go off alone and find her own way to safety. 

     

                Even if she could have, even if there wouldn’t be people on the lookout for a woman fitting her description, her recognisable face now on every news outlet in the country, perhaps even overseas, Lena wouldn’t have gone off alone. She didn’t trust the other women much and wanted to keep a close eye on them so there would be no nasty surprises. They’d allied themselves to get out and Lena wasn’t entirely convinced that Alex wouldn’t sell her out to buy freedom for the other three - at least if they were all caught together, there would be no bargaining or backstabbing. Besides, they still had to free Kara and if they were as committed to it as they said they were, she would use their help. Four minds were better than one, even if that one was the best mind in the world.

     

                Unslinging her backpack from her sore shoulders, Lena dropped it to the ground at Alex’s feet and sank down beside her pack, sweeping aside a patch of leaves and brush to bare the earth beneath. The ground was cold and damp, and Lena worked quickly to clear a sizable spot as Kelly started picking up branches and breaking some dead ones off the nearby trees and bushes. Lena wasn’t good at the outdoors stuff but the ex-soldier was efficient and deft as she assembled the basis for a fire while Lena dug out a box of matches and scraped a couple with no success until one flared to life with a weak orange flame, sheltered by her cupped palm as she lit a few of the leaves and pine needles until they smoked and glowed red. 

     

                It took a while before the fire properly caught, enough of the smaller twigs catching and smoking as the rock and tree cover sheltered the worst of the wind, and they all huddled close to it, hunched and sore and stiff as smoke stung their eyes and lungs. Lena could feel the prickling heat on her frozen cheeks and closed her eyes, feeling the warmth of the fire through her gloves. She remained seated, watching through half-lidded eyes as the other two women fussed over Alex, their voices low and gentle as they tried not to let their concern show. Briefly, Lena considered how much easier it would be if they had left Alex behind as the ex-guard had ordered. 

     

                Finally rousing herself, she rifled through her pack and Kelly’s and peeled back the lids of some canned foods, setting them in the fire to warm through a little before setting the metal thermos from her pack into the flames to boil. The water boiled first, the metal blackening from the flames, and she was glad for her thick gloves as she plucked it from the fire and dropped a tea bag into it, letting it steep and cool slightly before she hesitated and passed it off to Eliza first.

     

                Eliza made Alex drink before the three of them sipped their portions, heat searing their throats, not wanting to squander the warmth. She handed off the food for them to feed Alex next, tins of beans and chunks of sausages spoon-fed until Alex shook her head, her face a grimace of pain, before the three of them finished it off with the can of creamed corn, passing the spoon back and forth until they’d finished them and were still hungry but reluctant to deplete their stores too quickly. 

     

                “It’s going to be cold tonight,” Eliza said, her breath visible in the firelight as she helped Alex move into a comfortable position near the fire, pack beneath her head, hood drawn up and held closed at the neck with the velcro strips. “It would be smart to pair up for warmth.”

     

                Choking down a scoff of annoyance, Lena’s mouth twitched and her eyes darted between Eliza and Kelly, wondering which one of them would draw the short straw and pair up with her. It would be with great reluctance that Lena huddled with either of them for warmth but sharing body heat for survival, especially when one was outdoors in a bitterly cold region, was the wiser choice, regardless of her feelings for either woman. 

     

                Nodding, Lena pushed herself to her feet and wiped the damp needles and leaves from her snowsuit before vanishing far enough into the trees and shrubbery to relieve herself as she cursed the cold, and then returned with enough wood to stoke the fire. She made a few more trips in the dark, fumbling around for logs and thick branches long enough to make a lean-to. It wouldn’t do much, and they’d need to leave a gap for the fire and smoke but in short order, with Kelly’s help once she realised what Lena was doing, they had two lean-to’s constructed against the rocky wall behind them, triangulated with the fire. 

     

                Setting more wood onto the fire, making it smoke as the damp bark tried to catch, she dusted off her gloves and picked up her pack. Crawling into one of the lean-to’s, Lena shoved her pack into as comfortable a position as she could make and sank onto the cold, hard ground, curling in on herself. She had her hood pulled up, fastened closed at the front, only a small circle showing her face, and she burrowed into her warmth, feeling the radiating heat of the fire at her feet. A minute later, a pair of boots blocked out the light of the fire and Eliza shoved her pack in beside Lena’s crawling into the low space.

     

                “You’re with me,” Eliza stated the obvious. “We’ll go back-to-back.”

     

                Rolling over without a sound, Lena closed her eyes, a small pucker between her eyebrows, and scooted backwards as Eliza stretched out beside her, until her back met the firm presence of the doctor. Tugging her hood securely down over her face, Lena hugged her arms to her chest and tried to sleep. As exhausted as she was, body bruised and aching, it was hard to come, the sound of the wind whistling through the gaps in the wood, the rustling of leaves, bushes and branches putting her on edge for the sound of advancing agents, but she eventually did sleep. 

     

                It wasn’t particularly warm, even with the fire near to her feet and Eliza at her back, curled in on herself to conserve her body heat, but they didn’t freeze and Lena woke with the mortifying realisation that she’d rolled over during the night, her gloved hand gripping a fistful of Eliza’s snowsuit and her face pressed into her shoulder blades. Jerking up with her heart lurching in her chest, pounding with panic as she frantically looked around through the pale grey of pre-dawn light, Lena felt stiff and tense as she blinked away sleep. 

     

                The adrenaline waned quickly, leaving her dragging in quick, shallow breaths as she realised there was no danger, pulling the chin of her hood apart so she could breathe in the damp air. The fire had gone down to wet ashes and she crawled out of the lean-to and scrabbled for some of the wood they’d set aside, piling it on and fumbling with the matches with her clumsy gloved hands, filling the air with smoke as she coughed and sputtered until it was lit. The noise she was making roused Eliza, who sat up in the shelter behind her and reached out to touch Lena’s back, startling her.

     

                Letting out a rough sound of surprise, Lena skittered away and glanced back with wide eyes, sprawled on a damp patch of leaves. “It’s alright,” Eliza softly called to her. “It’s just me.”

     

                Squeezing her eyes shut, Lena shook her head and pushed herself up, climbing to her feet to get her blood flowing, her joints stiff and aching as she stretched her limbs. She slowly walked away from their makeshift camp, feeling cold all the way through, her lungs aching and her footsteps slightly unsteady as a headache pounded behind her eyes and the taste of the campfire clung to the back of her throat.

     

                Walking until she hit the road, Lena sank onto the dirt and stared down the long expanse of gravel vanishing into the distance, wondering how long it would take for a car to pass by. After a few minutes, her head clearer and her stomach rumbling, she retraced her footsteps to the camp where the others had risen and were heating a meagre breakfast in the fire she’d lit and Kelly had fanned bigger. 

     

                “So … what’s the plan?” Kelly ventured after they’d finished a tin of beef stew and a muesli bar each.

     

                “We stick to the shoulder of the road and follow it south,” Lena murmured, staring into the fire. “This part isn’t very populated but tourists and outdoorsy people will be on the road. We’ll try and hitch a ride, say our car broke down at our campsite.”

     

                “Alright, well, the daylight’s wasting,” Kelly agreed, climbing to her feet and kicking ashes over the flames until they guttered and died.

     

                They gathered their packs and made their way to the road, doing just as Lena said, the heavy clouds opening up on them as they walked, heads bowed and rain pattering against their shoulders, the wind buffeting them along in a staggering rush. The road wasn’t completely abandoned, although it was very isolated, with poor visibility and the bad conditions making it only suitable for the trucks travelling back and forth Deadhorse in the north, and within an hour of walking down the sloping elevation of the mountain passes, a truck blared past. Unfortunately, it was heading in the wrong direction.

     

                Walking onwards, passing by grave markers along the poorly maintained road, trying not to slip in puddles and pitted sections as they kept to the side, not wanting to be wiped out by a truck heading their way, they kept going. An hour turned into two, and then three, miserable and cold, so cold that Lena almost wished they were in the shelter of the crude lean-to’s, Eliza at her back and the fire at her feet so at least she could feel even a little bit warm. 

     

                It wasn’t until the fourth hour that a truck passed them by, the four women desperately staggering towards the road, waving their arms, shouting uselessly. But luck was on their side, the red tail lights visible as the driver slammed on their breaks, the semi-trailer screeching to a halt dozens of feet away as they hobbled after it, practically weak with relief at the thought of the warm cab, of not walking for a while. 

     

                Eliza reached the truck first, the driver climbing out of his idling 18-wheeler as he jerked up his hood, rounding the front of the cab to speak to the doctor. Somewhat sheepish and apologetic, Eliza recounted the story of their bad luck with their car engine troubles and a flat tyre, gesturing to the other three women as they closed the gap between them. The man looked a little wary and a little concerned as his eyes flitted back and forth.

     

                “It’s a dangerous road, ma’am, I’d say you weren’t thinking well at all to come out here in a car. Most folks wouldn’t dare risk it, not with all the dangers.”

     

                “I know,” Eliza self-deprecatingly laughed, ducking her head slightly. “It was silly of us to think the worst of the weather was over this time of year. We’d talked about it for years, you see, coming with my husband - that was before he passed away a few years back - so I thought I’d come with the girls. These two, my daughters.”

     

                Lena didn’t so much as blink when Eliza reached out to touch her shoulder after Alex’s back.

     

                “And my daughter-in-law,” Eliza finished up, touching Kelly’s arm. 

     

                Keeping her head ducked down, trying to avoid the man’s gaze, Lena hitched her backpack higher as Eliza kept talking, spinning the story as the man grew increasingly impatient. A moment later, he took a step back and gestured to the truck.
