                “Alright, well, I can’t stop, I need to keep going. I’ll be heading back to Fairbanks, of course. Not much place else to go this way. It’ll be a tight squeeze but I can’t leave you out here alone so … hop in.”

     

                They scrambled up into the cab, one after the other, Eliza waving them up before she climbed in to take the seat beside the driver. The cab only had two seats and room behind them for the mattress wedged in with blankets and pillows. No one had any complaints about the arrangements though, warm inside the cab as they hunkered down on the mattress, damp and shivering as the three women made themselves comfortable. 

     

                Lena was unfortunate to find herself in the middle of the two women, thanks to their mismanaged boarding, and she passed the pillows on to Alex so she could comfortably lean against the side of the cab, away from Lena’s shoulder. For her own comfort, the best she could do was draw her knees to her chest and wedge her backpack between her legs, her eyes watching the man from the sliver of his face she could see in the rearview mirror and the back of his neck from behind the headrest. Her trust didn’t go a long way, and a stranger on the road - no matter how helpful - was likely to be trusted even less than the three women who’d treated her in prison.

     

                Still, it was warm, almost stiflingly so once they’d gotten going again, too many bodies in the cramped space leaving them practically roasting in their snowsuits, but none of them complained. They’d been so cold that it was a relief to be so warm, especially after the danger of exposure last night, and Lena felt herself dozing, her eyelids growing heavy as she leaned against the back of the cab, jostling along as the voices of Eliza and the driver washed over her. 

     

                It was hours of driving and she woke with the movement of the semi-trailer rattling along the treacherous roads, shadows beneath her eyes as she blinked slowly, aware of Kelly pressed up on one side of her, aware of the knots in her shoulders from her coiled anticipation of something going wrong. Had he recognised them? Would he be able to radio someone and tip them off? As tired as she was, the jolt of worry hit Lena and she resolved to stay awake for the remainder of the trip, her mind turning to the pistol at the top of her backpack, wondering if it would be safer to kill the driver at their next stop, tie up loose ends even if it meant leaving a trail.

     

                She was still pondering the moral dilemma of killing the man who had helped them when she heard a faint droning sound over the noise of the truck, leaning forward as her expression turned severe. Staring out the window, her eyes darted back and forth across the wide expanse visible through the windscreen and she spotted the shape of something flying towards them.

     

                “What’s that?” she rasped, voice thick with sleep.

     

                “The chopper? It regularly flies this route for any emergencies. In all likelihood, they would’ve found you at your car if you hadn’t gone walking off,” the driver gruffly replied. “Ain’t much in the way of gas stops and emergency services along the highway so they have to do something to keep an eye out for accidents and the like.”

     

                “Oh,” she murmured, sinking back.

     

                Her mind quickly ran through the likelihood that they’d find the chopper, half-buried in shrubs and trees amidst the relatively sparse backdrop of the mountains. It would stick out like a sore thumb and after a quick investigation, it would be glaringly obvious where it had come from. It wouldn’t take long for the proper authorities to be contacted, the bodies of the two agents Kelly had shot up in Boulder undoubtedly found by now, and Lena had to swallow her curses at the obvious trail they were leaving behind. And now this driver knew too much and Lena resolved to do what had to be done to keep them alive.

     

                She’d been asleep when they’d passed through the small town of Coldfoot, not much there and no real opportunity for help with the limited population, Eliza desperately asking the driver to take them as far as he was going. Now, she didn’t risk sleeping, not with the threat of being found out hanging over them, and even though it was almost another seven hours to Fairbanks, most of the day eaten up in the cramped cab as their legs went numb and stiff and they shared muesli bars with the driver, seeming like four women interested in the outdoors as they stayed silent. 

     

                The CD player crooned quiet music and it was already heading towards late afternoon by the time they headed into Fairbanks, further south now and already getting dark. He waited just until they were far enough into the city limits to drop them off, pulling into a gas station and glancing over at Eliza.

     

                “Right, well, you ladies should be alright from here, I’d reckon.”

     

                “Yes, thank you so much for your help. You’re a lifesaver, literally,” Eliza said with a warm smile.

     

                In the back of the cab, Lena unzipped the backpack, reaching her hand in as she kept her eyes on the side of the man’s head from her point of view. She swallowed thickly, audibly, wondering if she had it in her to kill someone, to shoot him at such close range, her stomach twisting at the thought of blood and brains in the cab. But she’d spent enough time around blood and brains before, had seen multiple dead bodies, had enough of an interest in biology to have studied them up close and wouldn’t have considered herself a queasy person. 

     

                Steeling herself, she made to jerk the gun out of her bag and felt the vice-like grip of fingers around her right arm, strong as it pinned her wrist in place. Eyes flashing with anger, Lena glanced sideways at Kelly, who continued to stare straight ahead, as if she didn’t know what Lena was trying to do, as if nothing was amiss. She didn’t draw attention to them, just squeezed tight enough for Lena to heed her warning, letting go of the pistol and yanking her hand free. Reaching over, Kelly zipped the backpack up and gripped the top of it in a fist, covering the zips with her hand to stop Lena from trying again.

     

                The truck came to a final stop and Eliza opened the door to climb out, gathering up her bag and pocketing her trash, making a ditzy show of checking her belongings before she thanked him and climbed out. Tearing her bag from Kelly’s grasp, annoyed, Lena passed through the middle of the two seats and thanked the man, keeping her head turned away from him, disembarking onto the damp concrete below, tugging her hood up. She turned as Alex came next, face taut and eyes slightly glazed with pain, and Lena grimaced as she stepped forward to help her down, reaching up to take the brunt of her weight as she gingerly lowered herself to the ground, her lips bloodless as her brown eyes flickered to Lena’s face, a mumbled thanks offered up. 

     

                Kelly hopped down last, thanking the man with forced enthusiasm and sincere gratitude as she hoisted her backpack higher up, nodding and then shutting the door. The truck was still idling and the man slowly accelerated away from them, leaving the four women huddled together for a moment until Eliza walked into the gas station to ask for directions to a bus station or some other form of transportation southwards. Emerging with directions scrawled on the back of an old receipt, she pointed them in the right direction.

     

                “Here,” Kelly murmured, nudging Lena and holding out a trucker cap she’d stolen from the back of the cab, smuggled out for Lena’s use. “You won’t look so recognisable.”

     

                Snorting at the flimsy excuse of a disguise, Lena still thanked her and gratefully tugged it down low over her face, the beaver on the front of the cap making her seem more like the type of woman they were pretending to be. She quickened her pace to fall into step beside Eliza as the doctor led them down the road.

     

                “Unless you’re planning on preying on a bus driver’s empathy,” Lena started, narrowing her eyes as she stared ahead through the waning light of the blue dusk, “there’s no chance we’re going to get on a Greyhound south. We’d have better luck jacking a car; I’ll get my mom to track down the owner and wire money afterwards.”

     

                “We’re not stealing an innocent person’s car.”

     

                “And we’re not shooting anyone else,” Kelly pointedly replied from behind Lena.

     

                “No one said anything about shooting,” Eliza placatingly replied.

     

                Glancing over her shoulder, Lena raised her eyebrows and Kelly gave her a pointed look but didn’t pursue the issue. Lena knew that it probably was for the best to not leave an eighteen-wheeler idling on the outskirts of the city with a dead driver behind the wheel. He’d be quickly discovered and it would lead an even obvious trail to them - not that it wouldn’t have been obvious where they were heading, considering the lack of places to go - which was the opposite of what they were hoping to achieve. Even buying themselves an hour or two unnoticed in Fairbanks could make all the difference.

     

                “But it’s fine, we can buy tickets.”

     

                “Sorry, was there a secret salary you were being paid for treating all of the inmates that we were unaware of?” Lena scoffed, her gaze sceptical as she glanced sideways at Eliza.

     

                “No, there was petty cash at the black site though. Not a lot; just under a thousand dollars. Fake IDs too for the agents but they wouldn’t have worked for any of us. Either way, we can buy bus tickets to Anchorage and I assume you’ll take it from there?”

     

                Nodding, Lena had nothing else to say but was glad for Eliza’s foresight to grab what cash had been stashed at the black site before they’d left. 

     

                They had to walk for another hour before finding the bus station, a row of coaches lined up with kiosks, vending machines and the ticket booth lined up. There were people as well, so many people going about their lives that it was unnerving to see so much mundanity on display. Lena couldn’t remember the last time she’d seen so many in one place - at least ones that hadn’t wanted to hurt her - and it made her chest feel tight with panic, even as they passed by or milled about oblivious to the four escapees amidst them.

     

                “We need to split up,” Lena softly said, her eyes scanning people walking past, cautious and on edge. “Our faces will be everywhere.”

     

                “Yours,” Alex murmured, her attention darting to Lena. “No one else knows we’re out. They think it’s only you.”

     

                Lena sneered as her eyes hardened, “lucky for you, then. Still, four people can attract too much attention, and that’s the last thing we need.”

     

                “Four people will give you more cover. We’re just four women on a trip to Alaska, watching the bears come out of hibernation. It’s fine, it’s good, it’ll get us where we need to go.”

     

                “We’re heading towards Anchorage; that’s away from any sort of wilderness retreat bullshit you want to spin.”

     

                “Well, yes, people typically do go home after a holiday,” Alex flippantly replied.

     

                Eliza reached out to grab both of their arms, squeezing tightly as she shot them warning looks. “You two are going to draw more attention to us with your bickering than anything else. We stick together. Alex, go and buy four tickets. Kelly, you buy snacks. Maybe get a newspaper too.”

     

                She handed over a few folded bills to Alex and Kelly, watching the two of them walk off as Lena hung back, surly with her arms folded over her chest. Cap pulled down low over her face, she saw other people with bulging packs and sturdy boots, thick coats and gloves and all manner of outdoor equipment to make use of in Denali National Park, although snowsuits were glaringly absent with the weather too warm for it at that time of year as far south as they were. There was nothing to be done for the matching black ensembles of the four women though, except to hope everyone else was too preoccupied with their own trips, boarding and disembarking the buses that came and went, to take any notice of them.

     

                Alex was back first with four tickets in hand and Kelly returned a few minutes later, handing off bottles of water and handing Eliza the newspaper before she tore open a packet of chips. They all removed their thick gloves and shared the packets, as well as the bag of Sour Patch Kids she’d bought, setting their packs down and making an effort to talk and laugh at Kelly’s instruction, although the best Lena could manage was a twitch of her lips and a tightening at the corner of her eyes. 

     

                They waited forty minutes for their bus, queuing at their stand with the other passengers, and Eliza showed the driver their tickets before they climbed on board, filing to the back and claiming four seats, two in front of the other, on the left side. Lena filed into the window seat and Eliza sat beside her, their bags at their feet, with Alex and Kelly in front of them. It was ten minutes before the bus was on its way, the lights dimmed and the seats mostly full as the driver set off south.

     

                It was a nine-hour bus ride and Lena cursed every wasted minute of it, having already lost so much precious time since leaving the black site, and now wasting more on the slow ride towards Anchorage. The first couple of hours were filled with the palpable hum of quiet conversation, the sound of bags of snacks being opened and the general noise of a few dozen people crammed in close quarters, and Lena leaned her head against the window as they rattled along, closing her eyes and trying to resist the restless urge to fidget. 

     

                She was safe for now though, which was more than she could say for Kara, a pit in her stomach as she found herself reaching up to worry her fingers over her chapped lips. A single kiss, holding so much potential, so much confusion. Was it fuelled by the moment, by a brief moment of joy and adrenaline at the freedom they’d wrangled amidst the death and chaos they had wrought? Or had it meant something, something that Lena had never had for herself, forged in the loneliness of the prison, exacerbated by the round-the-clock time they’d spent together, getting to know the parts of each other that hadn’t been shared in so long, so many doubts and fears, vulnerabilities, dreams and wishes? Lena would do everything within her power to get the answer from Kara’s own lips when she pulled her from the depths of the sea and never let her go again.

     

                Unfortunately, that seemed an eternity away, the possibility of finding her, getting her out slipping further out of reach with each mile they drove away from her. Brooding over thoughts of Kara, over the puzzle of conducting a rescue mission, of evading capture long enough to do that, Lena eventually slipped off into sleep, swaying with the motion of the bus as her body sank into the blissful relief of hours of uninterrupted rest. And she needed it too, desperately, her body aching and bruised, feet blistered and bleeding in the thick socks she wore. And it was so warm too, the heat generated from so many bodies making them sweat in their snowsuits but none of them complained. The four of them just slept.

     

                They all woke periodically throughout the night, roused by a rough patch, roused by a cough or someone brushing past to use the restroom. For the most part, the four escapees slept though, all other needs set aside as they caught up on as much rest as possible in the uncomfortable upright position of their seats. The bus trundled southwards and the sun steadily rose and by the time Lena fully awoke, they were almost into Anchorage.

     

                When they pulled into the bus depot, they rose stiffly and filed off the bus with their bags, dry-eyed and not as rested as they would have liked, developing knots and aches in new places. Flagging a cab, Eliza asked the driver to drop them off at the Anchorage Public Library, using their sparse cash to pay for the trip, before repeating it with a trip to a coffee shop a block away from the university, before they flagged a final third cab and Lena gave the address near enough to a small building she owned across the city.

     

                They were dropped off near a pub and Lena led the way with the directions pulled from the depths of her mind, taking them to a narrow three-story building with a garage door covered in graffiti and boarded up. Using the two keypads to get them through the two sets of doors, she led them into the garage where an inconspicuous black Chevy RAM truck was parked, the windows tinted dark and in pristine condition. Of course, it hadn’t been driven in a long time, perhaps a couple of years, and as Lena murmured for everyone to take a seat or stretch their legs, she spent an hour attaching a new battery, swapping the oil and fan belt, lubricating the cylinder walls and replacing the coolant before she tried to start it and the engine rumbled to life.

     

                Piling into the truck, they all buckled up and Lena used the garage remote kept inside the truck to open it before backing out onto the narrow road behind the building. Shutting the garage door, she slowly set off down the road, passing by boarded-up businesses and dumpsters full of trash. It had been years since the last time she’d been in Anchorage but she still remembered the route through the city, moving with the flow of traffic, sticking to the speed limits and braking at lights, not wanting to draw unwanted attention to the inconspicuous car. She’d chosen that truck for the specific reason that it was the most popular in the state, just one of many going about its day, and she drove the Chevy to the industrial area without any issues.

     

                Slowing as she drove past grey warehouses and factories, Lena knew she was getting close to hers, nestled amidst two others she’d purchased under different shell companies as an added buffer for any undue attention. Finally coming to an idling stop outside a rusting chain link gate, she put the truck in park and opened the door, fishing a key out of the glove box and jumping out onto the asphalt below. 

     

                Glass and gravel crunched beneath her feet as she walked over to the padlock, fitting the key in and twisting, forcing the tumbling mechanisms to move with a little extra pressure. The lock clicked apart and she let the chain slither through the links before she dragged one half of the gate open and then the other before climbing back into the truck. Driving through, she paused again to lock up behind them and stowed the key before continuing across a yard of broken machinery, empty oil drums and rotted crates and pallets covered in filthy tarps and plastic sheeting. It could have been one of any warehouses along this section from the outside.

     

                There was another remote in the glovebox of the truck and Lena pushed the button to open the roller door of the warehouse’s loading bay, waiting patiently as it creaked and groaned its way up. It was large enough for the likes of the semi-truck they’d ridden to Fairbanks in and she drove the Chevy into the dark confines of the warehouse before closing the roller door behind them and killing the engine.

     

                Slamming her door shut behind her, Lena breathed in the smell of damp concrete and stale air as she moved blindly through the space. The power mains were nearby and she felt the tightness of unease in her chest as she moved through the dark, the sounds of the other three women climbing out of the truck and slamming the doors loud and echoing in the cavernous space. There was a draught, a chill to the warehouse that wasn’t the freezing temperatures they were used to but was uncomfortable all the same and Lena didn’t waste any time finding the mains box and flipping the switches for the lights beside it.

     

                Flood Lights flickered to life, casting a white harshness over the grey confines of the warehouse from where they hung from overhead beams. It was almost bare, a few pallets of carefully packaged necessities covered with tarps dotted in between machinery and equipment for any repairs she could conceive of ever needing, a wall lined with stacks of oil drums, filled with fuel for the car so she could avoid gas stations, and reinforced steel shuttered at every opening, hidden by the boarded up windows that made it look abandoned from the outside.

     

                Moving through a door off the ground floor, there was a spacious area that was originally a break room and had been upgraded somewhat to the basic utilitarian living standards for a secret hideout. There was a fridge, humming as it kept the bottles of water chilled, a camp bed tucked into one corner and a kettle on top of a counter, beside a stainless steel sink. Cranking a heater, Lena felt the pleasant brush of warm air caress her cheeks as she pulled off her gloves and moved over to the fridge to get a drink. Cracking the seal on the bottle, she took a swig as the other three joined her, filling the middle of the space, which was decently sized, and looking around. Kelly met her gaze as Eliza led Alex over to the camp bed, easing her down onto it.

     

                “This is it?” Kelly asked.

     

                “There’s a control room upstairs,” Lena replied, gesturing towards the damp-stained ceiling. “Bathroom next door as well. Hot water should be working once the gas is turned on.”

     

                Breezing back out of the room, Lena climbed the rickety staircase up to the office, rust staining her hands as she hauled herself up with the handrail, the steps groaning as her heavy snow boots stomped up them. Opening the door to the refurbished office, she flipped the lights on and stared at the wall of computer monitors, radar equipment, frequency scanners, stacked towers of stored data and bundles of extra equipment, printers, cameras, burner phones and computer hardware that she might have needed shoved into boxes or beneath the desk. 

     

                There was a safe as well, large enough to hide a few pistols, tasers, bundles of cash and credit cards under different names, and a rather extensive collection of fake IDs and foreign passports she’d forged herself with the use of the equipment in that room. She’d need to make them for the other three women too, once she had the time, once Kara was safe. She’d need to make four.

     

                Turning on the computers, she was satisfied by the hum and faint whir of the towers as they powered up, the screens flaring to life. Kneeling in front of the safe, she took another sip of water and unlocked it, using her keycode and fingerprint to access the interior, sifting through the contents to reassure herself that everything was as it should have been. Locking it behind her, she pushed herself to her feet and looked out the windows overlooking the warehouse below. 

     

                Feeling some of the tension unwind at the familiarity of a place she’d only frequented a few times, more homely and comforting than any place she’d been since they’d dragged her out of bed in the middle of the night. Sipping her water for a minute longer as she tried to plan her next move, she broke off her thoughts and screwed the cap back on, retreating downstairs to pick up her pack and fetch the phone she’d brought with her.

     

                As she stepped back into the breakroom, Eliza and Kelly glanced over at her as they broke off their conversation. Arching an eyebrow as she bypassed them and crouched beside her pack, unzipping it, Lena couldn’t help the stab of annoyance, the thin patience from her exhaustion and gut-wrenching worry for Kara.

     

                “Don’t stop on my account,” she said aloud, feeling their gazes shift over to the side of her face.

     

                “We were just discussing a supply run. Kelly and I-“

     

                “That’s too risky,” Lena interrupted.

     

                Sighing, Eliza grimaced. “Unless you have accommodation upstairs, we have one bed between the four of us. I’m sure you have decent supplies here, by way of food, but we need something fresh. Nutritious. Not processed and dried rations. Alex needs medicine.”

     

                “I have a stocked First Aid kit, of course.”

     

                “Of course but that doesn’t help with the rest of it.”

     

                “I’m not risking anything else until Kara’s been saved - and it’s my car.”

     

                “You won’t be coming,” Kelly informed her.

     

                Snorting, Lena turned to meet her gaze, raising her eyebrows. “If you think I trust either of you out of my sight for even a second-“

     

                “What do you think we’re going to do? Lead them right back to you, here? Where my sick girlfriend is holed up with a wanted criminal?”

     

                “We need supplies? Fine. But I’m going with one of you.”

     

                Making a sound of objection at the back of her throat, Eliza shook her head, already unzipping her pack and withdrawing the crumpled newspaper Kelly had handed her the evening before. She unfolded it and held it out to Lena, who was drawn forward by uneasy curiosity. Her stomach sank at the sight of her face on the front page and she snatched it from Eliza’s grasp, poring over the small text.

     

                “You’ll be in every news outlet. It’s too risky. We’re not going to betray you, not even if Alex’s life wasn’t on the line. Trust me.”

     

                Lena scoffed and that was all the response she was willing to give on that matter but her interest was consumed by the article now, and she had to call her mom. Dimly acknowledging the fact that they did need more supplies - it was a place furnished for one person - and fresh food would be good after so many months with a poor excuse for freshness, Lena waved a hand dismissively.

     

                “Fine. Keys are in the truck. Do whatever you want; I don’t really care.”

     

                “There’s just-“ Eliza faltered, wringing her hands. “Well, most of the cash I found paid for the tickets and the cabs and-“

     

                Swallowing a sound of frustration, Lena slapped the newspaper down on the counter and stalked out of the room. Cursing under her breath as she stomped upstairs, she withdrew a wad of cash from the safe and deliberated over the credit card before deciding it wouldn’t be much help if neither of them had an ID to present for any big purchases that cash couldn’t cover. 

     

                Walking back downstairs, she handed Eliza the cash and then picked up the newspaper again. It was a speculative piece about her sudden disappearance, whether she had been incarcerated, questioning the lack of a trial in that case, plus a lengthy section on her family, including her mother’s vocal and monetary support of President Baker and his anti-alien sentiments. It made Lena angry and she screwed the newspaper into a ball and tossed it into the trash, bracing herself against the counter of the kitchenette and raking a hand through her greasy hair.

     

                The break room was silent, a strange tension in the air, and she could hear the sound of the truck’s engine beyond the room as Eliza opened the roller door and backed out. That made her angry too, and Lena felt as if she was nothing more than a ball of frustration these days, her patience wearing thin, her nerves fraying. This wasn’t how it was supposed to have been.

     

                “You don’t have to worry about any of us turning you in, you know,” Alex replied after a minute.

     

                Lena straightened and tipped her head back, eyes closed and a weary sigh escaping her. She didn’t have the patience to withstand the ex-agent.

     

                “Don’t I?” Lena muttered.

     

                “How long are you planning on not trusting us? Because it’s going to be a lot harder to find Kara if-“

     

                “I’ll be six feet under and I still won’t trust you. You’ve done nothing to earn it. Not even taking a bullet for me is enough, so save it.”

     

                Alex let out a weak laugh, coughing as she smiled thinly at Lena’s back, pressing a hand to her aching shoulder. “I didn’t take a bullet for you to convince you to trust me. But we need to work together to rescue her, and it was only because we worked together that we made it out of the prison.”

     

                Whirling around, Lena gave her a derisive look, her mouth twisting with contemptuous amusement. “The only reason we made it out is because of Kara. We can pat ourselves on the back all we want about how well we planned and timed it but let’s not kid ourselves; without her, we wouldn’t have made it past the first section. Hell, without her, you never would have even considered helping me, so don’t preach to me about teamwork. I’ve worked alone my whole life and I’m sure I’ll manage just fine without you. Next time you take a bullet for someone, try and make sure it’s fatal so I don’t have to put up with you any longer.”

     

                Storming out of the room, she bristled with anger that made her vision dim at the edges, Alex’s words floating after her. “Well, next time it won’t be for you, that’s for sure. You’re a real asshole, you know that?”

     

                Ignoring her, Lena yanked open the door to the storage closet and fetched a packaged pair of cotton drill coveralls and the other packaged clothing items before slipping into the bathroom. A cupboard held towels and products and she selected what she needed as the water ran, the pipes groaning from years of disuse as it slowly warmed up. It was a pleasant sensation to kick off the too-big boots that had rubbed her feet raw and bloody through the thick socks, to strip off the thickly padded snowsuit and several layers underneath. 

     

                By the time Lena peeled off the thinner inner thermals, her skin was pimpling from the cold and steam was starting to billow from the shower stall. It felt like a luxury as she stepped beneath the hot water, a few degrees too hot just for the sake of the warmth, and she shampooed her hair and scrubbed her body clean, blood and sweat rinsed away with the dirt. Conditioning her hair for the first time in months, Lena lingered in the shower as she let it settle in before she rinsed it off and felt a weight off her shoulders as she stepped out and wrapped herself in a clean towel.

     

                She dressed in her thinner layers, feeling the cool of the place but grateful to leave the harsher weather garments behind, and then brushed her teeth, applied deodorant and snagged a pair of scissors before trimming a few inches off the bottom of her frustratingly long hair. She hadn’t had a haircut in eight months, hadn’t had a razor, hadn’t had nail clippers, nothing. It felt good to trim the split ends and clip her nails, basic things that she’d taken for granted.

     

                Feeling more human when she emerged, she paused before stepping into the breakroom and casting a fleeting glance at Alex before grabbing the brick-like phone. Hesitating as she turned to go, she grimaced.

     

                “The bathroom is outside, to your left, if you want a shower. Clothes are in the supply closet; it’s all in my size but we’re about the same.”

     

                “Thanks.”

     

                Nodding, she stalked outside, walking across the warehouse as she dialled her mother’s number. Muscles strung tightly, Lena paced, chewing her chapped lips as she felt the pressure of her self-imposed deadline pressing down on her. Truthfully, she had no way of knowing how long she had to pull the prison out of the sea, how long Kara and the others could survive in there, what the situation with food and water was, or even if there was oxygen. It made her chest feel tight with panic.

     

                “Hello?”

     

                “It’s me. We got away, we’re somewhere safe.”

     

                “Are you sure? Reports are saying they’re looking everywhere for you. Nationwide manhunt.”

     

                “As safe as I can be,” Lena amended, rubbing her forehead. “There’s safety in numbers. The others I’m with are unrecognisable; the DEO won’t even know they’re out.”

     

                “Right,” Lillian flatly replied before pausing a moment. “If you tell me where you are, I’ll send a man to fetch you. I have the house in Ecuador-”

     

                “I’ve told you - I can’t run. You said you’d help me recover the prison.”

     

                “And I will but you need to be safe first. Hell, go to Ireland - better yet, go to the Irish Embassy. I’ll charter my jet to take you to Washington and you can seek asylum.”

     

                “Mom,” Lena snapped, her patience worn thin. “No. No, I’m not doing that. I don’t care if that’s what you think I should do but it’s not going to help. I’ll just end up trapped inside a nicer prison while the government tries to knock down the door.”

     

                Lillian scathingly scoffed. “Well, this isn’t enough! Your story is being swept aside; the government is insisting that you fled the country on charges of embezzlement and tax fraud and the only ones who believe that the government has done something to you are those QAnon conspiracy theorists but they’re not exactly credible. Your words aren’t enough to clear your name.”

     

                Exhaling sharply, Lena pinched the bridge of her nose, turning on her heel and pacing back across the warehouse. “That’s all I have. I didn’t escape prison with a USB of DEO documents detailing the things they did to us all, did I?”

     

                “Pity you didn’t.”

     

                “So, what now? Is there someone else you can call or-”

     

                “Now … I’m starting to question whether the effort it will require for me to straighten out this mess would benefit me,” Lillian mused.

     

                Laughing hollowly, Lena’s lips twitched with a smile as her green eyes flashed with anger. “Of course. What can you get out of it, right? It’s not enough to help your daughter-”

     

                “Oh, don’t be like that, Lena. I love you, you know that I do. But that love was never supposed to extend to exonerating you, and it certainly doesn’t extend to hauling a prison from the depths of the ocean to save some alien you grew attached to. Why can’t you be content with my setting you up in a safe house overseas, where it will be nice and easy for me to pay off the local authorities? Most people in your situation would be grateful for that.”

     

                “There isn’t anyone else in my situation,” Lena stiffly replied. “If you’re not going to help then forget it. Forget I ever called; that should be quite easy, considering this is the most we’ve talked in years.”

     

                “Don’t be like that, I-”

     

                “I have to go.”

     

                “Lena,” Lillian sharply replied. “I’m trying to do what’s best for you but-”

     

                “I-”

     

                “But if this is what you want, if you want to risk your freedom, your own life , fine, I will continue to try for you. Get me real evidence, real proof, and then I’ll be able to help rescue that alien for you.”

     

                Pausing for a moment, wary and uncertain, Lena gently cleared her throat. “Kara. Her name is Kara.”

     

                “Well …”

     

                “I’ll try my best.”

     

                “And so will I. I promise you. Set aside your old grudges and trust me.”

     

                Mouth thinning, her trust not even fully extending to her mother without mountains of suspicion and doubt, Lena hummed noncommittally. “Thank you.”

     

                “We won’t talk until after you’ve given me what you can find. I’d suggest trying to be quick.”

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes as she hung up, closing her eyes for a moment, shoulders hunched as she stood in the middle of the warehouse for a minute longer. Raking a hand through her damp hair, she wandered back to the breakroom, absent of Alex, and made a bee-line for the kettle, digging out a tub of instant coffee with masked eagerness as she set the water to boil and waited. She hesitated and grabbed a second cup, adding two teaspoons of the grounds to it and filling them both with water. There was plenty of shelf-stabled powdered milk but Lena couldn’t be bothered with the effort of mixing it with water to add a splash to each mug, and besides, she hadn’t tasted coffee in so long that the bitter taste of it would be welcome.

     

                Taking a sip of her own, she closed her eyes as her shoulders slumped, some sense of normalcy rushing through her. It could’ve been any other night in her lab, puzzling over a new device and fuelling herself with another cup of coffee as the hour grew later. Instead, she was a fugitive trying her best to keep it together and focus on the sole task of rescuing her friend, and she didn’t have time to waste crying over something as trivially cherished as a cup of coffee. And it wasn’t even a good cup, not the freshly ground beans and espresso drip of the hissing machine at her favourite coffee shop she’d frequented, but the cheap tin of it that would be fine to sit on a shelf and gather dust for a few years in the off-chance she found herself in a sticky situation.

     

                Alex walked in as she was enjoying her second sip, and Lena turned at the sound of footsteps, watching as the guard towelled the ends of her reddish hair, raising her eyebrows as she met Lena’s gaze. “Did you call your mom?”

     

                “Mhm.”

     

                “And?”

     

                Shrugging, Lena took another sip of coffee, prolonging the moment of silence before she swallowed and lowered her mug, turning to walk over to the small table and dragging out the chair. She set her coffee down and sat, leaning back comfortably as her body ached from the ordeal of the last few days, and then she sighed defeatedly.

     

                “Apparently my version of events isn’t sufficient enough evidence for the general public to believe the government when they say none of it happened. So now I’m a wanted fugitive and we’re all fucked if they find us because I can’t clear my name without any actual evidence and if I don’t clear my name, I won’t be able to access any of the equipment I need to find Kara. And my mother’s love apparently doesn’t extend to finding the prison for me so the only way she’s really interested in helping is if I had something to prove what happened.”

     

                Finishing her rant, Lena clenched her jaw and toyed with her cup before she jerked her chin towards the other one sitting on the counter. “Coffee, if you wanted it.”

     

                “Thanks,” Alex said, crossing over to pick it up and taking a swig.

     

                She crossed back over to the cot she’d commandeered, taking a seat and setting the coffee cup down on the concrete floor before dragging her pack closer. Unzipping one of the little front pockets on the pack, she rummaged around and then pulled out a tiny thing, about the size of her thumb. It took Lena a second to realise it was a USB.

     

                “You know, I may not have officially graduated high school or had an Ivy League college education,” Alex repeated her words from two days prior with amusement, “but I was smart enough to save as many DEO classified documents to this as I could while we had access to the black site computers.”

     

                Lena had turned in her seat and went still at her words, a ripple of well-masked surprise crossing her face. Taking a sip of coffee, she set her cup down and cleared her throat before climbing to her feet.

     

                “For the record, I went to MIT; it’s not an Ivy League college,” Lena haughtily replied, plucking the USB from Alex’s hand and then walking upstairs to the computers.

     

                Plugging it in, she ran VPN software and used an untraceable email account, attaching numerous documents across half a dozen emails and sending them all to one of her mother’s old emails she remembered. She wasn’t sure if Lillian still monitored the account but she’d occasionally been sent papers, articles and links from it over the years, even when they hadn’t been talking, and it was the best bet she could think of, short of calling her mother back again.

     

                Ten minutes after sending them, she received an email back, a short, three-word reply; this will do.

     

     

                Two weeks since their escape passed by in the blink of an eye, with Lena growing more restless and short-tempered with each passing day. It didn’t help that the next dose of the birth control shots Eliza had given her monthly was weeks overdue, which had caused her period to start again, a lamentable annoyance without the added frustration of getting absolutely nowhere in terms of rescuing Kara. Then there was the issue of the close quarters they all resided in, the three extra camp beds Eliza and Kelly had come back with making for a very cosy breakroom with them all lined up in a row, able to reach out and touch each other if they tried. There was also the tiring cherry on top of their clashing personalities - or rather, Lena clashing with the others out of sheer stubborn dislike.

     

                It didn’t help that Alex had offered her up the golden ticket to debunk every lie the government had told about Lena’s absence, articles and journalists and news anchors talking about it non-stop as the documents circulated through the current news cycle. It didn’t help that their stolen helicopter and the bodies at the black site had been found, leaving a trail for a few agencies to follow, even if they evaded capture so far with Lena as the only suspected fugitive. It didn’t help that the White House was scrambling, trying to cover the story that President Barker had signed the paperwork himself for her unlawful imprisonment. It didn’t help anything. Lena’s mood grew fouler, no matter what went right for them. To her, nothing would be right until Kara was breathing in the fresh air as a free woman again. 

     

                Still, even with the classified documents and noise they were making, the government stubbornly insisted that it had all been falsified, or at the very least were unverifiable. The four women were frustrated and grasping at straws, holed up inside the warehouse together, trying their best, which just simply wasn’t good enough. 

     

                It was getting very close to three weeks since their escape when things gave. Perhaps most shocking of all was that it wasn’t Lena who caved. It wasn’t her who made the reckless decision, it wasn’t her leaving the others to fend for themselves while she tried to rescue Kara alien. Shockingly, it was Alex.

     

                Roused from her sleep by the faint squeak of the door opening, Lena, who hadn’t slept well the entire time she’d been out of prison, who was paranoid about being tracked down to the point where a minor disturbance had her heart pounding in her chest, sat up. Rubbing her eyes as she scowled at the door, she missed the shadow slipping through but heard the quiet thud of the door softly closing.

     

                Climbing out of bed, being quiet, she padded on socked feet across to the door and opened it as silently as Alex had. Stepping out into the pitch black of the warehouse as her eyes adjusted to the gloom and she was able to make out the grey shadows of the truck and other equipment and boxes, Lena saw the other woman quietly crossing over to the side door bolted shut beside the roller door. 

     

                Confused and wary, Lena followed after her until she’d almost closed the gap, suspicion nagging at the back of her mind until she broke the silence of the night, expecting the worst. “Where are you going?”

     

                Alex startled, whirling around, her face hard and serious. She raked a hand through her hair, mouth flattening with grim resignation. “I’m handing myself in.”

     

                Silent for a moment as she stared blankly at the guard, Lena’s eyebrows slowly furrowed together. “Why?”

     

                “Nothing’s going to give unless there’s a whistleblower for the DEO. The government will just deny, deny, deny and we don’t have enough time for that. I have enough information to verify everything we gave that reporter. That’ll help more than sitting here twiddling my thumbs.”

     

                “Are you-” Lena loudly started to object.

     

                Alex hissed, stepping in closer as she held a hand out to shush her. “Lower your voice.”

     

                “Are you out of your mind?” Lena hotly whispered. “If you hand yourself in, there’s a very good chance they’ll have you shot as a spy.”

     

                Mouth twisting wryly, Alex shrugged. “Probably not. They’ll start an investigation and I’ll probably do some time for it, but … I don’t know, what’s time compared to a sister’s life? She’s family to me, as twisted as the whole thing has been. We were just girls together inside there so … if I can save her … I’ll do it. Wouldn’t you?”

     

                “Of course I would. It’s what I’m trying to do, without getting us all locked up again.”

     

                “Well, one of us behind bars is a better trade-off.”

     

                “And now you’re just so noble that it has to be you, huh?”

     

                “It does have to be me. I know more about the prison than the three of you, so yes, it does have to be. I’m not noble, I’m not- I’m not brave or heroic or anything good , okay? You don’t have to tell me that. I just-” Alex closed her eyes, rubbing her forehead as she swallowed thickly. “You spent eight months in there, and they were awful, I know that, but … years of my life, my entire adult life, has been in that prison. It’s not exactly a good environment to grow up in but I am trying to do the right thing. I have a choice now, I have the freedom to choose, just like Kara did when she chose to stay, so let me choose to do the right thing. I want to do the right thing by my own choice.”

     

                And perhaps it was for the best that Lena didn’t hold any fondness for the guard in her heart, because it made it easier to let her do it. After a tense moment, Lena slowly nodded, her green eyes clouded but sharp as she gave Alex a scrutinising look and took in the gritted determination on her face. She had already resigned herself to the worst outcome possible in hopes that it would see Kara freed.

     

                “Okay,” Lena whispered. 

     

                Mouth turning down at the corners, Alex nodded in return, keeping her fear under tight wraps, although Lena could see it in the tautness of her face. Licking her lips, she hesitated, tugging at the bottom of the nondescript raincoat she’d put on, the coated nylon rustling. 

     

                “I know I- I don’t really have the right to ask but … could you do one thing for me?”

     

                Her stubborn expression faltered for a moment, the bravado dimming until she was just a scared woman, barely thirty, ignorant of the world beyond the prison she’d been raised in. Her brown eyes were bright with pain and Lena could see her visibly swallow the lump in her throat.

     

    “Can you look after them for me?” she asked, gesturing behind her, towards the breakroom used as a bedroom where her mother and girlfriend were sound asleep.

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena felt her throat painfully tighten. She nodded quickly, reassuringly, and saw some of the tension leak out of the set of Alex’s shoulders. Lips twitching in what almost seemed like a grim smile, Alex nodded in thanks and then turned to leave.

     

                “Hey,” Lena murmured, reaching out to snag the sleeve of her coat before she got more than a step away. “It probably doesn’t mean much to you, and, well, I still don’t like you one bit but … thank you.”

     

                Mouth hitching into an uneven smile, Alex’s eyes shone with amusement in the dark. “I’m not doing it for you.”

     

                “I know.”

     

                “Maybe once you get her out you can let her know where they’ve put me. I’d like to see her myself, to talk to her, to know my sister is safe.”

     

                “I will.”

    Chapter 21

                Hot blood splattered her face and Lena held the weight of the guard as she died slowly, sinking to the ground together, Vasquez choking on her surprise as blood spurted from her neck. But then it wasn’t Vasquez, it was Kara. Blonde hair spilling around her head, pale, freckled face staring up at her with blue eyes wide with disbelieving panic as she scrabbled at her neck, at the small hole the scalpel had gouged right through the skin and muscle to hit her artery. Lips flecked with foaming red blood at the corners, Kara tried to speak and Lena stared down at her in inhibited horror as the cold seeped into her, saltwater from the flooding prison rising around them too quickly for her to do anything to stop.

     

                “Lena. Lena, wake up. Wake up.”

     

                Waking with a hoarse shout, Lena breathed erratically as she bolted upright, the gun she’d hidden beneath her pillow while she slept held tightly in her hand, and made out the shadowed figure looming over her in the darkness of the room. She’d sweated through her undershirt and could feel it clinging uncomfortably to her skin as she raked damp hair out of her face, sniffing as she set the pistol down in her lap and swallowed thickly.

     

                “Are you alright?” Eliza softly asked, her voice sounding too loud in the stillness of the early hours of the morning.

     

                She reached out to touch Lena’s shoulder, fingertips just grazing the cotton of her shirt, when Lena jerked away, her face crumpling with contempt and anger. “Don’t touch me.”

     

                “I just want to make sure you’re alright. You were thrashing around. It sounded like you were having a nightmare. You were saying her name-”

     

                “I’m fine.”

     

                She bit the words out, cheeks flooding with colour, her heart still jackhammering in her chest as she closed her eyes, drawing in slow, shaky lungfuls of the damp warehouse air. Nodding, Eliza withdrew, wringing her hands from a few paces away, and Lena swung her legs over the side of the cot, the cold concrete burrowing into the soles of her socked feet as she hunched over, face in the palm of her hand and her eyes screwed shut. Eliza watched her for a moment and then shifted restlessly, turning to make for the small kitchenette.

     

                No one spoke as she quietly made two cups of tea, carrying one over to Lena and handing it off without a word. After a moment, she sank onto the cot, barely a dark outline in the gloom, and clutched her cup in her palms as she let out a resigned sigh.

     

                “You know, if you are having nightmares, I can go and pick some medication up for you. Something to help you sleep.”

     

                “You must be dreaming if you think I’ll willingly take any medications from you again,” Lena scoffed, taking a sip of her tea. 

     

                “Perhaps Kelly can-”

     

                “Kelly can worry about herself.”

     

                Sighing with regret, Eliza’s eyes strayed over to her daughter-in-law’s sleeping form before glancing at her daughter’s empty bed. It took her a moment to realise that it was empty, no vague lump to signify her daughter sleeping peacefully, and Lena was still as she sipped her tea, feeling rather than seeing the doctor grow wary.

     

                Climbing to her feet, Eliza crossed over to Alex’s cot and came up with a handful of blankets. Looking around the dark room, as if expecting her to be standing in the corner, unassuming. Even with her back to the other woman, Lena could feel her growing panic, feeling wooden as the muffled, cotton-wool feeling in her head left her rather indifferent. 

     

                “Have you seen Alex?” Eliza whispered, shaking Kelly awake.

     

                “Hm?”

     

                “Alex. She’s not in bed.”

     

                Sounding more awake now as she rubbed her eyes and sat up, Kelly murmured, “maybe she’s just gone to the bathroom.”

     

                “I’ve been up for ten minutes. Nothing.”

     

                Kelly was out of bed then, stumbling past the cots, cursing as she stubbed her toe, and flicking on the light switch beside the door. Hissing as she screwed her eyes shut against the sudden brightness, tears smarting, Lena turned her head aside.

     

                “Jesus.”

     

                Blinking rapidly as her eyes adjusted, she wiped her eyes on her sleeve and scowled as Kelly yanked open the stiff, rusting door with a squealing sound and stepped into the chill of the abandoned warehouse. Lena could hear her calling for Alex, her voice echoing slightly through the cavernous space, and she grimaced as she rubbed her eyes, letting out a forceful sigh.

     

                The sound of the metal staircase squeaking and shuddering as Kelly ascended it filled the quiet tension, her footsteps quickly returning, and Lena glanced over at her as she walked back into the room. Dark eyes wide with fear, Kelly’s face was pale and drawn and she restlessly toyed with her fingers as she hovered inside the doorway.

     

                “She’s not up there. I don’t- I mean … she couldn’t have left . Where would she even go?”

     

                “To turn herself in,” Lena murmured after a pause.

     

                Two sets of eyes landed on her and there was an awkward beat before a flicker of suspicion crossed Kelly’s face. Storming across the distance between them, she reached down to drag Lena to her feet, lukewarm tea splashing everywhere, the cup shattering as Lena lost her grip on it.

     

                “What the hell are you talking about?”

     

                Getting her feet beneath her, Lena pushed Kelly off and scowled as she shrugged her overalls back into shape, her face burning with anger as tea seeped into her socks. 

     

                “Don’t you dare put your fucking hands on me.”

     

                “What did you do?”

     

                “I didn’t do anything.”

     

                “Then where is she?”

     

                Shrugging helplessly, an aloof expression on her face, Lena raked a hand through her hair. “I don’t know. I woke up to her leaving, so …”

     

                “And you didn’t think to stop her?” Kelly demanded, her voice breaking as her face spasmed with anguish.

     

                Mouth thinning, Lena shrugged and waved off-handedly. “She’s free to make her own decisions. There’s nothing I can do about that.”

     

                Tears threatened to spill over as they rapidly welled in Kelly’s eyes, brought on by the realisation that her girlfriend was gone and unreachable now. Lena didn’t know what time it was but it had to be the early hours of the morning, long enough for Alex to have slipped into the city and vanished. Unless she wanted to be found, of course, but Lena didn’t think the ex-guard was stupid enough to hand herself in in the same city her loved ones were hidden away in.

     

                The silence after she finished speaking was tense and uncomfortable, her flat, indifferent tone feeling callous in light of their sudden loss, even though Lena found a certain sense of karmic balance in them being on level footing now, both having lost a person they loved. As if taking a moment to fully absorb her words, processing them as they stoked her anger, Kelly blinked in surprise, her lips parting.

     

                Lena watched her expectantly and saw the slap coming before it landed, quick and satisfying in the sharp sting of it across her cheek. She welcomed it, the numbness of the blow, almost smug in her haughtiness as she watched Kelly experience the same emotions she’d gone through weeks ago. There was that flicker of guilt though, cutting through the fog of her conflicting feelings, and she swallowed thickly as her cheek reddened.

     

                Eliza covered her mouth with both hands as she hunched over, her heartbreak written all over her face as she tried to muffle the choked sob of disbelief that clawed up her throat. Watching as Kelly turned away from her, Lena hovered for a moment but found their blatant displays of grief and anger unbearable as the initial satisfaction started to wear off. Hesitating, she turned and walked out of the room, making for the storage closet and fetching freshly laundered clothes from the shelves before she went to shower. 

     

                Emerging pink and warmed through, she dressed quickly and bypassed the door to the break room as she padded upstairs, socks slippery on the steps, and entered the office. She’d secluded herself there for hours and hours since arriving at the warehouse and picked her way through the room with familiar ease, reaching the safe and squatting in front of it as she unlocked it and started to remove things.

     

                Her main priority had been trying to find a way to save Kara, on top of spreading word of what was happening and liaising with her mother, but she’d also made time within all of that to forge a few fake IDs and passports. While she wasn’t an expert by any means, Lena knew enough of technology and from her past attempts to make her own - tried and tested - to make forgeries that would stand up against all but the most intense scrutiny and investigation. She grabbed wads of cash and a few of the IDs and locked the safe again.

     

                Walking downstairs, she hovered in the doorway of the break room with a guilty twist to her stomach as she took in the sight of Eliza and Kelly sitting on a cot, the latters face buried in the neck of her mother-in-law as she was comforted. A sudden bout of jealousy rose in Lena’s chest but she stamped it down, knowing that it was well beyond her now to have ever let someone comfort her in a moment of similar weakness. Crossing over to the cot, she tossed the cash and forged documents next to Kelly and cleared her throat.

     

                “Here. Fifty grand should be enough for you to get away from here and set yourselves up. I promised her I’d look after you so … I can send you more once you’re settled.”

     

                “Keep your money,” Eliza wearily replied, looking haggard as she raised her head to look at Lena.

     

                “You’ll need it to get-”

     

                “We’re not leaving. Not until Kara is safe, and Alex is safe, and all of our names are cleared, okay? That’s the promise we all made, that we’d get each other out. If- if Alex- if she wanted to do it her own way, I have to respect my daughter’s wishes, but I’m not giving up. Not on her or Kara. I know you don’t care one way or the other about any of us except for Kara, but that is my daughter, and I won’t abandon her.”

     

                A surly look clouded Lena’s face and she paused before turning and walking to the door, pausing again as a look of shame momentarily coloured her face. Looking back over her shoulder, she spoke to the floor.

     

                “I tried to stop her.”

     

                Leaving before anyone could say anything further, she made her way back upstairs, leaving the money and ID behind, and sank onto the desk chair as she slumped, a heaviness in her chest. Lingering with her thoughts for a while, Lena eventually heaved a sigh and picked up the phone, faltering before she called her mother. Lillian was the last person she felt like talking to but at least her mother would understand, wasn’t clouded by familial love, and Lena wanted that harsh reality right then. The overwhelming emotions downstairs were too unbearable to withstand and she needed to be useful.

     

                “Lena?”

     

                “I might have something useful lined up.”

     

                “Which is?”

     

                “One of us- she’s-” Lena started, her throat tight as she tried to explain things. “She left last night. She’s planning on handing herself in as a whistleblower for the DEO. To verify all of the information.”

     

                “This is the guard?”

     

                “Yes. I’m not sure when - she’ll have to get away from here first. She’s smart enough to know that. Um … but I don’t know, within the next few days I guess she’ll turn herself in. Not sure where or to whom but … it’s something.”

     

                “What’s her name?”

     

                “Alex Danvers. Alexandra ,” Lena corrected as an afterthought.

     

                “I’ll keep an eye on the news.”

     

                “Can you get the family lawyers brought on as her defence when it comes to it?”

     

                There was a pause and she could practically hear her mother’s eye-roll. “If it’s necessary.”

     

                “It is.”

     

                “Fine. What else?”

     

                “Any information leaking from the White House?”

     

                “Not yet. Still a lack of accountability from Barker. If this woman hands herself in, as you say, that should open a can of worms for him. Impeachment would be likely.”

     

                “Impeachment,” Lena contemptuously scoffed. “I want him in jail, I want him imprisoned a mile beneath the sea in squalor, I want him before a firing squad for what he’s done.”

     

                “The firing squad might be a little ambitious,” Lillian replied with amusement, “but he won’t get off easily. He should have stayed content to rule over his aliens but I can assure you I will not let him make a mockery of the Luthor name with what he’s done to you. He’ll rue the day he signed his silly warrant to take you in.”

     

                “Is that all you care about? The Luthor name? You’re not even doing it for me? ” 

     

                Lena couldn’t keep the bitterness out of her voice, that ugly jealousy from before rearing its head again as she thought about how lacking in maternal love her life had been up until that point. For all of Eliza’s compliance with the DEO’s orders, she’d shown Lena more tenderness than Lillian ever had and it was a pitying thought that a stranger who’d drugged her and cared for her many sustained injuries had been the closest Lena had come to a mother’s love in decades. She would have felt sorry for herself if she hadn’t had more important things to concern herself with, but she couldn’t help her bitter jibe.

     

                “Of course I’m doing it for you,” Lillian frostily replied. “Do you know how many hours of my day this has consumed since you called me? The lengths I’ve gone to, the people I’ve spoken to, all to get you home again. I’ve spent weeks-”

     

                “And it’s not quick enough.”

     

                “Would you like to do it yourself? The least you could do is show some appreciation for my help, a little bit of gratitude perhaps.”

     

                “I am grateful, but it’s taking too long.”

     

                “It takes as long as it takes.”

     

                “That’s easy for you to say. You’re at home, your face isn’t plastered all over the news. You’re not the one at the bottom of the sea right now.”

     

                “Neither are you.”

     

                Pinching the bridge of her nose as she hunched forward and squeezed her eyes shut, Lena clenched her teeth, her jaw aching from the pressure. “I don’t have time for this. Keep an eye out for Alex and help her if you can. I’ll call you in a couple of days.”

     

                Hanging up the phone without another word, Lena slammed the phone down on her desk, rattling the keyboard and a few pens and sheaths of paper. Putting her head in her hands, she wanted to cry, frustration building in her chest, mingling with her helplessness. She thought of Kara and the dream that had troubled her that morning, wondering how she was, wishing she could talk to her. What would she even say to her? All Lena would be able to do was apologise. It hadn’t been her choice but she’d left her behind. 

     

                Drawing in a deep breath, she forcefully exhaled and straightened in her seat, wheeling it closer to the desk and moving the mouse. Clearing her throat, Lena let her work consume her as she continued the task of compiling a list of names for the metahumans who had been imprisoned, with the help of the information Alex had exported from the DEO database. It was difficult, a spreadsheet of codes and prisoner IDs that Lena had to ask the other women for help with, not knowing who was who, and her knowledge of the prisoners secluded to her own cell block. 

     

                Puzzling through it for the remainder of the morning, she had amassed a decent number of metahumans - and Nia, half-human and half-alien - intending to pass it on to her mother to print the names of all of them. Surely some of them had family looking for them, surely the staff alone, also imprisoned there, had hundreds of family members who wondered what had happened to fathers, sons, daughters, cousins, even just friends, old colleagues. There must be hundreds of people wondering and giving the general public that knowledge was a good way to instigate mass uproar and the demand for the government to do something.

     

                She couldn’t wait for the other two women to calm down enough, to trust her enough to review her work, so Lena sent it off to Lillian and hoped it would be enough. Turning her attention to more pressing issues of the physics behind raising a broken underwater prison to sea level again, Lena researched naval vessels and private contractors, digging into how oil rigs were set up in the middle of the sea and other methods of recovery that could be used. She had separate folders for the different plans they’d cobbled together since arriving at the black site, and while she wasn’t optimistic about any of them, she knew that at some point they would have to find a solution. She’d charter a submarine and blast a hole in the side of the prison if it came to it, drag Kara out unconscious and leave as many of the others as she had to to, regrettably, drown.

     

                Avoiding downstairs, she starved her way through lunch and dinner and idled away the middle of the night at her desk, barely working as she lost herself in her thoughts. By the time the sun rose outside the warehouse, unbeknown to Lena beyond the windowless office, she was back to work, checking her emails for any response from her mother, going through the files Alex had stolen to see if the DEO had ever had a contingency plan for a rescuer mission, and she was left undisturbed as she worked.

     

                Skipping all three meals again that day, drinking nothing, and not sleeping at all, Lena didn’t do herself any favours. Dry-eyed and irritable, she felt despair threaten to consume her, and the worst part was that she used to be good at committing herself to her work, losing herself in it for days, but now with the lingering fog of drugs and her half-starved and sleep-deprived form, she couldn’t even think while she tried to push through it. An integral part of her work ethic had been taken away from her in less than a year. 

     

                Perhaps it was a good thing she could no longer get by with neglecting her needs while staying mentally sharp enough to continue her research, but it didn’t feel that way. If Lena could have stayed awake for a week with the mental capacity for clear, logical thought, she wouldn’t have hesitated to do it for Kara’s sake. Instead, she fell asleep at her desk just after dinner time and wasn’t roused until just before midnight.

     

                The sound of the door creaking open cut through the troubled dream she was having and Lena slowly reared her head, blearily blinking at the screensaver on the computer screen. Sitting up, her neck stiff from the angle she’d slept, with her head pillowed on her folded arms, she furiously rubbed her heavy eyelids and then glanced sideways as a moving figure caught her attention. 

     

                A tense moment preceded the breaking of the silence as Kelly approached and then stopped a few feet away. Clearing her throat as she wheeled her chair closer to the desk, Lena shook the mouse and logged back into the computer, waiting for the other woman to speak. 

     

                “Any news?” Kelly asked, her voice a dull rasp.

     

                “Nothing,” Lena murmured, the other woman’s agony eliciting a stab of pity, even as she tried to steel herself against any weaknesses. “Um … I don’t think we’ll hear from her for a- a while. She’s smart so … she’ll probably get away from here first. Depending on where she goes … it could be a week or more before we hear about her.”

     

                Running a hand over her face, Kelly choked on a laugh. “Not that smart, obviously. But she’ll go to the closest place possible - we don’t have time to waste.”

     

                “Right.”

     

                There was an awkward pause and Lena toyed with a pen as she stared blankly at the computer screen, willing the other woman to walk away. She wasn’t good around people at the best of times, let alone after being imprisoned with them, the reminder of their power imbalance and differing circumstances that had led to drastically different experiences inside hanging over them, and she just wanted it to be over. The day she saw the last of them would be the start of trying to process things and heal from it on her own terms.

     

                “I’m sorry for slapping you.”

     

                Shrugging indifferently, Lena swallowed thickly and stayed silent. It didn’t matter to her, hadn’t really hurt, hadn’t changed her indifferent opinion of the other woman. Mostly, Lena had suffered so much worse inside the prison that anything lesser didn’t even faze her in the slightest anymore. Before, maybe it would have angered her, wouldn't have wounded her pride, but Lena had swallowed so much of her dignity over the last nine months that it was just accepted. 

     

                Stepping in closer, Kelly set a bowl down on the edge of the desk and produced a bottle of water wedged beneath her arm. Gesturing to it, she cleared her throat. “You haven’t eaten anything so …”

     

                Eyes flitting down to the bowl of steamed vegetables, rice and grilled chicken, Lena nodded and paused momentarily. “Thanks.”

     

                “Sorry we haven’t been much help, um …”

     

                “It’s fine.”

     

                “If there’s anything you need us-”

     

                “I don’t.”

     

                “We’re here to help.”

     

                “You don’t have to be.”

     

                “We want to be.”

     

                “Just go to bed, Kelly,” Lena sighed. “I’ll let you know once she’s handed herself in.”

     

                She missed the ripple of pain that crossed the other woman’s face, brimming with anxiety as she wrung her hands. Nodding, her mouth a flat line, Kelly left without another word and Lena shovelled her dinner into her mouth and sipped the water until the bottle was empty. All the while, she continued her line of action, hoping something would come to fruition if she followed each avenue to whatever end. So far, nothing had.

     

     

                It was two weeks later when an email made it to her inbox with her mother asking her to call. Knowing that something must have come up, that it wouldn’t be a courtesy call or out of kindness and empathy as she checked on her daughter’s welfare, Lena snatched up the phone and called Lillian.

     

                “What’s happened?”

     

                “She handed herself to Canadian officials while crossing the border, heading for Vancouver. They denied her request for political asylum and detained her. Canada doesn’t want to piss off America so they informed the Ambassador to Canada and she was transported to the US Embassy in Ottawa.”

     

                “Ottawa?” Lena exclaimed, her heartbeat picking up speed as adrenaline coursed through her. She climbed to her feet, raking a hand through her hair. 

     

                Alex had gone further away than Lena had anticipated and she felt a stab of worry, wondering what the ex-officer was up to. Swallowing thickly, her throat suddenly dry, Lena rubbed her forehead as she frowned, trying to think.

     

                “Do you know what’s going on?”

     

                “I have contacts who have fed me some information. The Ambassador has informed the Secretary of State and it looks like they’ve taken custody of her and will be extraditing her to the States. It’ll need to go through the courts first before they determine if it’s even possible for them to extradite her but of course, Canada will surrender her; it’s just a matter of how long it takes. The last thing we want is for it to take months, or even worse, years for them to sort it out. It helps that they’d denied her political asylum, I suppose. They could have deported her immediately but given the threat she is to national security, it’s easy to understand why they didn’t. Anyway, it’s in the jurisdiction of the Department of State now but there are whispers that the Department of Justice and Homeland Security are trying to butt in and take custody of her. I guess the threat of the President being indicted by what could come out of her has thrown them into a panic.”

     

                “Surely the Attorney General-”

     

                “Don’t be too optimistic, Lena. Of course we’d like to believe the Attorney General will follow due process but the government has its fingers in every possible pie and who knows how much money Baker’s put in his pockets to keep him loyal.”

     

                “I’ll bring it to Congress myself.”

     

                “If that was possible, you already would have. Look, I’ve done some digging of my own, and rumour has it the DEO is a covert department of the Department of Justice, which means it directly reports to the Attorney General. He would know what they’re up to; chances are, he’s not going to want to be implicated in this either. So that’s not inspiring much hope in me, but the DEO might have shielded the truth about what they’re doing regarding the prison, and it’s been operational for so long that there have been a dozen Attorney Generals filling that position.”

     

                “I don’t care who’s in what position or who knew what. She needs to be put in front of the Senate with a dozen cameras shoved in her face and every reputable news source reporting on it until someone gives a shit and starts helping us.”

     

                “We can’t rush these things-”

     

                “You think I don’t know that? But it’s already been weeks ; I don’t know how much time they have. I know I could be chasing after a dead woman, I- I know that, but I won’t stop until someone helps me. I hate to admit it but … I don’t think I can find a solution to this. I need someone to care, I need help, and I just- I need people to start listening. You say you have contacts? Can’t you get them to speak to the right people and go down the right avenues to make things move along quickly? Once my name is cleared and they unfreeze my assets I can pay you-”

     

                “It’s not about money.”

     

                Raking a hand through her hair, she grew agitated, her frustration building at the helplessness she felt. Lena was used to buying or bribing her way to anything she wanted and it was unsettling to not know her mother’s motives, to not be able to snap her fingers and have things progress smoothly. It would have been easier to deal with corrupt officials if she could pay them off directly but she was stranded in Anchorage with limited power to move the pieces of this complex chess game that put all of their lives at stake. Until she was exonerated, she had to try and find her mother’s weak spot, find what she wanted and dangle it over her until she caved and helped Lena achieve what she wanted.

     

                “What do you want then? I’ll give you anything. The business? Take it. I’ll empty the vaults of my inventions and hand over every hard drive with any research the Government hasn’t already wiped. Whatever you want, I’ll give it to you if you can do this for me.”

     

                Lillian was quiet for a moment. “Keep an eye on your emails.”

     

                The line went dead after that and Lena was left spluttering as she stared at the hunk of plastic. Dropping it onto the desk she groaned as she put her face in her hands and lingered a moment before going to deliver the news to the two women downstairs. They were stoic and silent, unable to venture any questions as Lena bleakly offered them little comfort with her limited information.

     

                One good thing about the buzz Lena had already created with her information leaked to CatCo, along with Alex’s classified documents, was that there was soon information available that corroborated everything Lillian had told her. Whether it was at border security in Canada, from the Embassy itself, or within the various executive departments of the US government, word spread about the arrest of a wanted fugitive who had surrendered herself to the US government with the admission of her own guilt in releasing the classified documents that had been making the rounds through the news circuit over the last couple of weeks. If they hadn’t known Alex’s name then, it was certainly known then and Lena read every single article that came through with rapid succession as photojournalists snapped pictures of her in cuffs, being escorted out of the Embassy in Ottawa by the authorities and again when she was flown to Washington DC.

     

                Two days after her official arrest on US soil, there was a hearing for her initial arraignment, after being held at the District Court awaiting her charges.
