The legal documents were quickly obtained and splashed across the news and Lena read through the list of things Alex was being indicted for under the Espionage Act of 1917. Unlawful computer intrusion; Obtaining national defence information; Unlawful retentions of national defence information; Disclosure of national defence information; Disclosure of classified information; Obstructions of justice. Afterwards, she was taken to the United States District Court for the District of Columbia to await her post-indictment arraignment and that was the last Lena heard of her for the time being.

     

                It kicked off a storm though. If the government had been in a panic when Lena had initially come out with the truth of what had happened to her, having a DEO whistleblower in the spotlight heightened that panic to new levels. It started with a Congressional Hearing, Lena watching a glitchy livestream with the other two women standing behind her, listening to Senators discuss the recent arrest of the ex-DEO officer and the testimonials she and Lena had given. 

     

                Then there was some discussion about CatCo’s involvement, that they could be prosecuted for violating the Espionage Act as well, for publishing the documents that Lena had fed through to them. There were varying degrees of support for that ruling but Cat Grant gave a blithe interview, brusque and irate as was her usual demeanour whenever captured on video, where she expressed her right for the First Amendment claims of the press against the government’s proof by insisting that CatCo had reason to believe that the information they’d acquired could be used to the injury of the United States, or to the advantage of a foreign nation with less favourful intentions. Her nonchalant logic only furthered the tangled mess of too many parties involved.

     

                A week after Alex’s surrender and arrest had made the public press cycle, the Office of the Inspector General formally initiated an investigation into the DEO, as one of the departments of the Department of Justice. It was a shock for Lena when confronted with the appearance of Hank Henshaw, after so many months of being accustomed to his visage being attributed to J’onn, when photos of him showed up in a Google alert for Alex’s name. There were photos of a bunch of suits with him in the midst, somewhat grainy from the distance the photographer was from the Director, but it made Lena feel an uneasy twist as memories of being dragged out of bed in the middle of the night and locked inside a room to be interrogated by him resurfaced. It brought so much of it back, that confusion, the panic, the desperation and bleak disbelief as she was issued with her sentence without even a trial. She let Eliza take over her computer for the rest of the day and took a long shower to try and scour her mind clean with the comforting press of hot water against cold skin.

     

                Things moved slowly in the government but Congress was dragged into the midst of it all as evidence proved more than circumstantial, as rumours solidified into facts, and when the House Speaker initiated a formal House inquiry in light of Alex’s whistleblowing, President Baker dug himself a deeper hole. While three congressional committees deposed witnesses, Baker obstructed the inquiry itself by getting his administration to ignore subpoenas and testimony, with the White House Counsel informing the House Speaker that they would not be cooperating with the investigation due to concerns that there hadn’t been a vote of the full House of Representatives yet. It didn’t matter though, and witnesses were brought before Congress as the House Intelligence Committee held their first of many public hearings. Hank Henshaw was the first to testify.

     

                Tuning the TV into the channel, the three women sat at the small metal table and ate soup for lunch as the public hearing was broadcast live. Staring at the face of the man who had helped her out of prison, just as easily as he’d put her in there, even if there were two entirely different beings behind the faces, was disconcerting and Lena shifted restlessly as they got through all of the legal jargon and the hearing got underway. It was boring for a while but the three of them watched with rapt attention.

     

                “Can you please state your name and position for the Senate?”

     

                “Hank Henshaw, Director of the Department of Extra-normal Operations.”

     

                “What is the Department of Extra-normal Operations?”

     

                “It’s a covert government organisation, under the Department of Justice.”

     

                “And what is the objective of the department?”

     

                “Our jurisdiction is to monitor extraterrestrial presence and/or invasion of Earth, particularly regarding the safety of the United States.”

     

                “Are you aware of the allegations made against the Department of Extra-normal Operations by Miss Lena Luthor and Agent Alexandra Danvers?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Can you confirm Agent Alexandra Danvers is an employee of the Department of Extra-normal Operations?”

     

                The questions were endless, circling topics as Henshaw skirted the truth as much as possible, trying to avoid confirming anything that hadn’t already been verified by the initial inquiry and the investigation by the Office of the Inspector General. Henshaw and the Attorney General were both in hot water with the knowledge they’d kept under wraps, the unlawful crimes committed on behalf of the government and President, and it was a long hearing that they had to sit through, watching the Director sweat beneath the scrutiny, digging himself a deeper hole as evidence and testimonies were put forth.

     

                Three days later, they brought Alex forward. She hadn’t had the chance to publicly retell her version of events on camera and the three women eagerly watched the screen as they waited for a glimpse of her. She entered the floor to camera flashes of reporters admitted to the hearing, head ducked down, jaw and shoulders tense. She looked well though, and there was a palpable relief from her family as Lena glanced at them, the muttered reassurances that she was unharmed, that she was being looked after while held in custody.

     

                Alex was more forthcoming with her own answers, curt and serious as she told every shred of the truth, from her admission to the prison and future role to the function of the prison, the mistreatment of the prisoners - branding herself complicit as she recounted the abuse inflicted - the employees and management, the deliveries, bribery, buried secrets and dead aliens. Holding nothing back as she painted a truly terrible story, corroborating everything Lena had put in her initial statement, and even verifying that Lena had been brought in unconscious and without trial to serve a life sentence on President Baker’s orders. It went on for hours with interruptions for breaks, but Alex bore the whole thing with patience and grim resignation, flanked by security, and legal counsel Lillian had funded for her, as she was questioned again and again until they finally called it a day.

     

                Lena was left feeling relieved at the truth of a whistleblower being out in the world, of Alex backing up everything she’d said and highlighting the tragedy of hundreds of prisoners trapped beneath the sea. It sparked protests and further investigations by the United Nations into human rights violations by the United States, and other world leaders and politicians weighed in on the situation, garnering further attention for the cause. It all came to a head with the call for the impeachment of President Baker, the articles of the inquiry submitted to the Senate weeks later, almost two months since Lena had freed them from prison and left Kara trapped inside.

     

                She called Lillian the day after the news of the impeachment trial, knowing it could be months still before the Senate voted on the outcome of it, knowing they didn’t have that kind of time, and knowing that there was nothing else she could do now. Over the last couple of weeks, each time she’d called her mother it had resulted in some sort of conference call with lawyers, government officials and the other two fugitives she was hiding with, all of them playing a game of tug of war as the fugitives refused to turn themselves in and the Department of Justice and various other executive departments of the government tried, in tandem with the lawyers, to get them to surrender to the nearest authorities.

     

                Nine weeks after breaking out of prison, Lillian emailed Lena to turn on the news, and the three women watched as President Baker made an address to the American public to announce his resignation from the presidency due to the Fort Rozz scandal. Hidden away in their warehouse, the three women looked at each other, stunned by the way everything was falling into place for them so perfectly after months - and years for some - of the horrors of the prison. 

     

                When Lena called her mother, Lillian assured her that a pardon would be inevitable now, and three days later, when the former Vice President - now President Susan Brayden - held a conference at the White House to announce an official search-and-rescue effort by the US Navy, Coast Guard and Air Force into recovering Fort Rozz. Watching her efforts pay off as the government finally made a public statement to help recover the prisoners from the depths of the sea, Lena felt so weak with relief that she couldn’t do anything but sit there, pale and limp as the pressure to rescue Kara alone was lifted off her shoulders. 

     

                It was Eliza who ended up coaxing Lena to her feet and into the truck parked in the warehouse, the three of them climbing in and driving out of the warehouse, almost two months after arriving there. One part of Lena never wanted to leave the safety of the place after the instability of the prison and her subsequent escape; the other part of her never wanted to see the dismal, damp hideout again. She didn’t question where they were going though, even though the three of them were fugitives, and she didn’t feel frightened when Eliza pulled up outside the nearest police station in Anchorage, parallel parking the truck and killing the engine, knowing that it didn’t matter what happened to her now, what happened to any of them, because she’d instigated what she’d set out to do and even though Kara wasn’t free, the government was culpable and the public knew they were out there. They wouldn’t be able to stop until they rescued the prisoners or recovered the wreckage of Fort Rozz. Anything less than that would be seen as unacceptable, by the public and the Departments of Defence and Justice. 

     

                Outside the precinct, Lena stepped out of the truck in broad daylight and walked through the front door with the other two women behind her and when a cop looked up at her, there was a flicker of recognition in the man’s eyes as Lena quietly turned herself in. Arrested in the middle of the precinct as a wanted fugitive, she started to cry, but it wasn’t for the cuffs clapped around her wrists but with the relieved resignation of knowing that help was on its way, and she was finally going home. 

    Chapter 22

                Separated from the two women she’d lived in close quarters with for months now, Lena felt adrift as she was held in isolation, cuffed to a table as the precinct was sent into a panic, trying to call through the chain of command, trying to figure out who was responsible for taking custody of Lena, trying to identify the other two women who’d come in with her. They were technically fugitives as well but relatively anonymous in the public eye, even though they’d been on the list of employees within the prison that Lena had released. No one seemed to know what to do, as if they’d never anticipated she would show up in Anchorage, as if that was above their pay grade to search for a fugitive who was publicly known to have escaped at the very northern point of Alaska.

     

                They ended up locking her in one of their interview rooms, hands cuffed to the table in front of her with enough chain to allow her to sip the tepid cup of water that had been brought in for her. Her throat felt dry and she hadn’t been afforded a phone call, hadn’t been told to call her legal counsel or let anyone know she was there. Sitting in the ghastly light of the overhead fluorescents, Lena had the unsettling feeling of deja vu, of being put through the same unjust process once more.

     

                They’d driven there early afternoon and the hours slipped by, untraceable to Lena in the locked room, but her mind drifted to Eliza and Kelly with curiosity and perhaps a small prickle of worry. Her paper cup of water was refilled, another brought with black coffee as she sat stiff-shouldered and hollow-eyed with exhaustion as the evening dragged on. It was past dinner time when a vending machine turkey sandwich and a packet of Lay’s were set on the table in front of her. Eating with little relish for the food, Lena finished it all and rubbed her dry eyes as her patience started to wear thin.

     

                She could feel that it was late when a few FBI agents stepped into the room, flashing their IDs and stating their names, quickly forgotten, before Lena was uncuffed, cuffed again and escorted out. The precinct was tense and quiet, the hum of the lights, the click of computer keyboards and the coffee percolator filling the hallway as she was led outside, a SWAT team closing in around her as she was lifted into the back of a nondescript black van.

     

                Two SWAT members sat in the back, along with the two agents, and a convoy of three vans departed, driving out to a private airstrip where a government-issued plane was waiting for them on the tarmac. Lena shivered in the cold air as she was helped out of the van, the smell of gasoline and exhaust fumes tinging the breeze, and she wondered how long it would be until she was fully free to bask in the fresh air without the threat of imprisonment hanging around her. She wondered how long it would be before Kara was free to experience the same.

     

                Eliza and Kelly were hauled from the other two vans, likewise cuffed with grave expressions on their faces as the trio were escorted to the plane by the SWAT agents with rifles and faces hidden behind the visors of their helmets. The three of them had been searched for weapons when they’d been arrested and they weren’t a real threat to any of the FBI employees, but the rifles put them on edge and warned them off any attempts that might have suddenly arisen. They were kept separate on the plane, staggered on opposite sides and different ends, with Lena to the middle on the right. 

     

                She didn’t ask where they were going but the flight was long, taking off just before midnight and dragging. Leaden, Lena sank into her seat and dozed, head against the window, the relief of temporarily having nowhere to be and nothing to fight for stealing over her and leaving her drained. It wasn’t a restful sleep though and she woke with a sore neck and the unsatisfied feeling of cotton wool exhaustion, her mind slow and thick, but not from the effects of the drugs, which had been flushed out of her system after weeks without a new depot injection.

     

                Sleeping the entire way there, until the dipping of the plane as they rapidly descended woke her, Lena blinked at the harsh sunlight as she stared out the window. It didn’t take her long to realise they were descending into Washington; it should have been obvious. They touched down at an airstrip and were led off the plane and into three waiting vans and repeated the process of idly waiting as they were driven through traffic until they came to the FBI Headquarters in northwest Washington. 

     

                They were driven into an underground parking lot and the area was a buzz of activity after that, Lena finding herself inside, walking down the air-conditioned hallways of the blandly corporate building, until she was locked inside a room. Shortly afterwards, she was retrieved to be booked, her fingerprints and photograph taken as she stared blankly ahead while complying with the instructions that she responded to without comprehending.

     

                Afterwards, they made her a cup of coffee and a man and a woman in suits sat across from her, taking turns trying to get her to speak and open up to them. The entire time, she didn’t say a word, tired and resigned to wait for the next step. After a fruitless hour of gentle probing for information, for some sort of confession or explanation, they took her from the room and she was loaded back into a van.

     

                They took her to a federal detention facility, where she would stay in the custody of the FBI until there was a hearing or a pardon. She didn’t really know what to expect, but at least with a fair trial, she’d at least be afforded the right to defend herself, to have lawyers fight on her behalf. They couldn’t sweep it under the rug now that the whole world was watching it unfold.

     

                Still, as she was processed at the detention facility, it felt eerily similar to that first day at Fort Rozz, photographed and fingerprinted again , a bundle of drag beige prison uniform thrust into her arms, the public showers and watchful eyes of the prison guards. Eliza and Kelly were right alongside her the entire time, not a word exchange between any of them, and the other two women looked more frightened than Lena, who had been through it all before. This time, there was no shock collar, no electrified batons jabbed into her side, no struggling against the guards and no medical examination. It was all standard routine but it didn’t mean that Lena couldn’t feel that cold dread seep through her at the familiarity of it all.

     

                Locked in a cell, Lena sank onto her cot and her skin prickled from the cold and the unease of the dark room. It was almost lunchtime and she was brought a plastic tray with food on it, picking at it and drinking the water, before they let her out to make a phone call. Her mother’s number was still the only one she could think to call, dialling it as she had dozens of times over the last few weeks. Used to receiving calls from Lena on a private number, Lillian answered this one too and must have been playing a recorded message informing her that the call was coming from the detention facility. 

     

                “Where are you?” Lillian brusquely demanded as soon as the call connected.

     

                “We handed ourselves in. We were in Anchorage,” Lena confessed, rubbing the bridge of her nose as she screwed her eyes shut, frowning. “Um … we’re in Washington now. They handed us over to the FBI and they flew us in. I’ve been processed so they’ve put us in this … detention facility. I’m not sure what’s next. A hearing, I guess.”

                

                “I’ll call the lawyers.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Lena hesitated, her mouth flattening as she tried to resist asking for information that she knew her mother wouldn’t have the answer to. Still, she couldn’t help herself, not liking how she’d effectively been cut off from any news source.

     

                “Have they-”

     

                “It’ll take some time. Let them do their job and worry about yourself now.”

     

                “I don’t know if I’ll be able to call you again but if anything happens-”

     

                “I’ll be sure to send a letter,” Lillian snorted.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena ran a hand through her hair and sighed. “I’ll talk to you soon. If they let me.”

     

                She hung up the phone after that, lingering a moment until the guard cleared his throat and she allowed him to escort her back to her cell. Lena didn’t see Kelly or Eliza again, and wouldn’t for a long time - although she didn’t know that at the time - and she was left to her own thoughts for the rest of the day. 

     

                Dinner came, and night swiftly followed, and Lena slept fitfully as the sounds of the detention facility kept her awake. Heavy footsteps, the squawk of a radio, keys in the locks and banging doors. After so many weeks of relative quiet in the leaking warehouse and small black site, being back in a prison with so many others constantly around was too loud. Still, she did sleep, and the next day she had a hot shower and breakfast, frozen waffles and scrambled eggs with a cup of black coffee, wary of the better treatment than what she’d received from the DEO, even though the FBI had given her no cause to mistrust them. Lena had an inherent distrust of any sort of government law enforcement or military though, exacerbated after months in prison.

     

                Whatever she’d been anticipating next, it wasn’t a few hours sitting back in her room and then being hauled back out again, taken to a private visitation room where lawyers met with their clients, and left uncuffed as she sat on a metal chair with a guard inside the room with her. He was silent for a few minutes and then tried to make small talk with her, his hopeful probing for any information met with aloof silence. 

     

                Ten minutes later, the door unlocked and another guard entered, jerking her head for the man to leave, and then stood aside to let more people inside. Lena’s mouth parted with shock as she watched her mother sweep into the room, intimidatingly tall as she towered head above everyone else in her heels, cool and haughty as her sharp eyes fell on her daughter. There was a momentary pause as Lillian failed to mask her surprise at Lena’s appearance, before she continued further into the room and arched an eyebrow, lips twitching with a smile.

     

                “Surprised to see me?”

     

                The metal chair scraped against the tiled floor as Lena pushed it back, climbing unsteadily to her feet as her stomach swooped. She had no lost love for her mother but she felt like a child running to her for comfort after scraping a knee as her chin wobbled and her eyebrows furrowed together in stubborn composure.

     

                “Mom.”

     

                They stared at each other for a moment and Lillian stepped in closer and enveloped her in a hug. It surprised Lena, who flinched at the sudden contact, before hesitantly returning it, clutching fistfuls of the back of her mother’s coat as she pressed her face into her shoulder. It was brief but it knitted some of her back together, the presence of someone who preceded her time in prison somewhat comforting, even if it was Lillian.

     

                “You look awful,” Lillian commented.

     

                Letting out a broken laugh, Lena ran a hand over her face, smiling humourlessly. “I looked a lot worse, believe me.”

     

                She sank down onto her chair, knees weak, and her mother sat across from her, a man who had followed her in taking a seat, while another suited man remained standing. Lillian gestured off-handedly at the two of them.

     

                “Your lawyers.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “It’s a pleasure to meet you, Miss Luthor,” the man across from her said, extending a hand. 

     

                She shook it and the appropriate introductions were made before the man cleared his throat. “Firstly, this will be a bit unorthodox. You’re entitled to a hearing after an arrest has been made, just to inform you of your charges. Your arraignment will be where you plead but … well, as I said, it’s unorthodox, to say the least. Technically you’re a fugitive, but you haven’t committed any crimes, or been charged with anything. There is a warrant for your imprisonment that has been taken into evidence from the DEO, which means that, at least for the time being, you are required to stay in FBI custody. A hearing has been set for tomorrow but we’ll be expecting a pardon for you any day now from President Brayden.”

     

                “What about breaking out of the prison?” Lena rasped, a tremor in her voice as she curled her hands into fists on the metal tabletop. 

     

                The steel was cold to the touch and she felt her stomach lurch at the memory of Vasquez’s blood coating her hands. They didn’t know about that; she was reluctant to bring it up. 

     

                “That does complicate things, but you’ve been taken into custody again, which is the main thing. The unlawful nature of your imprisonment without a fair trial should hopefully afford some leniency.”

     

                “And the others?”

     

                There was an awkward pause and exchanged glances, the lawyer across from her shifting uncomfortably in his seat as Lillian stared at Lena, her gaze level and sharp. “Well … you’re our client so our priority is to exonerate you.”

     

                “I don’t care about that; I can stay in here for the next year if I have to. My priority is the prison.”

     

                “Just let them do their job, Lena,” Lillian sighed. “Clear your name first, take some time to adjust to reality, unfreeze your assets, and then you can worry about other people. Frankly, I’m not so sure why you’d want to help these people anyway, based on what I’ve heard come out of that woman’s mouth.”

     

                “I made a promise.”

     

                “You don’t owe them anything.”

     

                “Not to them.”

     

                Turning to the lawyers, Lillian gave them a tight smile, faint lines radiating from the corners of her eyes as they tightened. “Can you give us a moment? Please.”

     

                The two men climbed to their feet and made for the door, one knocking on the frosted window and waiting for the guard to let them out. The small room was silent and Lena felt tense like a caged lion as her mother shifted in her seat, metal groaning as she propped her elbows on the table and leaned in. There was a grave look on Lillian’s face and a faint downturn of dissatisfaction at the corners of her mouth.

     

                “I am trying to help you but you are making this difficult .”

     

                “This isn’t about me.”

     

                “Yes, it is. You don’t know that- that creature - you just think that you did. And you’re letting your false feelings cloud your judgment. This is very unlike you, and I understand that the circumstances have been … difficult for you, and you’re under a lot of stress right now, but you are not thinking clearly. You’re been manipulated and used by them all to get them out-”

     

                Lena’s response was frosty as she stiffened in her seat. “Don’t presume to know anything about my feelings - or her. She wasn’t manipulating me.” Her voice turned scornful and she rubbed her thumb over her closed eyes. “She was free. She got us out and she went back in to save everyone else.”

     

                “Then she made her choice.”

     

                “And I’m making my own. If you don’t like it, then leave.”

     

                “You’re being very ungrateful.”

     

                “I don’t care. ”

     

                “Don’t you? This is what you’ve always wanted; my attention, my love, my help. You’ve always been desperate to be wanted by someone. Why on earth would you pick an alien to be wanted by?”

     

                “She’s the first person to ever treat me with an ounce of kindness. And she’s been inside there for eighteen years. You don’t know what it’s like in there, how- how awful it is, and for her to come out of it with so much … humanity.”

     

                Lillian was slow to reply, the silence unbearable as they stared at each other, scrutinising and stubborn. “She’s not a person at all.”

     

                “No, she’s better than the rest of us,” Lena murmured, lowering her gaze to the scratched surface of the table.

     

                “That doesn’t change the fact that you’re stuck in here. And whether you’re in here or free, it’s not going to change her fate because you don’t have the means to recover that prison alone. Except, if they find her - if - she won’t be running into your arms if you’re tucked away inside a cell.”

     

                Her mother pushed her chair back and climbed to her feet, her tall figure casting a shadow across the table. “Something to think about.”

     

                Lillian’s heels clicked across the floor and she knocked on the door. It opened and her mother swept out without another word, leaving Lena slumped in her chair as she raised her eyes to watch her go, knowing that Lillian was right. Her mind weighed heavily with the truth of her mother’s words, that unbearable thought that they would find Kara and she would be alone in a world that had treated her so cruelly. Wouldn’t it be a kindness, in a sense, to let her mother pull her strings and have Lena out of the facility as soon as possible so that Lena could help whatever search effort was being conducted and be there when they found her friend, to protect her from the overwhelming loss of a world she was a stranger to?

     

                The guard returned after escorting her mother and lawyers out, and Lena was led back to her cell to await her fate.

     

     

                “Any luck?” Kara asked, sinking to a crouch.

     

                The scrawny man looked sharply at her, a gleam to his eyes as he fiddled with the knob of the clunky radio device he’d had her rip out of the command room. He’d tried in vain to repair it within the command room, but as days bled into weeks, parts stripped from other devices and computers, he had no luck with fixing it. As things progressively worsened inside the prison, a last-ditch effort had been made by tearing the thing out of the console and tinkering at it inside the cell block.

     

                “Nothing,” Winn sighed, a barely audible whine of the frequency grating on Kara’s sensitive hearing. “That doesn’t mean it’s broken though. I mean … it could just mean no one is close enough to contact us.”

     

                That thought lodged in Kara’s throat like a stone, sitting heavily behind her sternum. She ran a hand over her face, narrowed with hunger after they’d cut the rations even further recently. Admittedly, it was not the quick escape or rescue she’d anticipated for the prisoners, and things were looking bleak.

     

                “Keep trying,” Kara instructed him.

     

                Pushing herself to her feet, she felt weak and exhausted, hunger gnawing at her shrunken stomach as she picked her way through the packed floor of the cell block. The force fields had never gone back up after the day she’d helped her friends escape, and the floor was crowded with sleeping figures, prisoners and frightened staff huddled together in groups, blankets and pillows scattered everywhere, and stacked supplies in one of the open cells - the one that had originally been Kara’s. The one that had been Lena’s before her escape was being used as the sole toilet for everyone crammed in the cell block, the heavy entrance doors sealed shut against the rest of the prison and cutting them off from the showers.

     

                The noise of murmured conversation, of rattling coughs and rasping breaths was an overstimulating drone as Kara anxiously raked her fingers through her hair. It had been weeks. Weeks of cutting down on their food rations, until everyone was lean with the edge of starvation, hollow-cheeked with skinny wrists beneath dirty prison clothes they had no way of washing. With their limited facilities to even wash properly, the odour of a few dozen people crammed into one block was overpowering, old sweat, blood and sickness creating a thick malaise within the block. 

     

                Not only that but outside of the cell block, whenever a few of the more invulnerable ones left, there was the putrid smell of death, of decomposing corpses that had been unceremoniously dropped through the ceiling panels into one of the flooding sections to keep them out of the way. Even that wasn’t enough with the amount of blood and gore splattered throughout the hallways, and the freshly dead that showed up after an altercation with some of the other prisoners roaming about, growing increasingly violent as they tried to hoard supplies, tried to thin out the number of mouths to feed or just let the antsy claustrophobia of being stuck in a sunken prison get the better of them. In her forays out of the cell block, Kara had tried her best to clean the hallways, but the acrid smell of bleach only mingled with the vestigial smell of flesh and blood, faint rusty streaks coating the walls and floors, amidst the dank smell of mould as black speckles of it slowly overtook the plaster and ceiling panels.

     

                Leaks had sprouted in numerous places, a sheen of water constantly reflecting the flickering lights as puddles formed and water ran down the walls. They’d sourced as many buckets, pots, trash cans and other vessels as possible to try and mitigate the slow flooding of the prison but it was practically impossible. They were all waiting for the day they starved to death or illness ravaged them all from the poor living conditions. If they’d thought it had been bad in the prison before, which it had been, it was nothing compared to being cut off from supplies and basic necessities. It didn’t help to have the wild cards prowling the hallways at times, and with the lack of yellow radiation and the constant expenditure of her energy trying to keep people safe, Kara had earned herself a few scrapes and bruises and minor fractures as she solar flared, not even knowing what that meant or having any context for the sudden bouts of vulnerability and weakness that she’d only previously experienced after long hours of exposure to the red sun lamps in her cell.

     

                Finding a relatively quiet corner where J’onn had tucked himself away in, Kara sank to the floor with a morose look on her face. Even her endless optimism was starting to feel rather forced and thin of late.

     

                “Winn’s still not having any luck with the radio.”

     

                “It was always wishful thinking to hope it would work,” J’onn grimly replied, giving her a thin smile.

     

                Frowning, Kara rubbed her cheek, unease and confusion knotting in her stomach. “I know, I just- do you think they made it out okay? I thought … I thought someone would have found us by now. That if they all made it to land safely … they would have told people. Lena said-“

     

                A sharp laugh interrupted her muddled thoughts as she spoke them aloud. Looking up, Kara’s eyes landed on Andrea, who was stretched out on her back, one arm beneath her head as she tossed a foraged stress ball into the air and caught it with the other hand. She was smiling bitterly and her blue eyes slid sideways to Kara as she caught the ball again.

     

                “Well, that was your first mistake, KZ.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “Trusting her.”

     

                Anger lashed through Kara, making her cheeks redden. “That wasn’t a mistake. I know her, I know Lena will keep her word.”

     

                Scoffing, Andrea raised her eyebrows as she stared at the ceiling, a mocking edge to the twist of her lips. “Will she? I can tell you one thing I know for sure; I used to be just like her. I grew up in Argentina for most of my life and we were very well off - maybe not Luthor money but damn near close to it for a while - and I know for a fact that if my father hadn’t lost our fortune, and if I had still acquired some dodgy amulet to try and help and wound up in here all the same, if I got out … I’d forget this place ever existed. I’d go back to my mansion and forget I ever knew you. So don’t be upset when we all start dropping dead in the next month because your prison girlfriend didn’t stay true to her word. She’s a billionaire - she doesn’t give a shit about any of us now that she’s free.”

     

                Silent for a moment, doubt sown in the back of her mind, Kara pursed her lips and stubbornly jutted her chin forward. “You’re wrong.”

     

                Fumbling the ball as it fell back toward her, Andrea sighed as it skittered away across the concrete floor, coming to a rest against the base of the wall. Turning her head, she helplessly spread her hands as she gave Kara a wide-eyed, serious look.

     

                “Then where is she? How many days has it been now?”

     

                Eyes straying to the wall with the notches she’d been making for each day that had passed, Kara felt a lump lodge itself in her throat. Her eyes stung and she felt embarrassed, pushing herself to her feet and stalking off, her shoulders taut as she put some distance between herself and the other woman. Still, she could hear J’onn quietly berating Andrea for trying to kill Kara’s hope, insisting that it was harmless to let her believe that Lena was coming. The way he said it, it made Kara’s stomach sink with the realisation that he didn’t much believe her friends were coming back for them either.

     

                Curling up in her small patch of free space, she tried to sleep for a while but couldn’t. Restless and tense, unable to stretch out, unable to block out the sounds of other people or the overpowering smell of them all, Kara tossed and turned as her mind worried at the delay of their rescue. The worst part was not knowing, but she knew even if they didn’t come, she wouldn’t have changed her mind about coming back to buy everyone more time. Or maybe she would have; maybe if she had flown off to civilisation, she would have roused people to rescue them herself, but Kara knew they would’ve been rescuing corpses if she hadn’t sealed the doors back up as much as possible, hadn’t plucked supplies from flooding hallways and sectors to keep everyone fed, hadn’t broken them out of their cell blocks in the first place. 

     

                It was just a shit situation either way she looked at it but the reality at the moment was a dragged-out, inevitable death for them all in comparison to what could have been relatively quick. And hadn’t Querl said that drowning was quite peaceful? Not that she would have been on board if she’d flown away, but where would Kara have gone without her friends? If they truly had abandoned her - a thought she didn’t want to entertain - then they wouldn’t have wanted her with them anyway. Not even Lena.

     

                After a couple of hours of brooding, she rose to her feet and started sorting through the rations, which were under constant guard to ensure no one stole extras. There were a few dozen of them inside the cell block, but it was mostly the prisoners Kara had originally been with, a few others she recognised around the prison, who had been let loose and were frightened of the violence breaking out, and as many others that seemed placid as they could fit. She also had a few of the more helpful or knowledgeable guards and officials too, including the Deputy. The only one missing from their original cell block, who hadn’t been freed from the prison, was Mon-El.

     

                He’d made himself a nuisance though, banging on the doors and demanding they give him their supplies, cursing out Kara and demanding her to face him directly. She wasn’t worried about him, and he was easily scared off whenever she had to leave the block, all posturing and idle threats as hunger and fear got the better of him. It was the same for most of the other prisoners, all of them thin and hungry, fighting for supplies, covered in blood, wearing clothes they stripped off each other’s unconscious bodies, nursing injuries with looted medical supplies. Of course, more than a few of them had killed each other and Kara had endured a few broken bones splitting up those fights, trying to keep the prison together as Winn and Querl patched machines and equipment, kept the lights on and the oxygen and water running.

     

                Sifting through a couple of boxes of saltine crackers and canned apple slices, Kara nodded to Nia, who approached first and was handed her cut of dinner. It wasn’t much, barely more than a few bites as she was given two crackers with an apple slice on each. They had plenty of water though, which was fortunate, although there was a faint tang of salt to it as it came out of the faucet on the little sinks in each cell. They’d run out of tea and coffee weeks ago but at least it kept them all hydrated to have water, even if they slowly starved.

     

                Eating her own rations once everyone else had been served theirs, the complaints growing fewer as they all adjusted to their shrunken stomachs and dwindling food supplies, Kara felt defeated. She didn’t know how much longer they could last, not just physically but the way everyone’s mental health was so clearly deteriorating as well. In the beginning, when they’d made the effort to scrounge up as many useful items as possible, they’d taken novels and decks of cards from the rooms of staff members, as well as the half-missing chess set in the room they had their socials in, coloured pencils and paper, even a TV and a radio. That wasn’t enough to fill the time though and they were all restless and bored, cooped up together for too long.

     

                The cell block wound down for the night and Kara slept near the stockpile of food, along with her friends, Imra on watch for the next few hours as the rest bedded down, and she slept fitfully. The sound of coughing, sniffling and snoring kept waking her even when she did sleep, an interminable cold making the rounds as they remained in close quarters. She never got sick, fortunately for her, but it was a cesspool of bacteria inside the cell block, and no amount of attempting to stay clean could help as they were left to wear the same clothes each day, unable to wash properly, clean their greasy hair or brush their teeth with actual toothpaste. 

     

                Despite not being locked in their individual cells, with shock collars and armed guards, medical appointments and daily mandated walks around the same room, cold showers and pills and their set routine with portioned meals to their caloric intake, they were worse off than ever. It was a warped train of thought to wish for the orderly routine and care of the prison guards and their efficiently maintained schedule, with deliveries and staff rotation, but Kara didn’t think a single person inside the prison would object to that now. It would have been better than starving, would have been better than their current circumstances. Each night she went to sleep and dreamt of the faces of unknown guards and staff she’d killed to claw her way out of the prison and each morning she woke grey-faced with grief and regret, wishing she’d never done it. 

     

                But then she’d think of Lena, of her bloody, tear-stained face as Kara had kissed her goodbye and left her on the deck. To see the sunrise with her, that singular, beautiful event, and know that she’d freed her at least, was a balm to Kara’s horror at her own actions. Perhaps she deserved to stay inside that prison and die there in recompense for the hurt she’d inflicted, the damage she’d caused which had directly led to their current circumstances, but it was a consolation to know that Lena wouldn’t be there to die beside her. It eased the pain just a little to know she’d done that one good thing before the end.

     

                Waking early to the permanent brightness of the lights and the constant sound of other people, Kara climbed to her feet and tapped Nia’s shoulder to relieve the young woman of her watch over the food. Immediately finding space on the floor, Nia went to sleep and Kara stepped around other prone figures as she picked her way over to the sink. Running the water, she splashed it over her face and washed her hands, the frigid temperature not bothering her one bit, although many of the others complained about how it made their teeth ache, and was likely partially responsible for the chest infections and possible pneumonia some of them were suffering from, the cold and damp getting to them. Rinsing her mouth out and then drinking some water, Kara was drying off her hands and face with the sleeves when a whine filled the cell block.

     

                She paused and turned, a few of the others also disturbed by the sound. They settled back down again but a moment later there was another high-pitched whine and a crackle. Eyes zeroing in on the communications radio, the clunky piece of equipment with its knobs and buttons and speakers emitting the sound. Moving as quickly as possible, Kara tripped over Winn’s legs and fell to her knees before the device.

     

                Grumbling as he was woken up, Winn pushed himself up and rubbed his eyes, while Kara ignored him. She gripped the sides of the machine and stared at it with wide, desperate eyes, unsure whether she was imagining things or whether the sound was something. 

     

                “What?” Winn grumbled, pushing the blanket off. “What is it?”

     

                “A noise,” Kara hoarsely replied. “I thought I heard- there was a noise. A- a whining sound.”

     

                More people were waking up then because of the disturbance and Querl was on Kara’s other side, taking a knee as he cocked his head to the side. He glanced at Winn, who had shifted to a crouch beside Kara, frowning at the silent radio.

     

                “You’re convinced you’ve fixed it correctly?” Querl asked him.

     

                “As sure as I can be.”

     

                They were silent for a moment, the three of them - and the others who were awake - listening carefully. There was a faint crackle but nothing else and Kara’s expression furrowed with disappointment as she sat back, shoulders slumping. The silence inside the cell block was thick as she swallowed dryly.

     

                “I thought I- never mind,” she murmured.

     

                The machine stayed silent, the hum of it like a taunt as she closed her eyes. Then it whined again, with a faint crackle, and a split second later there was the sound of a broken voice.

     

                “-lo?”

     

                Kara’s eyelids snapped open as her heart hammered in her chest and she leaned in. The three of them sitting before it all shared glances as if reassuring each other that they weren’t imagining things.

     

                “That was-“

     

                “You heard it too, right?”

     

                “Hell- … is ther- … one there? Does … -one …py?”

     

                Winn anxiously started tuning the frequency as Kara picked up a headset with a mic attached to it, settling them over her ears. Pushing a button to talk, Kara licked her lips as her eyes flitted around restlessly.

     

                “Hello? Hello? Is someone there?”

     

                “Does anyone copy?”

     

                “Yes,” Kara breathlessly replied. “Yes, we copy. We- we’re here. Please. Please help us. You have to help us.”

     

                “Hello? Hello?”

     

                “Hello, we’re here. We’re right here.”

     

                “Copy. This is the MT Leviathan, we hear you. Can you please identify yourself?”

     

                Relief cut keenly through Kara and she felt the pressure of a sob building in her chest as her hands shook terribly. She had to curl one into a fist in her lap as she swallowed thickly, barely able to speak.

     

                “My name’s Kara Zor-El. I’m- I’m a prisoner on board the Fort Rozz. Um … we’re underwater. We’re sinking. I don’t know how- how many of us there are but-“

     

                “Did you say prisoner?”

     

                “Yes, sir. I- do you know Lena? Lena Luthor? I need to speak to Lena, I-“

     

                “Lena Luthor?”

     

                “Yes. Yes, that’s her. Is she coming? Do you know if she’s coming for us?”

     

                “Oh, shit!” The man said before his voice faded. “Gemma, I need you to radio whoever you can get in contact with. I think we’ve found that prison everyone’s been talking about. That one with all the aliens on it.”

     

                His voice grew louder again as he came back on the radio. “Kara? You said your name is Kara?”

     

                “Yes, sir.”

     

                “I’m Captain Khan, of the Leviathan. We’re a fishing tanker off the coast of Alaska. That’s where you are; do you- do you know where you are?”

     

                “Yes, sir. My friends- I helped them escape. They’re supposed to be coming back for us, um … it’s been weeks. Months. Do you know-“

     

                “They’re looking for you, Kara. Alright? Your friends … they’ve been all over the news. Can you- can you tell me anything else? How many of you are there?”

     

                “I don’t know. I don’t know. A lot of them are dead. They’re all sick. There’s not enough food. Um … we just- we need help. If you could- if you could tell them where we are, sir, that would be really good.”

     

                “We’re radioing in right now, alright? It’s going to be fine. Help is on its way, do you hear me, Kara? It’s a good thing your prison is so big, huh? Damn near gave me a heart attack picking you up on the radar. I thought for sure it was a shipwreck of a naval submarine. God damn, that’s some good luck.”

     

                He was laughing now, elated with disbelief, and a nervous laugh built in Kara’s chest as she rubbed a hand over her face. There was a faint feeling inside at the news that her friends were safe, had made it far enough to be on the news, and her whole body felt limp as if she would never be able to move again. 

     

                Captain Khan kept rambling on but she couldn’t concentrate on his words anymore, but she was conscious of the sound of an approaching vessel. Soon enough, the tanker seemed practically upon them and Kara’s eyes drifted towards the ceiling.

     

                “Captain Khan? You’re right on top of us, sir.”

     

                “Alright, well, my crew and I will stay right here until we get this sorted out, alright? Don’t you worry now, you’ll all be fine soon enough.”

     

                “Thank you, sir,” she faintly replied, biting her lip before she continued. “Do you- do you think you could ask them to let me speak to Lena? Or Alex, Kelly, Eliza, any of them. Do you think you could ask for me?”

     

                “Alright, Kara. I’ll ask.”

    Chapter 23

                A week went by since arriving at the detention facility and Lena was left feeling antsy and in the dark. Aside from her mother’s brief visit, she had no other contact with anyone who could offer up any information, and aside from the brief hearing, where there was a prolonged scramble to determine what to charge her with, she was charged under the Espionage Act, same as Alex, and left in the custody of the FBI for the time being.

     

                Of course, they could have charged her under that act for the information she’d helped leak to reporters, via her mother, and if her mother wasn’t so untouchable, with direct lines to the White House most of the time, they probably could have charged Lillian as complicit as well. But it was just a formality, a reason to hold Lena at the detention facility for the time being while the multitude of investigations played out. That could take months though, and Lena was left inside her cell with gritted teeth as she felt time pass by so quickly.

     

                There was nothing to be done for it though, and she had to swallow the hard pill that she was irrelevant in the grand scheme of it now. And what did it matter in the end? If they rescued Kara - and to a lesser extent, the others - what did it matter if she was the one who paid for the equipment and the manpower, who convinced the government and military and came up with the plan? Except that it mattered a great deal to her and it was unbearable to sit idly while waiting for political leaders to figure out what to do with her.

     

                Until a week had passed and they’d figured it out, Lena unaware of that fact until heavy footsteps stomped down the hallway just past lunchtime. She’d already eaten, her tray left on the floor, the meal inadequate but filling. Lena had long since stopped turning her nose up at food after being subjected to things she would have hardly called edible in her past. Under the impression that she would have been left alone for the remainder of the afternoon, until it was time for dinner, Lena was surprised to hear footsteps beyond. It could have been for another cell and she stared at her lap as her shoulders grew tense, waiting to find out what was going on.

     

                “Luthor.”

     

                Lena raised her head, eyebrows lifting inquisitively as she watched the guard set the key in the lock, metal scraping as the tumbler turned and the door swung open.

     

                “You’re free to go.”

     

                It took Lena a moment to make sense of what she was hearing, remaining seated on her cot as she blinked, staring at the man. There was a best of silence and the guard shifted impatiently, an expectant look on his face as he tucked his thumbs through his belt loops.

     

                “Free to go?” Lena echoed, her expression perplexed as she wrung her hands in her lap.

     

                “President Brayden signed your release this morning.”

     

                Taking another moment to absorb the new information, Lena hesitated before she slowly pushed herself to her feet. She felt as if she was dreaming, or was perhaps being subjected to some psychological torment as a prank, that she’d reach the door and they’d slam it in her face and laugh.

     

                Cautiously crossing the small cell, she paused on the threshold and the guard stepped aside, arching an eyebrow as he gestured her out. There were no handcuffs, just another guard waiting to escort her out, and Lena toyed with the hem of her prison beige clothes, fighting to swallow as she tried to wrap her head around things.

     

                They took her to a bare room just before the mesh grille and locked doors of the entrance, the clothes she’d come in with pressed into her hands. Shakily changing inside the room, she took a moment to fold her prison uniform and left it in a pile on the floor, unsure of what to do now.

     

                She was processed for her release quickly, all of the paperwork filled out, a few of the guards casting furtive glances, doors unlocked and the lobby of the detention facility open to her. And of course, her mother was there, rigidly occupying a vinyl-covered chair in the waiting area.

     

                Rising to her feet, Lillian arched an eyebrow as she gave her daughter an appraising look. “Well, I guess some allowances should be made for fashion choices in the Arctic Circle. Not to worry, I’ll have that taken care of. You’ll feel like your old self again in no time.”

     

                “What’s going on?” Lena asked, ignoring her.

     

                Already making for the door, Lillian glanced back over her shoulder, sceptically. “You’re free to go. Obviously.”

     

                “Obviously. But why?”

     

                “President Brayden and I had a nice long chat. I’ve been speaking to the White House for weeks, trying to orchestrate this, but then … well, things fell into place. She had the common sense to realise she needed to take a different stance from Baker if she wanted any chance at succeeding in the role. For starters, the anti-alien policies didn’t seem to do him any favours or garner any sympathy once word of the DEO got out. Brayden doesn’t want the same to happen to her so she’s decided to back your cause instead. Not that it’s for you, only that things seem to be swaying in that direction and it’s better to be seen on the right side, wouldn’t you agree?”

     

                They were outside, walking across the asphalt to the black car that her mother had arrived in. A driver was behind the wheel and he climbed out to open the back door for Lillian, who slid in first with Lena following after. Buckling herself in, she sank into the soft leather and breathed in the smell of the polish rubbed into the seats, her eyes closing as she was brought back to the hundreds of times she had been chauffeured around in her own car. 

     

                Once the driver was back behind the wheel, the engine rumbling to life beneath them, Lillian leaned forward and pushed the button to raise the partition separating the halves of the car. Leaning back, her mother cleared her throat, staring aloofly out the window as she spoke.

     

                “I have the jet ready and fuelled to go at an airstrip just outside the city. You’ll have to wait for them to return your assets to you - you know, unfreeze your accounts, return your devices, research, keys - so it would be best for you to stay with me for the time being until your apartment is made suitable.”

     

                “What?”

     

                Lillian turned to look at Lena, her expression cool as she met her daughter’s eye. Slowly blinking, Lillian exhaled. “You will come and stay with me until your apartment-”

     

                “No, I’m not leaving. I have to stay here, in DC, until- until things get sorted. The others-”

     

                “The others are where they should be. I doubt very much that they will be leaving anytime soon, at any rate.”

     

                “Why would you say that?”

     

                “Because they’re criminals , Lena. And that is where criminals deserve to be.”

     

                “You don’t even know what you’re talking about, okay? That’s not for you to decide-”

     

                “It’s not for you either.”

     

                “Yes, it is. I was there with them, I know what they did. And if you think they’re criminals, you have to believe the same of me. I was there too, I-”

     

                “You were wrongfully blamed. You didn’t hurt anyone, but they hurt you. Am I not allowed to resent them for the pain they inflicted on my daughter?”

     

                Lena’s mouth hitched into an uneven smile, her eyes glazing over as her mind seemed to slip away to somewhere else, some memory. Lillian couldn’t have known what was replaying in her mind, the heaviness of a limp body in her arms, hot blood on her hands, the way the scalpel felt digging into flesh, the way a light went out in the eyes as she felt dread pool in her stomach, the cloying smell of copper in the air as she was covered in so much blood.

     

                “I killed someone.”

     

                She didn’t mean to confess it, didn’t mean to let the words slip out and give truth to something that she’d intended to bury with the rest of what had happened to her. The silence in the back of the car was deafening and she stared at Lillian, her chest rising and falling quickly, and after a moment she shrugged slightly, cocking an eyebrow. It belied the disgust, the guilt, the grief and anger buried inside but she couldn’t let herself feel it then.

     

                Instead, she confessed it as if it was nothing, as if it wasn’t the thing that kept her up at night, the thing she had nightmares of, haunted by it. That was only a part of it too, the other things she’d endured, complicit in as well, a suffocating horror that suffused her every thought. It was largely thoughts of Kara drowning, of Kara trapped that bothered her the most and that was its own guilt to deal with.

     

                After a moment, Lillian shrugged in return and let out a frosty laugh. “Do you think that matters to me?”

     

                “It should. If they’re criminals, so am I.”

     

                “No, you’re not. It’s an entirely different situation. Whatever led you to kill someone must have warranted it.”

     

                “How do you know that? You weren’t there.”

     

                “I wasn’t, but you have been so painfully noble and self-righteous your entire life. It’s partially why this rift has existed between us since you were a child. Always so- so soft, so weak. You never had the stomach for the dirty, brutal, painful sides of science, the sides that drive innovation and creation. This person you killed … it could only have been a last resort.”

     

                Eyes stinging, Lena looked out the tinted window and swallowed thickly. “It was,” she whispered.

     

                “I’ll not ask you to tell me. It’s irrelevant anyway and clearly something that’s bothering you-“

     

                “Bothering me? I killed someone. Maybe not a good person but still … of course it’s bothering me.”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Lillian rolled her eyes. “You’re always so busy assigning morality to things. Whether they were good or not, they’re dead and you’re not and, thus, you have come out the victor. Accept that and move on.”

     

                Falling silent, Lena watched the city pass by for a while before she cleared her throat and looked at Lillian. Raising her chin, she frowned slightly, stubborn and serious.

     

                “I’m not leaving the city.”

     

                “Oh, Lena-“

     

                “I’m not. I’m not leaving. I need to stay close to all of this. Thank you for your help. Really. I know I haven’t always appreciated your methods but I’m grateful for everything you’ve done to help me. But this is where we part ways.”

     

                Still for a second, Lillian conceded with a nod. “Very well, if that’s what you want. I’ve been staying at the Waldorf; you can have my room.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                It was an uncomfortable ride for the rest of the duration as Lillian lowered the partition and instructed the driver to take them back to the hotel. Once they arrived, she bid the driver wait for her and swept out of the car as Lena lingered on the sidewalk, brimming with nervous tension as her eyes darted around. There were pedestrians but they didn’t give her a second glance as they carried on past.

     

                Making for a private entrance to the townhouse adjoining the Waldorf Astoria, Lillian was fishing her keys out of her bag and Lena’s stomach jolted with panic. Hurrying to catch up with her mother, she swallowed, her mouth dry as she looked at the building, two floors and no doubt the most expensive room available at the hotel, but also so easily accessible if anyone tried to break in and steal her away.

     

                “This is your room?” she hoarsely asked.

     

                “Yes, the Townhouse Suite. It’s the biggest they have; I’m not sure you’ll have much need of the second bedroom.”

     

                “I can’t stay here.”

     

                “Nonsense. It’s well-sized and they’ll cater to your every need. My card is on file so you’ll be able to take all of your meals here until you get things sorted.”

     

                “No, I-”

     

                “Christ, Lena, does it always have to be such an ordeal with you? What is it now? You’d think someone who has been in jail and on the run for the better part of ten months would be glad to stay in a townhouse at the Waldorf. Especially when your mother is footing the bill for you.”

     

                Closing her eyes as she raked a hand over her face, pale and tense as she breathed slowly, Lena’s face rippled with panic. “I am glad, I just- I’d like a different room. Please.”

     

                “This is the best they offer.”

     

                “I’m sure, I just- I’d like to stay in a room that’s a bit … higher up.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lillian clicked her tongue with exasperation. “Really? You think someone is going to come in and steal you away again? Heavens. Well, you always have had a flare for the dramatics - and considered yourself more important than you are. Very well, I’ll arrange a new room for you.”

     

                Inside the lobby, the receptionist kept glancing at Lena with mild shock on her face as she nervously fumbled about, typing on the computer, activating a keycard. It was slid across the counter and Lillian plucked it off the marble, holding it out to Lena with a thin smile on her lips.

     

                “There. The penthouse is sufficiently high enough for you?”

     

                With a surly look on her face, Lena took the keycard from her and pocketed it in her thick winter coat. As they moved away from the front desk, Lillian gave her a once over and opened her handbag, fishing out her purse and sliding a black credit card free.

     

                “Do me a favour and buy something more suitable to wear. I can’t bear to look at you dressed like some … hiking lumberjack.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, lips twitching with a ghost of a smile, Lena pocketed the credit card too. “Fashion isn’t particularly high on my list of priorities at the moment, but I’ll see what I can do.”

     

                “Well it should be. Anytime you set foot outside of this hotel, you’re going to have a horde of reporters and photographers outside. That should warrant some pride in your appearance; your name has already been besmirched.”

     

                “Not that I’m planning on any outings.”

     

                “Call if you need anything. You may think you don’t need my help but, well, you never thought you’d need me to get you out of prison. But here we are.”

     

                Disgruntled by her mother’s evident enjoyment in Lena being beholden to her, Lena turned around and jammed her thumb into the elevator button. Tense and still somewhat stunned by the fact that she was walking about freely, Lena stepped into the elevator and met her mother’s level stare until the doors slid shut and she started to rise to the penthouse at the push of a button.

     

                Stepping off at the top floor, the opulence of the place was disorienting as she walked to the door and let herself into her suite. The room was the traditional decor she had grown up with, all dark wood and heavy fabrics, the canopied bed made with crisp white sheets, the walls and furnishings a rich royal blue. Lena felt scruffy in comparison, wandering through the spacious rooms and feeling dizzy with the sudden change in her circumstances. Suddenly, the casual display of so much wealth felt sickening when she considered where Kara was, where she had been until recently.

     

                The thought made her uneasy, which made her hot beneath the heavy winter layers, and she quickly started to strip off layers as her heart pounded in her chest, breaths coming quickly as a hot sweat started to prickle her skin. Leaving her clothes scattered around her, until she was down to her underwear, Lena staggered over to the windows and fumbled with the heavy drapes until she dragged them across, before stumbling back over to the front door and locking it from the inside. 

     

                Then, she quickly walked into the bathroom and vomited in the sink before scooping a handful of water from the tap and rinsing out her mouth. Pressing a hand to her clammy forehead, she closed her eyes and breathed for a moment, feeling nauseous and frightened, before she stripped off her underwear and turned to the large tub. One of the things she’d been looking forward to upon her escape had been a hot bath, and while the presence of one was not quite the treat she’d anticipated, given the circumstances of her newly found freedom, Lena couldn’t pass it up.

     

                Running the hot water, the simple luxury of it feeling like a gift, she added some of the body wash to the running water and watched bubbles froth. Stepping in when the water barely covered the bottom of the tub, she gripped the porcelain sides, the bones of her back prominent as she hunched over and drew in heaving breaths, trying to wrestle with the confusion of the person she’d been and the person she now was, the life she’d had before and the life she’d lived recently. It was difficult to come to terms with the fact that she’d been subjected to awful conditions after a pampered life of decadence and wealth and the privilege of anything at her fingertips. Now, she was thrust back into it, of a sort, as if she was expected to just assimilate back into her old life, as if the rest of it had never happened.

     

                Once the bath was full enough, Lena shut off the taps and slipped beneath the water. It was stingingly hot, turning her skin pink as the heat flushed it, and she stayed under until her lungs ached and she was forced to resurface. Staying in the bath until the water started to cool, she drained it and ran a new one, this time making use of the shampoo and conditioner, the body wash, scouring herself clean and then climbing out before the heat faded. 

     

                Wrapping herself in a fluffy towel, she dried off and then donned a bathrobe before wandering back into the suite. Recovering her mother’s credit card from the pocket of her coat, Lena left her clothes on the floor and walked over to the bar fridge. Another thing she’d been looking forward to had been alcohol, and she definitely could have used it then. Although the bar fridge lacked the usual labels she favoured, there were little bottles of whisky, vodka, tequila, gin and rum. She plucked them all out with the bottle of champagne and carried them through to the bedroom.

     

                Setting her prizes on the mattress, Lena ensured all of the windows were locked and then dragged the drapes across before making her way back out to the open living area, grabbing a dining chair and wedging the back of it under the door handle for good measure. Returning to the bedroom, shutting herself inside, Lena walked over to the bed and sank onto the mattress, reaching for one of the bottles. 

     

                Draining the tequila in one long chug, she screwed the lid back on and set it down with a shaky hand. Reaching for the next one, she swallowed the rum in two mouthfuls and repeated the process until she’d gone through the spirits and popped the cork on the champagne. Having been sober for longer than she’d ever been since the age of eighteen, the alcohol worked quickly, her tolerance all but non-existent, and some of Lena’s jitteriness mellowed out.

     

                With that mellowing came the deep, gut-wrenching guilt and grief of leaving Kara behind. Sipping the champagne as she sat cross-legged on the bed, her skin soft and pink, her damp hair air drying as she stared blankly at the wall, Lena felt the horrifying pit in her stomach yawn wide open to consume her. It wasn’t even dusk yet but that day felt neverending as she drank and drank, the champagne sickly sweet and getting worse as it warmed, the bottle held tightly in her grasp. And Lena drank to forget but it didn’t make her forget at all, not one bit - instead, it made her feel vulnerable and alone, the line between her composure and falling apart very thin.

     

                The champagne made her feel sick and she had to stop, setting the mostly full bottle on the nightstand and then curling on her side in the middle of the bed. It was too soft, the quilt too thick, the bed too wide, and Lena’s head was spinning as the alcohol hit her. Her breathing turned shallow as she squeezed her eyes shut, and while she didn’t cry exactly, the breathless gasps and hitching breaths in the dark of the room were so clearly quiet sobs but she didn’t give in to the pressure of tears building behind her eyes, that choking tightness in her throat to let out ragged sobs that would have filled the silence.

     

                Falling asleep on her side, Lena slept fitfully, murmuring wordlessly, her eyes moving beneath closed eyelids as her face furrowed periodically. It was nothing new, nothing but the same nightmares that had plagued her since the night she’d been taken from her home. She woke a few times in a cold sweat, the darkness of the bedroom foreign and unnerving as she was left momentarily disoriented at the unfamiliar surroundings. The lingering effects of the alcohol didn’t help, leaving her confused, muddling through the fact that she was free until sleep came for her again.

     

                The following morning, she sat red-eyed and gaunt with exhaustion and the hangover she’d regretfully acquired. Sipping the bottle of Perrier she’d taken from the fridge, she curled up on a sofa and stared blankly at the wall until a knock on the door disturbed her. Head whipping to it, Lena’s heart pounded as her hands turned clammy around the bottle. Eyes darting around in a panic, she listened to the rap of knuckles repeat.

     

                A muffled voice sounded through the door and she stared at the chair, wedged beneath the handle, and refused to answer it. Eventually, the person left and five minutes later the landline phone started to ring. Hesitating, Lena crossed the room to answer it.

     

                “Hello?”

     

                “Miss Luthor, so sorry to disturb you. A delivery has arrived for you; a porter just tried to deliver it to your door but there was no answer. Would now be a good time for him to bring the delivery up?”

     

                “No,” Lena blurted out, her voice a rasp. “No, thank you. I don’t want any deliveries or- or housekeeping or anything like that. Thank you.”

     

                Slamming the phone down onto the receiver, Lena sank onto the plush armchair beside it, head tipping back as she massaged the headache at her temples. Ten minutes later, the phone rang again and she felt her patience immediately wear out, anger flushing through her as she yanked the phone free.

     

                “I don’t want to be disturbed,” she snapped.

     

                “Just answer the door,” Lillian drawled.

                

                Blinking in surprise, and suddenly abash at her curtness, Lena’s lips parted. “How do you know someone’s at the door?”

     

                “They have clothes for you. I took the liberty of ordering you a few things and they’ve called me to say you won’t answer the door.”

     

                “Sorry, I’m not particularly keen on opening the door to strangers anymore,” Lena snorted. “Can’t imagine why.”

     

                “Just answer the door.”

     

                Her mother hung up and Lena stared down at the phone for a moment before she hung it up with a scoff. Her relationship with Lillian had ever been a tricky thing. There was love there, to some degree, and a level of toxicity, and her mother had always pushed her to be better, even if in Lillian’s opinion that meant being worse , but there was also a coldness to their relationship, a lack of empathy and towards each other from both ends. Lena wouldn’t garner any sympathy from Lillian because of what she’d been through, but she knew her mother would fight tooth and nail for her out of principle. 

     

                She was a Luthor, and while that may not have gotten her anything maternal out of her mother, it offered her something better - someone who would never let anyone outside of the family mistreat Lena. Lillian also had the propensity to ignore the past and focus on what was ahead, which was unfortunate in the current situation as her brusque indifference afforded Lena no grace to adjust back to reality.

     

                Still, when there was a knock on the door five minutes later, Lena moved the chair and unlocked everything, jerking it open and then glancing from the porter to the taller, more imposing figure her mother cut at the young man’s side. Arching an eyebrow, Lillian barged inside, stepping around Lena, who moved back, opening the door wider, before the porter followed her inside with more discomfort and uncertainty, his arms laden with bags.

     

                Finding the light switch, Lillian flicked them on and then strode over to the windows, yanking the curtains apart. “Really, Lena, you’ll strain your eyes trying to see in this gloom.”

     

                Running a hand over her face, Lena sighed and the man quickly set down all the bags, giving her a courteous nod as he shifted uneasily, before backing out of the room and shutting the door behind him. Opening her eyes, Lena stared at her mother.

     

                “What are you still doing here? I thought you had your jet ready.”

     

                “Yes, well, that was for your benefit. Seeing as you’re determined to stay here, I thought I’d stay as well. You’ll inevitably need my help - even just my connections.”

     

                “And why is that? If you could have done something about the prison, you already would have, so I’m starting to doubt the usefulness of your connections. I know my assets are still frozen, but it wasn’t a matter of money for you to charter a ship to locate the prison if you wanted to do that for me - I gave you the coordinates - so what other use are you to me?”

     

                “You’ve been drinking,” Lillian noted.

     

                “Wouldn’t you?”

     

                Humming, Lillian gave her an appraising look before she walked over to the table and sank onto a chair. Gesturing to the bags, she unbelted the front of her coat and crossed her legs.

     

                “A few necessities for you.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “Have you eaten yet?”

     

                “No.”

     

                “I’ll order room service. What will you have?”

     

                “I’m not hungry.”

     

                “If you’re hungover, food will help.”

     

                “I can manage my own hangover.”

     

                “I’ll order anyway.”

     

                Trying to rein her temper in, Lena exhaled sharply through her nose and Lillian rose to her feet and crossed over to the phone. Dialling for room service, she rattled off a list of dishes and they sat in tense silence until there was a knock on the door. Lillian rose to answer it herself and in short order, the dining table was covered with silver trays, uncovered to reveal the dishes beneath them.

     

                Looking at the granola, the apple pancakes, seasonal fruit selection and eggs with bacon and breakfast potatoes, Lena felt her stomach turn. It was richer fare than she’d had in almost a year, and coupled with too much to drink on an empty stomach after a long stint of sobriety, she knew it wouldn’t stay down.
