Instead, she poured coffee from the carafe and had it black, taking small sips as the food cooled. Lillian didn’t touch it either, drinking her coffee as she eyed Lena shrewdly.

     

                Once it was evident she wasn’t going to eat a single bite of it all, Lillian sighed and folded her arms. “Well, seeing as you have no interest in anything but brooding, perhaps some information will cheer you up.”

     

                Expression sharpening as her interest was piqued, Lena straightened in her seat. “What information?”

     

                Deliberately taking her time, Lillian raised her cup of coffee and took a slow sip before setting it back down. Clearing her throat as she rotated the cup on the saucer, there was a glint in her eyes. Patience quickly wearing thin, Lena lashed out and dashed the cup from the table, coffee splattering over the floor as the cup rolled away on the rug.

     

                “Tell me,” she demanded, her voice dangerously low.

     

                Looking surprised by her outburst, Lillian raised her eyebrows and ran her finger against the rim of the saucer. Clearing her throat, she stared at her daughter, wanting to gauge her reaction to her words.

     

                “An Alaskan fishing boat picked up something on their SONAR. Radio communication was made and they called in to local authorities saying they’d found Fort Rozz.”

     

                Lena’s stomach swooped, her heart hammering as she leaned forward, lips parted, eyes wide. She hardly dared to believe her mother’s words, that bubble of hope expanding in her chest almost too impossible to believe. 

     

                “They’ve found them?”

     

                “Well, radio communication was made. But it’s definitely them; you were asked for by name.”

                

                “By whom?” Lena asked, her voice wavering as she clung to the desperate hope that it was Kara.

     

                “Who do you think?”

     

                On her feet in an instant, Lena was shaking as she helplessly stared around, unsure where to even begin. “I- I have to go. Where are they? Which boat is out there? I need to go-”

     

                “They’re not out there anymore; the call was made six days ago.”

     

                “Six days?” Lena hoarsely echoed, anger flashing across her face. “Six days and you didn’t tell me?”

     

                “Would it have helped to be in prison, knowing that they’d been found and you couldn’t help?”

     

                Voice wobbling as her eyes stung fiercely with tears she would never let fall in front of Lillian, Lena turned around and started picking up the bags of new clothes. “Yes . Yes, I think it would’ve helped a lot to know what was going on, to know that it was all worth it.”

     

                “Who can say if it was worth it yet? They still need to rescue them - if they can. It would have only added to your stress and worsened your mental health to be left in the dark after being given a spark of hope. I did it for your own good-”

     

                “Don’t give me that,” Lena snapped.

     

                She unearthed underwear, a pair of pants, a thick sweater, a pair of heeled boots and a wool coat with a fur collar. It was entirely inappropriate attire for where she needed to go but Lena tore the tags off and dressed quickly, unable to bring herself to feel self-conscious with her mother watching hawkishly as she verged dangerously close to breaking down before her. Perhaps being in prison for so long had desensitised her to normal etiquette in social situations but Lena didn’t care if she was being rude, snapping when Lillian insisted she was just trying to help, snubbing food she would have killed for months ago, essentially biting the hand that fed her. 

     

                Dressed, she scraped her hair out of her face and faced Lillian. Her agitation dimmed then, her shoulder slumping with defeat as she realised she was effectively stranded in DC. Blinking rapidly as her eyes took on a glassy sheen, she swallowed thickly, her throat tight as she was forced to stifle her pride.

     

                “Please,” she raggedly begged. “I need to go, I just- I need to talk to her. Maybe it’s asking too much after everything you’ve already done for me, and I’m grateful, I am, but I- please just tell me where they are or who I can talk to and I’ll- I’ll go. You won’t have to help me anymore.”

     

                Lillian’s eyelids shuttered and she sharply exhaled through her nose. Sitting straight in her seat, she opened the front of her coat and removed something from the inside pocket, setting down a little plastic card. She slid it across the table and Lena quickly closed the gap, curious now. Picking it up, she stared at a photo of herself and realised it was a driver’s licence. Glancing up at her mother, Lena’s face crumpled with confusion.

     

                “If you had eaten your breakfast and taken the time to shower and dress, we could have had this talk properly and would have left in time to make it to the airstrip for the flight I have scheduled to Anchorage,” her mother grumbled with disapproval. “As stubborn as you have always been, of course you wouldn’t listen to me - even when I am wasting my time to help you.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena felt her eyes water and she scowled fiercely at the lump in her throat. Hand clenching around the ID, she sat heavily on her chair and drained her cup of coffee. Her stomach was tied into knots though and she couldn’t stomach a bite even if she’d wanted to, even if it meant pleasing her mother so she would help her further. 

     

                Sighing as she rolled her eyes, Lillian pushed back her chair and climbed to her feet, belting her coat and picking up her handbag from the floor. “Finish getting ready and we’ll leave now.”

     

                Shooting out of her seat, Lena rummaged through the rest of the bags and hastily brushed her teeth, sprayed on deodorant and then packed the other clothes her mother had bought her into a leather duffel bag that had been purchased as well. There was a brand new MacBook and iPhone as well but Lena didn’t do more than unbox them and pack them with the charging cables before she was zipping everything up and hauling the bag over her shoulder.

     

                Pocketing her room key as well as her mother’s credit card, unwilling to give that back just yet, she stalked out of the room on Lillian’s heels and followed her down to the lobby in silence. Outside, Lillian’s car was parked with a waiting driver smoking as he leaned against the polished body of it. Stamping out the cigarette, he jerked open the back door and Lena paused on the threshold of the hotel entrance, a horde of photographers and journalists set up at varying positions on the sidewalk. 

     

                Muttering a curse at her mother’s correct assumptions, wondering if perhaps Lillian had called them herself, as right as she was, Lena ducked her head and shielded her face with a hand, ducking behind her mother as much as she could. Lillian had hired security though, and three burly men fended off the photographers to clear a path to the car and Lena ignored the shouts of her name until Lillian was shoving her into the back of the car and climbing in after her.

                

                “Well, that will be the cover of tomorrow’s papers,” Lillian dryly commented as the driver set off.

     

                Surly with her unease and contempt for the attention and the reason why, Lena didn’t respond as the tinted windows blotted out the chances of the paparazzi taking photos of her, even if the flashes were irritatingly visible to her as the car was practically mobbed. A cold sweat covered Lena’s back and she fiddled anxiously with her hands in her lap as they merged into traffic and the clamouring faded behind them. Her heart rate settled as she leaned back, closing her eyes and letting out a shuddering breath.

     

                “The navy has sent their biggest ship,” Lillian started to explain, capturing Lena’s attention even if she continued to stare out the window as if she hadn’t heard her. “The fishing boat gave them the coordinates and they got there four days ago. I only found out about it all three days ago after a bit of bribery and blackmail. I don’t think you’ll be opposed to that this time.”

                

                “No, not this time,” Lena murmured, her eyelids shuttering as worry knotted her insides.

     

                “There hasn’t been any news since. I don’t imagine they’ll let you on the ship that easily - I’m still trying to work that part out. But then, well, you are the easiest resource to tap for knowledge of the prison. Director Henshaw isn’t talking and it’s difficult to access all of the different facilities the others are being held in over and over again. Much easier to rope you, I should think, but, well, it’s the Navy. I’m not sure how accommodating they’ll be for the sake of you talking to your … friend. We’ll cross that bridge once we get to it, though.”

     

                She kept talking, theorising and musing over what would be done next, and Lena listened, of course she did, but she also wished her mother would stop talking. As much as she hated to admit it, it didn’t help to know that communication had been made but Kara was still stuck in the prison, but it was a weight off Lena’s shoulders to know that at least she was alive, that she’d held out this long. Lena just hoped that Kara knew she’d been trying her hardest to free her.

     

                Eventually, Lillian ran out of news and theories and fell silent, and shortly after that, they were at the private airstrip where she had been supposed to leave from the day before. Nothing was going to plan for anyone though and instead of her mother whisking her away to Metropolis, Lillian wearily chartered the jet to Anchorage and followed her daughter to Alaska.

     

                The flight took almost nine hours, an agonising ride that wasn’t helped by Lena’s old fear of flying. She thought that having flown a helicopter a few times by her own hand, she wouldn’t be afraid any more - surely a trained pilot was safer than experimentally pushing buttons and hoping for the best - but Lena’s emotions were all over the place and delving into her fear of flying was the only thing that distracted her from the impatient and worrying wait of touching down in Anchorage.

     

                Of course, once they landed in Anchorage, they were still a thousand miles away from where Kara was imprisoned beneath the waves and it only made Lena itch with anticipation. If she could just hear her voice, talk to her after the confusing way they’d parted, it would be a balm to everything that had happened over the last two months. There was the matter of the other three of the prison break group being in prison, of course, but Lena would gloss over that so Kara didn’t lose hope, and besides, Lena planned on dealing with that once her friend was free, safe from any governments and militaries and allowed to feel the fresh air on her face and bask in the sunlight without the threat of capture. Kara was owed the chance to make up for so many stolen years and Lena would make it happen, even if she had to make a fugitive of herself once more.

     

                “We’ll get a hotel for the night,” Lillian started to plan as they walked off the jet.

     

                “No.”

     

                “You need to rest and there aren’t any places up north that are offering accommodation to tourists. God knows how infrequent the visitors are to places like that. Unless you’d rather sleep in a motel along the side of a road somewhere.”

     

                “I’ll sleep on the ground beside the road if that’s what it takes.”

     

                Growing impatient, Lillian huffed. “Well you can’t. At the very least, let’s get a hotel for the night so I can make some calls. What’s the point in flying out to the middle of nowhere if we’re not even sure you will be allowed to speak to her? They’re in the middle of surveying the area for a rescue, you know. They might not want you interfering.”

     

                Raking a hand through her hair, Lena clenched her teeth and yanked open the car door before the waiting driver could do it for her. Shoving her bag at her feet, Lena buckled herself in and waited for Lillian to climb in, the door shutting behind her.

     

                “Fine,” she ground out. “One night. But you say whatever you have to to get me out there tomorrow, alright?”

     

                “I’ll do my best.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                High-strung, as if she could feel the distance between herself and Kara shrinking, Lena was irate and tense as Lillian instructed the driver to take them to the best hotel in the city. When they arrived, Lena opted to wait in the parked car while Lillian reserved two rooms for them, before ducking her head and making a fast bee-line to the elevators once her mother fetched her.

     

                “I was staying here,” Lena murmured, staring at the closed elevator doors as she broke the uncomfortable silence. “In Anchorage, while I tried to sort it out. This is where I was hiding. I have a safe house here; I could have gone there instead.”

     

                “You’d rather sleep in some dingy, off-grid shoebox than sleep in a decent bed, purely out of your resentment of me? I am hoping it’s a decent bed, even if it’s not the Waldorf. If only you weren’t so predictably impulsive; we could have stayed in DC a few more days in better conditions.”

     

                “It was a warehouse,” Lena curtly replied.

     

                The elevator dinged and the doors parted, spitting them out onto the top floor. Not that it made a difference which floor they were on, the hotel much the same regardless of the room type. Lillian led them down the hallway until she stopped outside a door and then her mother handed Lena a room key in silence and they unlocked their adjacent rooms. It was gloomy and quite cool, making Lena shiver in her coat, the unwelcome familiarity of the bitter cold stealing back over her as she found herself back in Alaska once more. She hoped this would be her last trip to the state.

     

                Sliding the chain across the door and fiddling with the thermostat, she had hot air blowing out of a vent and moved over to the windows, dragging the curtains closed, plunging herself into further gloom. Sinking onto the foot of the bed, she kicked off her shoes, the heeled boots hurting her feet, which had only known thin-soled canvas shoes and thick winter boots for a long time now, and then tipped backwards. The mattress jostled and she let out a deep sigh. Despite not eating anything that morning, and with the growing lateness of the day, she still had no appetite.

     

                As the room warmed, she shed her coat and turned on the TV, sitting against the pillows at the head of the bed and watched the news with a brooding look on her face as she thought about Kara and the prison and the military. There were so many factors, so many moving pieces now that she didn’t know what to expect, wasn’t sure who to trust, what to believe. All she knew was that she would steal a car, buy a plane, do whatever she had to do tomorrow to get back to Barrow and find a way to Kara from there. She would charter a little fishing boat that wasn’t seaworthy for the rough, icy waters of the Arctic Sea if that was what it took to find the naval ship working to recover the prison. Her determination was her most inexhaustible resource, that was for sure.

     

                Falling asleep without meaning to, the faintly nauseous exhaustion of her hangover, as well as the ordeal of the last few days, catching up to her, Lena was roused a few hours later by a knock on the door. It jolted her from sleep in a panic, sweating in the heat of the room as she looked around, wild-eyed, trying to pinpoint the disturbance that had torn her out of her nightmares. Her hand scrambled for the pistol beneath the pillow that was no longer there, left behind in the warehouse with the rest of the things she’d wanted to part ways with for good.

     

                There was another knock on the door and her mother’s impatient voice drifted through, muffled by the wood. Her relief was keen as clarity swept through her muddled mind, the fog of sleep lifting as she climbed out of bed.

     

                “-need to eat something.”

     

                Rubbing her eyes, Lena scowled as she moved over to the door, peeking through the hole first before she drew the chain across and unlocked it. Her mother held a paper bag aloft with a withering look on her face.

     

                “Dinner.”

     

                Looking at the logo for Big Belly Burger on the greasy bag, Lena’s mouth thinned but she stepped back, opening the door wider to admit Lillian to the dark room. Clicking her tongue, her mother flipped on the lights and walked further into the room, setting the bag down on the table tucked into the corner. There was a drinks tray as well with two cups of soda and Lena locked the door before joining her.

     

                Sitting in the weak yellow glow of the overhead lights and the flickering TV, they ate in silence. As much as she felt like she was going to be sick, Lena picked at her cheeseburger out of the sole desire to make her mother leave faster, even if the food was greasy and bland in her mouth. She had to periodically sip her soda to force the mouthfuls down her throat and the food sat heavily in her stomach as a wave of nausea swept over her. 

     

                Eating just enough to satisfy Lillian, she wiped her fingers on a paper napkin and cleared her throat as she scrunched up the greaseproof paper of her cheeseburger. “I think I might sleep.”

     

                “Christ, Lena, can you at least let me finish my dinner first?” Lillian softly exclaimed, her face rippling with annoyance as she raised her own half-eaten burger.

     

                “I’m tired.”

     

                “I know you’re tired, and I know that you’re not going to sleep. The only thing you’re going to do is sit around and mope and that’s not good for anyone. I know none of this is ideal - God knows I have better things I’d rather be doing with my time - but you need to look after yourself. And seeing as I know you’ve never done that well - perhaps I’ve done a worse job of that myself, but you are still alive, so it can’t have been that bad - I suppose it’s up to me to try to help you now. As much as you will inevitably resent me for it, I’m sure.”

     

                Lena rankled at her mother’s snide comments and couldn’t stop her bitter reply. “Well, I didn’t ask you to baby me. You never have and it’s far too late for you to start now, so why don’t you spare us both the misery and go back to your own room.”

     

                Setting her burger down, Lillian wiped off her hands and fixed Lena with a piercing stare. She was silent for a moment and Lena felt her stomach twist with unease at the awkwardness of it, a flush creeping up her neck as she shifted on her chair. She didn’t avert her gaze from her mother’s stare though, and after a second, Lillian’s thin mouth of disapproval parted as she let out a resigned sigh.

     

                “This isn’t you,” Lillian said with surprising softness, tinged with sadness. “I know there’s no lost love for me, but you aren’t this bitter and angry. Perhaps I’m not the most sympathetic person, and I’ve never pretended to be, but whatever happened to you out there … if you wanted to talk about it-”

     

                A scoffing laugh of disbelief escaped Lena as her face split with a genuinely amused smile, she turned her head and ran a hand through her hair. Leaning back in her seat, she glanced sideways at Lena, her smile turning crooked.

     

                “Are you serious?”

     

                “I’m trying to help you.”

     

                “Well, thanks but no thanks. Talking isn’t going to help; all they did was try to make us talk but you know us - therapy would never be anything but a joke to our family.”

     

                “They made you … see a therapist?” Lillian slowly asked, bewilderment creasing her face. “In prison?”

     

                “Kelly - the, uh, one of the women who escaped - she was sent there as a psychologist. Mandatory monthly sessions for all prisoners.”

     

                “Oh, well …”

     

                “But thank you anyway,” Lena brusquely replied, her voice a pained rasp now as her throat felt tight. She kept her eyes averted, confused and embarrassed, a shallow divot between her brows as she rubbed her forehead. “I, uh, I just- I don’t want to talk about it. I just want to forget it all happened and just- just move on, so if we could … I don’t know, just stop talking about it and just be normal … that would be good. I don’t need you to feign maternalism, okay? I- I don’t need you to pretend to care or-”

     

                Heaving a sigh, Lillian closed her eyes and shook her head slightly, almost regretfully. “I do care. Not in the way you would have liked, perhaps, but I’m the only person you have. I can’t remember the last time we spoke this much, or this often, and you can hate me as much as you’d like for being here, hindering you if it means you look after yourself, but it’s not feigned maternalism. You’re my daughter, like it or not, and I said I would help. Until I’ve kept my word, we’ll have to endure it, but I would like to see the daughter I raised, not this … I don’t know what you are. Traumatised? I’d hardly believe you’d have it in you to be anything less than what you already were. You have always been so defiant.”

     

                Letting out a soft laugh, Lena’s mouth twitched at the corners and her eyes flickered to Lillian with something akin to fondness in them. She might have hated her at times but Lena loved her mother. Trust Lillian to be so dismissive of it all, to expect better from Lena, even in the face of so much trauma; it was comforting in a twisted way.

     

                “Nothing’s changed,” Lena agreed with her assessment, shrugging nonchalantly. “Traumatised though? I don’t know, I didn’t get much of a choice in that.”

     

                Pausing, the moment weighted as they stared at each other, Lillian’s expression softened minutely. She shifted forward slightly and Lena thought for a moment that she was reaching for her hand, before Lillian picked up her soda and took a sip, clearing her throat.

     

                “What happened to you?”

     

                Stomach lurching at the brazen question, Lillian not one to tiptoe around the sensitivity of it, Lena opened and closed her mouth, floundering as she tried to formulate a response. She didn’t want to talk about it, and aside from glossing over the details in an email for the sake of getting her story out there to save Kara, Lena had refused to voice what had happened to her. Perhaps it was easier to stamp it down, to make it small enough to overlook while she was conscious, if she didn’t speak about the things that had been done to her, but it wasn’t very small right then. As Lillian pressed on the pain like a fresh bruise, the hurt felt all-consuming.

     

                Rubbing her eye with a thumb as the silence continued, Lena didn’t know whether to tell her or not. Her voice wavered as she stalled. “Um …”

     

                It took her a few minutes, a distant look in her eyes as she stared at the table filled with their dinner, brow furrowed with thought, before she continued. In fits and starts, she slowly started to talk, her usually ordered mind trying to piece things together as the memories overlapped, the timelines muddled, months of the foggy drug-induced confusion making it difficult to know what had happened when. Her voice shook, her hands were white-knuckled fists in her lap, and her eyes occasionally stung or watered, but she didn’t lose her composure, even as her pulse quickened and her breaths turned shallow. Her chest hurt with the memory of so much pain and helplessness.

                

                Lena didn’t know why she ended up divulging it all to Lillian. Perhaps it was the knowledge that her mother wouldn’t pity her, that she only wanted to know out of curiosity - or did she? Lena was having a hard time guessing her mother’s motives these days - but the words spilt out of her in a rasping torrent of confession and admission. She told her how they’d come for her, how they’d interrogated her for hours, drugged her, beat her, stripped her and processed her. Eliza had poked and prodded her and injected her with whatever she’d been told to, the guards had beat her some more, starved her and denied her basic privileges, isolated her to the point of desperation that led her to swallow the pills just to get out of the tiny, hot cell for a minute. 

     

                There was the bitter cold and sicknesses from the damp confines, her broken leg from her escape attempt, her bruised and battered body from misbehaving. The guards who hated her, the guard Alex had killed for her, the people Kara had torn apart to get her out, the way they’d used Kara against her, and her against Kara. The freezing cold showers, the shock collars that had been incapacitating, the heaviness of their boots and the batons slammed against her bones, the little cells that were enough to drive them all to madness.

     

                Then there was getting out. How she’d plotted and planned with Kara and Alex, how Alex had wound up inside a cell too, how they’d drugged her until she was limp and defeated and underestimated, how Alex had escaped because of Lena’s meddling with the electrical circuits, how the lights had been cut and they were out of their cells and in the ceiling before the guards knew what was coming for them. How Kara, away from her red sun lamps, was stronger and more powerful, tearing through them with horrifying ease, how that guilt, along with her loyalty, had been the thing to make her stay behind for the others. The sickening flight from the top of the prison, Alex bleeding, the other two women frightened as Lena wrestled with the helicopter and her breaking heart, before they’d landed on the northern coast of Alaska and Kelly had shot dead the DEO agents manning the black site.

     

                She skimmed over the trip to Anchorage and their wait there until she’d handed herself in, and Lena felt exhausted by the time she fell silent, her mind so crowded after dredging it all back up. Reaching for her soda, she sipped as Lillian stared at her, her face ever so slightly slack with the shock of everything Lena had endured, and perhaps surprise that she’d even told her. Throat dry, Lena drank until the melting ice cubes were all that was left at the bottom of her cup, setting it back down and avoiding her mother’s gaze. She felt raw and vulnerable and didn’t want to be observed, didn’t want to be perceived . 

     

                Clearing her throat, she licked her lips and closed her eyes so she could face Lillian head-on without having to look at her, to try to judge her expression. Repeating herself, softer this time, weary and defeated, Lena felt a twinge in her chest as she fought back the urge to cry. “I think I might sleep.”

     

                This time, Lillian didn’t object, just pushed her chair back and started cramming the wrappers and containers into the paper bag. Lena sat still, eyes still shut as she tried to breathe slowly, evenly, the building pressure in her chest difficult to stamp down. Listening to her mother move around, putting the bag in the trash, pushing her chair back in, Lena felt impatient for her to leave, the burning behind her closed eyelids unbearable, the awareness that she was dangerously close to losing her composure. 

     

                The touch to her cheek surprised her. Startling as she flinched back, her eyelids fluttering before she fought to keep them shut, Lena calmed at the realisation that it was just her mother. Her mother, who had barely offered her any comfort since her father had brought her home, had rarely shown her any affection, who had hugged her so infrequently that Lena could count the times on both hands with fingers to spare, including the most recent one at the detention centre.

     

                Finding herself leaning into her touch for a brief moment, the cool softness of her mother’s palm cupping her face, thumb stroking her cheekbone, Lena pulled away slightly and Lillian briefly curled her fingers under her chin to hold her in place. 

     

                “I’m glad that you’re safe.”

     

                Clamping her mouth shut, teeth grinding together, Lena squeezed her eyes closed as Lillian left, the door clicking shut behind her a moment later before she unravelled. Letting out a gasping breath, she opened her eyes, stinging furiously with tears that fell quickly now, wrapping her arms around her midsection as she curled inwards. Letting out a choked sob, she furiously dashed her sleeve across her eyes and angrily climbed to her feet, stalking to the door and locking it securely, dragging a chair to wedge beneath it as well. 

     

                Once she was done, she placed her palms against the door and tried to swallow another sob, tears running down her cheeks as her dark hair fell around her face. Covering her mouth with a hand, she stayed that way for a long minute, trying to reel it all back in, stamp it back down to that space behind her sternum where she could overlook it, pretend it wasn’t there, that she was unaffected by it all. It had been a bad idea to tell her mother the details of what had happened; the only thing worse than having spent her whole life desperate for her mother’s attention was finally getting it.

     

                She couldn’t rein it in though, the thing that had been building inside of her, all that pent-up anger and grief and guilt that she’d felt, no doubt about it, but not to the extent of its existence. It came out of her in a torrent and she grabbed at her clothes, her cheeks flushed, eyes bright with tears as they just kept coming, frustration getting her worked up as she all but tore them off her body, working up a sweat. 

     

                Letting out another sob, she sank onto the edge of the bed and put her head in her hands as she tried to cry quietly, worried her mother would hear her through the walls. It had all been too much and Lena felt close to the breaking point, seemingly no closer to rescuing Kara, even as she appeared to be within arms reach. Swallowing the next sob, her throat bobbing painfully, Lena lowered herself onto her side and faced the wall, tears running down her temples and across the bridge of her nose before they soaked into the pillow beneath her head.

     

                The tears kept coming until she fell asleep without meaning to, raw-eyed and gasping for breaths, clutching at the sheets as she felt her heart breaking. Next thing she knew, it was morning, a sliver of pale blue sky visible through the curtains as she woke with the puffy-eyed, scratchy throat memory of her crying jag. Crossing over to the window, she peeked through the curtains to find a clear day.

     

                It was summer but Anchorage was still colder than she had been used to, and colder than she would ever like it to be again, and she dressed quickly in the warmth of her room. Feeling restlessly cooped up once more, seeming to go from one place of confinement to another of late, she paced her room for a while and then made for the door. 

     

                Grabbing the spare key card from the light switch, she heaved the chair away and fumbled with the locks and chain before slipping out into the hallway. Knocking on her mother’s door, she fidgeted as she glanced up and down the hallway, empty at that time of the morning, and listened to footsteps approach. Lillian was showered and dressed, looking sleek and polished in new clothes she must have had delivered sometime yesterday.

     

                “Oh. Morning.”

     

                Anxiously glancing over her shoulder, Lena stepped forward and her mother moved aside to accommodate her. Shutting the door behind herself and locking it, Lena trailed her past the steamy bathroom, the cheap carpet soft underfoot, and hovered restlessly in the narrow strip between the table and queen bed as Lillian took a seat at the table. Her mother was halfway through a coffee brought up by room service, today’s newspaper spread out on the table.

     

                “So … what’s the plan?” Lena asked.

     

                Gesturing to the seat, Lillian picked up her newspaper and shook it out. “First, you’re going to make yourself presentable and we’ll have breakfast.”

     

                Closing her eyes, a headache pounding from how hard she’d cried last night, Lena felt frustration bubble up in her chest and had to take a moment to speak. “Can we at least figure out the rest of it first?”

     

                “I’ve made a few calls. Military personnel and the like. No luck yet but I think within the next couple of days we’ll-”

     

                “Not in a couple of days ,” Lena tersely replied. “Today.”

     

                “I can’t command the US military, navy or air force.”

     

                “Well President Brayden does and surely I’m owed some goodwill with her after everything her predecessor put me through.”

     

                “I think you used your goodwill up on being pardoned.”

     

                “I would rather have stayed in there than waste it on the inevitable.”

     

                “It wasn’t inevitable; you could have been in there for months before a trial was brought to the courts. They would have let you go eventually but you would have been even less help from within there. At least give me the day to try and pull some strings though. If they’ve made radio contact and she’s asking for you, I’m sure another day won’t hurt.”

     

                Lena didn’t bother trying to explain how much it hurt her. Sitting heavily at the table, she braced her elbow on top and cupped her head. Eyes skimming over the fine newsprint, Lillian absentmindedly reached for the leather bifold menu and handed it over to Lena. Roughly sighing as she took it, shoulders sagging, Lena opened it and perused the list of items. Shutting it a moment later, she folded her arms and Lillian glanced up, raising her eyebrows.

     

                “Know what you’re getting?”

     

                “Eggs.”

     

                “Coffee?”

     

                “Black.”

     

                Nodding, Lillian browsed her newspaper for a few more minutes before rustling the pages and folding it in half, leaving it on the table. Rising to her feet, she moved over to the bedside table and picked up the phone, calling the extension to place an order and rattling off the items. She asked Lena how she wanted her eggs cooked and, when answered with a shrug, ordered them poached before hanging up and returning to the table.

     

                Sitting in tense silence as Lillian resumed reading her newspaper while Lena restlessly bounced a leg and bit her nails, her mother softly chastising her without raising her eyes from the pages. Twenty minutes later there was a knock on the door, and at the ashen look of unease on Lena’s face, Lillian climbed to her feet to answer it herself. 

     

                A laden tray was set on the table and Lena’s shoulders tensed at the feeling of some unknown person behind her, keeping her head ducked down as she tried not to flinch at the quick movements of the man as he unloaded everything. Once he left, she slowly reached for the cutlery wrapped in the napkin and shook the cheap square of cotton out, draping it across her lap and reaching for her coffee. Taking a swig, she found it better than any cup she’d had since being locked up and took another sip before sliding her plate closer.

     

                Eating with no enthusiasm or evident appetite, she split open the yolks and watched the vivid yellow spill across her toast, steam rising from the heat of the meal. Forgetting what it was like to have something made fresh, made hot to eat - she didn’t count Big Belly Burger from the night before - she wished she felt hungry enough to enjoy it. Instead, Lena ate with the clinical detachment of pure nourishment, not tasting a thing as she chewed and swallowed. In a way, it was no different from the calorie-calculated meals she’d been given in prison, fed only enough to sustain her energy requirements and maintain a healthy body weight. 

     

                Lillian ate her own food and watched Lena closely, badgering her until she’d cleared her plate, before she was satisfied that her daughter was fed. Setting down her knife and fork, Lena drained the rest of her coffee and set her napkin on the table before arching an eyebrow.

     

                “So?”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lillian reached for her cell phone. “Let me make some calls.”

     

                What followed was an agonisingly long morning. Pacing back and forth, perching on the end of her mother’s bed, and then pacing some more, Lena listened as Lillian made call after call, was transferred through to various people, bribed and made nicely veiled threats, as she tried to get through to someone who could pull the strings that would get them onto the naval ship in the middle of the sea. Lena felt like a spring coiled tight, her muscles tense, her headache pounding as her patience wore thin.

     

                Lillian ended up banishing her back to her own room to shower and dress in some of the clean clothes Lena had brought with her, which only marginally made her feel better while she was in the shower before she returned to her previous anxious fidgeting. Lingering in her room long enough to set up the new Macbook and iPhone, Lena connected to the hotel wifi and spent half an hour searching her own name, along with Kara, Fort Rozz, and the other three women in her escape party. Scouring articles for information to corroborate Lillian’s relayed news, she grudgingly had to admit that her mother was telling the truth; although there was nothing in there mentioning Kara by name, there were articles confirming the US Navy had made radio contact with Fort Rozz. That alone was enough to satisfy Lena’s doubts.

     

                Shutting the laptop, she returned to Lillian’s room and her mother answered the door on the phone, beckoning Lena inside and snapping at someone on the other end. Lena blinked in surprise, feeling like she was intruding, and sank onto the edge of the mattress, listening as her mother’s ire grew, as her voice turned downright icy, her face hard. Lena knew that anger all too well and was glad it wasn’t directed at her. She’d been on the end of it one too many times herself, which was never a fun prospect, and just hearing her mother’s raised voice made her stomach jolt with the memory of it.

     

                Lunch passed by and Lena sat cross-legged in the middle of the bed, hugging a pillow to her stomach as she watched her mother pace, resisting the urge to wear a path into the carpet as well. As the afternoon dragged on, Lena couldn’t get comfortable, and couldn’t sit still as she waited for the green light. Nothing short of being locked up again or physically restrained would stop her from leaving the moment they were given approval. That didn’t come until just after six o’clock, the sky still a clear blue outside, daylight showing no sign of fading yet.

     

                “Thank you for your assistance,” Lillian said to the phone. “It’s very much appreciated. Yes, yes, the shares will be transferred as soon as I can arrange for it, you have my word. Yes, the Luthor family is happy to offer patronage- of course, yes, thank you. If there’s anything else I can do for you … as always. I’ll wait to hear from you.”

     

                Hanging up, Lillian turned to Lena, an air of satisfaction about her as she smiled, slightly smug as her eyes creased faintly at the corners. “I should hear back within the hour to arrange a pickup from the hotel by a Marine Corps escort.”

     

                “And then?”

     

                “They’ll drive us to their base where a helicopter will fly us to Barrow. They have a base there where we’ll refuel before heading out to the ship. They just need to confirm their clearance with the Navy first.”

     

                “What’d it cost?” Lena asked.

     

                Arching an eyebrow, Lillian smiled thinly. “What’s the matter? Not willing to pay the price?”

     

                “Of course I am. I’d just like to know how much I’m paying so I can make arrangements. You mentioned shares …”

     

                “My shares. A small amount, at that.”

     

                Face crumpling with confusion, Lena stared at her mother. “Of your L-Corp shares or Cadmus?”

     

                “L-Corp. With all of the attention and your release, share prices are rising. It makes sense they’d want a cut of the profits for their help.”

     

                “Why not mine?”

     

                “For starters, I’m not sure you even have yours until everything is resolved. Second of all, because I wanted to.”

     

                “And what do you want in exchange? My shares once I have access to my portfolio?”

     

                Waving a hand as her expression rippled with annoyance, Lillian scoffed contemptuously. “Is it so difficult for you to think I might want to help you without expecting anything in return?”

     

                Silent, Lena cocked an eyebrow and Lillian rolled her eyes. “Consider it a late birthday gift then.”

     

                “No, I’ll pay you back. Once it’s all done.”

     

                “There’s nothing you have that I would want.”

     

                “L-Corp,” Lena blurted out. “I’ll give you the company.”

     

                Letting out a breathless scoff of laughter, Lillian smiled slightly. “Don’t be ridiculous.”

     

                “I mean it. I don’t want it anymore.”

     

                “Is one girl really worth that much? Is that the price tag for her freedom? A thirty-billion-dollar company?”

     

                A thin, wry smile crossed Lena’s face as her eyelids shuttered. “Well, I’m only worth a tenth of that anyway so the rest isn’t my money to begin with.”

     

                “You’re being irrational. Besides, I don’t want the business. I would have taken it from you when you vanished off the face of the earth, presumably in one of your reclusive episodes of research, but I didn’t.”

     

                “What did happen to it? I never did ask.”

     

                “You’ve changed a lot to not give the company you lived and breathed for a single thought,” her mother mused. “Your CFO, Samantha Arias, has been running it in your stead. She assumed the title of acting CEO when it became apparent that your leave of absence was indefinite. It will be yours for the taking once you’re back in Metropolis.”

     

                “I don’t want it.”

     

                “You just need time to adjust-”

     

                “No, that’s really not it. I’m just- I don't want to do it anymore. Once this is all over … I’m not sticking around in Metropolis. I can’t be somewhere like that anymore and I- it’s not that I didn’t love what I did, it’s just that so much has changed and I- that’s not the life I can go back to. I need to go away somewhere for a while, maybe a long time, and … I don’t know, process it all. Get past it.”

     

                “Where will you go?”

     

                “I don’t know,” Lena admitted before she let out a soft laugh. “Somewhere warm.”

     

                Lillian was silent for a moment and then let out a weary breath before she nodded. “Well … I still don’t want your company.”

     

                Shrugging indifferently, Lena stared at the carpet. Her mother might have thought she was being irrational, that it was some impulsive decision made out of her desperation to save Kara, as if this was the price she’d thought her mother was asking for and she was willing to pay it. The truth was that it wasn’t irrational at all, that Lena had spent so many months in a cell, irrevocably changed by that, that she didn’t think she would be able to return to her old life for a long time, if at all. 

     

                It wasn’t just that it had been a long time since she’d stepped foot inside L-Corp, had no idea what their last three quarters had looked like, which projects were in what stage, if there had been any major staff changes - aside from herself - or new board members replacing old ones, if there were any new big investors and what new contracts had been negotiated with manufacturers and suppliers. It was a daunting position to be CEO of such a big corporation and being divorced from the everyday running of it was something that Lena would be able to get up to speed on with relative ease if that was what she desired, but how could she sit behind a desk all day as if she hadn’t been gone for a large chunk of time, make small talk at meetings and prance around in her Louboutins, dishing out orders and trusting the words out of people’s mouths while her every need was catered to? 

     

                She needed time and space, away from the attention it would bring to live in Metropolis, photographed going in and out of the office, stalked to her apartment building, feeling claustrophobic as she was hounded by the media. It would be nigh on impossible for her to slip back into that role without being overwhelmed by the storm it would create, even if the positive press would have helped boost L-Corp’s revenue even higher. Lena had put the business before herself so often, doing the work that ordinarily wouldn’t have fallen to the CEO purely because she enjoyed it, she enjoyed her creations and inventions and the advancements she made, more than the endless meetings and conferences, the emails, spreadsheets and paperwork. But that was lost to her now; Lena had nothing in her mind to create, no drive to develop anything new.

     

                Of course, her mind was only driven to rescue Kara at the moment, but even after that, she knew she just didn’t have it in her yet. Utterly spent, she needed time to rest, to reflect and heal as best as she could. Even then, the scars were too deep, the trauma too fresh and unmanageable that she didn’t think she would ever recover enough to assimilate back into her old life. Maybe a semblance of it, one day, but she needed to go somewhere where she wouldn’t be found easily, where she could be overlooked in a house for her to sit and bask in the warmth of the sun and simply enjoy her freedom. That was what she needed.

     

                As promised, within the hour Lillian had received a call back, and in short order - despite the day inching towards dusk - mother and daughter found themselves in the lobby of the hotel as they waited for the military convoy to arrive. Just before seven o’clock, three Jeep J8s pulled up outside, engines rumbling loudly, and Lillian rose to her feet as the sliding doors parted to admit three uniformed members of the Marine Corps. Rising, her pulse quickening with the anticipation of what came next, Lena swallowed thickly.

     

                In short order, she found herself in the back of one of the Jeeps, the conversation her mother had with one of the indistinguishable men washing over Lena without her taking much of it in, and she swayed along with the movement of the vehicle. It was just her and Lillian in the back of theirs, the other two Jeeps holding the bulk of their escort, which seemed like overkill but for which Lena was grateful, and she cleared her throat, looking at her mother across the narrow space between the benches.

     

                “Who’s your contact?”

     

                “Jim Harper. He used to do some work for me with Cadmus on the side when he was an officer but he was promoted to Colonel of the Marine Corps a few years ago. It always pays to have corrupt friends in high places. You would know his predecessor; Lauren Haley.”

     

                Lena’s stomach lurched as her lips parted. “Haley? As in-”

     

                “Your Warden, I believe. That was news to a lot of people when you revealed that piece of information; I think most people in the Navy were under the impression she’d died. The presence of the DEO and what they’ve been doing must have rattled them all.”

     

                Stewing in her silence as she processed what her mother was saying, and second-guessing whether a man who had taken the spot of the woman in charge of the prison’s day-to-day running, a man who had worked for her mother, doing God knew what for her, was reliable enough to give Lena what she wanted. But then, she was in the back of a Marine Corps escorted vehicle, on her way to their base as her mother’s bribe worked its magic. Perhaps Lillian was right and that it paid to have corrupt friends in high places. Lena just hoped it paid off in her favour.

     

                Arriving at their base, they idled at a checkpoint while passes and clearances were reviewed before they let their retinue through. It was getting cold now, the daylight fading quickly as the sky darkened, and Lena drew her coat tighter around herself as she stepped out of the Jeep and looked around with interest. The base was an orderly sprawling of buildings; offices, barracks, warehouses, mess halls, and workshops. One of the officers called for them to follow after him and the two women fell into step behind him.

     

                There were a few introductions with other Marine Corps officials, which Lillian smoothly commanded, and an hour and a half later, they were strapped into a plane as the final checks were being made before takeoff. Closing her eyes as she gripped the straps, her face pale, nervous now that she was getting so close, Lena breathed slowly. When the flight took off, her stomach swooped with adrenaline and suspense. 

     

                It wasn’t a long flight either, especially not in a military jet, and in less than two hours they were setting down onto a grey airstrip outside of Barrow. There were no windows for Lena to look out of and it would have been too dark anyway, but she knew in the daylight the landscape would have been unsettlingly familiar from her own aerial views she’d taken in of the surrounding coastline and austere land. She was glad she couldn’t see it, thinking of that little box of a building where she’d lived for a couple of weeks, still foolishly clinging to the belief that they would go back for Kara and leave Alaska with her. That hadn’t gone anywhere close to plan.

     

                At the base, they shook the hands of a few more officials and were led to a conference room, commercial grey and so ordinarily corporate that it was like sitting in a business meeting, cups of black instant coffee set before them, a jug of water in the middle of the table, harsh fluorescent lights overhead and a vent pumping out warm air. As late as it was starting to get, Lena was keyed up and impatient to get going again, taking sips of her coffee as she listened to the conversation, the man asking after Lena’s wellbeing, offering up snippets of news that hadn’t made it to the press cycle yet, and outlining a plan.

     

                “We have rooms for visitors in the main building; I’ll have someone show you to them once we’re done here.”

     

                “But-” Lena blurted out, the first thing she’d said in hours. She quickly glanced at her mother and then back to the man, her brow furrowing. “Aren’t we leaving now?”

     

                “In the morning. You’ll stay the night and a crew will fly you out to the ship tomorrow morning.”

     

                “But-”

     

                “You’re on their time now, Lena,” Lillian murmured. 

     

                Shoulders sagging with disappointment, a lick of anger flashing through her, Lena clenched her teeth and raised her cup of coffee to her lips, draining it and squeezing the paper cup so tightly that she crumpled it. Setting it down, her expression was wooden and she had to stop herself from outright glaring at the man and his apparent apathy for her time constraints.

     

                There was nothing she could do about it though and was left to be escorted to her room by the officers once the meeting wrapped up. It made her uneasy to be walked through the drab hallways with uniformed officers, armed and stiff, escorting her, and Lena broke out in a cold sweat at how familiar it felt to being walked through the hallways of the prison. Sure, this place wasn’t damp concrete and these officers were there to help her, but she couldn’t shake that heart-pounding panic as she anticipated handcuffs, a beating, a cell.

                

                Instead, she was shown to a small room, neat and sterile, the bed made with hospital corners, a nightstand next to it and a desk at the foot of the bed. She had her bag, which had been checked before she’d been allowed to bring it onto the base, and then again into the building, and she set it down on the desk. Tired as she was, she knew she wouldn’t be able to sleep in a base full of government-armed officials, who for all their differences weren’t easily differentiated from the DEO by Lena and her mistrust, so she slipped the laptop from from her bag and turned it on. 

     

                There was the issue of the wifi and she didn’t want to find someone to ask for the password, or if they would even give it to her in the first place, so she ended up playing chess against the computer for a few hours before she stretched out on the bed. Staring up at the ceiling, the light off as she lay awake in the dark, she ached for the sound of Kara’s voice, imagining how different it all would have been to have her there. 

     

                The pain cut so deeply that her breathing turned shallow, with faint gasps as she gripped the front of her shirt and pretended that she was just in the next room. It was just like in their prison, a little gap at the base of the wall for air ventilation, and if she wanted to, she would be able to talk to her, and the only reason that she didn’t was that it was the middle of the night and Kara was asleep. It might have been delusional to pretend that, and she knew it wasn’t true, but it was a comforting thought to think of it as one of the many nights they’d slept next door to each other, the solace of each other’s presence just on the other side of the wall.

     

                Dry-eyed and exhausted, Lena was roused from her thoughts by a knock on the door, climbing to her feet to answer it with no pretences that she’d been trying to sleep. It was just after six o’clock and she was led to a small room where her mother was waiting, drinking coffee and eating the breakfast that had been brought for them from the mess. It was better than the prison food but not Michelin level and she was surprised her mother was eating it, sitting down to join her as well.

     

                After they finished eating, Lena wolfing hers down purely to speed things up, they were given warmer clothes to wear, the bitterness of the far north already palpable from within the walls of the building, and Lena knew it would get far worse out on the sea. Despite it being summer, it would be icy and the winds would be so harsh that it would feel as if it burrowed right into them instead of parting around their solid forms. Showering in a private bathroom, Lena dressed in the white and grey camo utility fatigues, cold-weather boots with a snow camouflage parka over the top. She was dressed like any of the others, pulling on tan gloves as well and a matching beanie over her dark hair.

     

                Emerging, she almost laughed at the sight of her mother dressed identically to her, so out of place and evidently uncomfortable in the Marine Corps-issued winter gear that Lena got a prickle of satisfaction out of it. She’d never seen her mother dressed in anything other than business casual, professional or cocktail attire and it was as ludicrous as the rest of it. Fighting back a smile, she arched an eyebrow at her and Lillian bristled with resentment as her mouth tightened.

     

                Spirits buoyed now, as if the rest of it seemed inevitable, that of course it would be easy now, Lena felt as if she could walk on water with how much hope nestled in her chest. She would speak to Kara on the radio and the Navy would have a plan in place and in a few days - at most , she was sure - Kara would be in her arms and Lena would be able to rest. Eagerness filled her and she was quickly on the heels of their escorts, anticipation making her stomach knot itself.

     

                The aircraft that had flown in from the aircraft carrier ship was a Grumman C-2A Greyhound, used for supply runs, transporting cargo, mail and passengers, a boxy-looking thing with a capacity for 26 passengers. It was just shy of 60 feet long and Lena felt trapped inside the windowless interior as she boarded after the flight crew, picking a seat at the front. Lillian picked the seat directly across the aisle from hers, with only a single column of seats on each side, and Lena glanced sideways at her. It was far from her mother’s usual use of her free time but Lena was oddly grateful she was with her. 

     

                When they were finally cleared for take-off, she gripped the armrest and closed her eyes, her heart beating rapidly as she thought she might be sick. There was something about her nervous optimism that made her queasy, thinking of all the ways something could go wrong, how it felt hard to believe she was so close now, and Lena was stiff through the entire duration of it. Fortunately for her, the professional pilots were a lot better than she had been with the military-grade helicopter she’d stolen, and they didn’t detour from their planned flight route. At the speed the plane could fly, they made it from land to the the prison in under two hours.

     

                Feeling them slow, tilting at the descent, she gripped the armrest and swallowed thickly. There was a shakiness in her chest and her throat felt tight as she stared wide-eyed ahead, waiting for the jostling landing. When it came, her stomach dropped , and Lena had to press her lips into a flat line to stop her chin from wobbling. Lillian took the pinched look on her face as a product of her fear of flying.

     

                “Are you alright?”

     

                “Fine,” Lena replied, her voice wavering.

     

                Unbuckling her seatbelt as the engines whirred, the propellors slowing as they lost momentum, Lena was on her feet with her bag slung over her shoulder before the aircraft was fully off. Shifting from foot to foot, she waited for them to prepare to disembark and was on the heels of the flight crew the moment they stepped off the plane. Feet landing on the damp deck of the aircraft carrier, so big that it made Lena feel tiny to be standing on top of the stretch of grey runway, she tried to ground herself as the wind assaulted her. It was bigger than the prison had been but was strikingly familiar to that day she’d escaped, staring out at the chilling sight of the sea and ice floes tossed by them.

     

                “This way,” the pilot said, jerking his chin for her to follow.

     

                They were met by naval officers and Lena shook their hands, names instantly forgotten, her bag taken from her as she was led inside the aircraft carrier. This felt more like the prison, the metal and concrete of the ship and the dampness of water making the hairs rise on her arms and the back of her neck. As it hit her all at once, she came to a sudden stop in the hallway, her mother walking straight into her before she clicked her tongue and pushed her forward.

     

                “What is it?” Lillian asked when Lena didn’t move.

     

                “This place, it- I just- it feels so … similar,” Lena forced out, her larynx aching from the effort it took, her voice gravelly and strangled.

     

                “Well, it’s different. Put one foot in front of the other and keep going; you’re almost there. She’s waiting for you.”

     

                That, along with her mother’s vice-like grip on her arm, urging her forward into a stumbling motion, was enough to spur Lena onwards. Feeling lightheaded as she breathed shallowly, she walked down the hallways in a daze, until she was brought to an open command room, computers, control panels and servers lining the walls as sailors of various ranks and divisions worked away. The Captain of the aircraft carrier was there and came to introduce himself before leading them over to a portion of the room with communication devices and radios with a variety of knobs, screens and gauges.

     

                “We’ve been communicating with them regularly,” the Captain gruffly told them, his eyes straying to Lena with curiosity. “Each time, they ask to speak to you.”

     

                “Are they there now?” Lena hoarsely asked.

     

                Clapping his hand on the man sitting at the radio, the Captain nodded to him. “Contact the prison.”

     

                “Yes, sir,” the sailor said, a headset with a mic covering his ears as he fiddled with the knobs for the radio frequency, eyes fixated on the screens in front of him. “This is USS Gerald R Ford, do you copy, Fort Rozz?”

     

                It was a tense minute of silence and the sailor had to repeat himself before a voice came on the radio. Lena had been anticipating Kara and the desperate bubble of hope in her chest deflated with disappointment as a man’s voice came through the main speakers.

     

                “Good morning, USS Gerald R Ford, this is Agent Winn Schott on the line. What can I do for you?”

     

                Lena wanted to groan at the thought of the mousy agent she’d knocked unconscious in the ceiling crawl space manning the radio and her mouth thinned with exasperation. 

     

                “Agent Schott, thanks for answering the call. We have Miss Lena Luthor on board the aircraft carrier to speak to you, as requested.”

     

                “Lena Luthor? Shit. Sorry, wait, just- hang on a second,” Winn babbled, his voice fading but still audible to them. “J’onn. J’onn, where’s Kara? No, it’s Lena. She’s on the ship; someone needs to find Kara. Now. Don’t tell her, okay? Don’t say anything or she’ll freak out, just bring her back here. Um … hi, are you still there, USS Ford?”

     

                “Copy, Agent Schott.”

     

                “Someone’s just going to look for her. She’s not on the cell block at the moment. Can you- can you stand by?”

     

                “Standing by.”

     

                Lena’s shoulders sagged and she rubbed her forehead, her breaths coming quickly now, feeling far too hot in the thick winter layers, even though she knew it was just because she was getting herself worked up. The carrier was warmer than the prison had been but she knew even that would have been colder than she would have liked if she hadn’t been so anxious that she couldn’t help but sweat in her layers.

     

                “Here,” the man said, removing the headset and climbing to his feet, gesturing to the chair. “You sit and put this on. You’ll be able to hear her clearly and talk back.”

     

                Nodding in thanks, a lump caught in her throat that made Lena believe she wouldn’t have been able to speak even if she’d wanted to. Sitting heavily on the desk chair, she wheeled it in close and nestled the headset over her ears. It muffled the sound of voices, machines and typing and Lena listened to the loud thud of her heart in her ears as she tried to breathe evenly.

     

                It felt like an eternity, minutes slipping by with silence on the faint crackle of the line. Eyes straying to the time on the digital clock, she swallowed thickly, and then again, her throat so dry that she couldn’t force the lump down. Then she heard a faint whine of static and a voice came through.

     

                “This is Kara Zor-El.”

     

                Her voice was as gentle as Lena remembered, but she was all business, not knowing it was Lena on the other end. The sound of her voice cut cleanly through Lena and the air rushed from her lungs as she sagged, her vision immediately blurring as her eyes filled with tears.

     

                “Hello?” Kara haltingly pressed at the ensuing silence.

     

                Straightening, hunching over as she gripped the edge of the table, Lena drew in a rattling breath, a pitiful sound escaping her before she swallowed and tried again. “It’s me,” she managed to force out, a breathless whisper, her voice cracking.

     

                She was met with silence for a long moment before a hoarse laugh came through, elated and relieved and evidently thick with Kara’s own fought-back tears. “It’s you.”

     

                Her murmured response was warm, laced with laughter, with adoration, and Lena’s heart spasmed in her chest. “It’s me,” Lena echoed, a small laugh escaping her as well as she dashed her sleeve across her eyes, trying to pretend like she wasn’t wiping away tears, aware of the trio at her back. “Um … it’s good to hear your voice.”

     

                “And yours. I thought- it’s just- it’s been a while. I was worried you didn’t make it home.”

     

                “I did. We all did. I’m sorry it’s taken me so long; I’ve been trying to come back for you. The whole time.”

     

                “I know. I didn’t expect anything less.”

     

                It bolstered Lena’s determination to hear that Kara hadn’t lost hope, which Lena had privately feared, and she let out a forceful breath, rubbing a thumb into her eyelid as she swallowed a sob. “You’re okay?” she hesitantly asked.

     

                There was a pause. “I’m fine. We’re all doing good in here. Um … well, hopefully, it won’t be for much longer. They keep telling us we have to wait for- for reconnaissance and submarines and all of that but I’m sure you have a plan, right?”

     

                “You know me,” Lena breezily replied with false bravado. “Of course I have a plan. I would’ve been here sooner but … well, I was a fugitive. Had to clear my name so I could come and get you myself. You know I wouldn’t leave it up to the others.”

     

                “No, you wouldn’t, would you?” Kara replied, a smile in her voice. 

     

                They lapsed into silence and Lena blinked rapidly, a severe frown on her face as she tried to keep her composure. “I’ll get you out of there soon, alright?”

     

                 “Yes, ma’am, I’ll see you soon.”

     

                “See you soon.”

     

                “And Lena? I- thank you for leaving. I’m sorry, I just- I had to.”

     

                Eyelids shuttering, Lena’s mouth thinned as pain knifed through her, her voice a mere whisper. “I know you did.”

     

                “I meant what I said though. I would find you anywhere, even in the dark. I can- I can hear your heartbeat up there and I- … I’ll tell you later, okay? But I would really like that sunset together.”

     

                Remembering Kara’s wishful thinking, that she would have liked to fall in love with Lena on a beach somewhere, with ice cream and sunset. It felt like she was repeating that sentiment, albeit without stating it for their respective audiences, and Lena let out a quiet huff of laughter. 

     

                “Me too. I still have to keep my promise; ice cream and sunset on a beach, right? With birds.”

     

                “You already gave me a sunrise.”

     

                “I’ll give you ten thousand sunrises and sunsets.”

     

                “Just as long as you’re there.”

     

                “I will be. Just … wait a few more days, okay? Wait for me a little longer.”

     

                “I’d wait forever if you asked me to.”

     

                Pausing at that, Lena’s face spasmed with bewildered surprise, warmth in her chest as she felt better than she had in months. Kara was okay, things were alright in the prison, and Lena was going to get her out of there in a day or two and everything would be fine. It would be better than fine; they’d have each other with ice cream and sunsets, on a beach somewhere with seagulls and hot weather. Just a few more days.

     

                “Just a few more days,” Lena promised, her voice wavering as tears ran down her cheeks. She didn’t have it in her to be embarrassed to be seen crying, it all just felt so raw and shocking. “It’s not forever, just a few more days. I promise.”

    Chapter 24

                “Why didn’t you tell her the truth?” Querl asked, crouched beside Kara as he listened to the radio communication.

     

                Running a hand over her thin face, Kara shrugged, her expression clouding. There were tears in her eyes and her cheeks were wet, quickly wiped dry as Kara cleared her throat.

     

                “I just- I don’t want her to worry.”

     

                “They’re probably going to tell her on the ship. They won’t send anyone down here while there are hostiles running around; they won’t risk the lives of their sailors.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Kara didn’t want to listen to his logic, exhaling softly as her shoulders sagged with exhaustion. “I know, I know. But it’s Lena; she’s the one who will make the plan. I bet she already has one. You’ll see, trust me.”

     

                Querl squeezed her arm but his expression wasn’t optimistic or hopeful, only grave and doubtful. “I do trust you.”

     

                “We just need to keep it together for a few more days, you heard her. It’ll all be over after that.”

     

                “Should we- should we hand out the rations?”

     

                Her eyes flitted around the crowded room, at the number of starving prisoners and staff members trying to fill the empty hours of their day, no longer interested in the working radio as help seemed just as distant as before. Swallowing thickly, Kara’s mouth thinned with grim resignation and she hesitated before shaking her head.

     

                “No. No, don’t- we’ll stick to the usual rations. We can’t know for sure how long it’ll take. They probably need … I don’t know, just more resources, I guess. How heavy do you suppose the prison is?”

     

                “Somewhere between fifty to sixty-thousand tonnes, I’d estimate. Then you have to calculate the force of the water pressure as well. That’s the tricky part.”

     

                “Have humans done that before? Retrieved a sunken ship that weighed that much?”

     

                “Maybe half that weight.”

     

                Eyelids shuttering as her hopes were dashed, Kara raked a hand through her lank hair. It was getting harder to stay hopeful that things would resolve themselves quickly. It had already been months since she’d helped her friends out of the prison, and even with the Navy above them, touching base regularly to try and reassure them that they were working on a solution, their freedom seemed no closer.

     

                Swallowing thickly, a tightness in her throat as panic knifed through her, Kara glanced at Querl. “They mentioned winches. What’s that? Will it- can they do it with that?”

     

                “Marine winches. They’re like a big reel. They use them to tow other boats or salvage wrecks.”

     

                “And they’re big enough to do that?”

     

                “No,” Winn answered as Querl hesitated. “He’s right; they’ve retrieved a wreck maybe half the weight of the prison, but the salvage winches won’t be able to lift that much. I think the biggest would be maybe … forty-tonnes?”

     

                Blinking as she stared at him for a moment, Kara shook her head slightly as if confused by his response. “How can it be forty-tonnes but they’ve recovered one half the size of this prison? It doesn’t make sense.”

     

                “I- well, I’m not sure about that one but most wrecks … aren’t in one piece. Um … it’s actually really difficult to recover a wreck and- I don’t know if they’ve managed to recover a full ship with trapped passengers before … well, you know.”

     

                “They’ll need a lot of winches,” Querl murmured, his eyes darting around as he did the math. “That’s probably the holdup.”

     

                “How long do you think it’ll take them to work it out?” Kara asked, her wide blue eyes so serious and hopeful.

     

                Winn opened and closed his mouth, shrugging, and Querl was silent. A hand clapped her on the shoulder and she looked up at J’onn, who was smiling down at her, his expression kind as he nodded reassuringly.

     

                “They’ll work something out. Lena’s with them now, and didn’t you always say she’d find a way to come back for us all? There’s no point worrying about it now; let’s leave her to work, alright? We’re all safe for the time being, even if not so comfortable. Put your worries aside and give her a few days. I’m about to meditate if you’d like to join me?”

     

                Hesitating, glancing back at the radio, which was silent as they’d made them keep the transmissions brief, Kara nodded. Uncrossing her legs, she rose to her feet, lanky and jittery, and followed J’onn to a peaceful corner. He sank down onto the concrete floor and crossed his legs, his shoulders slumping.

     

                Mirroring his pose, Kara let out a heavy breath, looking worried as her eyes darted around the room. Reaching out, J’onn placed a hand on her knee and Kara jerked her attention back to him, her shoulders sagging with exhaustion. 

     

                “You’ve done well. It’ll be over soon. Now, take a deep breath in.”

     

                Nodding, Kara swallowed the lump in her throat and closed her eyes, inhaling deeply as she tried to make her tense muscles go slack. As J’onn spoke, the soothing rumble of his voice washing over her, Kara couldn’t quite empty her mind, her thoughts straying to Lena. She couldn’t begin to explain her relief to hear her voice once more, a thing she’d dreamed of each night, and replaying their conversation in her mind as she listened to the familiar, barely audible sound of her pounding heart above the surface of the sea, was enough to instil Kara with a little bit of peace. Breathing in and out, she listened to Lena’s heart and found solace in the fact that she was free.

     

     

                “She mentioned submarines and winches,” Lena said as she rose from the chair, her composure regained and her expression smooth, despite the faintly bloodshot eyes.

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “There aren’t any winches that can withstand a load that heavy.”

     

                The Captain gave her a dismissive once-over. “The Navy has access to better grade equipment; we’re also working with the Coast Guard and looking into foreign aid. Rest assured, we’re doing everything we can.”

     

                “I can help. I can map the prison for you-”

     

                “That won’t be necessary. We’ve acquired blueprints from the DEO.”

     

                “Well, what about the mechanics? It sits about a mile down, usually, with an anchor system-”

     

                “Yes, thank you, Miss Luthor, we’re aware of the anchor mechanics via our ROVs. Unless you’re a qualified marine engineer, your assistance is not necessary.” 

     

                He was busy staring at the SONAR imaging of the prison beneath them on a screen, rattling off a few instructions to nearby personnel as Lena stepped up beside him, a defiant jut to her chin as her stare hardened.

     

                “I have invaluable information-”

     

                “You were a prisoner. The only personnel with invaluable information I’m interested in talking to are Director Henshaw, Warden Haley, and perhaps Deputy Lane. Two of them are trapped in the prison below and are being very cooperative. You weren’t brought here as a consultant, so unless you have some other expertise you can provide-”

     

                “But I-”

     

                “Are you a naval officer, Miss Luthor?” the Captain asked with exasperated amusement.

     

                She blinked, affronted by his question as she bristled. “No.”

     

                “And are you Captain of this vessel?”

     

                “No.”

     

                “Nor are you Admiral of the fleet, whom I take my orders from,” he continued, his words clipped. “So please remove yourself from the office. If your presence is required, it will be requested.”

     

                Quietly seething as she let out a scoff, Lena arched an eyebrow. “Make no mistake, Captain, if I was in charge, they’d already be free.”

     

                Stalking off without another word, Lena shouldered her way out of the room and glanced over her shoulder at the sound of heavy footsteps falling in behind her. Drawing up short, she looked at the young man and arched an eyebrow. 

     

                “Yes?”

     

                “I’m your assigned escort.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena carried onwards. “Do you know where my room is?”

     

                “Your berth is this way,” the man said, slipping past her and leading the way.

     

                She was led to an empty berth with rows of triple-stacked bunks lining both sides of the space. It was more enclosed than she’d anticipated, with not much space between the foot of each bunk and not much space between them either. Her bag had been set down on the bottom bunk mattress of the ones closest to the door and her escort lingered on the threshold.

     

                “You’re prohibited from wandering the vessel unescorted, due to your credentials. I’ll fetch you at mealtime, otherwise you’re to stay inside your berth.”

     

                Lena stared at him with open ire, silent as he shifted from foot to foot, waiting for some sort of acknowledgement. Once it became apparent that she wasn’t going to, he nodded and then turned to leave. Turning to her bag, Lena hesitated and then turned back around to him.

     

                “Hey, do you guys have wifi?”

     

                He shook his head, shrugging apologetically. “Sorry. Not until we dock.”

     

                Frustration bubbled up in her chest and she pressed her mouth into a thin line, nodding in thanks and turning around.
