Picking up her bags, she carried them to the far end of the berth, tucking herself away in the bottom bunk of the furthest corner, the sailor shutting the door behind him as he left. Sinking onto the bed, Lena stretched out and stared up at the underside of the bunk above her before closing her eyes and letting out a shaky breath.

     

                She was alive, she was okay. The thought, the keen relief of it, made her eyes prickle with fresh tears and she let out a breathless sob as her body went slack, covering her face with a hand as her composure wavered. It all felt so rushed, so confusing, and Lena didn’t even know where to begin processing it all. She would have liked to sit there and talk to Kara for hours, but it was only a brief communication with eyes and ears all around her, a mere reassurance to each other that they were alive and okay - for now.

     

                After a sleepless night, Lena was flagging, her body aching and energy waning, but the aircraft carrier reminded her too much of the prison so she couldn’t bring herself to nap away the hours. It was cool inside, the mattress too thin beneath her, the room too cramped and the sound of heavy boots tramping up and down the hallways. All she needed was a shock collar and the effect would have been complete. 

     

                A while later, the door squeaked open and Lena shot upright, on alert as she glanced around, knowing there was no other exit. “Lena?”

     

                Her shoulders slumped at the sound of her mother’s voice drifting through the berth, and the fight quickly bled out of her. “Back here.”

     

                Lillian’s footsteps loudly approached and Lena stared at her winter jacket and pants as Lillian rounded the foot of the bunks and then ducked her head down to look at her. Expression pinched with displeasure, possibly from the cold or just the general inconvenience of being in the Arctic Circle instead of amusing herself elsewhere, she gave Lena a once-over glance.

     

                “Are you done with your little performance back there?”

     

                “They’re undermining me,” Lena seethed, bristling with indignation.

     

                “Maybe they are. Maybe they just don’t want a visitor telling them how to do their job. Perhaps they don’t trust an ex-fugitive who spent the better part of a year in that prison. Who knows what your motives might be?”

     

                Scoffing as she rolled her eyes, Lena smiled thinly. “Oh, come on. What other motives could I possibly have, aside from a rescue mission?”

     

                Lillian was silent, fixing her with a long look before she sighed and straightened. “At least you got to speak to her. Are you satisfied now?”

     

                “Hardly,” Lena grumbled before she softened slightly. “But thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Lillian tapped the metal of the bunk ladder. “Just try not to cause any trouble for the time being, hm? Any actions could have drastic consequences out here; this is the Navy, they’re not going to take it lightly.”

     

                Resisting the urge to roll her eyes, Lena raised her eyebrows quickly in a look that didn’t inspire confidence but was definitely sarcastic enough to convey how she felt. Sighing, Lillian turned and left without another word and Lena sank back onto the thin pillow, brooding in silence as she resumed staring up at the slates and plotted. It had very quickly become apparent that she was the only one operating on a short timeframe, with any real sense of urgency. 

     

                She spent the next few days trying to rein in her agitated anger as she tried to find openings, ways to insert herself into the Navy’s plans, which from her understanding amounted to sitting around waiting. Four days passed by with Lena eating her meals with a surly look on her face, being denied even a handful of minutes to speak to Kara again, and nothing else seeming to happen. She was shut out of most conversations and only gleaned a little information, but by the fifth day, she’d had enough and had made enough of a nuisance of herself to earn the Captain’s ire in full.

     

                “As I’ve mentioned before, that’s classified information. If you intend on causing trouble on my vessel, I will have you flown back to Alaska and you can await the outcome of the recovery mission from shore.”

     

                “Then why am I here, if not to help?” Lena demanded, a haughty look on her face as she jutted her chin forward.

     

                The Captain let out a quiet laugh, a placidly patronising smile on his face as he braced his hands against the edge of the table. “We were cautioned that your, ah, friend is a wild card, and with that comes trying to mitigate the risk of what could happen if she goes rogue down there. Countless lives are at stake, you see.”

     

                “She wouldn’t,” Lena stiffly replied. “She only went back because she wanted to save everyone else. She’s not- she’s not a threat.”

     

                The Captain gave her a tight smile, his hands clasped behind his back. “And we intend to keep it that way … with your co-operation.”

     

                Blinking as sudden understanding swept through her, Lena’s mouth opened and closed soundlessly for a moment before her cheeks flooded red with anger. “So I’m- I’m … what, blackmail?”

     

                “Insurance.”

     

                Her flinty stare cutting across to Lillian, Lena gave her an accusatory look. “And I’m assuming you were on board with this?” she derisively asked, her lip twisting contemptuously as wounded betrayal filled her eyes.

     

                “It was the only way to get them to agree to bring you out here.”

     

                “You weren’t given clearance to board a naval vessel to sit and talk to your friends on a radio the whole time; you were cleared for the sole purpose of acting as emotional support to keep her calm. That is why you are here. Now, if you will please leave me be so I can speak to the submarine reconnaissance crew, thank you, Miss Luthor.”

     

                His final words were curt, an effective dismissal, and Lena rankled as she glared at his back. Lillian reached out and snagged her arm to drag her away and Lena shrugged her off, glowering at her mother before stalking off. Falling into step beside her, Lillian heavily sighed, their escorts tailing them.

     

                “You don’t have to take everything so personally.”

     

                “You’re unbelievable,” Lena quietly snapped. 

     

                Slowing, Lillian spread her hands pointedly, raising her eyebrows. “You’re here, aren’t you? I did what you asked.”

     

                “You set me up to be used as blackmail.”

     

                “You always view my actions so negatively. If you’re so convinced that your friend, this- this Kara, wouldn’t be a threat to anyone, then it shouldn’t be an issue that your purpose here is to make sure she doesn’t hurt anyone. It’s a moot point.”

     

                “You manipulated me; that’s not moot.”

     

                “Well, I’ll tell you outright, if you continue to cause trouble, you won’t be used as insurance anymore. Just … sit tight. Let them do their jobs. Distracting the Captain won’t help anyone but having a little bit of patience goes a long way. You said it yourself, the winch on this carrier isn’t enough to lift the prison; they’re waiting for aid to get here.”

     

                “Even that isn’t going to be enough,” Lena snapped. “Okay, maybe I’m not a marine engineer but just basic maths and physics alone can answer that question. This is the biggest aircraft carrier in the Navy, its winch can tow … I don’t know, forty-five tonnes? The next biggest one can probably tow about the same. That’s a fifth of the prison’s weight. Come on , mom, you expect me to just sit there while they take a week to figure that out?”

     

                “That’s the only way.”

     

                “No,” Lena firmly denied, a gleam of panic in her eyes as she fell silent, swallowing thickly before she lowered her voice, continuing hoarsely, “no, it isn’t.”

     

                “If there was another way, you would have found it by now. There’s nothing on this earth that would be able to lift that in one go, so just-”

     

                Lena closed her eyes, her shoulders slumping as the breath was expelled from her lungs. It was logical, of course, to think that nothing on earth would be able to lift half a million tonnes in one go, no piece of equipment manoeuvrable enough to raise the prison in one piece. And therein lay the issue, that they couldn’t break the prison into sections without destroying its structural integrity, without depressurising the entire thing, without causing it to completely flood and killing everyone inside it. If they could break it apart, that would have made things a hell of a lot easier, salvaging usable materials to repurpose, but it was the presence of live individuals, who were intended to remain alive, that complicated things.

     

                But the prisoners weren’t normal, they weren’t just ordinary humans locked away in there, otherwise, they would never have been beneath the surface of the sea in the first place. And while the others may have been powerful, been restrained and had their powers stifled, there was only one person onboard who had the potential to do what Lena needed. Perhaps not within the prison, without being suffused with pure, unfiltered radiation from a yellow sun, but say Kara was out, recharged her powers to beyond comprehensible constraints of human ability, perhaps then.  

     

                She was singular in her existence, and she was the singular answer. How often had Lena thought about how easy it would have been with Kara at her side, knowing that her powers seemed so limitless, so full of potential? She had been the plan all along, in a way, the key to Lena’s original escape, the one who did break them out in the end. Nothing had changed, only that she was inside and Lena was outside. Except, Lena hadn’t been able to reach her again, cut off from Kara as the prison sank beneath the surface once more, lost as she circled over the patch of water in a helicopter trying to locate her. If she’d had access to diving gear at the time, would it have still been futile?

     

                And now, on the largest aircraft carrier, filled with naval officers and millions of dollars worth of equipment, from jets, to ROVs, to diving gear, would it still be futile? Lena didn’t need to find a way to get the prisoners out, she just needed to find a way in to get one prisoner out, and wasn’t that a lot more doable?

     

                “I have to go,” Lena cut Lillian off, her mind racing faster than she could comprehend as she suddenly turned, rubbing her forehead as she rushed off.

     

                “Whatever you’re planning,” Lillian murmured as she snagged Lena’s arm to stop her a moment, shrewd enough to see Lena’s mind turning, “make sure you’re willing to suffer the consequences.”

     

                Ignoring her, Lena shrugged her off and then doubled her pace, her escort following after her, and retraced the path back to her berth. Opening the door, she hesitated, glancing at the sailor as her mouth twitched with a ghost of a smile.

     

                “I might take a nap before lunch.”

     

                Frowning slightly, he lingered a moment and then nodded, leaving her to her room. It was perhaps a good thing that Lena hadn’t left her room except for mealtimes and the occasional request to speak to the Captain, often denied, all of them escorted by her sailor, because it afforded her some goodwill as the man left her alone with the impression that she would remain in there until lunchtime. 

     

                Of course, she had no intention of that, lingering in her room for five minutes to ensure the coast was clear before she cracked open the door, poked her head out and made sure the hallway was empty before stepping out. Easing the door shut behind her, she kept her head ducked down as she quickly made herself scarce. Fortunately, the borrowed fatigues and winter outer layers were the same grey and white standard camo for the other sailors, dressed to withstand the freezing temperatures of the Arctic, and anything that came with the recovery mission, so if anyone saw her, pending they didn’t catch a good glimpse of her face, there was a good chance she would blend in, as long as she didn’t look suspicious or lost.

     

                From her limited outings on the aircraft carrier, she knew there was the flight deck, and then the gallery below, housing air traffic control, catapult launching valves, cabins, the fan room and other electrical and weapons rooms. Lena definitely had no plan on heading up to that level, steering clear of the Captain and any other higher-ranking officials. Her berth was situated on the second deck, along with storerooms and machinery, the same as the deck below, and the third deck below housing the fan room and trade shops for mechanical and electrical work. She didn’t want that deck either.

     

                It took her almost an hour to find the dive locker, following the periodic maps and striking them off one by one until one of them denoted its location with the Carrier Compartment Usage Codes. Tucking herself away in a corner, she waited until lunchtime before entering the room, finding that it wasn’t locked, and wasn’t staffed either, a row of lockers with no actual combination locks holding the diving equipment necessary for Mobile Diving and Salvage Unit 2, the diving crew on board.

     

                Opening one of the lockers, Lena started to pull out all of the gear, finding that they used a dry suit to protect them from hypothermia in the freezing water, scuba gear with twin oxygen tanks for relatively shallow work - she’d seen through glimpses of the screens that Fort Rozz hadn’t sunk more than twenty metres beneath sea level - and she pulled out boots, wrist and neck seals, valves, a hood and mask, tubes and fins. It was all black and rubbery and she was left helpless for a moment, knowing she couldn’t carry it all with her to the side of the ship unseen and unquestioned. 

     

                Pausing for a brief moment to consider it, Lena shed the thicker outer layers of her winter pants and jacket, removing her wool gloves and beanie and shoving them in the jacket pocket before she picked up the dry suit. Lena hated the sea, had never been a strong swimmer, if much of one at all, and she didn’t give herself time to think things through. 

     

                All she knew was that she was on a naval aircraft carrier, with known divers onboard, as well as other submersible equipment, and had deduced they would have gear, and that if she could access that gear, nothing was stopping her from throwing herself off the side of the carrier and diving to the prison to sort things out herself. Was it reckless? Undoubtedly so. Stupid? Lena preferred to believe she never did stupid things. Terrifying? Absolutely. Still, she would do it anyway. For Kara.

     

                Struggling into the parts, trying to work on the seals, unsure whether she’d done it correctly or not, pulling on the boots, Kevlar gloves and hoisting the tubes onto her back and fastening the straps of the buoyancy control device around them, after checking they were actually full of oxygen first. She’d attached the tubes and the regulators and the pressure gauge. There was a flashlight attached to the strap of the BCD and Lena checked everything before pulling on the mask, leaving it on her forehead for now.

     

                Stopping to pick up the fins, she swallowed her fear and awkwardly waded out of the diving locker. She was already on the correct level for the aircraft elevator, where they moved aircraft from the hangar to the flight deck via the elevators on the side of the carrier, and she followed the map to the nearest one. Perilously close to the hangar, where pilots were running safety checks or replacing parts, servicing the aircraft for duty, she tried to remain unobtrusive as she ducked inside. 

     

                Unfortunately, dressed head to toe in black scuba gear didn’t make for an unnoticed trespasser. Still, she was so close to the open mouth leading from the hangar to the elevator, cavernous and exposing a stretch of pale blue sky beyond. It was probably fifteen feet above sea level, maybe twenty, so she couldn’t see much of the sea from her point of view but she was quick to move across the concrete floor of the hangar as more voices rose.

     

                “Hey! Hey, what are you doing?”

     

                “Who is that?” one of them called out.

     

                “Somebody stop them! Call the Captain, now!”

     

                She wasn’t fast, with the weight of the gear she was lugging with her, but no one could have stopped Lena. Bootsteps followed after her, pounding on the concrete, but she was running through the mouth of the hangar now, the wind ferociously assaulting her as she met the unmitigated force of it. Staggering to a stop near the edge, she hunched over, pulling on one fin and then the other before she heard more shouts behind her.

     

                Glancing over her shoulder, Lena felt panic wrench her stomach at the sight of three sailors gaining on her. They were out on the elevator too, sprinting towards her, and Lena fumbled with the valve to open the tank as she inflated the BCD before releasing the inflator button and deflating it. She didn’t have time to check for leaks or to make sure it was all working, glancing over the edge of the elevator. The wind was so rough that she thought it might drag her straight over the edge anyway.

     

                Dragging her mask down over her face, she didn’t allow herself to pause, to doubt herself and feel the terror of the seething waves below, churning dangerously and freezing cold. Deflating the BCD, she jammed the regulator in her mouth and turned, taking in the sight of the closest sailor, six feet away from her with an arm outstretched.

     

                Staring at him, at the panicked look on his face, wind buffeting him as his words were swallowed up by the howling of it, Lena stepped backwards. The drop made her stomach plummet quicker than she did, her hands clamping the regulator to her mouth and the mask to her face, terror suffusing her as air rushed around her and she struggled to keep her legs together, fins pointed toward the rapidly approaching surface. It felt like an eternity and the blink of an eye at the same time, and then she hit the roiling sea.

     

                The force of it was enough to knock her breathless, and it was only the regulator forcing oxygen into her that kept her from letting in a lungful of salt water. Blindsided by the disorienting current dragging her about as she tried to get her bearings, Lena couldn’t think straight for a minute past the blind panic of it all, of being in the sea, barely able to classify herself as a swimmer.

     

                As she started to adjust to it, getting past the initial shock, able to situate herself so she wasn’t being tossed about aimlessly, hesitantly letting go of the mask. It stayed in place and after a moment she managed to let go of the regulator too, fumbling for the flashlight on the BCD until a small glow of light radiated from it.

     

                The water seemed so blue as she was swept by the current, the sunlight breaking through the surface to highlight the endless water surrounding her. And there, below her, thirty feet off the starboard side of the aircraft carrier and not so deep enough that she couldn’t swim to it, the shadowed deck of the prison. Lena’s heart pounded in her chest, audible in her ears, as adrenaline coursed through her.

     

                As she struggled to stay in place, fighting the current, trying to kick properly with the fins and failing miserably, she steeled herself for what came next. There were no thoughts about what could be out there - whales or seals, polar bears - about how much oxygen she had, whether there were any leaks in the hoses or her suit seals, and whether Lena had the strength to fight the current and the pressure to go that deep. The dry suit felt uncomfortable too, the boots too big, the suit air adding more buoyancy and insulation as she tried to dive deeper.

     

                Exhaling, a stream of bubbles rushing out around the regulator, she let her body’s buoyancy decrease and tried to work the valves on the suit to let out some of the trapped air. She didn’t feel the cold as much as she would have in a wetsuit but it was still palpable and Lena swallowed thickly, trying to keep breathing as she slowly sank. The suit pinched her skin as it was squeezed against her body in the descent, itching Neoprene rubber, and she was uncoordinated and helpless as the water swept her with the current. 

     

                There was simply nothing she could do about it, and she was worried about spending all of her energy fighting against it, opting to focus on diving instead of swimming ahead until she was over the prison. Slowly but surely, she descended through the water, her visibility decreasing as the sunlight grew further away, the blueness of the water becoming darker as her flashlight cast a small glow about her. Fortunately for Lena, the current swept her in a trajectory across the deck of the prison, and by the time she managed to dive the twenty metres down to it, she was able to grapple with the rough surface to slow herself, the friction of her Kevlar gloves helping her resist it better. 

     

                It was easier then, clinging to the deck as she kicked furiously from spot to spot, grasping at handholds - fraying ropes, rusted mooring cleats, deck railings and large knuts drilling the thick sheets of metal together - until she made it to the sliding doors where the elevator shaft rose from the depths of the prison to the deck. 

     

                It had already been twenty minutes by her reckoning, her slow, clumsy descent taking far longer than it should have to sink roughly twenty metres, and she was growing more confident now, determination lending her a franticness as she grasped the lip of the square outline of the shaft. It was already parted, the pressure of the water over the last three months slowly working them apart, no hydraulics and electrical controls keeping it shut, the seals broken and useless. That was perfect for her though; it was just wide enough for her to squeeze through with some struggle, fumbling to unclasp her BCD with the tanks to make herself thinner, swimming through first before she jerked the tanks through after her.

     

                And just like that, Lena was back inside Fort Rozz.

     

     

                Kara had spoken to the Captain that morning, as had become the norm over the last week and a bit, seeking reassurance in an update and comfort in the knowledge that there were people up there, people working hard to free them all. There was no greater comfort than the sound of Lena’s heartbeat up there though, a steady presence throughout the last five days, and even though she couldn’t differentiate the blend of overlapping voices, too many sailors and too much stimulation for her to pick out the details, that heartbeat was a sound she would have known anywhere, could pick out with ease when she tuned in to the aircraft carrier above.

     

                And that was all she was afforded after that first day, after the handful of minutes spent talking to Lena, not nearly enough to satiate Kara’s desperate need. But every time she spoke to the Captain, begged and pleaded with him to put Lena on, he apologetically informed her that Lena was busy, of course, tirelessly working with marine engineers and consultants flown in with expertise in physics and nuclear engineering. And Kara believed him; that was exactly the sort of thing Lena would be doing, even though it cut deep to know she was there but just out of reach, unable to speak to her with the same ease as when they’d shared neighbouring cells and talked all day and night. How Kara missed those moments, even as awful as they had been. She just missed Lena.

     

                But then she heard a panic onboard, an alarm wailing throughout the aircraft carrier, raised voices and people rushing back and forth. She’d been sitting by the radio in case an unexpected transmission came through, daring to hope that this time it would be Lena, and had been playing cards with Nia, Imra, a janitor, chef and Deputy Lane when the fuss managed to cut through her tuned out attention. When it did become noticeable, Kara’s gaze cut up to the ceiling as she frowned.

     

                “What?” Nia asked, glancing at her as the movement snagged her attention.

     

                “Something’s going on up there,” Kara murmured, cocking her head to the side and closing her eyes as she tried to filter through the overwhelming number of noises to figure out what it was.

     

                “Is it- have they done it?” Lucy anxiously asked. “Are they rescuing us?”

     

                “No, it’s … alarms.”

     

                Kara’s stomach jolted as she picked up the sound and she quickly turned her attention to zeroing in on Lena’s heartbeat to check if she was safe. Except, Lena’s heartbeat wasn’t as high up as it should have been, usually restricted to a few of the highest decks. Except now, as Kara honed in on it, it was so low that she might have thought it was beneath sea level if she could judge the distance correctly. But that was ridiculous because Lena was terrified of water and the only people underwater were the prisoners; there was no submarine crew investigating them today, not at that time.

     

                But it was unmistakably Lena’s heartbeat, Kara was certain of that. And she was certain that it was lower than any other heartbeat on the ship. Listening for a moment as the others badgered her with questions, which she tuned out, Kara tossed her cards down and climbed to her feet, her gaze fixated on a point across the room. She could clearly pinpoint Lena’s heartbeat, isolated from any other noise surrounding it, in between the endless racket of the prison, and the dimmer sounds of the prison above, somehow suspended between the two. And Kara knew, she didn’t know how or what, but she knew that Lena was in the water.

     

                “Lena,” she breathlessly murmured before lurching into motion, trampling the card game, tripping over the chef’s leg as she stumbled forward.

     

                Making a beeline for the door, Kara paid no attention to the others as her sudden movement stirred them up, people rising from their spots, calling questions. She made it to the sealed doors and tried to pry apart the seams, using what little inhuman strength she had right then to dent the metal enough to create a shallow groove, a little handhold to pull one door aside. Metal groaned and she heaved it open with relative ease then, until a hand came down on her shoulder and she jumped, head jerking to look at J’onn.

     

                “What’s the matter?”

     

                “It’s Lena,” Kara babbled, “I can- I can hear her heart. She’s- she’s not on the carrier, she’s coming here.”

     

                “Kara. Kara, Kara, hang on a second, okay? You’re probably just hearing things; Lena wouldn’t be able to make it down here. Even if she did, she wouldn’t be able to get us out, so there wouldn’t be any point.”

     

                A prickle of rare anger nettled Kara as she braced her foot against the other door and pushed it apart as well, hauling them both open wide enough for her to walk through with ease. “I’m telling you it’s her. I would know her anywhere. It’s her, I need to go. I need to go before the others-”

     

                She didn’t finish her thought, already through the doors, taking off through the prison as she tuned in to the other prisoners, tracking their heartbeats, wondering if any of them had the ability to pick up on Lena. If they hadn’t yet, surely someone would soon enough. Kara didn’t pause, just kept going, intent on reaching her first.

     

     

                The central chamber of the prison was pitch black as Lena swam deeper, her flashlight offering the only light for her to see by, but the current was gentler, not the violent thrashing of the sea, and she descended with relative ease. Still, it was a sort of fumbling, swimming blindly as she tried to pinpoint a foot, fear making her skin prickle as she kicked her legs and exhaled streams of bubbles through the regulator.

     

                Then she saw the first body. It was a bloated, grotesque thing, the skin practically luminescent white in the glow of her light, the face split open and in varying stages of decomposing, the irregular patches of skin making it very clear that various marine life had been feasting on it. The sudden glimpse of a person - no, a corpse - sent Lena’s heart thundering, a hoarse shout forced up her throat as terror seized her. It was only slightly less terrifying to realise it was a body.

     

                Swallowing her gorge, the threat of bile caught at the back of her throat, Lena pushed on. That was only the first body though, not to mention the limbs that she caught sight of, perhaps torn off by Kara, perhaps the flesh and muscle disintegrating and eaten away by fish and whatever else had managed to get in. Either way, it was unsettling and Lena didn’t want to linger. 

     

                Hurrying now, her sense of urgency redoubled, and not purely out of a desire to get away from the bodies, but out of a desire to see Kara, she swam until she hit a wall. Hand fumbling for it, she followed the curve until she found a doorway - sealed - and then continued to follow it to the next one. The second one stood open, not completely, but enough for her to squeeze through once she unbuckled the BCD again. It was a tighter fit this time though, and she didn’t think she was going to be able to get through, even side on, until her desperation forced her to ignore the pain of her shoulder, her ass, surely to leave bruises as she made herself fit. 

     

                Treading water in the hallway, she rebuckled the BCD and tanks onto her back and set off. This entire section was underwater, something Lena thought she ought to have expected, and she swam down the hallway, taking in swollen desks and rusted filing cabinets through office doorways as her flashlight illuminated glimpses, more bodies here - more than she remembered there being, with prisoners too, much to her surprise - and sodden cardboard, solitary cans of green beans, bags that may have held bread at one point. She didn’t want to linger there either.

     

                And then she was at the office she remembered them coming through, having counted the doors by number, visualising the map they’d created in her mind. Swimming inside, she found it easier this time, the buoyancy of the water lifting her right up to the ceiling with the hole of the missing panel. Of course, by that point she could have shifted any panel with ease, the waterlogged pieces gone soft with months of constant exposure to water. 

     

                Still, after the struggle of swimming, her muscles unused to the strain of exercise, it was still an effort to climb out of the water. The exertion made her arms shake as she braced herself, the added weight of the oxygen tanks making it more difficult, but she was nothing if not persistent and gritted her teeth against the effort, straining herself until she was half out, legs still in the water until she wriggled forward, kicking frantically. Sprawled in the wet, narrow confines of the ceiling, Lena tore the regulator from her mouth, panting as she lay propped up on her elbows for a moment.

     

                Then a spark caught her attention, her breaths still ragged and eyes wide behind the goggles as she saw the exposed wires, how wet it was up there, and suddenly realised that she was precariously close to electrocution. Without further pause to catch her breath, she carried onwards, scurrying on all fours, fins scraping along the beams as she tried to be quick, she counted panels beneath the soggy insulation until she was sure she was through to the next section. 

     

                Confident in herself, she flung handfuls of insulation aside, barely covering the panel here because of where it had been used for the same purpose she was using it for now. She had to lean down from her perch on the beam and couldn’t reach the next structural support, bracing her hand against the panel instead, only for it to be wet as well, giving way beneath her hand without hesitation. She didn’t have time to process the fact that she was falling, headfirst, through the ceiling without any chance of stopping, the heavy weight of her gear dragging her quickly.

     

                And then she hit something solid, except it wasn’t hard and cold and it didn’t hurt , and it was arms winding safely around her in a tight embrace, cradling her carefully as her feet hit the floor and her knees buckled, legs refusing to hold her weight. Sinking to her knees, Lena tore off her mask, tossed it aside and then threw herself at Kara, arms around her neck as she let out a choked sob.

     

                She hadn’t had time to properly process it but she knew. If it wasn’t Kara, who else was it? That searing warmth of her touch, that palpable strength of her body, that comfort that her presence instilled in Lena, from that very first day she’d been locked away in the cell beside hers. Breaking down, Lena sobbed into Kara’s shoulder as she clutched at her for dear life.

     

                “You’re okay, you’re okay,” Kara whispered, stroking Lena’s hair, her face screwed up with fierce protectiveness as she held her close, one arm around the twin oxygen tanks, the other cupping the back of her head, the diving hood still covering Lena’s dark hair. 

     

                Despite her dryness, Lena still felt cold and she shivered, the adrenaline leaving her, her whole body shaking, exhausted and shocked. Eyes closed, shoulders hunched and head ducked down, Lena slowly pulled away. Her cheeks were wet with tears and saltwater and her lips trembled as her eyelashes fluttered, as if she didn’t dare open her eyes and shatter what may very well have been an illusion.

     

                But there she was, kneeling on the wet floor, flooded half a foot deep as the adjoining sector slowly spilt over into this one, cupping Lena’s shoulders as she stared at her with surprise and panic. Kara’s face was hollowed out with hunger, her blonde hair gone brassy and lank without the facilities to properly wash, her clothes dirty and hanging off her lanky frame. But her eyes were the same, that searing blue, so warm and earnest, and Lena let out a strangled sound of relief, feeling as if her chest was caving in at the sight of her. 

     

                Reaching out with a gloved hand, shaking terribly, she touched Kara’s cheek as her vision blurred, her voice a cracking whisper as she spoke. “Hi.”

     

                Kara let out a husky laugh, her eyes creasing at the corners, and she covered Lena’s gloved hand with her own. “Hello.”

     

                Swallowing painfully, Lena sniffed and steeled herself as she reached for the clasp of the BCD and undid it, the oxygen tanks clanging loudly onto the floor as she slipped the straps free. The unburdened weight made her feel so much lighter, rolling her sore shoulders before she quickly started stripping off the rest, fins, seals, boots and gloves all amassing into a small heap as Kara watched her with confusion as Lena started to babble.

     

                “We have to be quick.”

     

                “What are you doing?” Kara softly exclaimed, reaching for a glove as Lena cast it down. “You need to put this back on, you need to go-”

     

                “No.”

     

                “Lena-”

     

                “Listen to me,” Lena insisted as she staggered to her feet and started working on the dry suit next, shimmying out of it as Kara tried to yank it back up. “You need to-”

     

                “No, you need to go,” Kara said with more urgency this time, her voice fraught with panic. 

     

                Pausing, her feet out of the suit now as she held the dripping form of it in her hands, staring at Kara with bewildered surprise, Lena watched her friend go rigid as she turned, hurrying away from her. A sound of protest escaped Lena as she dropped the suit and stepped over the pile, insistent on Kara leaving in her stead, unwilling to give in without a fight at least, but then Kara faltered a step just before the intersection of hallways, glancing back over her shoulder, her eyes wide with fear, her face shockingly pale.

     

                “Go back,” she called to her, voice wavering. “Please.”

     

                And then she turned back around just as something moved quickly, a person, and punched her squarely across the face, sending the Kryptonian reeling before she hit the wall. It happened so quickly that Lena couldn’t stop the scream that escaped her, clapping a hand over her mouth as her stomach plummeted. And because she was Lena, she would never have turned away. 

     

                Not when the quickly moving being slowed into the distinct shape of Mon-El, nor when his eyes landed on her and he smiled thinly, his attention captured by her now. She’d caused so many issues, made so much of a nuisance of herself during her imprisonment that he hated her almost as much as he hated Kara, holding onto millennia-old feuds between the planets even in a prison on Earth, and while Kara was there to have it out with him, he knew that she loved Lena, and there Lena was. Of course, she was nothing in comparison to a Daxamite’s strength and speed, but he was nothing to a Kryptonian’s, and before he could take more than a step in her direction, Kara tackled him to the floor with a splash.

     

                His head cracked the concrete floor and Kara grabbed a fistful of his hair, which had grown longer in the last three months, and then slammed his head into it again, blood blooming in the water. Face twisting with pain and anger, Mon-El tried to wriggle out from under her, driving an elbow into Kara’s stomach, eliciting a gasp, and then rolling over as he tried to pin her under his back. He was only half successful at that, both of them splayed on the floor, and Kara rolled out of the way, anticipating him trying to pin her down. On her feet in a heartbeat, she raised her foot to stomp on him, knock him unconscious until she could lock him up again, she was left standing on one leg for a moment as Mon-El grabbed her ankle and then heaved, throwing her across the hallway. 

     

                Managing to slow herself slightly, palms slapping the wall before she could fully crash into it, Kara used the momentum to push back off, getting some height before she drove her fist into his face. Blood spurted from his broken nose and Mon-El swore as he staggered backwards, hands rising to cover his face.

     

                “You stay the fuck away from here, do you hear me?” Kara hoarsely commanded him, her voice frayed and unrecognisable as fear coloured it.

     

                Spitting blood, Mon-El bared his teeth. “I heard her heart. She came back for you, didn’t she? Over my dead body am I going to let you get out of here, while I’m rotting away with the rest of them.”

     

                “There isn’t a way out,” Kara panted, running a sleeve over her face as she put herself between him and Lena, a bruise mottling her cheek. “We’re all stuck down here.”

     

                “No, we’re not,” Mon-El said, gesturing to the pile of gear Lena had shed. “I’ll be taking that. Right after I make sure neither of you ever leave this place again.”

     

                “You’re not going to lay a finger on her.”

     

                “You think too highly of yourself; you might think you’re stronger than me, but you’ve deluded yourself into believing them. The truth is, without the sun, you’re barely more than a good punch, whereas I , on the other hand, don’t need the sun to make me what I am. Down here, you and I? We’re a fair fight.”

     

                Scoffing, derision twisting her face as she gave him a once over, Kara shook her head with weariness. She’d put up with his presence for years, and as Lena watched on, she knew Mon-El had underestimated Kara once again. Sure, Kara might be a shadow of her true strength in full sunlight, in an atmosphere saturated with radiation, but she was still a Kryptonian in a universe with a yellow sun, and that counted for more than what he was.

     

                He feinted but Kara could see the way his muscles shifted and got him around the middle as she tackled him back into the wall, before Mon-El picked her up around the waist and flipped her over his shoulder. It didn’t quite go in his favour though as Kara ended up with her legs wrapped around his neck, thumbs jamming into his eyelids as he hissed with pain, trying to drag her off him. Forcing her crossed legs apart, he tossed her to the ground and Kara took a cheap shot at his groin as she lay sprawled on her back. Making a low sound of anger and warning at the back of his throat, Mon-El tried to punch her, hunched over with his fist coming down fast, but Kara was quicker than him, shifting to the side so his fist struck the floor, and then toppled him by wrapping her legs around his, throwing him off balance as he fell to his knees.

     

                Lena watched the whole thing unfold with helplessness. She couldn’t even keep track of what was happening, their movements so quick that it was almost beyond what a human could comprehend, and Lena anxiously chewed her lip as she hovered around, fighting the urge to jump to Kara’s defence. She would be useless, of course, but it made her stomach lurch sickeningly to hear the cry of pain as Mon-El got ahold of Kara’s arm, twisting it so that it hurt the socket at her shoulder, threatening to dislocate it. But then Kara was out of his hold, headbutting his chin as Mon-El swore, spitting blood at her before getting her in a chokehold.

     

                Unable to stand it any longer as Kara scored deep furrows on his forearms, Lena looked around for a weapon and her eyes landed on the BCD. Stumbling over to it, she detached a hose and hefted a tank in her arms, hurrying over to the aliens with the intention of braining the Daxamite. Unfortunately, he was not so easily injured by any human strength and the oxygen tank didn’t cave his head in as Lena had been hoping. Still, it surprised him enough to let his hold on Kara go slack, the Kryptonian drawing in ragged breaths as she rubbed her reddening throat. Mon-El’s attention was similarly distracted as he turned towards Lena, who dropped the oxygen tank with a dull thud before he grabbed a fistful of her Navy fatigues and tossed her like a ragdoll.

     

                That had more of the intended effect on Lena, who wasn’t as heavy as Kara was, her muscle mass and bone density that of a regular human, so, naturally, she went flying. Her shoulders smacked into the wall first, followed by the sicking sound of her head striking concreted with the whiplash of the momentum, before she sagged to a heap, tasting blood in her mouth as her vision danced with black spots. Trying to make the walls stay still as her vision swayed precariously, she took in the fight with a dazed look on her face, watching as Kara’s grim resolution to fight Mon-El turned into unmitigated anger. Nothing would have held her back then, no more trying to render him unconscious until authorities could deal with him, lock him away again with the risk of another prisoner freeing him - that was what she’d deduced had happened.

     

                Instead, Kara pummelled him, the thud of her fists sinking into flesh, striking his face as she turned it into a bloody mess, filling the hallway. He was helpless under the relentless torrent of her beating, his face split with cuts, nasty bruises and his eyes, cheeks and mouth swollen into an unrecognisable depiction of him. And still, Mon-El wouldn’t give up, spitting out curses as he tried to stop Kara, attempting to sneer as he hurled insults at her, getting in a few punches of his own but nothing that could have stopped an enraged Kryptonian. 

     

                Even when he managed to get his arms around her in a bear hug, driving Kara backwards until they burst through a locked door together, into one of the storage closets, the two of them creating such a commotion as things clattered around, it wasn’t enough to overpower her. Shakily climbing to her feet, using the wall for support, Lena inched along it until she lined up with the door, she tried to peer inside and see what was going on. A shelf had collapsed, bleach and other cleaning supplies mingling with the salt water as the noxious smell of it wafted out of the closet, and she watched as Mon-El disentangled himself from beneath a mess of iron, plastic bottles and paper towels. 

     

                His eyes fell on her and Lena couldn’t bring herself to move, cold water soaked into her socks as she stood shivering in the hallway, watching the Daxamite see his opportunity and knowing there was nothing she could do. She could try to run, sure, but he would catch up to her with ease and she was more concerned with whether or not Kara was okay, knowing that if she could withstand a little bit of pain, there was a good chance her friend would save her. It was a heavy burden to put on someone, but there was nothing Lena could have done otherwise, and if he killed her before Kara pulled herself together, and crawled out from beneath the mess, so be it.

     

                Then Mon-El was on her, his hand around her throat as he started to squeeze, looming over her as he pinned her to the wall. Lena couldn’t breathe, could feel the pain in her throat, the tightness in her chest as she looked up at him, wide-eyed.

     

                “I can’t kill her, but I can make sure I take you with me,” he venomously whispered. “They should have put you down the minute you arrived here.”

     

                “I should have done the same to you,” Kara grimly replied from behind his shoulder as she thrust an iron pipe right through his back and out of his abdomen in one smooth motion. 

     

                It happened so quickly that Mon-El didn’t have time to stop her, her movement from the closet to the other side of the hallway so fast that the pipe was bursting out just above his hip before he could do much more than let out a hoarse cry of pain. And then Lena felt it too, the pain of it as Kara’s strength drove the pipe not just through Mon-El, but into Lena as well, the jagged end of the pipe she’d torn free shearing through her clothing and into the left side of her waist. And she couldn’t even cry out in pain as Mon-El still had a hand around her throat, a hand that was quickly going slack as Kara jerked the pipe out of the two of them, casting it aside, and watched as the Daxamite’s hands fluttered around his hip.

     

                He staggered backwards, blood running out of his gaping wound, and Kara stood behind him with a regretful look on her face, breathing heavily as she watched him flounder for a moment. When he fell to his knees, she swooped in quickly, cupping his shoulders and easing him down into the water as his eyelashes fluttered, his mouth opening and closing as if he was suffocating. Staring down at him with a distaste for what he’d forced her to do, Kara’s mouth twitched slightly, betraying the solemn look on her face for the true guilt, grief and horror she felt inside.

     

                “Sorry, cousin,” she murmured. “I wish it had been a fair fight.”

     

                Letting out a choked sound of surprise, blood running down his chin as he coughed it up, his face and body such a mess that it almost seemed kinder to kill him than to let him endure the pain, Mon-El drew in a shuddering breath and then exhaled softly before he went still. Lena was still braced against the wall for support, her right hand pressed against her left side, and she watched with wide eyes, still reeling from everything. It had barely been five minutes since she’d fallen through the ceiling and now Mon-El was dead and she had a wound in her side that was bleeding more than she would have liked, and the noise had started to draw attention, the sight of movement from the corner of her eye catching Lena’s attention as she found herself staring at familiar faces.

     

                Then Kara was in front of her, palms skating over Lena’s shoulders and down her arms as she sniffed, swallowing thickly as she nodded. “Okay, we need to get you out of here now.”

     

                “I can’t. It has to be you.”

     

                “No, I-”

     

                “It has to be,” Lena interrupted, reaching out to grab Kara’s wrist in a vice-like grip. “Do you understand? I came back here to get you out.”

     

                Kara had stopped listening at Lena’s touch, her eyes dragged down to the sticky wetness of Lena’s hand on her skin. Going pale, Kara’s lips parted as she took in the vivid red of the blood. “You’re bleeding.”

     

                “I know,” Lena whispered. “It’s okay. I just- you need you to listen to me, okay? You were always the plan - not me. I always needed you to be the muscle, and they’re just- they’re twiddling their thumbs up there trying to find answers and none of them will listen to me, so it has to be you because you’re the only thing on Earth that’s strong enough to lift this prison out of the water. I need you to go back up there and sit in the sun until you’re strong enough to lift us all out.”

     

                “But-”

     

                Lena’s eyes were swimming with tears now and she gently squeezed Kara’s wrist, her expression pleading. “Please. You made me leave you behind last time; I’m asking you to do the same. Just for a little while.”

     

                “You need help,” Kara said, her voice breaking as she reached out to cradle Lena’s waist, her eyes darting up to her face at the ripple of pain as Lena went rigid, her mouth flattening to a bloodless line. “Let me bring you with me.”

     

                Shaking her head, swallowing the pain until she could draw in a hitching breath, Lena smiled tightly. “I can’t. I’m not a good swimmer, I won’t be able to make it back up there, even without this. I think it was … sheer dumb luck that I made it down here. You need to go … without me, alright?”

     

                “I’ll hold onto you-”

     

                “Kara,” Lena softly sighed. “There’s only one respirator. I knew I was staying when I came, so … just go now and … I’ll see you in a couple of days, okay? I promise you. It’ll all be alright.”

     

                Face crumpled with frustration at how unfair it all was, her cheeks coloured pink, her eyebrows drawn together in a scowl as her deep blue eyes shone with tears, Kara jerked her chin forward. “You said a couple of days before and it was longer than that.”

     

                “I know, I’m sorry. I thought they wanted my help but they didn’t, so I had to come myself. It’s me and you, just like last time. I make the plan, you execute it, right?” she said with a quick smile, trying to force her voice lighter with amusement, trying not to worry Kara.

     

                Leaning in, Kara touched her forehead to Lena’s as she cupped her shoulders. “I’m not going anywhere until you’re looked after, okay? I’m sorry. I’m sorry, I didn’t mean to-”

     

                Lena closed her eyes, leaning in closer, bumping Kara’s nose with her own as she softly shushed her. “I know, I know. It’s alright, I’ll be fine. ”

     

                Kara couldn’t quite swallow the strangled sob that worked its way up her throat, but she pulled away, glancing over at the prisoners and staff hovering far enough back to stay out of the way. Her eyes landed on J’onn as her shoulders sagged, a desperate plea in her eyes.

     

                “J’onn-”

     

                “I’ll get one of the medical packs,” he said without her needing to say another word, moving off quickly.

     

                Kara didn’t say anything else, just stared at the others until Imra warily stepped forward, her splashing footsteps breaking through the relative silence of the hallway. She walked over to Mon-El’s side and sank to a crouch, checking his pulse before nodding to herself, her mouth thinning with dismay.

     

                “He could be nice sometimes.”

     

                “Yes, he could,” Kara sorrowfully agreed.

     

                “Querl? Can you come give us a hand?” Imra called out without looking back.

     

                Hurrying forward, Querl glanced down at Mon-El with mixed feelings and Imra gestured to Lena. He came to help Kara, slinging one of Lena’s arms around his shoulder as Kara propped her up on the other side, her other hand pressing to Lena’s side as she worried about the blood loss. The section was flooded to half a foot but there were still rooms that held empty bunks and occasional desks and they shifted Lena into the nearest one, Kara sweeping aside the pot of pens, the computer monitor and keyboard, stacks of paperwork that hadn’t been looked at since the escape and consequent sinking of the prison.

     

                Getting Lena up on the desk, stretched out as her face turned grey with the pain and strain of it, Kara’s fingers shook as she unbuttoned the naval shirt and then pushed up the beige t-shirt underneath. It was perhaps an inch deep but it was bleeding freely and Kara tore off her prison sweatshirt and tamped the wound as Querl began rattling off medical protocols and procedures. J’onn was back in no time, setting down a pilfered first aid kit and rifling through the contents. It held no drugs in it, locked away in Eliza’s old office, and they didn’t have time for it to work anyway so Lena made do with squeezing Kara’s hand as Querl disinfected the site and packed it with gauze before he taped it over and bandaged her midriff. It would need stitches, and soon, but that was the best they could do down there without Eliza or any other living doctor on board.

     

                Lena knew that Kara was reluctant to leave her but she also knew that it would drive her to be quicker, to rescue them sooner if she knew Lena needed medical attention. It was unlucky to be injured now, at the very end of it all, but also lucky in a way. She didn’t think she would have been able to convince Kara to go without her if she hadn’t been pierced by the end of the pipe. Now, at least, they would all be out in a day or so, practically no time at all considering how long they had all waited for this moment.

     

                “You need to go now,” Lena rasped, sweating as she breathed heavily, her energy spent. 

     

                “I-”

     

                “I’m alright. I’ll be waiting here for you, okay? You and I … we’ve got a date to catch,” she thickly told her, smiling brightly as tears pricked her eyes.

     

                A laugh bubbled up in Kara’s chest and her face was pinched with worry but she nodded quickly, squeezing Lena’s hand. “What flavour ice cream will you pick?”

     

                “Can’t go wrong with classic vanilla. You?”

     

                “I’d really like to try this chocolate everyone keeps talking about.”

     

                “Chocolate ice cream,” Lena whispered, her eyelids shuttering as a smile stretched across her face. She made a low hum of agreement. “Good choice.”

     

                “We can share.”

     

                “Sounds perfect. You should- you should go now. Bring the gear here; I’ll tell you what you need to do.”

     

                Kara was gone in a blur of motion and back a minute later with an armful of black tubes and rubber, the oxygen tank Lena had tried to cave Mon-El’s head in with hanging from one hand. Talking her through the steps as best as she could, Lena watched Kara fumble with the pieces, and it was Lucy who ended up stepping in to pull the seals over her wrists and neck, connect the hoses to the tank and tighten the straps. Lena hated the Deputy with a burning passion but it filled her with a sense of peace to know that Kara would be able to make her way to the surface safely.

     

                Once she was all geared up, the mask over her forehead, regulator in hand and fins tucked under one arm, Kara stepped up beside the desk. Looking down at Lena, Kara gave her a pained smile, still tender and warm despite the anguish that wrenched her heart to be parted so soon, and Lena felt it too, ashen-faced and trying to be brave as pain pulsed in her side, nauseous and exhausted from the day.

     

                “It’ll be okay. I’ll see you soon.”

     

                With a final squeeze of her hand, Kara swallowed the lump in her throat and nodded. “Soon.”

    Chapter 25

                Swimming was a vaguely familiar activity to Kara, who had only done it a few times on Krypton when her family had taken trips out of Argo City to visit the Dandahu Ocean. Not that it wasn’t common for other Kryptonians, the two continents surrounded by vast seas of turbulent water, only that her parents were always so busy with work that they hadn’t had time to go that often. Still, she managed, cutting through the water with ease as she breathed freely with the regulator, dodging bodies she’d left there, bodies she’d created, her superior vision making it glaringly obvious what destruction she’d inflicted in the flooded sector and the central chamber beyond.

     

                It was oddly freeing, in a way, to swim, and Kara thought it might have been peaceful under other circumstances. This time though, she moved as quickly as possible, arms arcing and legs kicking as the fins propelled her upwards as quickly as an Olympic swimmer, even if her form was terrible. Within a minute of sinking through the empty hole of the ceiling into frigid water that didn’t bother her in the slightest, Kara was at the parted doors to the central chamber, which she forced apart to make it easier to slip through. 

     

                Two minutes after that, she was at the elevator shaft, jerking those doors further apart as well before she was fully exposed to the sea. The current was stronger there, but Kara moved with such ease and speed that it didn’t have time to drag her off course as she paddled up to the light blue light of the surface just ahead. It wasn’t far at all, a fraction of the distance she’d already swam, and what had been a long struggle down for Lena was a quick trip back up for Kara.

     

                And then she saw a funny little thing, a machine with lenses and flashlights attached to a thick wire as it moved around underwater. It spotted her and she frowned beneath her mask as she continued upwards, suddenly greeted by the big splashes and torrents of bubbles as other figures jumped into the Arctic Ocean in gear identical to what she was wearing. Recognising them as sailors from onboard the aircraft carrier, Kara swam straight to them, surfacing next to a black rigid-hulled inflatable boat with two other divers onboard and a man in fatigues similar to what Lena had been wearing with the insignia of a lieutenant on it. 

     

                Removing the regulator from her mouth as she pushed the mask up, Kara grabbed the side of the boat and hauled herself up. The others tried to help, all of them talking over one another, grabbing the straps of her BCD to drag her safely into their vessel, and Kara sprawled in the bottom of it, breathing heavily with her eyes closed as she tasted the salt on the fresh air and the sunlight on her face. It was warmer than last time, stronger now that summer was here, and she wanted to bask in it but had more important matters to attend to.

     

                “Are you crazy?” the lieutenant was yelling at her. “Stealing diving gear and throwing yourself into the water like that. Do you know how easily you could have died? The Captain will have you sent back to sh- who the hell are you?”

     

                As he’d ranted, Kara had dragged the soaked diving hood off her head, exposing blonde hair gone a dull mousy colour in the water, a stark difference to Lena’s dark brown hair. Drawing in a deep breath, Kara straightened, unclipping the BCD and kicking off the fins.

     

                “Tell the Captain I want to speak to him.”

     

                “Who are you?”

     

                Kara ignored him, climbing to her feet in the rocking boat as she shaded her eyes and stared up at the massive aircraft carrier. There was so much activity going on inside it, growing louder and louder as she stood in the pale sunlight, her whole body prickling with the feeling of the radiation, soaking it up, straightening as the minute hurts of her beating quickly vanished, her body becoming stronger by the second, her senses flaring to an almost overwhelming capacity. 

     

                It was worse than last time, the late winter radiation weaker than the early summer sunlight suffusing her now, and Kara felt slightly sick as she blinked back the dizzying rush of power rushing through her muscles, her veins, her bones. It was so disorienting that she clapped her hands over her ears, squeezing her eyes shut as she rocked with the boat, the lieutenant’s words ignored as she breathed quickly, trying to stamp it all down. In the months since her brief bout of freedom, Kara had forgotten what it was like. It made her want to pitch herself off the side of the boat and swim back down to the prison, hole herself up in a windowless room twenty metres beneath sea level.

     

                She wouldn’t, of course. Lena was injured and she needed to get her out so she could receive medical aid, which meant speaking to the Captain, which meant getting on the carrier. Slowly dropping her hands, she blinked at the brightness until her eyesight adjusted. 

     

                “Where’s the Captain?” she asked without glancing at the divers.

     

                “The Captain is onboard; we’ll contact him now. I just need you to tell us who you are.”

     

                “Kara Zor-El.”

     

                The lieutenant relayed that to the command room via a little handheld radio, warily watching Kara as he spoke, taking in the way she fidgeted, rolling her shoulders, screwing her eyes shut, blinking rapidly as she chafed beneath the roughness of her prison uniform. She was trying to retain her composure, to adjust to the sensitivity of being a Kryptonian beneath a yellow sun, feeling the strength that slowly recovered itself after years of being subdued, and she could feel how light she was, as if she could walk on water if she wanted to. Of course, Kara knew her body mass and bone density were greater than that of a human, but the radiation brought out powers that she’d never had the time to explore, beyond that scuffle as a thirteen-year-old girl on a beach, out of her depth and terrified out of her mind at this foreign world and the aggressors that had manhandled her into cuffs with green kryptonite.

     

                Clenching and unclenching her hands, Kara was dimly aware of the radio communications as the Captain responded. She didn’t have time for that though, the inevitable request that they return to the aircraft elevator and wait to board the vessel, the whole process that would doubtlessly overcomplicate things. Kara didn’t have time for the fuss of rigging the boat up to the pulley system and securing everything, waiting for the safety clearance to be authorised so they could board the carrier. After waiting a few minutes, as the divers were recalled and the ROV hauled into the inflatable boat, Kara pitched herself off the side of the boat and swam to the carrier herself, alarmed shouts following after her before the water closed over her head.

     

                The swim was even easier this time, her speed ramping up, her muscles flexing as she cut through the waves and little pieces of ice that hadn’t fully melted with the heat the carrier emitted. She reached the carrier’s hull in less than a minute, surfacing in the swell of the waves as they battered the vessel’s side, craning her neck as she stared at the underside of the aircraft elevator. It was no more than twenty feet above her and with the apparent strength that was returning to her, Kara was confident she’d be able to reach it. She just needed a little bit of momentum.

     

                Drawing in a deep breath, the tang of salt strong at the back of her mouth, she submerged herself and dove a few metres deeper before angling back up. With a powerful kick as she used her arms to propel her upwards, Kara shot out of the water and ten feet into the air before crashing back down with a splash. Undeterred, she went deeper this time, staring up at the wavering blue surface above her as she gritted her teeth, and then tried again, angling herself so that when she shot out of the water, she hit the hull, using her momentum to lever herself higher. 

     

                She couldn’t quite fly yet, probably not for a good hour at least, but there was that weightless feeling, that knowledge of the potential there, and she just grazed the lip of the aircraft. Fortunately, she was strong enough that dangling by the very tips of her fingers was doable, and as she fought against the precarious slipperiness of her wet hand, she managed to swing the other one up, getting a better hold and then hauling herself up with ease. It was so easy and Kara had forgotten what that was like, pushing herself up as if she wasn’t relying solely on her hands and arms to bear her weight. It frightened her to think about what she could really do after a day of exposure to unfiltered yellow radiation, what she could do after a week , every cell of her being completely saturated. So far, this was only slightly more than nothing, than what she’d been able to do in the prison when she hadn’t been sitting under red sun lamps all day.

     

                Crawling onto the edge of the aircraft elevator, a sodden heap as seawater ran off her in rivulets, pooling beneath her, Kara drew in a deep breath and then climbed to her feet. Five sailors stared at her from varying positions on the elevator pad, mouths slack, eyes wide, and Kara didn’t even consider her appearance - bruises that were already fading mottling her cheek and jaw, blood down the front of her clothes and streaking her face in half-dried scabs. Staring at the human with wariness, she opened and closed her mouth before clearing her throat.

     

                “Can you direct me to the Captain of this vessel?”

     

                Then panic unfolded as the sailors started yelling over each other, one of them radioing to the command deck, another running to close the door to the hangar, the other three squaring up with stubborn looks of determination as one of them babbled about not having weapons while the biggest one snapped at him to be quiet. When the biggest one stepped forward and punched her squarely across the jaw, Kara forgot to move out of the way, blinking as his fist slammed into her face with the sound of bones crunching before he let out a cry of pain, his momentum carrying him over the edge. Reaching out, Kara snagged the collar of his uniform and held him aloft, his face gone shockingly white as he stared at her with fear in his eyes.

     

                “The Captain?” Kara repeated.

     

                Then he started to squirm and she exhaled with an impatient sigh before setting him down on the elevator pad with overcautious gentleness. She wasn’t sure of her limits, didn’t know how much force to calculate to touch them without injuring them badly. That thought made her think of Lena and how it would be a long while before Kara would trust herself to touch her without having to take a moment to think about it, to move with deliberate care so she didn’t shatter her bones without meaning to. She didn’t have time to dwell on that then though, although she didn’t want to injure any of these bystanders either - not if she didn’t have to.

     

                But then the door to the hangar was closing, already halfway down as two of the sailors had gone back in and the other was nervously inching closer to take her injured comrade back inside with her. Kara watched as she helped gather the big man up to his feet and usher him back towards the closing doors, knowing they wouldn’t make it in time. Darting ahead, she gripped the edge of the closing door and stopped it in its tracks. Machinery whined as the door tried to obey the mechanics but met the resistance of the Kryptonian, who held it with only a slight tremor in her arm, not quite strong enough for it to be easy yet. Still, Kara slowly managed to fight back, pushing it up until it was shoulder height.

     

                The two sailors stared at her with unabashed fear and shock and she frowned, jerking her chin towards the door, before they ducked beneath it and into the hangar. Following them inside, Kara dusted her greasy hand on the damp thigh of her pants and then raised her eyebrows at the faces that greeted her.

     

                “I’m looking for the Captain.”

     

                An alarm wailed and Kara’s face furrowed with a displeased frown before she grimaced and set off quickly. She had no way of knowing which heartbeat amongst the deafening pounding of hundreds of them belonged to the Captain, but she knew she couldn’t wait around to ask person after person until someone pointed her in the right direction, not knowing what they might start doing - one of them mentioned weapons and she wouldn’t put it past humans to very quickly rely on those - so she took off at a run, which was faster than she’d moved in almost two decades, a blur dodging around sailors and taking the stairs three at a time as she tried her best to parse the amount of information she was processing with her senses.

     

                People rushed back and forth on the different levels of the carrier but Kara could hear the stationary heartbeats consolidated in one portion of the upper decks, towards the centre of the vessel. She made that her target, moving quickly through the hallways as she caught sight of pale, stricken faces that barely had time to process her before she was pushing past them. 

     

                A couple of sailors were blocking the closed doors leading to the communication deck and Kara slowed a moment at the sight of them before she squared her shoulders and forged ahead. Hands grabbed at her, trying to stop her, an arm going around her throat in an effort to slow her, two sailors clinging to her arms, and she kicked open the locked double doors with ease. There was a stunned moment of silence as she waded inside with the sailors clinging to her and then she gently shoved them off her and broke the hold of the woman’s arm around her neck.

     

                “I’m looking for the Captain,” she announced.

     

                There was a pause before a man stepped forward, clearing his throat. “You’re trespassing on my vessel.”

     

                “My name is Kara-“

     

                “Zor-El. Yes, I know who you are. I’m glad to see you match your profile,” he drawled, pushing a button on a keyboard and gesturing to a screen.

     

                Kara glanced at the mugshots that had been taken of her, updated regularly in the system as she’d grown. There was an entire dossier on her that the DEO had compiled and she was curious to know what was in it but had more important things to concern herself with then.

     

                “Although, I would like to know what you’re doing above sea level, considering you’re supposed to be in prison.”

     

                “Lena-“

     

                “Yes, I’m aware of Miss Luthor’s meddling as well. However, it isn’t her obvious absence that I’m interested in; you are not authorised to board a United States naval aircraft carrier, and yet here you are, in the middle of my communications room. Some might perceive that as a threat to the security of everyone onboard.”

     

                “Sir, I’m not a threat to anyone,” Kara firmly replied, her face furrowing.

     

                Of course, she’d forgotten the bruised face, the bloody clothes, and the fact that not an hour ago she’d killed someone she’d shared a cell block with for years. She was only there for one thing though, and Kara raised her chin as she stared down the Captain.

     

                “I’m here to help, sir. Lena came to fetch me-“

     

                “Thank you, Miss Zor-El, but your assistance isn’t needed here. It is not within Miss Luthor’s jurisdiction to determine who can and cannot board my vessel, and it is not within her jurisdiction to take command of this rescue mission that the United States government has authorised. If you aren’t a threat, as you insist you aren’t, then you will turn yourself into our custody and cooperate with my staff until our mission has been completed.”

     

                “You aren’t listening to me.”

     

                With a sigh, the Captain glanced at a sailor and then gestured towards Kara. She bristled but was confident in her ability to withstand any sort of physical assault from them. Right up until two sailors pulled the pins from twin canisters and tossed them at her feet, neon green smoke spilling out of them as Kara quickly registered what it was. The moment she realised was also the moment that crippling pain swept over her as she choked on a burning lungful of air, knees buckling as she stared wide-eyed at the smug Captain.

     

                As veins of green traced over her face, he walked towards her, hands clasped behind his back until he was standing over her. His shadow cut across her and she stared up at him with venom in her eyes.

     

                “You are an international threat to global safety, Miss Zor-El. I may have been sent here to safely retrieve everyone onboard Fort Rozz, but your alienness has not been forgotten and I will use any means necessary to contain you if I believe you are a risk to the success of my mission. I will have your cooperation. My men will show you to your quarters.”

     

                Hauled to her feet as she choked down the roiling nausea that swelled in her stomach, Kara had to blink back tears as she rasped a response. “You’re making a mistake. You’re not the plan; I am. I’m Lena’s plan-“

     

                “That’s quite enough from you.”

     

                He gestured dismissively and turned his back on her as sailors started forcing her out of the room. Before she was dragged out, Kara caught sight of an older woman in the same uniform as the other sailors - sans any insignias or name tags - an anxious look on her face as she stepped forward, her pale eyes sharp and piercing as she stared right at Kara. 

     

                And then she was in the hallway, struggling to breathe as the green kryptonite burned her lungs. Wobbly on her feet, Kara allowed herself to be limply dragged along as she scrambled to think. She wasn’t sure why, but she’d imagined they’d be grateful for her sudden appearance, would have known what Lena intended to do, had been picking her brain for the last few days to figure out how to put her plan into place. Or at least that was what they had made it sound like. Now it seemed like that hadn’t been the case at all.

     

                Coming to a stop outside a door identical to the others lining the hallway, she was pushed inside and the door was locked from the outside before a light was flicked on. The light cast a red glow over the room and Kara felt a dizzying wave of weakness wash over her - not by much but enough to let her know it was a red sun lamp, and it would slowly sap her strength as she sat in that cell and waited. 

     

                Swearing, she kicked the door, metal twisting as it bent out of its frame. Alarmed shouts greeted her from the hallway and Kara was tempted to fight her way out but there was something that stopped her, the knowledge that they knew what her weakness was, had that information and green kryptonite on hand to subdue her. Except, it didn’t really matter, because Lena was injured and locked in an underwater prison with no doctor onboard, and Kara would weather any amount of green kryptonite to save her.

     

                She was steeling herself for another kick to take the door off its hinges when she heard a voice on the other side of it, brusque and impatient. “How much will it cost to get you to open this door?”

     

                “Um …”

     

                “Name a number. Seven of them, if you’d like. Quickly.”

     

                “A million dollars?” the man replied with uncertainty, as if warily asking a question.

     

                “A million dollars it is. Open the door and I’ll have it transferred into your bank account within the next three business days.”

     

                There was the rattling of a key before the door suddenly swung open to reveal the woman who’d been staring at her inside the communications room. Taller than Kara even, with a severe expression that verged on smug, or perhaps condescendingly amused, she gave her a once over as Kara stared at her, bewildered. Unsure whether she should attack or not, Kara cleared her throat and opened her mouth but was cut off.

     

                “Where’s Lena?”

     

                “Inside Fort Rozz.”

     

                Quietly cursing, Lillian’s mouth flattened with annoyance. “That foolish girl,” she muttered to herself before glancing at Kara. “You said you’re her plan?”

     

                “Yes. She came to get me.”

     

                “And stayed behind, of course. Is she okay?”

     

                “She- she’s injured, she needs medical attention.”

     

                Nodding, Lillian stepped aside. “Go.”

     

                Hesitating a moment at the command, Kara opened and closed her mouth, staring at Lillian. “You’re her mother?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                Nodding, Kara gave her a stern look. “I’ll bring her back safely.”

     

                “See that you do.”

     

                The haughtiness surprised her but Kara was already moving quickly, brushing past the sailor in the hallway, the weakness that had slowly been creeping over her quickly banished as she moved further from the red sun lamp.
